Appetite push measured at ~100 kcal per kg lost

blocks.text: Set point or settling point?

It's tempting to conclude that everyone has a fixed weight their body is determined to return to. Researchers argue about that. One camp talks about a *set point*, a weight the brain actively defends. Another prefers the idea of a *settling point*, a weight that emerges from the balance between your biology and your environment: what food is around, how much you move, how you sleep, how stressed you are. Change the environment for long enough, and the settling point moves.

The evidence above fits a middle position. The defense is real, and it appears lopsided: strong against loss, much weaker against gain, which is what the leptin story predicts when high levels barely register. But the asymmetry is also why the modern food environment pushes weight up so easily: the system barely resists a surplus. That means the same features that make regain likely also make prevention comparatively cheap. Keeping weight from creeping up in the first place is far easier than taking it off later, because you're working on the side of the system that doesn't fight back.
Working with the alarm, not against it

None of this means weight change is impossible or that regain is a personal failure. It means the hardest part of changing weight usually isn't losing it, and that people who regain aren't simply weaker than people who don't; they're up against a system built to pull them back. It's holding the new weight while the body sends steady, unconscious pressure to go back. People who understand that tend to plan differently.

Sleep is one lever that's easy to overlook. Lab studies of short sleep have found the same hormones moving in the same unhelpful direction as after a diet, with leptin down, ghrelin up and hunger higher, even though no fat has been lost. On a watch rotation where sleep is already scarce, a cut layered on top of short nights is fighting the alarm on two fronts.

blocks.title: Making the defense easier to live with
items: Aim for modest changes you can keep, since the push back follows the loss no matter how fast it came
Build meals around protein, fiber and volume, which help fullness signals do their job
Keep meal times as regular as your schedule allows so hunger has a predictable rhythm
Protect sleep, since short nights push hunger hormones the wrong way
Lift weights to hold on to muscle while you lose fat
Treat maintenance as its own phase with its own plan, not the end of the diet

blocks.text: Expect hunger and treat it as information, not a verdict on your willpower. A rising appetite after weight loss is your physiology doing exactly what it evolved to do. If you're planning a significant change in weight, or considering any medication, talk with your corpsman, a doctor or a registered dietitian first.

The bigger lesson reaches past food. Many systems in your life have a set point they defend: sleep schedules, fitness, habits, even mood. Pushing hard against a defended system for a short time usually produces a short-term result. Changing the inputs it responds to, steadily and for a long time, is what moves the set point. Leptin taught scientists that lesson the expensive way.

takeaways: Leptin acts more like a famine alarm than a brake: falling levels trigger strong responses, high levels barely register.
Ghrelin rises before meals and learns your usual meal times.
After weight loss, hunger hormones stay shifted for at least a year, and appetite rises about 100 kcal a day per kilogram lost.
Losing weight slowly or quickly led to the same regain; the defense follows the loss, not the speed.
Plan for maintenance as its own phase, and use protein, fiber, regular meals, sleep and lifting to make it easier.

title: Enough Is a Number: What 49 Experiments Say About Protein
dek: The gym rules about protein sound like physics. The research says something more relaxed, and more useful: protein works like a threshold, not a dial.

blocks.text: Spend a week around any weight room and you will hear three rules repeated like laws of nature. Eat a gram of protein per pound of bodyweight. Get a shake down within thirty minutes of your last set or the workout is wasted. And don't bother eating more than thirty grams at once, because your body can't use it.

All three sound precise. All three sound like they came out of a lab. One of them is roughly right for a reason almost nobody who repeats it knows. The other two fall apart once you look at how they were tested.

The more interesting story isn't any single number. It's how a fuzzy range of evidence gets hardened into gym rules, and how the actual science, once you read it, points to an idea that applies far beyond nutrition: some inputs work like a volume knob, and some work like a light switch. Protein is much closer to a switch.
The floor, not the target

Start with the official number. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein in the US and Canada is **0.8 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day**. For an 80 kg (about 176 lb) adult, that's 64 grams, roughly two chicken breasts' worth.

The RDA is often misread as a recommendation for everyone. It isn't designed for that. It's set to cover the basic needs of almost all healthy adults, meaning enough to avoid deficiency and maintain the tissue you already have. It was never meant to answer a different question: how much protein does someone need who is deliberately trying to build muscle?

It helps to know what protein is actually doing. Your muscles aren't static objects. They're constantly being taken apart and rebuilt, protein by protein, every hour of every day. Muscle grows only when building outpaces breakdown over weeks and months. Training is what tips that balance toward building; dietary protein provides the amino acids the rebuilding crew needs. Without the training signal, extra protein mostly gets burned for energy or used elsewhere.

To answer that one, you need experiments where people lift weights for weeks, some eat more protein and some don't, and researchers measure what happens to their muscle. Lots of those experiments exist. The problem is that most are small, and small studies bounce around. So in 2018 a team led by Robert Morton at McMaster University pooled them.
The study that pooled everything

Morton's group gathered every randomized controlled trial they could find that met two conditions: participants did resistance training for at least six weeks, and some of them got extra protein while others didn't. They ended up with **49 trials and 1,863 people**, published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine*. It remains one of the largest analyses of its kind.

items.label: Randomized studies pooled, with 1,863 participants
Average extra fat-free mass gained with added protein
Daily intake beyond which extra protein added no more muscle

blocks.source: Morton et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

blocks.text: Two results matter. The first is that extra protein did help. People who supplemented gained more strength (about 2.5 kg more on their one-rep max) and more fat-free mass than those who didn't. The second is how *much* it helped: an average of **0.30 kg** of extra fat-free mass over the course of the studies. That's real, and it adds up over years, but it's about two-thirds of a pound. Training did the heavy lifting. Protein topped it off.

There were also two telling patterns. The benefit shrank as people got older, and it was larger in people who already had lifting experience. Younger, trained lifters got the most out of extra protein, which makes sense: they're the ones whose training is pushing hardest against the limits of their materials.
Where the curve goes flat

The most cited part of the paper is a break-point analysis. The researchers plotted each study group's total daily protein intake against how much fat-free mass it gained. Gains rose with protein up to about **1.62 g/kg per day**, and above that the line went flat. More protein, no more muscle.

Here's the part that usually gets left out. The uncertainty around that number is wide: the 95% confidence interval runs from **1.03 to 2.20 g/kg**. The break-point model itself didn't quite reach statistical significance (p = 0.079). The authors were upfront about this, and because of that uncertainty they suggested that people who want to be sure of maximizing gains could aim for about 2.2 g/kg, the top of the range.

blocks.title: Daily protein for an 80 kg (176 lb) adult
blocks.note: Multipliers from the meta-analysis applied to an 80 kg body; 2.2 g/kg is the top of the plateau's 95% confidence interval.
blocks.source: Morton et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

blocks.text: Remember too that a plateau in pooled data is an average across hundreds of people. Some individuals will top out lower, some higher. That's exactly why a range is more honest than a single magic number, and why the sensible move is to aim somewhere inside it rather than argue about the second decimal place.

Now the gym rule makes sense. One gram per pound is 2.2 grams per kilogram. It isn't the amount most people need; it's the conservative top of the range. It works, but mostly because it overshoots. If you hit 1.6 g/kg consistently, you're already at the point where, on average, extra protein stopped producing extra muscle in the pooled data.

Think of protein as building materials and training as the work order. Below a certain amount, a shortage of bricks slows the job. Above it, piling more bricks on the site doesn't make the crew build faster. The work order is what sets the pace.
The anabolic window that wasn't

The thirty-minute window is a more instructive case, because it shows how a myth can be born from honest research. Early studies compared people who drank a protein shake right after training with people who drank nothing. The shake group often did better, and the conclusion was that *timing* mattered.

But look at what actually differed between the groups. The shake group didn't just eat protein at a particular time. They ate *more protein, total*. Timing and total amount were tangled together, so there was no way to tell which one was doing the work.

In 2013, Brad Schoenfeld, Alan Aragon and James Krieger untangled them. They pooled 23 studies on muscle growth covering 525 people and used a statistical model that accounted for each study's total protein intake. A simple pooled analysis did show a small benefit for timing. Once total protein was controlled for, the effect of timing disappeared. The strongest predictor of muscle growth was simply how much protein people ate across the day.

That's a useful mental move to keep in your pocket for any health claim. When someone says X causes Y, ask what else was different between the people who did X and the people who didn't. Often the hidden variable is doing all the work.
The thirty-gram ceiling

The idea that your body can only use around 25 to 30 grams at a sitting has a real origin too. Short-term studies measure muscle protein synthesis, the rate at which muscle builds new protein, over a few hours after a meal. In those windows, synthesis rises with dose and then levels off around that range.

A 2013 study by José Areta and colleagues tested how to spread protein across a day. Trained men did a leg workout, then drank 80 grams of whey over 12 hours in one of three patterns: eight 10 g doses, four 20 g doses, or two 40 g doses. The middle pattern, **20 grams every three hours**, produced the highest synthesis rates. That's a decent argument for spreading protein across several meals.

But a ceiling on how fast you build in a short window isn't the same as a ceiling on how much you can use. In 2023, Jorn Trommelen and colleagues in the Netherlands gave people either 25 grams or 100 grams of protein after a workout and tracked where it went using multiple isotope tracers. The 100-gram dose produced a bigger anabolic response that lasted **more than 12 hours**, and very little of the extra was burned off as fuel. The body didn't waste it. It just processed it more slowly.

blocks.title: Gym rules vs the evidence

left.head: What you hear
items: Eat 1 g per pound or you won't grow
Shake within 30 minutes or the session is wasted
Over 30 g in one meal is wasted
Protein builds muscle

right.head: What the research shows
items: Gains flattened around 1.6 g/kg (0.7 g/lb); 1 g/lb is a safe overshoot
Total daily intake predicted growth; timing didn't once total was controlled
Large doses are used, just more slowly
Training builds muscle; protein supplies the materials

blocks.text: A caveat on both of those studies: they measured synthesis rates for hours, not muscle size over months. They tell you about mechanisms, not final outcomes. The honest practical summary is that spreading protein across three to five meals is sensible and convenient, and a big protein-heavy dinner after a long day isn't wasted.

The same goes for the popular advice to eat protein before bed. A 2023 trial gave young men 45 grams of casein, 45 grams of whey, or a placebo before sleep after an evening workout. Both proteins raised overnight synthesis compared with placebo, and the expensive slow-digesting casein did no better than whey. It's a reasonable way to fit in another protein feeding. It isn't a secret weapon.
Turning it into meals

Converted to pounds, the plateau is about **0.7 grams per pound**. For a 165 lb person, that's roughly 115 to 120 grams a day. Eaten over four meals, that's about 30 grams each, which is a can of tuna, three or four eggs plus a glass of milk, a chicken breast, or a cup of Greek yogurt with something else on the side.

blocks.title: Setting your own number
items: Find your weight in kilograms (pounds divided by 2.2).
Multiply by 1.6 for your daily target; use up to 2.2 if you want a margin of safety.
Divide by the number of meals you actually eat, usually three to five.
Anchor every meal with one clear protein source before filling in the rest.
Check your intake honestly for a week, then stop counting and keep the pattern.

blocks.text: Notice what isn't on that list: powder. In the Morton analysis, supplements helped because they raised people's total intake, not because there's anything special about protein that comes in a tub. Powder is a convenience food. If the galley serves eggs at breakfast and meat at dinner, and you add milk, yogurt or jerky in between, you can get there without it. If a shake is the easiest way to close a gap during a long watch rotation, that's fine too. It's food, not magic.

One situation where aiming toward the top of the range makes extra sense is when you're eating less than you burn, for example while trying to lean out before a deployment. A calorie deficit makes the body more willing to break down muscle along with fat, and sports nutrition researchers commonly suggest higher protein during those phases to help hold on to what you've built. Combined with continued lifting, it's one of the simplest ways to make sure the weight you lose is mostly fat.

Two practical notes. First, these intakes are common in studies of healthy adults, but if you have kidney disease or another medical condition, talk to a doctor or your corpsman before raising protein a lot. Second, the age finding cuts both ways. Older adults respond less to protein, which is one more reason muscle built in your twenties is worth having: it's the account you'll be drawing on for decades.
The real lesson: find the bottleneck

Protein is a nice example of a common trap. People pour energy into the variable that's easiest to buy and measure, such as grams, timing, brands and windows, and comparatively little into the variable that drives results. In every one of those 49 trials, the participants were training consistently. That was the signal. Protein only mattered because it supported the signal.

Gamers will recognize the pattern. Once your frame rate is above what your monitor can display, buying a faster graphics card doesn't make you aim better. Below that point, hardware is a real handicap; above it, the limiting factor is practice. Protein is the frame rate. Get it high enough that it isn't holding you back, then stop shopping and start training.

Once you understand that protein behaves like a threshold, the strategy changes. You don't need to optimize it forever. You need to get to *enough*, make that automatic, and then spend your attention on the things with no ceiling in sight: showing up, adding weight or reps over time, and sleeping. Enough is a number. Find it, hit it, and move on to the hard part.

takeaways: About 1.6 g of protein per kg per day (0.7 g/lb) is where muscle gains flattened in the pooled data; 2.2 g/kg is a safe upper target.
The RDA of 0.8 g/kg prevents deficiency; it isn't designed for building muscle.
Total daily protein matters far more than timing. There's no 30-minute deadline.
Big protein meals aren't wasted, but spreading protein over 3–5 meals is easy and sensible.
Protein supplies materials; consistent hard training is what actually builds muscle.

title: Hot Rooms and Ice Baths: What the Evidence Actually Says
dek: Saunas and cold plunges went from Finnish habit and locker-room trick to wellness religion. The real data is more interesting: one looks surprisingly good, and the other works best when you know what it costs.

blocks.text: In the 1980s, researchers in Kuopio, a city in eastern Finland, signed up 2,315 middle-aged men for a long-running heart study. Among hundreds of questions about their health and habits was one that only makes sense in Finland: how often do you take a sauna? Then the researchers waited. About twenty years later, they checked who had died.

The results, published in 2015 in *JAMA Internal Medicine* by Tanjaniina Laukkanen and Jari Laukkanen, were startling. Men who used a sauna four to seven times a week had a much lower risk of sudden cardiac death than men who went once a week, along with lower rates of fatal heart disease and death from any cause. The study became the founding text of a modern wellness movement: sauna for heart health, and its partner in the trend, the cold plunge, for everything from fat loss to mental toughness.

Heat and cold are real physiological stressors, and the body's responses to them are fascinating. But the evidence behind each claim varies enormously, from solid lab physiology to observational hints to marketing. Sorting them out also reveals something useful about stress in general: the same response that helps you in one situation can quietly work against you in another.
The sauna data, read carefully

Here's what the Kuopio numbers look like. After adjusting for heart-disease risk factors, men who used a sauna two to three times a week had a hazard ratio for sudden cardiac death of 0.78 compared with once-a-week users, and men who went four to seven times had 0.37. Similar patterns held for fatal coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease and all-cause death.

Session length mattered too. Compared with men whose sessions lasted under 11 minutes, men who stayed in for more than 19 minutes had about half the risk of sudden cardiac death, with a hazard ratio of 0.48. Longer sessions were linked to lower risk of fatal heart disease as well, though not to lower death from all causes.

blocks.title: Sudden cardiac death risk by sauna frequency
blocks.note: Adjusted for heart-disease risk factors; 1.0 is the reference. About 20 years of follow-up.
blocks.source: Laukkanen et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015

blocks.text: The obvious question is whether sauna caused any of that. This was an observational study, so it can't say. In Finland nearly everyone uses a sauna, which helps, because it's not an exotic habit of the rich. But men who can sit in a sauna most days may still differ in ways that matter: more free time, less physical disability, different work, better baseline health. Only 201 of the 2,315 men were in the four-to-seven group, so the most dramatic estimate rests on a small slice of the sample.

There's a plausible mechanism, which is why researchers take the finding seriously. Sitting in intense heat raises your heart rate, widens blood vessels and pushes blood toward the skin to shed heat. In some ways, the cardiovascular system responds as it might to light exercise. Regular heat exposure also triggers adaptations, the same ones soldiers and athletes rely on when they acclimatize to hot climates.

A small study shows what that can do. In 2007, Guy Scoon and colleagues in New Zealand had six male distance runners sit in a humid sauna at about 90°C for around 30 minutes after training, roughly a dozen times over three weeks. Compared with their normal training, their run time to exhaustion rose by 32 percent, which the authors estimated was equivalent to about a 1.9 percent improvement in a race. Their blood plasma volume rose by about 7 percent, which likely explains much of it: more plasma means more fluid for sweating and for carrying blood to working muscle. Six runners is a tiny sample, but the mechanism matches what's known about heat acclimation.
What heat costs

Heat isn't free, and one cost is rarely mentioned in sauna hype. In a 2013 study by Andrea Garolla and colleagues in Padua, ten healthy men with normal sperm used a Finnish sauna at 80 to 90°C for 15 minutes, twice a week, for three months. At the end, sperm count and motility were strongly impaired, along with markers of sperm DNA packaging and mitochondrial function. The good news: every one of those changes had fully reversed six months after the men stopped. It's a small study, but anyone planning a family soon should know about it.

The bigger risks are simpler. Long sessions dehydrate you. Alcohol and heat combine badly, because both widen blood vessels and can drop blood pressure. People with heart conditions or blood-pressure issues should talk to a doctor before using intense heat regularly. And you should leave when you feel dizzy or unwell, not when a timer says so.
The first minute in cold water

Cold water is a much more abrupt stressor, and it can be dangerous. When you hit cold water, your skin's cold receptors fire all at once and trigger what physiologists call the **cold shock response**: an involuntary gasp, rapid breathing and a surge in heart rate and blood pressure. Your ability to hold your breath collapses.

Cold-water researchers, notably Michael Tipton's group at the University of Portsmouth, have spent decades showing that this first reaction, not hypothermia, is the immediate danger. Hypothermia takes a long time to set in. A gasp underwater takes a second. That's why you should never plunge alone, never jump into cold open water you can't get out of easily, and never hold your breath under cold water for sport.

Then comes a more encouraging finding: the cold shock response can be trained down. In a 2013 study, Tipton and colleagues found that a handful of short, five-minute immersions in 12°C water, enough to cool only the skin, significantly reduced the breathing part of the cold shock response on the next immersion. People who do regular cold exposure really do learn to stop gasping. That's probably the most solid physiological adaptation the cold plunge offers.

items.label: Rise in blood noradrenaline after 1 hour in 14°C water
Rise in blood dopamine in the same test
Increase in metabolic rate

blocks.source: Šrámek et al., European Journal of Applied Physiology, 2000

blocks.text: You may have seen those numbers quoted online. They come from a 2000 study by Šrámek and colleagues in Prague, who immersed a small group of young men up to the neck in water at three temperatures.

The comparison is the clever part. In comfortable 32°C water, heart rate and blood pressure actually fell, likely an effect of being immersed rather than of cold. At 20°C, metabolic rate nearly doubled. Only at 14°C did the big stress-hormone surge appear.

The numbers are real, but notice the conditions: one hour in 14°C water, with core temperature dropping. That's very different from a two-minute plunge, and the dopamine measured was in the blood, not the brain. The test shows that cold is a powerful trigger for the sympathetic nervous system. It doesn't show that a quick dip gives you a lasting dopamine boost.
Cold after lifting: the hidden trade-off

The best-tested use of cold water is athletic recovery, and here the evidence produced a surprise. In 2015, Llion Roberts and colleagues in Australia had 21 physically active men lift weights twice a week for 12 weeks. After each session, half sat in cold water for 10 minutes while the other half did a light active cool-down. The cool-down group gained more strength and more muscle. Their fast-twitch fibers grew by 17 percent, while the cold-water group's didn't grow significantly. Muscle biopsies showed that cold blunted the signaling and stem-cell activity that drive muscle growth after training.

A 2024 meta-analysis by Alec Piñero and colleagues pooled eight studies and reached a similar, more cautious conclusion: cold water immediately after resistance training *may* reduce muscle growth, though the studies were of fair to poor quality. The logic is intuitive once you see it. The inflammation and stress signaling after a hard session aren't just damage to be cleaned up. They're part of the message that tells muscle to adapt. Shut down the message, and you may shrink the adaptation.
If your goal is building muscle, don't plunge right after lifting. Separate the two by several hours, or plunge on a different day.
The mood and immune claims

The most cited human trial on cold and health is a Dutch study published in 2016 by Geert Buijze and colleagues. They randomized 3,018 adults to end their usual hot shower with 30, 60 or 90 seconds of cold water every day for 30 days, or to keep showering normally. The cold-shower groups reported **29 percent less sickness absence** from work. But they didn't report fewer days actually being ill. People seemed to feel well enough to work more often, not to get sick less. Participants also knew which group they were in, which matters when the outcomes are self-reported.

Beyond that trial, the case for cold water as a mood or immune booster rests mostly on small studies, short follow-ups and enthusiastic self-reports. Some find people feel less stressed or sleep a bit better afterward; others find little. Cold exposure also produces a short spike in inflammatory markers right afterward, which is a normal stress response rather than a sign of harm. It's an area where the popularity has far outrun the trials.

If you want to try the version Buijze tested, it fits even a cramped life with a tight water budget. Take your normal shower and turn the dial to cold for the last 30 to 90 seconds. It uses no extra water and no special gear. In that trial, 79 percent of the people assigned to it stuck with it for the full 30 days, which says something about how manageable it is. Just be honest about what it's likely to do: make you feel more awake and practice your tolerance for discomfort, not make you immune to the next cold that sweeps through berthing.

What about fat loss? Adults do have **brown fat**, tissue that burns energy to make heat. Since the late 2000s, imaging studies have shown that many adults have active brown fat that switches on in mild cold. It's a real system. But nobody has shown that occasional cold plunges add up to meaningful fat loss on their own, and it would be a mistake to treat them as a weight tool.

blocks.title: Sauna vs cold plunge: what the evidence supports

left.head: Sauna
items: Strong observational link to heart health
Plausible mechanism; heat acclimation is real
Can improve endurance via plasma volume
Costs: dehydration, temporary sperm impairment

right.head: Cold plunge
items: Cold shock response can be trained down
May reduce muscle growth if used after lifting
Mood, immunity and fat-loss claims are weak
Costs: cold shock can cause drowning in open water

blocks.text: Using stress on purpose

On a submarine, neither a sauna nor an ice bath is on the menu, and fresh water is precious. But the core idea travels. Heat and cold are both *hormetic* stressors: doses of stress that trigger the body to adapt. The benefit, when there is one, comes from the response, not the stress itself, which is why dose and timing matter so much. The same alarm reaction that teaches your body to handle cold can drown out the signal your muscles needed from yesterday's workout.

The most dependable benefit of cold may be psychological. Standing in cold water while your body screams to get out, and choosing to breathe slowly anyway, is a direct rehearsal of staying calm under pressure. The cold shock studies show the gasp reflex really does fade with practice. Whether that skill transfers to the rest of life hasn't been rigorously tested, so treat it as a reasonable bet rather than a promise.

Used sensibly, both can be good tools. Sauna has the stronger case for long-term health, though it's still built on observational data. Cold water has a narrower set of real benefits and some real risks. Neither should replace sleep, training and decent food, which have far better evidence behind them. Never plunge alone in open water, get out if you feel unwell, and if you have a heart condition, talk to a doctor or your corpsman before trying either.

The bigger lesson is about stress itself. We often talk about stress as something to minimize. These studies suggest it's better thought of as a signal. The right dose at the right time tells your body to get stronger. The wrong dose, or the right dose at the wrong time, just adds noise.

takeaways: Frequent sauna use is strongly linked to lower cardiac risk, but the evidence is observational.
Heat acclimation is real and can boost endurance by expanding plasma volume.
The cold shock gasp is dangerous in open water, but short repeated exposures train it down.
Cold water right after lifting may reduce muscle growth; separate them by hours or days.
Claims about cold plunges for mood, immunity and fat loss rest on thin evidence.

title: The Bus Driver Problem
dek: In 1953 a doctor noticed that London's bus drivers had worse heart disease than the conductors who climbed the stairs. Seventy years on, we know what long sitting does, and the fix is smaller than you'd think.

blocks.text: In the early 1950s, London ran on double-decker buses, and every bus had two men working it. The driver sat in his cab for the whole shift. The conductor collected fares, which meant climbing the stairs to the top deck and back down again, over and over, all day long. Same company, same routes, same city air, same social class. One man sat. One man climbed.

A physician named Jerry Morris saw a natural experiment hiding in that arrangement. In 1953 his team published a study in *The Lancet* comparing coronary heart disease in London's busmen. The drivers were more likely to die suddenly from heart attacks. When the conductors did develop heart disease, it tended to be less severe and less often fatal early on. Morris went on to argue that physical activity at work protected the heart, an idea that sounds obvious now and was genuinely new then. His work is widely credited as a founding moment for the science of exercise and health.

Seventy years later, most of us have the driver's job. We sit to work, sit to eat, sit to game, sit to scroll. On a submarine, a watch can mean hours at a panel. So the question Morris opened is more relevant than ever: what does long sitting actually do to the body, and how much movement does it take to cancel it out? The answers turn out to be more specific, and more encouraging, than the scary headlines suggest.
A study with a catch

First, a caveat Morris himself took seriously. Drivers and conductors weren't randomly assigned. Maybe heavier, less healthy men chose or were steered into driving. In 1956, his team published a follow-up with the memorable subtitle *Epidemiology of uniforms*, which looked at the busmen's physiques using their uniforms as data, a way of checking whether drivers simply started out bigger.

That kind of problem, called confounding, haunts almost all research on sitting. People who sit all day differ from people who don't in a hundred ways: job, income, health, age, habits. Worse, illness itself makes people sit more, so some of the link between sitting and poor health runs backward. Keep that in mind through everything below. The strongest evidence comes when observational studies, lab experiments and plausible biology all point the same direction. For sitting, they mostly do.
Your muscles go quiet

Here's the biology that makes sitting more than just the absence of exercise. Your muscles aren't only motors. They're also huge metabolic organs, pulling sugar and fat out of your bloodstream to burn or store. That job depends partly on the muscles actually contracting, even gently.

In 2003, Lionel Bey and Marc Hamilton at the University of Missouri studied an enzyme called *lipoprotein lipase*, which muscles use to grab fat from the blood. When they prevented rats from using their hind legs normally, roughly **90 to 95 percent** of this enzyme's activity in those muscles disappeared. Inactivity also reduced how much fat the muscles took up from the blood and lowered HDL, the so-called good cholesterol. Then, when the rats walked on a treadmill, enzyme activity rose about eightfold within four hours.

There's a reason this matters more than you might guess. In their 2022 paper, Hamilton's group pointed out that the entire human musculature, despite being the body's largest lean tissue, accounts for only about 15 percent of the body's oxidative use of glucose at rest. In other words, a resting muscle is mostly idling. All that metabolic capacity sits unused until the muscle starts working.

These were rats, and human muscle is not a rat's. But the finding shifted thinking. It suggested that standing and moving lightly through the day keep certain metabolic machinery switched on, and that this isn't the same thing as a workout. A muscle that sits motionless for hours behaves differently from one that contracts now and then, even if neither ever does anything strenuous.
The two-minute interruption

If inactivity switches things off, how often do you need to switch them back on? In 2012, David Dunstan and colleagues in Melbourne tested this directly in people. Nineteen overweight or obese adults aged 45 to 65 came into the lab three times. Each time they drank a standard sugary, fatty drink and stayed for five hours. In one session they sat the entire time. In the other two, they got up every 20 minutes for a two-minute walk, either at an easy pace or a moderate one.

blocks.title: Blood sugar rise after a meal, 5 hours
blocks.note: Walk breaks taken every 20 minutes. Lower means a smaller glucose spike.
blocks.source: Dunstan et al., Diabetes Care, 2012

blocks.text: Both kinds of break cut the post-meal rise in blood sugar by about a quarter, and insulin dropped by a similar amount. Look closely at the result that matters most: the easy walking breaks did almost as well as the brisk ones. What mattered was getting up regularly, not how hard you worked when you did.

Again, the limits. This was a short lab study in middle-aged, overweight adults, and their responses are likely bigger than those of a fit 20-year-old. But it fits the rat biology neatly, and it points at something practical. Interrupting sitting isn't a fitness plan. It's maintenance, like cycling a pump so it doesn't sit idle.
Can a workout cancel a day of sitting?

This is the question most people actually care about. If you train hard for an hour, does it matter that you sit for the other fifteen waking hours? In 2016, Ulf Ekelund and colleagues pooled data from 16 studies covering **more than a million people** to find out, harmonizing everyone's reported sitting time and physical activity so they could be compared directly.

items.label: People in the pooled analysis of sitting and mortality
Higher death rate for the least active people who sat over 8 hours a day
Daily moderate activity that appeared to erase the extra risk of long sitting

blocks.source: Ekelund et al., The Lancet, 2016

blocks.text: The results were striking in both directions. People who were the least active and sat more than eight hours a day had a death rate 59 percent higher during follow-up than the reference group of active people who sat less than four. But among the most active quarter, long sitting time was no longer linked to higher mortality at all. The activity level that seemed to do it was high: about 60 to 75 minutes a day of moderate activity, such as brisk walking.

There was one exception worth noticing. TV time was harder to offset. Watching three or more hours a day was linked to higher mortality in every group except the most active, and even there the link appeared at five hours or more. Researchers can only guess why. TV time often comes in long unbroken blocks, in the evening after eating, sometimes with snacking. Whatever the reason, not all sitting appears equal.

It's a guess, not a finding, but a marathon gaming session probably looks more like the TV pattern than like a desk job: hours in one position, few natural reasons to get up, often late and often with snacks. The fix is the same as for anything else. Build in a reason to stand, like refilling water between matches, so the session has breaks even when the game doesn't.

blocks.title: Sitting myths and what the data says

left.head: Common belief
items: Sitting is as bad as smoking
A gym session undoes a day in a chair
Only hard exercise counts
A standing desk solves it

right.head: What the evidence suggests
items: Risks are real but smaller and largely offsettable
It can, but it takes about an hour a day of moderate activity
Light movement and short breaks matter too
Moving matters more than which way you face

blocks.text: A 2019 follow-up by Ekelund's group used a more objective tool: accelerometers that measure movement directly rather than relying on memory. Pooling data from about 36,000 mostly older adults, they found that risk climbed steeply with time spent sedentary, and that activity of any intensity, even light, was linked to lower risk.

blocks.title: Mortality risk by daily sedentary time, measured
blocks.source: Ekelund et al., BMJ, 2019

blocks.text: Read that curve with care. The participants averaged about 63 years old, and people who are already becoming ill tend to move less, so some of the steep climb likely reflects sickness causing sitting rather than sitting causing sickness. The researchers adjusted for what they could, but no observational study fully escapes that problem. The direction of the finding lines up with the lab work, though, which is what makes it believable.

That last finding matters for anyone who can't fit in an hour of exercise every day. You might have heard that sitting is the new smoking. It's a catchy line, and epidemiologists have pushed back on it, because the risks aren't comparable in size and because, unlike smoking, the harm of sitting appears to be largely offset by movement. The useful version of the message isn't fear. It's that movement counts at every scale, from a two-minute walk to an hour-long workout.
What counts, and what doesn't

Steps are a simple way to keep score. A 2022 meta-analysis by Amanda Paluch and colleagues pooled 15 studies of about 47,000 adults. Compared with people averaging around 3,500 steps a day, those averaging about 5,800 had a 40 percent lower risk of death during follow-up, and the benefit kept growing up to a plateau. For adults under 60, the curve flattened around 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day.

Standing desks are less of a fix than they look. Standing still isn't the same as moving, and the biology above is about muscles contracting, not about which way you're oriented. A standing desk helps mostly if it gets you shifting, walking and changing position more often.

For people stuck in a seat, there's an intriguing but early lead. In 2022, Hamilton's lab reported that a repeated seated calf movement, a kind of heel raise they called the *soleus pushup*, could keep a small calf muscle working for hours without fatigue. In their lab tests it cut the post-meal glucose spike by 52 percent and insulin by 60 percent. That's a big effect from a small study, and the authors disclosed that their university intends to patent related intellectual property and that they have been developing ways to teach the movement. Treat it as promising, not proven. Still, the principle is sound and costs nothing: working muscles in your legs, even while seated, is better than none.
A plan for the long watch

Put the evidence together and a practical approach for a sitting-heavy life emerges. It has two layers. The background layer is breaking up long sitting so muscles never go fully quiet for hours. The foreground layer is real activity that builds fitness and seems to offset much of the risk that remains.

blocks.title: Moving more inside a sitting job
items: When you're tied to a panel, do calf raises or heel-and-toe pumps under the desk every so often
At every natural break, such as turnover, logs or a head call, stand up and walk
Take the long way and the ladder when you have the option
Stack short bouts: a few minutes of walking after meals adds up and blunts the glucose rise
Aim for a daily block of real exercise when the schedule allows, since high activity offsets the most risk
Cap long, unbroken screen sessions off watch, or break them up with movement

blocks.text: You don't need to hit every item. The research rewards consistency over intensity at the low end: the biggest jump in benefit in both the steps data and the accelerometer data came from moving out of the very least active group. If you only change one thing, make it the habit of standing up and moving for a couple of minutes whenever you notice you've been still for a long stretch.

None of this requires a gym, which matters in a space where a few square feet is a luxury. It requires noticing when you've been still too long and doing something small about it. If you have a heart condition, circulation problems or any health concern, check with your corpsman or doctor before changing your activity much.
The bus conductor wasn't an athlete. He just never stayed still for long. Movement works best as a background process running all day, not a single event you check off.

That's the reframe Morris's busmen offer. We tend to think of health in terms of workouts, discrete events with a start and an end. The sitting research suggests the body also keeps a running tally of the hours in between. A good workout still matters a lot. But the person who climbs the stairs all day is running a quieter, constant program of their own, and that one is open to anyone, even in a seat.

takeaways: Muscles that stay still for hours switch off some fat- and sugar-handling machinery; light movement turns it back on.
Two-minute walking breaks every 20 minutes cut post-meal blood sugar by about a quarter in a lab trial, and easy walking worked nearly as well as brisk.
About 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day appeared to erase the extra mortality risk of long sitting in a million-person analysis.
Light activity counts too: any movement was linked to lower risk.
Treat movement as a background process: break up sitting all day, then add real exercise when you can.

title: The Sugar Rush Is a Myth. The Crash Is Complicated.
dek: Sugar doesn't give you the boost everyone talks about, and the 'crash' is usually not what you think. Here's what blood sugar and insulin actually do, and what really drives your energy.

blocks.text: Ask almost any parent whether sugar makes kids hyper and you'll get a laugh and a story about a birthday party. It's one of the most confident beliefs in everyday life. So in the 1980s and early 1990s, researchers put it to the test properly. In the trials they gathered, children got either a known dose of sugar or an artificial sweetener that tastes the same, and nobody involved, not the kids, not the parents, not the researchers, knew which was which.

In 1995, a team led by Mark Wolraich pooled those experiments in *JAMA*: 16 reports covering 23 separate studies. The conclusion was blunt. Sugar did not affect children's behavior or thinking. The authors couldn't rule out a small effect or an effect in some subset of kids, but the dramatic sugar high wasn't there. What *was* there was belief. Parents expect sugar to cause chaos, so they see chaos.

Adults have their own version of the myth: the sugar rush that gets you through a midwatch, followed by the crash that leaves you staring at a panel with heavy eyes. The truth is more interesting. The rush mostly isn't real, the crash partly is, and the reasons have less to do with dramatic blood sugar swings than most people think.
What actually happens when you eat sugar

Your body treats blood sugar, more precisely blood glucose, like a reactor operator treats a key parameter: it keeps it inside a tight band, all day, automatically. Your brain depends heavily on glucose for fuel, so letting it drop too low is dangerous, and letting it stay too high damages blood vessels and nerves over time. Two hormones from the pancreas do most of the control work.

blocks.title: After a sugary snack
items: Sugars and starches are broken down into glucose, which enters the blood from the gut.
Blood glucose rises. Cells in the pancreas sense it and release insulin.
Insulin signals muscle, liver and fat cells to pull glucose in, store it as glycogen, or burn it.
Glucose falls back toward its normal range, usually within a couple of hours.
Between meals, the hormone glucagon tells the liver to release stored glucose so levels don't sink too far.

blocks.text: That's the whole system in a healthy person. Drinking a soda doesn't send your blood sugar to the moon and back like a cartoon. It produces a rise, an insulin response, and a return to baseline. How steep the rise is depends on the food. Liquid sugar hits fastest. Sugar eaten with protein, fat and fiber gets absorbed more slowly, so the curve is lower and wider.

This also explains why you don't need sugar to keep your brain running. Between meals, overnight and during a fast, your liver releases stored glucose and can even build new glucose from other materials. A healthy person who skips a snack doesn't run their brain out of fuel; the system was designed for an animal that often went many hours without food. The feeling that you *need* something sweet to think is mostly habit, taste and fatigue talking, not an empty tank.

Think of it like a well-designed control loop on a plant. A disturbance comes in, the sensor picks it up, the controller responds, and the parameter settles back near setpoint. The interesting failures aren't single disturbances. They're slow drifts in the controller itself, which is exactly what happens in diabetes, and what this article will come back to.
The rush that isn't

If sugar gave you a real energy boost, you'd expect to see it in experiments. In 2019, the psychologist Konstantinos Mantantzis and colleagues at the University of Warwick, Lancaster University and Humboldt University of Berlin pooled 31 studies covering almost 1,300 adults. They looked at how eating carbohydrates, mostly sugar, affected mood, alertness and fatigue compared with not eating them.

Sugar had essentially no effect on mood, no matter how much people ate or whether they then did something demanding. And within an hour of eating it, people were *more* tired and *less* alert than people who hadn't had any. The authors titled their paper with a question, rush or crash, and the data pointed to the second answer.

items.label: Studies pooled on sugar and mood
Adults across those studies
Time until sugar left people more tired and less alert

blocks.source: Mantantzis et al., Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2019

blocks.text: So why does a candy bar *feel* like a pick-me-up? Partly because it tastes good, and pleasure is real even when energy isn't. Partly because it's a break: you stopped, you got something, your brain registered a small reward. And partly expectation, the same force that made parents see hyperactive kids. When you believe something will energize you, you notice every hint that it did.
So what is the crash?

The popular explanation goes like this: sugar spikes your blood glucose, your pancreas overreacts with too much insulin, your glucose plunges below normal, and you feel shaky and drained. That chain does exist. It's called **reactive hypoglycemia**, and some people genuinely experience it, especially after surgery on the stomach or in the early stages of blood sugar problems. But in most healthy people, the post-snack slump happens while blood glucose stays in a normal range.

Other mechanisms probably matter more. Your body clock has a natural dip in alertness in the early afternoon that happens whether you eat or not, which is why the post-lunch slump gets blamed on lunch. Large meals of any kind can leave you drowsy. Animal research suggests that rising glucose can quiet the brain cells that produce orexin, a chemical that keeps you awake, which would mean sugar can make you sleepy without any crash at all. And if you're already short on sleep, a lot of what you call a sugar crash is just your sleep debt showing up when the stimulation stops.

blocks.title: The sugar story vs what the evidence says

left.head: What people believe
items: Sugar gives a burst of energy
Sugar makes kids hyper
The crash is blood sugar plunging below normal
Every glucose spike is harmful

right.head: What studies show
items: No mood boost; more fatigue within an hour
No effect in blinded trials
Usually normal glucose plus body clock, meal size and sleep debt
Spikes are normal; what matters is long-term control

blocks.text: The glucose-spike panic

Lately, continuous glucose monitors, small sensors stuck to the arm that read your blood sugar every few minutes, have spread from diabetes care into wellness culture. Influencers post their graphs and warn you to avoid every spike. There's a real study behind some of this excitement, and it's worth knowing what it did and didn't show.

In 2018, a Stanford team led by Michael Snyder had 57 people, mostly healthy or prediabetic, wear monitors for about two weeks. In a sub-study, participants ate standardized breakfasts. Eighty percent of them spiked after a bowl of cornflakes and milk, and more than half of the people who had tested as healthy on standard tests showed spikes in a range normally seen in prediabetic or diabetic people. The researchers grouped people into 'glucotypes' by how spiky their patterns were.

items.label: Spiked after a bowl of cornflakes and milk
People who wore glucose monitors for about two weeks

blocks.source: Hall et al., PLOS Biology, 2018 (via Stanford Medicine)

blocks.text: That's genuinely useful. It shows that standard one-time blood tests can miss how differently people handle the same food, and that a breakfast marketed as wholesome can behave a lot like candy. What it doesn't show is that a spike in a healthy, active 20-year-old is damaging. Spikes after carbohydrate-heavy meals are normal physiology. The research question that matters, whether spike patterns in people without diabetes predict future disease, is still being worked out.

The bigger, quieter problem is the one the monitors were invented for. According to the CDC, about 98 million American adults, more than one in three, have prediabetes, and more than 80 percent of them don't know it. Prediabetes means the control loop is drifting. Usually the issue isn't the spikes themselves but **insulin resistance**: muscle, liver and fat cells stop responding well to insulin, so the pancreas has to push harder and harder to keep glucose in range.

items.label: US adults with prediabetes
Of them don't know they have it

blocks.source: CDC, Prediabetes Risk Test

blocks.text: Is insulin the villain?

If you spend time in fitness corners of the internet, you'll run into a stronger claim: insulin is a fat-storage hormone, sugar raises insulin, therefore sugar and carbs make you fat in a way other calories don't. It's called the carbohydrate-insulin model, and it has serious scientists on its side. Insulin really does tell fat cells to hold on to fuel. The question is whether that matters for long-term body fat once total calories are accounted for.

Most of the tightly controlled feeding studies, where researchers keep people in a metabolic ward and measure everything they eat, haven't found the dramatic advantage the model predicts for very low-carb diets at the same calorie level. People lose fat on low-carb diets and on low-fat diets, mostly in proportion to how much less they end up eating. The debate isn't fully closed, but 'insulin is evil' oversimplifies a hormone you literally cannot live without. People with type 1 diabetes, who can't make it, waste away without injections.

Where sugar really does cause trouble is quieter and more practical. Sugary drinks and sweets pack a lot of energy into something that barely registers as food. A 500 ml soda doesn't make you feel like you just ate a meal, so you eat the meal anyway. Sweetness combined with fat, like in pastries, cookies and ice cream, is especially easy to keep eating past the point of hunger. That's not insulin magic. It's food engineered, deliberately or by trial and error, to slip past your fullness signals.

So the honest summary looks like this. Sugar isn't poison, and an occasional sweet thing won't wreck your metabolism. But it's an easy way to take in a lot of calories without noticing, it doesn't give you the energy it seems to promise, and a habit of liquid sugar on top of little movement and poor sleep is a reliable path toward the insulin resistance that actually hurts people.
What actually controls your energy

Insulin resistance builds slowly, and the main drivers are well known: carrying a lot of excess body fat, especially around the gut, not moving much, sleeping badly, and a diet heavy in refined carbs and sugary drinks. Notice that sugar is on the list but not alone at the top. A lean, active person who eats some sugar is in a completely different position from a sedentary person drinking several energy drinks a day.

Muscle is the biggest glucose sink in your body. When muscles contract, they can pull glucose out of the blood through pathways that don't fully depend on insulin. That's why even a short walk after a meal tends to flatten the post-meal rise, and why strength training improves blood sugar control over time. The more muscle you have and the more you use it, the more room your system has to absorb a carb-heavy meal.

Underway, this gets practical fast. Midwatch, the easy move is a sugary energy drink and a pastry. The caffeine masks fatigue for a while, the sugar adds nothing to alertness, and then the stimulation wears off on top of the sleep debt you already had. A better setup: eat real meals with protein, keep carbs paired with protein or fiber, move around during long watches when you can, and treat sleep as the main energy source, because it is.

items: Pair carbs with protein, fat or fiber to slow absorption.
Go easy on liquid sugar; it hits fastest and fills you least.
Move after big meals, even ten minutes of walking or a few sets of squats.
Don't expect sugar to fix tiredness. Ask whether you're short on sleep instead.
Build muscle; it's the biggest glucose buffer you have.

blocks.text: None of this is medical advice. If you have episodes of shakiness, sweating, confusion or a pounding heart a few hours after eating, or if diabetes runs in your family, get checked by a doctor or corpsman. A simple blood test can tell you where your control loop stands.

The reframe: energy isn't something you top up with sugar like a fuel tank. It's the output of a well-tuned system: sleep, muscle, regular meals and a body clock you respect. Sugar doesn't charge the battery. It just changes the reading on the gauge for a while.

takeaways: Blinded trials found no 'sugar high' in kids; a 31-study meta-analysis found sugar leaves adults more tired and less alert within an hour.
Most post-snack slumps aren't blood sugar crashing below normal; body clock, meal size and sleep debt matter more.
Glucose spikes after carb-heavy meals are normal. The real long-term risk is insulin resistance, and most people with prediabetes don't know they have it.
Muscle, movement and sleep do more for steady energy than avoiding every spike.
Pair carbs with protein or fiber, go easy on liquid sugar, and walk after big meals.

title: The 500 Calories Nobody Decided to Eat
dek: Twenty people lived inside a federal research hospital for a month so scientists could answer a simple question: does processing itself change how much we eat?

blocks.text: For one month, twenty adults lived at the Clinical Center of the US National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland. They weren't sick. They were volunteers in an experiment designed to answer a question that nutrition science had argued about for years without a clean test: does the *processing* of food, separate from its sugar, salt, fat or fiber, change how much people eat?

For two weeks, their meals were built mostly from ultra-processed foods. For the other two weeks, their meals were built from unprocessed or minimally processed foods. The order was randomized. The rule for both diets was the same: eat as much or as little as you want.

On the ultra-processed diet, people ate about **500 more calories a day**. Not because anyone told them to, and not because they rated the food as tastier. They simply ate more, and they gained weight. Then, on the other diet, they ate less and lost it. It's one of the cleanest demonstrations we have that our food environment can make decisions for us that we never consciously make.
What counts as ultra-processed

Almost everything we eat is processed in some way. Milk is pasteurized, rice is milled, beans are dried and canned. So the term needs a sharper definition, and the most widely used one comes from a system called **NOVA**, developed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in Brazil. NOVA sorts food not by nutrients but by the extent and purpose of the industrial processing behind it.

blocks.title: The NOVA scale, from least to most processed
items: Unprocessed or minimally processed: fresh or frozen fruit and vegetables, eggs, plain meat, milk, rice, dried beans.
Processed culinary ingredients: oils, butter, sugar, salt, used to cook the first group.
Processed foods: simple combinations of the first two, like canned vegetables, cheese, cured meat or fresh bread.
Ultra-processed foods: industrial formulations built from refined substances and additives, like soda, packaged snacks, sweetened cereals and many ready meals.

blocks.text: The fourth group is the interesting one. Monteiro's team describes these as products assembled from substances extracted or modified from whole foods, often with ingredients you would rarely find in a home kitchen: high-fructose corn syrup, hydrogenated oils, protein isolates, and cosmetic additives like flavorings, emulsifiers and colorings. They're designed to be cheap, shelf-stable, convenient and very easy to like.
A useful rule of thumb from the NOVA researchers: if the ingredient list contains things you wouldn't recognize as food you could buy and cook with, it's probably in group four.
The experiment

The NIH study was led by Kevin Hall, a physicist turned metabolism researcher known for running tightly controlled feeding studies. The design had one especially clever feature. Hall's team worked to match the two diets on the things nutrition debates usually focus on. The meals offered were designed to be matched for calories, energy density, protein, carbs, fat, sugar, sodium and fiber. The main thing left to differ was how processed the food was.

The ten men and ten women, with an average age of about 31, were offered meals and snacks totaling about twice the calories each person needed to maintain their weight. Staff weighed what was left on every plate, so researchers knew exactly what each person ate. Body weight and other measures were tracked throughout.

items.label: Extra calories eaten per day on the ultra-processed diet
Average weight gained in two weeks on that diet
Average weight lost in two weeks on the unprocessed diet

blocks.source: Hall et al., Cell Metabolism, 2019

blocks.text: The extra calories came almost entirely from carbohydrate and fat. Protein intake barely moved: about two calories a day of difference, which is statistically nothing. And weight changes tracked intake closely, a strong sign the effect was real rather than a quirk of water or measurement.

blocks.title: Where the extra calories came from
blocks.note: Protein intake did not differ meaningfully between the two diets (about −2 kcal/day).
blocks.source: Hall et al., Cell Metabolism, 2019

blocks.text: Two more details are worth noticing. First, people rated the meals on both diets as about equally pleasant. The ultra-processed food wasn't simply more delicious. Second, people ate the ultra-processed meals noticeably faster, about **17 more calories per minute**. Soft, easy-to-chew food goes down quickly, and fullness signals from the gut take time to reach the brain.

There was a biological echo of this, too. On the unprocessed diet, blood levels of PYY, a gut hormone that suppresses appetite, went up, and ghrelin, a hormone that drives hunger, went down compared with baseline. The body seemed to be signaling more satisfaction from the less processed food, even though people's own ratings didn't register the difference.
Nobody in the study felt like they were overeating. Their hunger and fullness ratings were similar on both diets. The extra 500 calories happened below the level of conscious choice.
Why it might happen
The study showed *that* processing changed intake. It didn't prove exactly *why*. Hall and his colleagues discussed several candidate explanations, and they aren't mutually exclusive.

items: **Eating speed.** Food that requires little chewing gets eaten before satiety signals catch up.
**Protein leverage.** One theory says people keep eating until they hit a protein target; if protein comes diluted among refined carbs and fat, you overshoot calories getting there.
**Engineered combinations.** Many products pair fat, sugar, salt and refined starch in ways rarely found in whole foods, which may encourage overconsumption.
**Gut-brain signaling.** Refined, pre-broken-down food may trigger weaker fullness signals than intact food that digests slowly.

blocks.text: One detail complicates the clean story, and Hall's paper says so directly. The two diets were matched for energy density when drinks were included, but the ultra-processed diet relied on diet sodas to get there. Looking only at the solid food, the ultra-processed meals were about **85% more energy-dense**, meaning more calories packed into each bite. The authors think that likely contributed to the overeating. So part of what makes ultra-processed food easy to overeat may simply be that it's calorie-dense and quick to eat, which raises the question of whether processing is the cause or just a marker for those features.

There was also a sobering practical finding. Using prices from a local supermarket, the team estimated that a week of ultra-processed meals at 2,000 calories a day cost about **$106 in ingredients**, versus about **$151** for the unprocessed version. Ultra-processed food is cheaper and quicker, which goes a long way toward explaining why it dominates.
How much of our food it is

Dominates is not an exaggeration. In 2025, the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics reported that from August 2021 to August 2023, ultra-processed foods made up **55% of calories** eaten by Americans aged one and older. For young people aged 1 to 18 it was nearly 62%; for adults, 53%.

blocks.title: Share of calories from ultra-processed food, US
blocks.note: Data from August 2021 to August 2023.
blocks.source: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief 536, 2025

blocks.text: The biggest single sources were sandwiches including burgers, followed by sweet bakery products, salty snacks and sweetened drinks. In other words, for most Americans, ultra-processed food isn't an occasional treat. It's the main source of energy.

Large observational studies have linked diets high in ultra-processed food with worse health. A 2024 umbrella review in the *BMJ* pulled together 45 pooled analyses covering nearly 10 million people and found higher ultra-processed food intake associated with a higher risk of 32 of the 45 health outcomes examined, including heart disease deaths, type 2 diabetes, anxiety and depression.

The honest caveat is important. These are associations, not experiments. People who eat a lot of ultra-processed food differ in many other ways, such as income, sleep, stress and exercise, and those differences are hard to fully control for. The review's own quality grading rated most of the evidence as low or very low quality. The signal is consistent, but observational data can't by itself prove cause.
The newer test

That's why controlled trials matter, and Hall's 2019 study had real limits: twenty people, two weeks per diet, in a hospital. In 2025 a larger and longer trial in England, published in *Nature Medicine*, asked a sharper question. What if both diets follow official healthy-eating guidelines, and the only difference is processing?

Fifty-five adults each spent eight weeks on a minimally processed diet and eight weeks on an ultra-processed one, with both built to fit the UK's Eatwell Guide. The ultra-processed version used reformulated, nutritionally improved products such as breakfast cereals, ready meals and plant-based alternatives, many carrying health claims on the label. All the food was delivered to participants' homes in its normal branded packaging, and they ate as much as they liked.

That design matters. Earlier trials, including Hall's, took place in hospital wards, which are about as far from real life as eating gets. Here people ate at home, at work and with their families, much as they normally would, just with someone else doing the shopping.

items.label: Body weight change on the minimally processed diet (8 weeks)
Body weight change on the ultra-processed diet (8 weeks)

blocks.source: Dicken et al., Nature Medicine, 2025

blocks.text: People lost weight on both diets, likely because both were healthier than what they usually ate. But they lost about twice as much on the minimally processed version. The gap was modest, and the trial was still small. Yet it points the same direction as Hall's: even when the nutrient numbers look good on paper, how food is made seems to matter.
The critics have a point too

Not every scientist is convinced that ultra-processed is the right category. NOVA lumps together foods with very different nutritional profiles: a packaged wholegrain bread and a can of soda can sit in the same group. Some studies find that certain ultra-processed foods, such as some breads, cereals and yogurts, aren't linked to worse outcomes at all. Critics argue that the real culprits may be specific features, like energy density, eating speed or particular combinations of ingredients, rather than processing as such.

Hall's own paper acknowledged that the NOVA system has been criticized as too imprecise to base dietary advice on, even as Brazil's national dietary guidelines use it to advise people to avoid ultra-processed food. Two serious groups of experts looking at the same evidence can reasonably land in different places about what the category means.

That debate is healthy, and it's ongoing. Researchers are now trying to separate out which features of ultra-processed food drive overeating. The answer will probably end up more specific than the category itself.
What to do with this

None of this calls for food purity or guilt. On a submarine especially, a lot of the food is processed out of necessity: it has to survive months of storage. The goal isn't zero ultra-processed food. It's noticing that some foods quietly push your intake up, and adjusting where it's easy.

A few moves follow directly from the evidence. Build meals around foods that look like what they are: eggs, meat, fish, rice, potatoes, beans, fruit, vegetables, milk. Eat a little slower, especially with soft, easy foods. Get protein in every meal so you're not chasing it through snacks. And be aware that the bag of chips during a long watch isn't a moral failure; it's simply food that's engineered to be easy to keep eating.

It also helps to think in swaps rather than bans. Oatmeal instead of a frosted cereal some mornings. A sandwich built from sliced meat and bread rather than a breaded, pre-fried patty. Nuts, fruit, cheese or a hard-boiled egg as watch snacks instead of something from a crinkly bag. Water or milk instead of soda most of the time. None of these changes is dramatic, and that's the point. Based on what the trials found, the effect of processing works through many small, unnoticed differences in how much gets eaten, so the fix can work the same way.

And if a meal is mostly ultra-processed, because that's what's on the menu tonight, you can still apply the eating-speed lesson. Put the fork down between bites, drink some water, and give your gut a few extra minutes to report back before going for seconds.

The bigger idea is about agency. We like to think every bite is a decision. Hall's volunteers weren't trying to overeat, didn't feel like they were, and didn't find the food more delicious. They ate 500 extra calories a day anyway. The lesson isn't that willpower is useless. It's that the smartest place to apply it is upstream, in what you put on the plate and in reach, rather than downstream, in a fight with every individual bite.

takeaways: In a tightly controlled NIH trial, people ate about 500 more calories a day on an ultra-processed diet without trying to.
The diets were matched on sugar, fat, sodium and fiber, so processing itself seemed to drive the difference.
Ultra-processed food supplies about 55% of calories in the US.
Observational links to disease are consistent but mostly low-quality evidence; the trials are small but point the same way.
Build meals around recognizable whole foods, eat a bit slower, and shape your environment rather than fighting every bite.
