Increase in heart stroke volume after interval training

blocks.source: Helgerud et al., Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2007

blocks.text: The mechanism was the heart itself. After interval training, the amount of blood pumped with each beat rose by about 10 percent, and the VO2max gains tracked that change. Hard efforts appear to push the heart to its limit in a way that steady easy work doesn't, and the heart adapts by getting better at filling and emptying.

blocks.title: Zone 2 vs hard intervals

left.head: Easy steady work (Zone 2)
items: Low stress; can be done often
Builds a base and lets you accumulate time
Good for recovery days and active rest
Less efficient at raising VO2max per minute

right.head: Hard intervals
items: High stress; needs recovery between sessions
Strong stimulus for the heart and VO2max
Big return when time is short
Too much too often leads to burnout

blocks.text: Putting it together with limited time and space

None of this means easy training is useless. It still counts toward the weekly activity targets, it's gentle enough to do on tired days and it builds the base that makes hard sessions possible. The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines recommend 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix. Vigorous minutes count roughly double, which is the guidelines' way of acknowledging what Helgerud's runners showed.

For most people, a sensible approach looks like this: one or two short sessions a week that are genuinely hard, plus as much easy movement as your schedule allows. You don't need a heart-rate monitor or lab-tested zones. Easy means you could talk in sentences. Hard means you can only get out a few words at a time.

On a rotating schedule, it helps to match intensity to how you feel. Put the hard session on a day when you've slept and eaten reasonably well, because intervals done exhausted are miserable and less productive. Save easy sessions for the tired days, when a steady 20 or 30 minutes still counts toward your weekly total and often leaves you feeling better than when you started. Strength training and hard cardio can live in the same week; just avoid stacking the hardest of both on the same tired day.

blocks.title: A 4×4 interval session, adapted for any machine
items: Warm up for about 10 minutes at an easy, conversational pace
Go hard for 4 minutes: breathing heavily, only a few words possible, but sustainable to the end
Recover for 3 minutes at an easy pace, keeping moving
Repeat the hard 4 minutes and easy 3 minutes for a total of four rounds
Cool down for a few minutes and note what you did so you can beat it next time

blocks.text: The protocol works on a treadmill, a stationary bike, a rowing machine or a stair climber, whatever is available and fits the space. With no machine at all, hard circuits of step-ups, burpees or shadowboxing can push your heart rate high, though they are harder to pace. Build up gradually if you haven't trained hard in a while, and talk to a doctor or your corpsman first if you have any heart symptoms, chest pain or a known medical condition.
The question isn't which zone is magic. It's whether you're regularly asking your heart to do something hard enough that it has to get better.
The engine you build now

The Zone 2 debate is a useful lesson in how fitness ideas spread. A real observation about elite athletes gets simplified, repeated and turned into a rule for everyone, and the context that made it true, twenty hours a week of training, falls away. The underlying science is less catchy: total activity matters, intensity matters more when time is short, and both feed the same engine.

That engine is worth taking seriously at twenty, even though the payoff in those mortality studies shows up decades later. Fitness declines with age for everyone. Starting from a higher peak means more years above the levels where daily life gets hard. And unlike almost every other number your doctor tracks, this one rewards effort directly. Run, row, ride or climb hard enough a couple of times a week and the body has no choice but to build a bigger engine.

takeaways: In a study of 122,007 patients, the least-fit group had about five times the adjusted death risk of the elite group, with no upper limit of benefit found.
The evidence is observational, but fitness is one of the few major risk factors you can actively train.
Zone 2 is useful for base and volume, but it is not proven to be the best intensity for ordinary people with limited time.
Hard intervals such as 4×4 minutes raised VO2max more than steady training of equal total work.
A practical mix: one or two genuinely hard sessions a week plus as much easy movement as you can fit in.

title: The Warm-Up Is a Workout in Disguise
dek: Warming up makes you stronger for the next hour, but the best evidence for injury protection points somewhere stranger: to what a good warm-up trains over months.

blocks.text: In 2026, a panel of 23 sports scientists from 12 countries tried to settle a question that every gym class, coach and PT instructor has an opinion on: what is a warm-up actually for? They worked through 122 statements in three rounds of voting. They reached strong agreement on 72 of them. One of the conclusions would surprise most people who have ever been told to warm up so they don't get hurt.

The panel found no support for the idea that a warm-up protects you from injury in the session you are about to do. Including certain exercises in a warm-up may reduce injury risk over the long term, they wrote, but that is the same benefit those exercises would have at any other point in training. The warm-up doesn't work like a seatbelt you click on before driving. It works more like a training program that happens to be scheduled at the start of every session.
That reframe changes what a good warm-up looks like. It also explains why the version most people do, a few lazy arm circles and a long hamstring stretch, gets the science almost exactly backwards.
Why warm muscle works better

Start with the part that holds up beautifully. Muscle is a chemical machine, and like most chemistry, it runs faster when it's warmer. Raising muscle temperature speeds the enzymes that release energy, makes nerve signals travel faster, and lowers the internal stiffness the muscle has to overcome to move. David Bishop's review of the mechanisms lists these temperature effects as the main reasons warm-ups work, alongside a few non-thermal ones such as a slightly elevated baseline oxygen uptake when hard work begins.

The size of the effect is not trivial. In a review of temperature and neuromuscular function, Racinais and Oksa reported that short, explosive performance improves by roughly 2 to 5 percent for every 1 °C rise in muscle temperature. The same review adds an important limit: once your *core* temperature climbs too high, the relationship flips and performance falls. Warm muscle is good. An overheated body is not.

One clever line of research tested how much of the benefit is really about heat. Bishop's review describes *passive* warm-ups, where muscle temperature is raised from the outside with hot water, heated garments or warm rooms instead of exercise. Because passive heating warms the tissue without tiring it, it lets scientists separate the temperature effect from everything else exercise does. Experiments like these are a big part of why researchers attribute most of a warm-up's effects to temperature rather than to the movement itself. Still, active warm-ups add things heat alone cannot, like rehearsing the movement you're about to load.

items.label: Gain in short-duration performance per 1 °C rise in muscle temperature

blocks.source: Racinais & Oksa, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2010

blocks.text: Does that show up when people are actually tested? A 2010 meta-analysis by Fradkin and colleagues gathered 32 studies of warm-ups that included activity beyond stretching. Warming up improved performance in 79 percent of the outcomes measured, and there was little evidence that it ever made things worse. The authors also flagged a weakness: few of these studies were well-controlled randomized trials. So the direction is clear, and the exact size depends on the task.

items.label: Share of performance measures improved by warming up, across 32 studies

blocks.source: Fradkin et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2010

blocks.text: The stretching flip

For decades, warming up meant static stretching: hold a hamstring stretch for 30 seconds, switch legs, repeat. Then studies started showing that long static holds right before explosive work made people slightly weaker and slower. The pendulum swung so hard that some coaches banned stretching before training entirely.

A 2016 review by David Behm and three colleagues sorted out the mess. Tested right after stretching, static stretches cut performance by about 3.7 percent on average, while dynamic stretches, meaning controlled movement through a range like leg swings and walking lunges, improved it slightly. The dose mattered a lot. Holding a stretch for a minute or more per muscle group cost about 4.6 percent. Holding it for less than a minute cost about 1 percent.

blocks.title: Performance change right after stretching
blocks.note: Testing usually happened 3 to 5 minutes after stretching, with no movement in between.
blocks.source: Behm et al., Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism, 2016

blocks.text: Here is the detail that most summaries drop. In most of those studies, people were tested within a few minutes of stretching, with nothing in between. When studies added dynamic activity after the stretching, the way a real warm-up would, no clear performance loss showed up. The review's conclusion was moderate: short static stretching inside a warm-up that ends with dynamic movement is fine, and it improves range of motion for a short window, typically under half an hour.

Static stretching before training isn't poison. Long holds right before explosive work are a small, real cost. If a muscle feels tight, stretch it briefly, then move through the range dynamically before anything heavy or fast.
The injury surprise

Now back to the puzzle from the start. If warm-ups don't protect you in the moment, why do so many coaches swear they prevent injuries? Because one kind of warm-up really does, and the reason is revealing.

In 2008, Torbjørn Soligard and colleagues ran a large trial with 1,892 teenage female soccer players across 125 clubs in Norway. Half the clubs replaced their usual warm-up with a structured 20-minute program, later known as the FIFA 11+. It wasn't just jogging. Once players learned it, it took about 20 minutes and was done at the start of every practice. It opened with running drills, then moved to a strength, jumping and balance block with planks, side planks, slow Nordic hamstring lowers, squats, jump landings and single-leg balance work. Over one season, the program group had a lower risk of injuries overall, and roughly half the risk of overuse injuries. The headline outcome, lower-limb injuries specifically, did not quite reach statistical significance, which is a fair reminder that single trials are noisy.

A 2017 meta-analysis by Thorborg and colleagues pooled the controlled trials. The FIFA 11+ cut overall injury rates by 39 percent. The older version, the FIFA 11, which was shorter and less demanding, showed no detectable effect at all.

items.label: Reduction in football injuries with the FIFA 11+ warm-up program
Detectable effect of the older, lighter FIFA 11

blocks.source: Thorborg et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2017

blocks.text: Look at what separates the version that worked from the one that didn't. The effective program was essentially a small strength-and-control session performed two or three times a week for months. It built stronger hamstrings, steadier knees and better landings. That is exactly what the 2026 expert panel was getting at: the injury protection comes from adaptations accumulated over a season, not from being warm on a particular afternoon.

There is a design detail in the 11+ that is easy to miss. Each strength exercise came in three difficulty levels. A player started with a basic plank held for 20 to 30 seconds, then progressed to alternating leg lifts, then to holding one leg up. The Nordic hamstring lowers went from a handful of reps toward a dozen or more. In other words, the warm-up applied progressive overload, the same principle that drives any strength program. It was built to get harder as the players got stronger, and that is part of why it kept working across a whole season.

blocks.title: What people think a warm-up does vs what the evidence shows

left.head: Common belief
items: Prevents injury in today's session
Long static stretches are the core of it
Any light movement counts
Skippable if you're short on time

right.head: What the evidence shows
items: Improves performance today, mostly via muscle temperature
Long static holds before explosive work cost a little power
Structured strength and control drills protect over months
A short, specific warm-up still beats none

blocks.text: Building one that does both jobs

The 2026 consensus described the warm-up in three layers. First, general activity to raise temperature. Second, movements specific to what you are about to do. Third, an optional set of brief, hard efforts meant to sharpen the nervous system for the main work, an effect researchers now call *post-activation performance enhancement*. They also stressed that more comprehensive warm-ups tend to work better and that the right one depends on the activity.

That third layer deserves a word of caution. The idea is that a few brief, near-maximal efforts can temporarily make the following work more powerful, but the effect depends on getting the dose right. Too little does nothing, and too much leaves you tired instead of sharp. For most people training for general fitness, the honest version is simple: a couple of quick, crisp reps of something explosive near the end of the warm-up, then a short rest. Don't build a second workout before your workout.

The panel made one more point that is easy to overlook: the warm-up is also a check-in. How your body responds during those first minutes tells you something about your readiness and fatigue that day. That makes it a built-in diagnostic. If your usual ramp feels sluggish and heavy, the session that follows can be adjusted before you find out the hard way halfway through it.

blocks.title: A 10-minute warm-up for a small space
items: General: 3 to 4 minutes of easy movement that gets you breathing harder, such as jumping jacks, marching in place, shadowboxing or an easy spin on a bike or rower.
Mobility in motion: leg swings, walking lunges with a reach, hip openers and arm circles, about 5 to 8 reps each, building range each time.
Strength-and-control block: a few slow hamstring lowers or single-leg hip bridges, a short plank and some single-leg balance work. This is the part that pays off over months.
Specific ramp: do the first exercise of your workout at an easy load, then two or three progressively heavier sets with fewer reps.
Sharpen: two or three short, fast efforts, like a few quick jumps or explosive push-ups, then rest a minute before the main work.

blocks.text: For lifting, the specific ramp is where most of the value lives. If your working sets are push-ups with your feet elevated, start with a set of incline push-ups, then a set of standard ones, then go. If you are squatting with a loaded pack, do a set with no pack, then a lighter one. These ramp sets warm the exact tissues you will use, rehearse the movement pattern, and give you a read on how you feel that day. If the ramp sets feel unusually heavy, that's useful data before you commit to a hard session.

For running or rowing, ease in. The first five minutes at a truly easy pace do most of the temperature work, and a few short pickups at the end of that period handle the sharpening. Cold muscle in a chilly space takes a bit longer, so add a couple of minutes when the room is cold.

The same logic applies outside physical training. Competitive gamers spend time in an aim trainer or a deathmatch before ranked games, and musicians run scales before a performance. Those routines work for the same reason a lifting ramp does: they rehearse the precise movements you are about to need, at increasing speed, until the system is running at full capacity. A generic warm-up helps. A warm-up that looks like a slower version of the real task helps more.
When time is tight

On a rotating schedule with ten spare minutes between obligations, the honest question is whether to spend three of them warming up. The research suggests yes, but compress it. Skip the long stretching. Do a minute or two of general movement, then two ramp-up sets of your first exercise. You get most of the temperature benefit and the movement rehearsal in very little time.

The strength-and-control block is the one piece you shouldn't throw away permanently, because it is the piece that builds durability. If you can't fit it before training, put it somewhere else in your week. A few minutes of hamstring lowers, single-leg work and planks, done consistently, is closer to what actually protected those Norwegian soccer players than anything about being warm.
The real lesson

Most people think of the warm-up as overhead, the toll you pay before the real work starts. The science suggests the opposite framing. The first ten minutes of a session are the most consistent training time you have, because they happen every single time you show up. Programs that used that slot for genuine strength and control work cut injuries substantially. Programs that used it for token movement didn't.

That idea travels well beyond the gym. The routine parts of any practice, the boring setup before a match, the checks before a task, are either filler or they are training. The difference is whether you design them to build something. A warm-up that you do three hundred times a year is not a preamble. It is one of the biggest workouts you do.

takeaways: Warm muscle performs better: roughly 2 to 5% per 1 °C for short, explosive efforts.
Long static stretches right before explosive work cost a little power; brief holds followed by dynamic movement are fine.
Warm-ups don't protect you in the moment; structured strength and control drills reduce injuries over months.
Use ramp-up sets of your first exercise as the core of a lifting warm-up.
Short on time, compress the warm-up but don't skip it.

title: People Would Rather Shock Themselves Than Be Bored
dek: Boredom feels like a waste of time. It's actually a signal, and every time you kill it with a phone you lose the message it was trying to deliver.

blocks.text: The room was almost empty. No phone, no book, no pen. Volunteers at the University of Virginia were asked to put their belongings away and simply sit alone with their thoughts for up to 15 minutes. That was the whole task: think about whatever you like, stay in the chair, don't fall asleep.

It sounds easy. It turned out to be hard enough that psychologist Timothy Wilson and his colleagues built a series of experiments around it, published in *Science* in 2014. In the early studies, nearly half of the 409 participants said they didn't enjoy the experience. When the researchers sent people home to do the same thing on their own, nearly a third admitted they had cheated, sneaking a look at a phone or getting up to do something.

Then came the version that made headlines. Before sitting alone, participants got a small, unpleasant electric shock, and many said they'd pay money to avoid feeling it again. Then they were left alone in the room for 15 minutes, with a button that would deliver the same shock if they pressed it. Nobody told them to. Two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed it anyway.

blocks.title: Gave themselves a shock rather than just sit and think
blocks.note: Participants had already felt the shock, and many had said they would pay to avoid it.
blocks.source: Wilson et al., Science, 2014 (via Nature News)

blocks.text: Think about what that means. Faced with nothing but their own minds, a large share of people chose pain over boredom. Not because pain is fun, but because *anything* felt better than sitting with the empty feeling. That empty feeling is boredom, and in a world built to make sure you never feel it, it's worth understanding what it's actually for.
Why sitting alone with your thoughts is so hard

Wilson's results are often summarized as 'people hate thinking', but that's not quite right. Thinking is something you do constantly. What people struggled with was *undirected* thinking with no task attached: no problem to solve, no conversation, no input. Without a target, the mind tends to drift toward whatever is unresolved, worries, regrets, the argument from last week, and that is not a pleasant place to sit.

The participants who did enjoy the time alone tended to have something to steer toward. According to reports on the study, they often thought about future events, frequently involving people they cared about. That's a clue worth keeping. Being alone with your thoughts goes better when you bring a topic, the same way a long drive goes better with a destination in mind. Thinking for pleasure, it turns out, is partly a skill: you pick the subject instead of letting the loudest worry pick it for you.

It also helps explain why the shock button got pressed. When there's nothing to engage with, even a mildly painful stimulus is at least *something*. It breaks the loop, gives the mind an event to react to. That's the same pull that makes people pick at a scab, crack their knuckles or refresh an app they checked thirty seconds ago. The urge isn't for pleasure. It's for any change at all.
What boredom actually is

Boredom isn't the same as having nothing to do. You can be bored in a packed schedule, bored during a mandatory training, bored while scrolling an endless feed. Psychologists usually define it as an uncomfortable state of *wanting* to be engaged in something satisfying and not being able to get there. It's not emptiness. It's a gap between the engagement you want and the engagement you have.

In 2018, the psychologists Erin Westgate and Timothy Wilson proposed a model that breaks that gap into two parts. They call it the **MAC model**, for meaning and attentional components. According to the model, you get bored when an activity fails on one or both of two counts: your attention doesn't fit the task, or the task doesn't feel meaningful to you.

blocks.title: Two roads to boredom (the MAC model)

left.head: Attention mismatch
items: Task is too easy: under-stimulated, mind drifts
Task is too hard: can't get a grip, attention slides off
Fix: change the difficulty
Example: a lecture way below or way above your level

right.head: Meaning deficit
items: Task doesn't connect to anything you care about
Even if the difficulty is fine
Fix: find or build a reason it matters
Example: paperwork that feels pointless

blocks.text: This explains why boredom shows up in such different situations. Copying numbers into a log is boring because it's too easy. A dense technical manual can be boring because it's too hard to follow, so your attention keeps sliding off it. And a task at the perfect difficulty can still be boring if you can't see why it matters. Notice that the opposite of boredom on both counts, a challenge that fits your skill and feels worth doing, is basically a description of flow.
Boredom is a signal, not a bug

Many researchers now see boredom the way doctors see pain: unpleasant on purpose. Pain tells you to take your hand off the stove. Hunger tells you to find food. Boredom tells you that what you're doing right now isn't a good use of your attention, and that you should change something, either the task, how you're doing it, or what you're doing it for.

From an evolutionary angle, that's valuable. An animal that could happily stare at the same patch of ground forever would never explore, never find new food, never learn. A creature that gets restless when nothing is happening gets pushed toward new information. Boredom is the push. In that sense it's less like a void and more like an engine warning light: annoying, but there to make you look.
Boredom is a question your brain is asking: *is this worth my attention?* The answer can be 'no, change it' or 'yes, and here's why'. What matters is that you actually answer it.

The trouble is that the push can go in good or bad directions. The same restlessness that drives someone to start a project can drive someone else to pick a fight, drink too much or make a reckless choice. Researchers have found that people who get bored easily, what they call high boredom proneness, are more likely to report problems like depression, overeating, gambling and substance use. Those studies are correlational, so they don't prove boredom causes the problems, but they do suggest that handling boredom badly is not a harmless habit.
The case for a wandering mind

Boredom may also have a creative upside. In a 2014 study, the British psychologists Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman had some participants spend 15 minutes copying numbers out of a phone book, a task chosen to be mind-numbing. Then everyone did a classic creativity test: list as many uses as you can for a pair of polystyrene cups. The bored group came up with more ideas. In a follow-up, people who had to *read* the phone numbers, an even more passive task, did better still, possibly because reading leaves more room for the mind to wander.

The idea behind this is that boredom loosens the grip of focused attention and lets the mind drift. That drifting, daydreaming state is when the brain links distant ideas, replays problems from new angles and sometimes hands you the answer you couldn't force. Lots of people have had the experience of solving a bug in the shower or on a walk, after giving up at the keyboard.

An honest caveat: these creativity studies are small, use simple lab tasks, and haven't always replicated cleanly. Boredom doesn't automatically make you creative, and you won't write a great game just by staring at a wall. The more defensible claim is narrower. Mind-wandering is where a lot of loose thinking happens, and boredom is often the doorway into it. Close the doorway every time and you get less of that thinking.
What the phone actually takes

For almost all of human history, boredom was unavoidable. You waited in lines, sat through long evenings, stood watches with nothing to look at. Now there's a device in your pocket that can end boredom in under a second, every time. That sounds like pure progress. But think about what happens to a signal that's always silenced before it's heard.

If boredom is a message that says *change something*, the phone answers it with the cheapest possible change: a new stimulus that asks nothing of you. The restlessness goes away, but nothing about your situation improved. You didn't fix the boring task, find a better one or figure out why it bored you. Do that hundreds of times a day and you never learn what your boredom was pointing at.

blocks.title: The numbing loop
items: Feel a flicker of boredom
Reach for the phone
Instant relief, no real change
Tolerance for empty moments drops
Boredom shows up sooner and feels worse

blocks.text: There's also a tolerance effect, which anyone who has struggled with doomscrolling will recognize. Wilson's participants were ordinary college students and community members, and many of them already found 15 minutes alone hard to bear. The more reliably you escape boredom, the less practice you get at sitting with it, and the more unbearable short gaps start to feel. Scrolling doesn't cure boredom. It often just moves it, leaving you oddly flat afterward, bored and overstimulated at once.

Long deployments put this in sharp relief. Underway, much of the endless feed disappears, and the empty stretches come back: between watches, waiting for a drill to end, lying in the rack before sleep. For people used to filling every gap, that can feel brutal at first. It's also a rare chance to find out what your mind does when nothing is feeding it, and what it starts asking for.

It's worth separating boredom from rest, because they get confused. Rest is when you're not engaged and you're fine with it; your body and mind are recovering. Boredom is when you're not engaged and you want to be. After a brutal watch, an hour of staring at the overhead may be genuine rest. Feeling restless, irritated and itchy for something to happen is the signal. The response to rest is to let it happen. The response to boredom is to ask what it's pointing at.
How to use boredom instead of killing it

None of this means you should seek out misery or throw your phone overboard. The goal is to stop treating every flicker of boredom as an emergency and start treating it as information. A few simple habits help.

blocks.title: When boredom hits
items: Notice it and name it: 'I'm bored.' That alone breaks the autopilot reach for the phone.
Ask which kind: is this too easy, too hard, or pointless to me?
If it's too easy, make it harder: race the clock, add a constraint, turn it into a game.
If it's too hard, shrink it: break off a smaller piece you can actually grip.
If it feels pointless, connect it to something you care about, or decide it really isn't worth doing.
If it's just empty time, let your mind wander for a few minutes before filling it.

blocks.text: The middle steps are where the MAC model earns its keep. Field day is boring because it's too easy, so make it a race or a challenge with someone else. A qualification card full of dense system diagrams is boring because it's too hard to grip, so cut it into one small piece you can actually trace. A chore that feels pointless might connect to something real if you look for it, and if it truly doesn't, at least you know why it drains you.

The last step is the strangest one, and maybe the most valuable. Try a short walk, a workout or a stretch of rack time with no input at all, not even music. Keep a small notebook handy. The first few minutes will feel itchy. After that, a lot of people find their mind starts producing things: ideas for a project, a solution to a problem, a decision they'd been avoiding. That's not wasted time. It's the thinking that never gets a turn when every gap is filled.

And when a task is boring because it's genuinely pointless, boredom has done its job. Sometimes the right response to a boring thing is not to push through it but to ask whether you should be doing it at all, or whether there's a version of your life with less of it. A lot of people who built something of their own started with exactly that kind of restless question.

The reframe: boredom isn't the absence of something to do. It's your mind telling you it wants something better than what it's getting. Silence that message every time and you never find out what 'better' would be.

takeaways: In Wilson's 2014 study, 67% of men and 25% of women shocked themselves rather than sit alone with their thoughts for 15 minutes.
Boredom comes from attention mismatch (too easy or too hard) or a lack of meaning, and each has a different fix.
Boredom is a signal to change something; the phone silences it without changing anything.
Small studies suggest boredom can open the door to mind-wandering and creative thinking, though the evidence is limited.
Next time you're bored, name it, ask which kind it is, and give your mind a few minutes before you fill the gap.

sources.by: Wilson, Reinhard, Westgate et al., Science, 2014

title: Part of Your Brain Is Still on the Last Thing You Did
dek: Every time you switch tasks, some of your attention stays behind. A management researcher gave it a name, and it explains why 'just checking quickly' costs so much more than it seems.

blocks.text: You sit down to work on your game. You've got the script open, you know what the next function needs to do, and you're about two minutes from getting into it. Then your phone buzzes. It's nothing, a reply in a group chat. You read it, answer it, put the phone down and look back at the screen. And the code looks oddly unfamiliar, as if someone else wrote it. What were you about to do?

That fog isn't laziness and it isn't a weak attention span. It has a name. In 2009, Sophie Leroy, a management researcher now at the University of Washington Bothell, published a paper with a title that sounds like a complaint scrawled on a whiteboard: *Why is it so hard to do my work?* Her answer was a concept she called **attention residue**.

The idea is simple. When you switch from Task A to Task B, your attention doesn't all move with you. Part of it stays stuck on Task A, still chewing on it, still wondering how it will turn out. You're physically doing Task B, but you're doing it with a partial brain. And the more often you switch, the more of yourself you leave scattered behind.
What Leroy actually found

Leroy ran two experiments in which people worked on one task, then moved to a second one. She measured how much the first task was still occupying their minds and how well they performed on the second. Two findings stood out, and one of them is surprising.

The unsurprising one: if people left the first task unfinished, thoughts about it lingered and their performance on the next task suffered. The surprising one: simply *finishing* the first task wasn't enough to clear the residue. What helped was finishing it under **time pressure**. When people had a tight deadline on the first task, they disengaged from it more cleanly and did better on the next.

Why would a deadline help? Leroy's explanation is that without time pressure, even a finished task stays open in your head. You keep evaluating it: could it have been better, did I miss something, what will people think? A hard deadline forces closure. The task isn't just done; it's *over*, and your mind accepts that it's over. Leisurely work tends to leave a longer tail.
Attention residue means the cost of switching isn't the few seconds it takes to change tabs. It's the reduced quality of everything you do while part of your mind is still somewhere else.
How often we actually switch

If residue is the tax, the next question is how often we pay it. Gloria Mark, an informatics professor at the University of California, Irvine, has spent about two decades timing how long people stay on a single screen before switching to another, first by shadowing office workers with stopwatches and later with software that logs computer activity as people go about their real work.

In her 2003 observations, published in 2004, people averaged about two and a half minutes on one screen before switching. By 2012, it was 75 seconds. In her more recent studies, the average was 47 seconds, and the median was around 40, meaning half of all stretches were even shorter. Other research groups have found similar figures.

blocks.title: Average time on one screen before switching
blocks.note: Office workers' real computer use, observed and logged. 'Recent' covers roughly the last several years before 2023.
blocks.source: Gloria Mark, UC Irvine, via University of California (2023)

blocks.text: Mark's work turned up two more numbers worth knowing. People spent about ten and a half minutes on a given project before switching to a different one, and when a project was interrupted, it took about 25 and a half minutes on average to get back to it, often after detours through other tasks. And here's the uncomfortable part: people interrupted themselves about as often as anything outside interrupted them.

Put those findings next to Leroy's and the picture gets grim. If you switch every 47 seconds and each switch leaves residue, you may almost never be working with your full attention. You're always carrying a little of the last thing, and the thing before that. It's like trying to run a full-power test on a plant that never gets a chance to stabilize.

blocks.title: The fragmentation loop
items: Switch to check something
Residue from the last task lingers
Current work feels harder and slower
Feel behind and restless
Switch again for relief

blocks.text: Why your brain won't let go

Why would a mind cling to a task it has already left? One old idea comes from the Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik, who reported in the 1920s that people remembered interrupted tasks better than completed ones, as if unfinished business stays switched on. The so-called Zeigarnik effect gets quoted constantly in productivity writing, but honesty requires a warning: attempts to replicate the memory part have produced mixed results over the decades. The broader intuition, that open goals keep tugging at attention, is better supported than the specific memory claim.

Leroy's work fits the broader intuition. Your brain is a goal-tracking machine. When a goal is still open, or when you're unsure whether you did it well, some background process keeps monitoring it, the way an alarm panel keeps a light lit until someone acknowledges it. That monitoring isn't free. It takes a share of the same limited attention you need for whatever is in front of you now.

Gamers know this feeling under a different name: tilt. You lose a round to something that felt unfair, and the next round you're still replaying it. Your crosshair placement gets sloppy, you take fights you shouldn't, and the loss bleeds into the next loss. That's attention residue with a scoreboard. It's why good players build a reset routine between rounds or matches, a breath, a quick note on what to fix, a deliberate turn of focus to the next fight. It's the competitive version of a ready-to-resume plan: acknowledge the loop, park it, move on.
Deep work: why intensity matters

In 2016, the Georgetown computer scientist Cal Newport popularized Leroy's idea in his book *Deep Work*. He split work into two kinds. **Shallow work** is the logistical, easy-to-repeat stuff: messages, scheduling, admin, quick checks. **Deep work** is focused effort that pushes your ability to its limit and produces something hard to replicate, like writing a complex system, learning a new technical skill, or designing a level that actually plays well.

Newport's argument is that the value of deep work depends on two things multiplied together: time and intensity of focus. Attention residue attacks the second term. You can sit at a desk for four hours, but if you check something every few minutes, you never get anywhere near full intensity, and four fragmented hours can produce less than one undistracted hour.

blocks.title: Shallow vs deep

left.head: Shallow work
items: Easy to do while distracted
Easy for someone else to replicate
Feels productive in the moment
Fills any time you give it

right.head: Deep work
items: Needs sustained, undivided attention
Builds rare, valuable skills
Often feels slow and uncomfortable at first
Needs protected blocks of time

blocks.text: There's an honest caveat here. *Deep Work* is a persuasive book, not a controlled experiment, and the related claim you may hear, that heavy media multitaskers are permanently worse at focusing, comes from research that has been mixed. A well-known 2009 Stanford study by Eyal Ophir, Clifford Nass and Anthony Wagner found heavy multitaskers were worse at filtering out distractions, but later studies have not always agreed on how big or reliable that effect is. Leroy's core finding is narrower and better grounded: switching carries a cost into the next task.
The one-minute fix: a ready-to-resume plan

Most of us can't eliminate interruptions. A chief needs something, the watch changes, a teammate pings you about a bug. So Leroy asked a more practical question: if you have to switch, can you reduce the residue? In a set of studies published in 2018 in *Organization Science* with Theresa Glomb of the University of Minnesota, she tested a simple technique.

The team first surveyed 202 working professionals about what interruptions felt like, then ran lab experiments. In two of them, with 66 and 44 student participants, people were pulled off one task and asked to switch to another, which involved reviewing résumés as if making hiring decisions. Some wrote a quick **ready-to-resume plan** before switching: where they were, what was still unresolved, and what they'd do next when they came back.

The people who wrote the plan showed less attention residue during the new task, made better hiring decisions, and remembered more about the candidates. The plan didn't need to be elaborate; the researchers stressed that about a minute was enough. Writing it down seems to tell the brain that the open loop has been safely parked, so it can stop guarding it.

blocks.title: Write a ready-to-resume plan (about a minute)
items: Where exactly did I stop? Note the file, line, step or page.
What's unresolved? One line on the problem you were in the middle of.
What's the very next action when I come back?
Put it somewhere you'll see it first when you return, then switch fully.

blocks.text: One limit is worth knowing: those studies measured how well people did on the *interrupting* task, not whether the plan helped them pick the original task back up. It probably does, since you've left yourself a map, but that part wasn't directly tested. Still, it's a one-minute habit with a solid lab result behind it, which is rare in productivity advice.
Designing your day around residue

Once you see attention residue, a few rules almost write themselves. **Batch the shallow stuff.** Answer messages in two or three blocks instead of the moment they arrive, so the residue from messaging lands in fewer places. **Use deadlines on purpose.** Leroy's time-pressure finding suggests that giving a task a short, hard end point, say 25 minutes to finish this function, helps you walk away from it cleanly.

items: Batch shallow work into set blocks rather than reacting all day.
Give focused tasks a hard stop; time pressure helps you let go cleanly.
Before any switch, spend one minute on a ready-to-resume note.
Keep the phone out of reach and out of sight during deep blocks.
Start deep blocks with the hardest part, before residue piles up.

blocks.text: Newport adds one more idea that runs against instinct. Instead of scheduling breaks from focus, he suggests scheduling breaks from *distraction*: decide in advance when you'll check your phone or messages, and outside those windows, don't. The point isn't purity. It's training. If every flicker of boredom gets answered with a quick check, your brain learns that discomfort always ends in a switch, and the urge to switch gets stronger. If you sit through the urge again and again, it tends to lose its grip.

Treat it like building endurance under a barbell. The first deep block of 30 minutes may feel long and itchy. That's normal, and it's not proof you can't focus. Add time gradually, notice roughly how long you stayed on task without switching, and let that stretch grow.

Life on a boat makes some of this easier and some of it harder. Off-watch time gets chopped up by drills, field days, qualifications and sleep, so long blocks are rare. But underway, you also lose the constant stream of notifications. For a lot of people, that's the closest thing to a true deep-work environment they'll ever get, and the trick is to use it on purpose instead of filling it with shallow stuff out of habit.

The same logic explains why games feel so easy to focus on. A good game gives you one clear goal, immediate feedback and no reason to look away, which is close to the conditions deep work needs. You don't lack the ability to concentrate. You just rarely set up the rest of your life the way game designers set up a match.

The reframe: focus isn't something you summon by willpower in the moment. It's something you protect by controlling when and how you switch. You can't stop every interruption, but you can stop leaving pieces of yourself behind at each one.

takeaways: Attention residue: when you switch tasks, part of your attention stays on the old one and drags down the new one.
Finishing isn't enough; finishing under a deadline helped people let go more cleanly.
Average time on one screen fell from about 150 seconds to 47 in Gloria Mark's studies, and people interrupt themselves as often as others do.
A one-minute ready-to-resume note before switching reduced residue and improved performance in lab studies.
Batch shallow work, protect deep blocks, and use offline time underway on purpose.

title: Why Future You Always Loses
dek: Your brain doesn't just prefer rewards now. It flips its preferences as a choice gets closer, and once you see the pattern you can use it against itself.

blocks.text: In the late 1990s, the behavioral scientists Daniel Read and Barbara van Leeuwen ran an experiment with snacks. They asked 200 people to choose a snack they would receive one week later. The options included healthy picks, like fruit, and unhealthy ones, like junk-food snacks. A week later the researchers came back with the snacks and said, in effect: here's what you ordered, but you can swap it for anything on the cart right now.

Look at the people who were not hungry at either moment, the cleanest comparison. When choosing a week in advance, 74% of them picked a healthy snack. When the cart was actually in front of them, 70% walked away with junk. Same people, same snacks, same lack of hunger. The only thing that changed was distance in time.

blocks.title: Chose a healthy snack (people not hungry)
blocks.note: 50 participants who were full both times. Most switched from healthy to junk when the snack was in reach.
blocks.source: Read & van Leeuwen, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1998 (Table 1)

blocks.text: This isn't a story about willpower failing under pressure. Nobody was starving. It's a story about a predictable flaw in how humans weigh the future, one that economists and psychologists call **delay discounting**. And the specific *shape* of that flaw explains a huge range of everyday failures, from skipped workouts to empty savings accounts to the game you planned to work on tonight.
Discounting is normal. The shape is the problem

Valuing things less when they're further away isn't irrational on its own. A reward later is worth less than the same reward now. You could die, the offer could vanish, plans change, and money now can be invested. Economists have a tidy model for a rational version of this: lose the same fixed percentage of value for every unit of delay. Under that model, called exponential discounting, your preferences are *consistent*. If you prefer A to B when both are a year away, you'll still prefer A to B when both are tomorrow.

Humans don't work like that. Our discounting is steep for short delays and flattens out for long ones. Researchers usually describe it with a hyperbola, a curve where value drops roughly in proportion to one divided by one-plus-the-delay. In plain terms: the difference between *now* and *tomorrow* feels enormous, while the difference between *a year from now* and *a year and a day from now* feels like nothing.

You've lived this a hundred times with an alarm clock. At 2200, setting the alarm for 0500 to work out before quarters feels like an easy, obvious call. The workout is the bigger reward; the extra sleep is small. At 0500, with the alarm actually going off, the extra hour in the rack is no longer a small thing far away. It's right here, and it suddenly outweighs everything. You didn't change your mind about fitness overnight. You just moved along the curve.

The economist Richard Thaler captured this in a famous 1981 thought experiment about apples. Some people would rather have one apple today than two tomorrow. But many of those same people would happily wait the extra day if the choice were one apple in a year versus two apples in a year and a day. The trade-off is identical: wait one extra day, get double. Yet the answer flips depending on whether the choice is close or far.

blocks.title: The same choice, seen from two distances

left.head: Far away
items: The larger, later reward looks obviously better
You plan to train, save, study, eat well
The cost feels abstract
Your choices match your values

right.head: Up close
items: The smaller, sooner reward suddenly looms huge
You skip, spend, scroll, snack
The cost feels immediate and real
Your choices match your impulses

blocks.text: This flip is called **preference reversal**, and it's been demonstrated over and over. In one well-known version by Kris Kirby and Richard Herrnstein, people who chose a smaller, sooner reward switched to the larger, later one when both options were pushed into the future with the same gap between them. The gap didn't change. Only the distance did.
The planner and the doer

Preference reversal means you are, in a practical sense, two different decision-makers. There's a version of you who plans from a distance and clearly sees what matters. And there's a version of you standing right in front of the snack cart, the phone, the Exchange, or the bunk, for whom the immediate option looks massive.

Neither one is the fake you. The planner isn't the “real” self and the doer a weak imposter. They're the same brain applying the same curve from two different spots on it. That matters, because it means trying harder to be the planner in the moment of temptation is fighting the shape of your own valuation. You'll win some of those fights, but you're the underdog every time.

Why would a brain be built this way? One plausible reading is that for most of human history, a reward that was sitting right in front of you was a sure thing, while a promised reward later might never arrive: the food could spoil, a rival could take it, plans could fall apart. A bias toward the near and certain would have paid off often. In a world of retirement accounts, long training programs and multi-year projects, that same bias misfires constantly. The hardware isn't broken. It's tuned for a different environment.

Psychologists who study procrastination describe the same split. Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl argue that when we put off a task to feel better now, the relief goes to present-you while the cost lands on a later version of yourself, who isn't around to object. Piers Steel's model of procrastination, built on hundreds of studies, has hyperbolic discounting at its core. The gym you skip, the money you spend, the study session you push back: all of them are the same curve, applied to different currencies.

The costs are real even when they're invisible. In a 1997 study, Dianne Tice and Roy Baumeister followed college students over a semester. Early on, the procrastinators were less stressed and less sick than everyone else. By the end, they were more stressed, sicker, and had worse grades on every assignment. They had borrowed comfort from their future selves, and the loan came due.
Future-you can't vote in today's decisions. Every plan that depends on future-you showing up and choosing differently from how present-you would choose is a plan built on the wrong curve.
Use the curve against itself

Here's the thought that changes everything. The same curve that makes you weak up close makes you wise from far away. When both options are distant, you reliably choose the better one. So the trick isn't to become stronger in the moment. It's to make the decision while you're still far away, and then **lock it in** so the up-close version of you doesn't get a vote.

This is an ancient idea. In Homer's *Odyssey*, Ulysses wants to hear the Sirens' song, which drives sailors to steer onto the rocks. He doesn't trust his future self to resist, so he has his crew tie him to the mast and plug their own ears, with orders to ignore anything he says until they're past. He decided at a distance, then removed his up-close self's ability to change the decision. Economists call this a **commitment device**.

The most striking modern example is a savings program called Save More Tomorrow, designed by Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi. Asking people to cut their take-home pay today to save more triggers the full force of the curve, because the pain is immediate. So the program asked a different question: would you agree *now* to put part of your *future* raises into savings? Since the raise hadn't arrived yet, the cost sat far away on the flat end of the curve, where people are reasonable. And because savings only went up when pay went up, take-home pay never visibly shrank.

items.label: Of employees offered the plan who joined
Of those who stayed in through the fourth raise
Average saving rate, start vs. 40 months later

blocks.source: Thaler & Benartzi, Journal of Political Economy, 2004

blocks.text: Nearly quadrupling a savings rate without anyone feeling a pay cut is what happens when you stop fighting the discount curve and design around it. Notice the structure: the decision was made far away, it was automatic after that, and quitting required effort. Inertia, normally the enemy, was put to work for the future self.

There's a second move that works alongside commitment: drag future rewards closer. If the payoff of a habit is months away, add a small payoff that arrives today. Track your lifts so you can see the number go up after every session. Mark each day you work on your project so a visible chain grows. Pair a task you avoid with something you enjoy, like a favorite playlist you only allow yourself during workouts. None of these change the long-term reward. They just put something on the steep, near end of the curve, where your brain is actually paying attention.
Commitment devices for real life

You don't need a research team to build these. You just need to notice when you're in “planner” mode, far from temptation, and use that window to make the up-close choice harder to get wrong. Deployment is almost a natural experiment in this: underway, a lot of temptations simply disappear. The danger is the return to port, when they all come back at once.

blocks.title: Deciding at a distance
items: Notice planner moments: Sunday nights, the start of a watch rotation, the week before pulling in.
Make the decision then, in specific terms: what, when, how much.
Automate it so the default does the work: automatic transfers, a preset contribution, gear packed the night before.
Add friction to the tempting option: log out, delete the app, keep junk food off the shelf.
Tell someone who'll notice if you back out. Social cost is a strong rope.
Expect up-close you to argue. Don't renegotiate; the deal was made by the version of you who could see clearly.

blocks.text: Money is the cleanest place to apply this. It's easy to come back from a long patrol with a pile of saved pay and watch it evaporate in a few weeks, because every purchase is up close and the future is far away. The fix is to decide where the money goes before you pull in, and to automate it so the decision executes without you. That can mean raising your Thrift Savings Plan contribution percentage or setting up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account. Rules and matching for the TSP and the military retirement system change, so confirm the current details with your command financial specialist or the base finance office before you set anything up.

The same logic works for fitness. Up close, the bunk beats the workout almost every time. So don't make the workout a decision you face at the moment of maximum tiredness. Make it a standing rule decided earlier: same time, same place, already planned, gear already out. You've removed the moment where the curve gets to vote.

It's worth noticing that game designers figured all this out long ago, and often use it on you rather than for you. Daily login bonuses, streak rewards and limited-time offers are engineered for the up-close self. A reward that disappears at midnight is maximally near and maximally urgent. A store that lets you buy now and grind later takes advantage of the same steep curve. Once you can see the pattern, you can recognize when a system is deliberately making the near option loom large, and you can choose to step back to the planner's distance before you click.

And it works for building things. If you're working on a game, a channel or a business, the payoff of any single session is months away, so it barely registers next to rewards that pay out tonight. Commitment helps here too: a set build time each day, a partner who expects progress, a public schedule for uploads. Each is a little rope around the mast.
A note of honesty about commitment

One famous study that supported self-imposed commitment devices has recently fallen apart. A 2002 paper by Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch on self-set deadlines was retracted in 2026, after a replication failed and investigators found signs that the data had been manipulated. That doesn't knock down the broader idea of commitment, which rests on many other lines of evidence, including the Save More Tomorrow results. But it's a reminder to judge each technique by whether it actually works for you, not by how good the story sounds.

The deeper lesson holds either way. You're not one consistent decision-maker who sometimes fails. You're a creature whose values seem to shift with distance, predictably and in the same direction every time. That's not a reason for shame. It's a design spec. Once you know which version of you shows up up close, you can stop asking him to be stronger and start arranging the world so he doesn't have to be.

takeaways: Humans discount the near future far more steeply than the distant future, so preferences flip as choices get closer.
Your far-away self chooses well; your up-close self chooses the quick reward. Both are you.
Make decisions while the temptation is still far away, then lock them in with automation or commitment.
Save More Tomorrow raised saving from 3.5% to 13.6% by tying it to future raises instead of current pay.
Before pulling into port, decide where your money goes and automate it; confirm TSP rules with your finance office.

title: What Happens When People Actually Quit
dek: Economists have paid tens of thousands of people to switch off Facebook and Instagram. The results are more modest than the headlines, more interesting than the skeptics admit, and they point to one thing most digital detoxes get wrong.

blocks.text: In the fall of 2018, a team of economists ran an unusual auction. They asked Facebook users a simple question: how much would we have to pay you to deactivate your account for four weeks? People took the question seriously, because the answers could turn into real money and real deactivation. After weighting the sample to look like the average American Facebook user, the median answer was $100. The average was $180.

Then the researchers, Hunt Allcott, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer and Matthew Gentzkow, paid a randomly chosen group to actually do it, and checked repeatedly that their accounts stayed off. When the four weeks were over, about 80% of that group agreed the break had been good for them. And yet, when asked again what it would take to make them quit for another month, they still wanted a lot of money. Their price dropped by up to 14%, but only that much.

That contradiction, “this was good for me” sitting right next to “I'd still need to be paid to do it again,” is the most honest picture we have of our relationship with social media. The study, published in the *American Economic Review* in 2020, became one of the most important experiments on the subject. Here's what it found, what later experiments added, and what it means if you want to change how you use your phone.
The four-week experiment

The team recruited through Facebook ads that offered money for an “online research study about internet browsing,” careful not to mention deactivation so they wouldn't attract only people who already wanted to quit. Everyone had to use Facebook for more than 15 minutes a day. People whose price was below $102 were randomly split into a group paid to deactivate and a control group that kept using it. The main analysis covered 1,661 people.

The first finding was simple: deactivation freed up about 60 minutes a day for the average person in the treatment group. That time didn't just flow into other websites. The treatment group actually spent *less* time on other social media and other online activities, and *more* time offline, including watching TV alone, doing other things alone, and spending time with friends and family.

items.label: Daily time freed up by deactivating Facebook
Of the deactivation group who said the break was good for them
Median price to give up Facebook for four weeks

blocks.source: Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer & Gentzkow, American Economic Review, 2020

blocks.text: The well-being results were real but small. An index combining happiness, life satisfaction, depression, anxiety and related questions improved by 0.09 standard deviations. The authors pointed out that's roughly 25–40% of the effect of typical psychological interventions like self-help therapy or group training. It's not nothing. It's also not the transformation that a lot of “I quit social media and my life changed” stories promise.

Some effects cut the other way. People who deactivated spent about 15% less time consuming news and scored lower on a test of current events. They also became somewhat less polarized in their political views. Facebook, it turns out, was both informing people and riling them up, and taking it away did both less.
The surprise: the habit stayed broken

The biggest effect in the study wasn't on mood. It was on what people did after the experiment ended. Nobody was stopping them from going right back to their old usage. Many didn't. As the four weeks ended, the deactivation group planned to cut their future use far more than the control group did. About a month later, they reported using the Facebook phone app about 12 minutes a day less than the control group, roughly 23% less. Some had simply stayed away: five percent of the treatment group still had their accounts deactivated nine weeks after the experiment ended.

There's an honest caveat buried in the appendix. Among iPhone users who reported their usage straight from their phone's built-in screen-time tracker rather than estimating it, the drop was less than half as large and not statistically significant. Self-reported numbers may have overstated the change. Still, multiple measures pointed the same way, including how quickly people reactivated their accounts.

The researchers offered two explanations, and both are useful to know. One is habit: the less you use something, the less it pulls on you, the same way caffeine cravings fade after you cut back. The other is learning: some people discovered that life without Facebook was better than they had expected. You can't fully judge something while you're inside the habit. A break is a way to collect data from the outside.

The price people put on Facebook fits that second explanation. Before the break, their valuation included things they hadn't really tested, such as how much they'd miss it and how bad being out of the loop would feel. After the break, they'd tested it, and their price dropped a bit. The drop was small, which suggests Facebook really was worth something to most of them. But it moved, which suggests people had been guessing.
You can't accurately judge what a habit is doing for you from inside it. A deliberate break is how you collect the data.
The bigger sequel: smaller effects, and a warning

Before the 2020 US election, Allcott, Gentzkow and a large team working with Meta ran the experiment again at a massive scale: 19,857 Facebook users and 15,585 Instagram users, all spending at least 15 minutes a day on the platform. The treatment group was paid to deactivate for six weeks. The control group was paid to deactivate for just one week, a clever design that made both groups go through the same hassle.

Six weeks off Facebook improved an index of happiness, depression and anxiety by 0.060 standard deviations. Six weeks off Instagram improved it by 0.041, though that result became uncertain after the researchers corrected for testing many outcomes at once. Exploratory analyses suggested the Facebook effect was concentrated among people over 35, and the Instagram effect was strongest for women aged 18 to 24, at 0.111 standard deviations.

blocks.title: Well-being gains from deactivation
blocks.note: Standard deviations. The last bar is the average psychological intervention, as cited by the 2020 study's authors.
blocks.source: Allcott et al., American Economic Review, 2020; Allcott et al., NBER Working Paper 33697, 2025

blocks.text: Then came the finding that matters most for anyone trying to change their habits. In 2020, the researchers could see app-usage data. When people deactivated Facebook, most of the freed-up time went to other smartphone apps. When they deactivated Instagram, *all* of it did. People didn't put the phone down. They opened something else.

Compare that with 2018, when more of the freed time went offline. We can't prove that's why the 2018 effect was a bit larger, since the studies differ in many ways. But it's suggestive, and it lines up with common sense. If you delete one app and your thumb finds another one, you haven't changed your habit. You've changed the logo.
How big is “small”?

A tenth of a standard deviation can sound like a rounding error. The 2020 authors offered a few ways to picture it. In their sample, everyone's mood dipped in the tense weeks around the election, and deactivating Facebook or Instagram erased more than half of that dip. In the original survey units, the average effect was like 3.8% of people moving from feeling happy “sometimes” to feeling happy “often.” And it was roughly 15–22% of the effect of a typical psychological intervention.

Smaller studies have reported bigger effects. In a 2018 experiment, Melissa Hunt and colleagues asked 143 University of Pennsylvania students to limit Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day for three weeks. The limited group showed significant drops in loneliness and depression compared with controls. That's a much smaller sample, and over a shorter time, than the economists' studies.

Averages also hide people. The 2018 authors noted that their qualitative interviews suggested the average effect likely masked substantial differences between individuals. In free-response answers, the deactivation group also wrote more about both the good and the bad that Facebook did in their lives, which is what you'd expect if the break made people see the trade-off more clearly. An average of 0.09 can come from a few people improving a lot and many barely changing. The only way to learn which group you're in is to run the test on yourself.

The evidence is genuinely argued over. In 2025, psychologist Christopher Ferguson published a meta-analysis arguing that, taken together, social media reduction experiments don't show reliable mental health benefits. Critics, in essays published on Jonathan Haidt's *After Babel* site, have disputed his methods in detail. A fair reading for now: on average, quitting produces small, real improvements for many people, the effect varies a lot from person to person, and it depends heavily on what you do with the time.
Quitting isn't the same as replacing

That last point is the core of what computer scientist Cal Newport calls *digital minimalism*, in his 2019 book of the same name. Newport's argument isn't that technology is bad. It's that most people never actually chose their online habits. They accumulated them, one free app at a time, each offering a little value, until the total cost was hours a day. His alternative is to focus online time on a small number of carefully chosen activities that strongly support things you value, and to happily miss out on everything else.

His method is a 30-day “digital declutter.” Step away from optional technologies for a month. Use that time to deliberately rebuild offline activities: exercise, reading, making things, seeing people. At the end, add back only the tools that clearly earn their place, with rules about when and how you'll use them. The key feature, and the one the 2020 data backs up, is the middle step. A detox that leaves a hole will be refilled by whatever is easiest.

What fills the slot matters more than how virtuous it looks. It can be a workout, a book series, studying for the next qual, sketching out a game design on paper, writing scripts for a channel, or a card game with the people in your berthing. The test is simple: does it leave you feeling like the time was yours? Feeds rarely pass that test. Most other things do.

blocks.title: Detox vs minimalism

left.head: Digital detox
items: Take a break, then go back
Removes an app and leaves a gap
The gap gets filled by another feed
Judged by how hard it felt

right.head: Digital minimalism
items: Take a break, then rebuild
Removes an app and fills the slot on purpose
Offline activities get scheduled
Judged by what you added back, and why

blocks.title: Run your own 30-day experiment
items: List your optional apps and sites, the ones life doesn't require
Pick a start date and remove or log out of them for 30 days
Choose two or three offline activities to fill the freed time, and schedule them
Notice what you actually miss, and what you don't
At the end, add back only what clearly earns its place, with a rule for when you'll use it

blocks.text: The detox you already get

Life underway runs a version of this experiment whether you want it or not. Connectivity is limited or gone, and the feeds stop. That makes it a natural chance to notice what you reach for when the usual apps aren't there, and how you feel a few weeks in. It also creates the classic rebound: back in port, signal returns, and the phone catches up on everything at once.

It's worth treating that moment as a decision rather than a reflex. Downloaded games and videos are still screens, so the offline phone isn't automatically a minimalist one. But the deployment gives you something the paid participants in these studies had to buy: weeks of data about life with less of the feed. Pay attention to what you find. Then, when the signal comes back, choose what to let back in.

The deepest lesson of the Facebook experiment is in that opening contradiction. People valued the app highly and also felt better without it. Both were true. Social media really does deliver things, news, connection, entertainment. It also takes more than most people realize while they're using it. You don't have to settle that debate for everyone. You only have to run the experiment on yourself, from the outside, and see which side of the ledger is bigger for you.

takeaways: In the biggest early experiment, four weeks off Facebook freed about an hour a day and slightly improved well-being.
The largest effect was lasting: many people used Facebook less after the break, though phone-measured data showed a smaller drop.
In 2020, most freed-up time went to other phone apps. Quitting one feed often just means opening another.
Average effects are small and debated. What you replace the feed with likely matters more than what you remove.
Treat breaks, including underway, as data. Then add back only what earns its place.
