title: The Year Chips Stopped Getting Faster
dek: For decades, software got quicker just by waiting for new hardware. Around 2005 that free ride ended, and nearly everything about computing has been bent around the loss ever since.

blocks.text: In November 1971, Intel advertised its first microprocessor, the 4004. It had 2,300 transistors, with circuit features about 10 microns, or 10,000 nanometers, across. Today, a single Nvidia Blackwell GPU carries 208 billion transistors. That's about 90 million times as many.

Now look at a different number. In 2004, Intel's Pentium 4 reached 3.8 gigahertz, meaning its clock ticked 3.8 billion times a second. Twenty years later, in 2024, Intel billed its Core i9-14900KS as the world's fastest desktop processor. Its top boost speed: 6.2 gigahertz. In two decades, while transistor counts kept exploding, clock speed went up by less than a factor of two.

So here's the puzzle. If we kept cramming in more and more transistors, why did processors stop getting dramatically faster at the thing everyone used to brag about? And where did all those extra transistors go? The answer explains why phones and laptops have so many cores, why AI runs on graphics cards, and why the next big gains in computing may come from programmers rather than physicists.

items.label: Transistors on the Intel 4004 (1971)
Transistors on an Nvidia Blackwell GPU
Top Intel desktop clock speed, 2004 vs 2024

blocks.source: Intel; Nvidia Blackwell architecture page; Intel Microprocessor Quick Reference Guide; Intel Newsroom, March 2024

blocks.text: A prediction that became a schedule

In 1965, Gordon Moore, then research director at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote an article for *Electronics* magazine. He had five data points, from 1959 to 1964, showing how many components could be put on an integrated circuit at the lowest cost per component. The count was doubling every year. He extrapolated boldly: by 1975, a chip could hold 65,000 components.

He was roughly right. In 1975, now at Intel, Moore revised the pace to a doubling every two years, crediting better lithography, bigger wafers and what he called circuit and device cleverness. Somebody, often said to be the engineer Carver Mead, started calling it Moore's law, and the name stuck.

It's worth feeling how strong that compounding is. Doubling every two years for fifty years is 25 doublings, and 2 multiplied by itself 25 times is about 33 million. Few things people build have ever improved like that. Cars, planes and power plants got better by percentages per decade. Chips got better by factors of millions. That's why it was so easy to believe the trend was permanent.

Two things about the law are easy to miss. First, it was never a law of nature. It was an observation about economics: how many components you could put on a chip *at the lowest cost*. Second, it became self-fulfilling. Historian Cyrus Mody has argued that the whole semiconductor industry, from equipment makers to chip designers, used Moore's law as a shared target, planning years ahead to hit the next doubling on schedule. It worked less like a prediction and more like a drumbeat.

blocks.title: Fifty years of shrinking
items: Moore predicts components per chip will double every year
Intel 4004: 2,300 transistors, about 10-micron features
Moore revises the pace to doubling every two years
Clock speeds rise more than 200-fold
Pentium 4 reaches 3.8 GHz; the power wall arrives
Clock speeds plateau; chips go multicore
TSMC starts volume production of 2 nm-class nanosheet transistors

blocks.text: The free ride called Dennard scaling

Here's the part almost nobody outside chip design knows. Moore's law alone only promised *more* transistors. What made computers *faster*, for decades, was a second rule, described by IBM engineer Robert Dennard and his colleagues in 1974. It's called *Dennard scaling*, and it was the greatest free lunch in engineering history.

The power a chip burns switching its transistors goes roughly as capacitance times voltage squared times frequency. Dennard's group showed that if you shrink a transistor's dimensions by some factor and also lower its operating voltage by the same factor, everything works out beautifully. The transistor gets smaller, it switches faster, and it uses less power, so much less that the power per square millimeter of chip stays about the same. You could pack in more transistors, run them at a higher clock speed, and the chip wouldn't get any hotter.

blocks.title: Dennard scaling: why shrinking used to be free
items: Shrink every dimension of the transistor.
Lower the voltage in proportion.
Capacitance drops, so each switch takes less energy.
Shorter distances let the transistor switch faster.
Power per transistor falls as fast as density rises.
Result: more transistors and higher clock speeds at the same heat per square millimeter.

blocks.text: That's why, for a generation, software developers could be lazy and win anyway. Write slow code, wait a couple of years, and new hardware would run it faster without you touching a line. According to a 2020 analysis by Charles Leiserson, Neil Thompson and colleagues at MIT, clock speeds rose by more than a factor of 200 between 1985 and 2005. Then they stopped.
Hitting the power wall

Dennard scaling depended on lowering the voltage each generation, and the voltage couldn't keep going down. A transistor is a switch, and below a certain voltage it can't switch cleanly between on and off. Worse, as transistors shrank to tiny sizes, they began to *leak*: current trickled through even when they were supposed to be off, like a valve that never quite seals. Leakage wastes power and makes heat whether the chip is doing useful work or not.

Once voltage stopped falling, the math flipped. Packing in more transistors and running them faster now meant more heat per square millimeter, generation after generation. The MIT team pinpoints the shift: by around 2005, microprocessor design had become power constrained. Engineers could still build faster chips. They just couldn't cool them. That's why the Pentium 4 topped out at 3.8 gigahertz in 2004 and why, two decades later, the fastest desktop chips boost only into the 6 gigahertz range.

If you've stood watch on electrical equipment, this will feel familiar. Every system has a thermal limit, and the limit isn't about how much power you can supply. It's about how fast you can take the heat away. Chips hit that limit in the mid-2000s, and the industry has been designing around it ever since.
Moore's law gave us more transistors. Dennard scaling made them fast for free. When Dennard scaling broke around 2005, transistors kept coming, but speed stopped arriving automatically.

So where did the extra transistors go? Into more cores. If you can't make one processor faster, put two, then four, then dozens on the same chip. Within a few years, dual-core and then quad-core processors were standard in ordinary PCs. Transistors also went into bigger caches, and increasingly into *specialized* hardware: graphics units, video encoders, AI accelerators, each built to do one kind of job far more efficiently than a general-purpose core.

There's an even stranger consequence. Modern chips have more transistors than they can afford to power all at the same time without overheating. Researchers call the idle portion *dark silicon*. It sounds wasteful, but it's part of why specialized hardware makes sense: if most of the chip has to sit dark at any moment anyway, you might as well fill it with circuits that are extremely good at one job and switch them on only when that job comes up.

But more cores come with a catch. A program only gets faster on many cores if its work can be split up. Any part that has to run step by step, in order, gets no help at all. Computer scientists call this *Amdahl's law*: if a tenth of a program is stubbornly sequential, then even infinite cores can't make it more than ten times faster. The free lunch didn't just end. It turned into a bill, and the bill was paid by programmers.
Nanometers that aren't

You've probably seen chips marketed as 5-nanometer, 3-nanometer or 2-nanometer. It sounds like the transistors are that small. They aren't. According to *IEEE Spectrum*, node names stopped matching any physical feature back in the mid-1990s. A 130-nanometer node transistor had gates around 70 nanometers long, and by 2011 Intel's 22-nanometer node had 26-nanometer gates. One industry veteran, Paolo Gargini, said the node number had absolutely no meaning in physical terms. Most critical features of a 7-nanometer transistor are considerably larger than 7 nanometers.

The names now work more like model years. Real progress still happens, but increasingly through cleverer geometry rather than raw shrinking. Transistors went from flat to fin-shaped, standing up off the surface so the gate could grip the channel on three sides. The newest generation uses *nanosheets*, thin stacked ribbons of silicon with the gate wrapped all the way around. TSMC says its 2-nanometer process, built on nanosheet transistors, started volume production at the end of 2025.

Chips are also growing sideways and in layers. There's a limit to how large an area a lithography machine can print in one exposure, and the biggest chips already hit it. So designers now stitch multiple dies together. Nvidia's Blackwell joins two maximum-size dies with a link moving 10 terabytes per second, so they act as one GPU. Moore's law, in other words, isn't dead so much as more expensive. As *IEEE Spectrum* put it, smaller doesn't necessarily mean less expensive anymore, and Moore's original prediction was about cost.
Plenty of room at the top

If the physics is getting harder, where will future speed come from? Leiserson and his co-authors gave a memorable answer in the journal *Science*. They split computing into the Bottom, meaning semiconductor physics and manufacturing, and the Top, meaning software, algorithms and hardware architecture. With the Bottom slowing, they argued, the Top would have to drive the gains.

To show how much room there is, they took a basic task, multiplying two 4,096-by-4,096 matrices, and wrote it the simple way in Python. It took about seven hours. Then they improved it step by step on the same machine: rewriting it in Java, then C, then splitting it across all of the machine's processor cores, then reorganizing the work to fit the processor's caches, then using the chip's vector instructions. The final version finished in 0.41 seconds. That's 62,806 times faster, from software alone, on hardware that didn't change.

blocks.title: Speedup from each rewrite of a matrix multiply
blocks.note: Multiply the steps together and you get about 62,806 times faster than the original Python: 7 hours down to 0.41 seconds.
blocks.source: Leiserson et al., Science, 2020

blocks.text: Even that final version used only about 40 percent of the machine's peak arithmetic capacity. The point isn't that Python is bad; it's a fantastic tool for getting things built quickly. The point is that a huge amount of computing power sits wasted under layers of convenience, and recovering it takes real understanding of how the hardware works: memory, caches, parallelism, data layout.

The MIT authors also warned that gains from the Top will be uneven and sporadic, not the smooth, automatic doubling people grew up with. Some fields will see huge leaps from a better algorithm or a custom chip. Others will see little. That's exactly what has happened with AI, where specialized hardware like GPUs and tensor processors delivered enormous gains for one kind of math while ordinary desktop speed crept along.

blocks.title: Two eras of computing

left.head: Before about 2005
items: Clock speeds climbed every year
Old software sped up automatically
General-purpose CPUs did nearly everything
Shrinking transistors was the main lever

right.head: After about 2005
items: Clock speeds roughly flat
Speed has to be earned in software
Specialized chips for graphics, AI and video
Cores, chiplets, new transistor shapes and better code

blocks.text: For anyone who wants to build things with code, this is good news hiding inside bad news. When the tide lifted every boat, skill mattered less, because the hardware covered for sloppy work. Now the tide has gone slack. A game that runs smoothly on cheap phones, a script that finishes in seconds instead of hours, a server bill that's a tenth of a competitor's: those wins belong to people who understand what's happening underneath.

The biggest wins usually aren't exotic. They come from choosing a better algorithm. Checking every object in a game against every other object for collisions means the work grows with the square of the number of objects: ten times the objects, a hundred times the work. Sorting them into a grid first, so each object only checks its neighbors, can turn a frame-rate killer into a rounding error. No new chip required, just a better idea about how to organize the work.

That's the reframe worth keeping. For fifty years, progress in computing looked like a law of physics, something that happened to us. It was really a lot of people working very hard on a schedule. The schedule has broken, but the work hasn't stopped. It has just moved up the stack, closer to the people writing the code.

takeaways: Moore's law was an economic forecast about transistors per chip, revised in 1975 to doubling every two years.
Dennard scaling made shrinking transistors faster at the same power; it broke around 2005 when voltage stopped falling.
Since then, extra transistors go into more cores and specialized chips instead of higher clock speeds.
Node names like '3 nm' no longer measure any real feature on the chip.
In one MIT test, rewriting code made a task 62,806 times faster on the same hardware. Future speed will increasingly come from software skill.

title: The Machine That Makes Light From Exploding Tin
dek: Every cutting-edge chip on Earth passes through a machine that blasts falling metal droplets with lasers 50,000 times a second. Here's how it works, and why only one company can build it.

blocks.text: Inside a vacuum chamber, a tiny bead of molten tin, about 25 microns across, roughly a third the width of a human hair, falls through empty space at 70 meters per second. A laser pulse hits it and flattens it into a thin pancake. A fraction of a moment later, a second, far more powerful pulse vaporizes the pancake into a plasma hot enough to glow in a color of light that does not exist naturally anywhere near the surface of the Earth. Then the next droplet arrives. This happens 50,000 times every second, around the clock, for months.

That flash of light is the starting point for the processor in your phone, the GPU running an AI model, and nearly every other leading-edge chip made today. The machine that produces it is built by one company, ASML, in the Dutch town of Veldhoven. It weighs close to 200 tons, contains around 100,000 parts and costs well over a hundred million euros. Intel has called it the most precise and complex machine it owns. To see why anyone would go to this much trouble just to make a flash of light, you have to start with how chips are printed.
Printing with light

A modern chip is a city of billions of transistors, wired together by layers of metal, all built on a disk of ultra-pure silicon called a wafer. Nobody places those transistors one at a time. They are printed, layer by layer, with a process called **photolithography**, which is basically very advanced photography.

blocks.title: One layer of a chip, simplified
items: Coat the silicon wafer with a light-sensitive chemical called photoresist.
Shine light through a mask (the reticle) that holds the pattern for that layer.
Lenses or mirrors shrink the pattern and project it onto the wafer.
Develop the resist, so exposed areas wash away (or stay, depending on type).
Etch, implant or deposit material where the resist is open, then strip it off.
Repeat for the next layer, dozens of times, aligning each to the last within nanometers.

blocks.text: A finished chip can go through this cycle many dozens of times. The machine that does the exposure step, called a scanner, is the bottleneck of the whole factory. It sets the smallest feature you can print, which sets how many transistors fit on a chip, which sets how fast and efficient that chip can be. And the single biggest thing limiting how small a scanner can print is the wavelength of its light.

One warning about the numbers you see in chip marketing. When a company advertises a '3-nanometer' process, nothing on the chip is necessarily 3 nanometers long. Node names stopped matching any single physical measurement years ago and are now closer to generation labels, like model years on a car. The real features, such as the spacing between the tiny metal wires, are larger. But they are still small enough that the light used to print them has become the central engineering problem of the industry.
The wavelength problem

Try drawing a fine line with a fat marker and you'll understand the core issue. Light spreads out as it passes through small openings, a property called diffraction, and that blurring gets worse as the features you are trying to print approach the size of the light's wavelength. Engineers summarize this with a rule known as the Rayleigh criterion: the smallest printable feature scales with the wavelength divided by the numerical aperture, a measure of how wide a cone of light the optics can gather. Shorter wavelength or bigger aperture, smaller features.

Numerical aperture is easier to picture than it sounds. Imagine trying to focus sunlight with a magnifying glass. A wide lens gathers light from a broad cone and can squeeze it into a tight, sharp spot; a narrow one can't. Chip optics work the same way. But making the optics wider gets harder and more expensive very quickly, and there are physical limits on how wide you can go. Shortening the wavelength is the more powerful lever, which is why each new generation of lithography is defined by its light.

blocks.title: Lithography light, generation by generation
blocks.note: Each step let chipmakers print smaller features. EUV's wavelength is about 14 times shorter than ArF's.
blocks.source: ASML, Light and lasers

blocks.text: For decades, the industry walked down this ladder. Early scanners used blue and ultraviolet light from mercury lamps, which ASML says could print features down to around a micron. Then came deep ultraviolet lasers, first krypton fluoride at 248 nanometers and then argon fluoride at 193. ASML says 193-nanometer systems can print features as small as 38 nanometers, smaller than the wavelength itself, thanks to clever tricks.

Those tricks got heroic. Chipmakers began filling the gap between the lens and the wafer with water to bend light more sharply, a technique called immersion lithography. Then they started splitting a single layer's pattern into two, three or four separate exposures, each printing part of the design, a process called multiple patterning. It worked, but every extra exposure added cost, time and chances for misalignment. The industry needed a much shorter wavelength. The obvious candidate, extreme ultraviolet at 13.5 nanometers, came with a catch so severe that many engineers doubted it would ever work in a factory.
Making light that barely exists

The catch is that EUV light is absorbed by almost everything. Air swallows it, so the entire light path has to sit in a vacuum. Glass swallows it, so you can't use lenses. Even the best mirrors absorb a big share of it at each bounce. And no practical lamp or ordinary laser produces it. You have to manufacture it, one explosion at a time.

ASML's solution is the tin-droplet source described at the start. A powerful carbon dioxide laser, built by the German company Trumpf, fires two pulses at each droplet: a gentle one to flatten it, then a strong one to blast it into plasma. ASML puts the plasma temperature at about 500,000 kelvin, dozens of times hotter than the surface of the Sun. As the ionized tin cools, it emits a burst of light around 13.5 nanometers, which a collector mirror gathers and sends into the machine.

items.label: Tin droplets turned into plasma every second
Temperature of the tin plasma
Speed of each falling droplet

blocks.source: ASML, The hottest thing about ASML machines

blocks.text: Think about the engineering hidden in that one sentence. The droplet generator has to fire identical drops at a perfectly steady rate. The laser has to hit each one twice, on target, while it is moving at highway speed. The tin debris can't be allowed to coat the mirrors. And it all has to run reliably enough that a factory can depend on it 24 hours a day. Getting the light source bright and stable enough for mass production took many years beyond the first working prototypes.
Mirrors smoother than a country

Since lenses won't work, EUV machines shape and shrink their light with mirrors made by ZEISS, the German optics company. They aren't ordinary mirrors. Each surface is coated with up to 100 alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, each only a few nanometers thick, arranged so that the weak reflections from every layer add up. Even so, ZEISS says each mirror reflects up to about 70% of the light. Bounce off a series of them and most of what the tin plasma produced is gone by the time it reaches the wafer, which is one reason the source has to be so powerful.

The mirrors also have to be almost unimaginably smooth. ZEISS offers a comparison: if one of its EUV mirrors were scaled up to the size of Germany, the biggest bump on it would be only about 0.1 millimeters high. Another: a mirror that precise could steer a laser beam to the Moon and hit something the size of a golf ball. The optics shrink the mask's pattern by a factor of four on its way to the wafer.

Then there is the motion. The wafer sits on a stage that races back and forth under the beam, exposing one chip area after another. According to ASML, it positions the wafer to within about a quarter of a nanometer for each exposure, correcting itself 20,000 times per second. A silicon atom is roughly a quarter of a nanometer across, give or take. The machine is lining up layers at close to the scale of individual atoms, while moving fast enough to process a steady stream of wafers every hour.

The Rayleigh rule gives two knobs: shorter wavelength or wider optics. EUV turned the first knob as far as anyone has dared. The newest High-NA machines turn the second, widening the numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55.
The most complex machine on Earth

Put it all together and you get a system that is less a machine than a building-sized ecosystem. Intel describes a standard EUV scanner as roughly the size of a school bus, weighing nearly 200 tons, with about 100,000 parts. Shipping one takes three Boeing 747 cargo planes, 40 freight containers and 20 trucks. ZEISS's optical system alone has more than 35,000 parts. After arrival, the machine has to be reassembled, calibrated and qualified inside the customer's cleanroom.

The price matches the complexity. In early 2024, ASML's newest High-NA EUV machine was reported at about €350 million, roughly twice the price of a standard EUV tool at around €170 million, according to figures published by Tom's Hardware. ZEISS says High-NA lets chipmakers fit roughly three times as many transistors in the same area, and that the first chips made with it reached the market in 2026.

blocks.text: ZEISS says its part alone took more than two decades of research and development and produced well over 1,500 EUV-related patents. The total effort, across ASML, ZEISS, Trumpf, US national laboratories, chipmakers like Intel, TSMC and Samsung that co-funded it, and hundreds of smaller suppliers, ran into the billions and spanned most of three decades. For long stretches, plenty of serious people thought it was a money pit that would never pay off.
Why only one company can build it

ASML is the only company in the world that sells EUV scanners. That's not because nobody else has heard of the physics; the basic ideas are published and taught. It's because the machine depends on a web of suppliers who each solved one impossible problem, plus decades of hard-won, unwritten knowledge about how to make all those pieces work together. Many of those suppliers effectively work only with ASML, and the know-how lives in the heads of thousands of engineers rather than in any manual.

That concentration has made EUV a geopolitical chokepoint. The Netherlands, under pressure from the United States, has blocked sales of EUV systems to China, and Chinese efforts to build a domestic equivalent face the same problem anyone would: you can copy a blueprint, but you can't copy thirty years of fixing what went wrong. Whoever controls these machines controls who can make the most advanced chips, which increasingly means who leads in AI, phones and weapons.

Even this machine won't keep shrinking chips forever. Each step down gets harder and more expensive, and transistors are approaching the scale where individual atoms and quantum effects start to matter. Chipmakers increasingly get their gains from clever 3D structures and stacking chips together rather than from printing smaller lines alone. But for now, every leading-edge path forward still runs through Veldhoven.

There's a lesson in this that reaches well past semiconductors. We like to imagine breakthroughs as single moments of genius. EUV is the opposite: it's what thousands of unglamorous, solved problems look like when stacked on top of each other. A droplet generator that never hiccups. A coating that survives tin debris. A stage that corrects itself 20,000 times a second. None of those makes a headline, and none can be skipped.

Anyone who has qualified on a nuclear plant knows a version of this. A reactor plant isn't impressive because of any one component. It's impressive because thousands of systems, procedures and people all have to work, and the whole thing is only as good as its least reliable piece. The most complex machine on Earth is a reminder that hard things usually get done the same way: not with one brilliant idea, but with stubborn, careful work on every single part, for longer than seems reasonable.

takeaways: Chips are printed with light, and the wavelength sets how small the features can be.
EUV light at 13.5 nm is made by hitting tin droplets with lasers 50,000 times a second.
Because EUV is absorbed by air and glass, the machine runs in vacuum and uses ultra-smooth mirrors.
A single EUV scanner is roughly 200 tons and 100,000 parts; High-NA versions cost around €350 million.
ASML's monopoly comes from decades of accumulated know-how across a web of specialist suppliers.

title: The Clocks in the Sky Run Fast
dek: GPS doesn't tell your phone where it is. It tells your phone what time it is, very precisely, from several places at once, and without Einstein the answer would be off by kilometers a day.

blocks.text: In October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, a metal ball with antennas that did little more than beep. American scientists tuned in, and some noticed something useful: the pitch of the signal shifted as the satellite approached and then pulled away, the same Doppler effect that makes a passing siren drop in tone. If you knew where you were, you could work out the satellite's orbit from that shift. Flip the problem around and something bigger appeared: if you knew where the *satellite* was, you could work out where *you* were.

At the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, physicists Guier and Weiffenbach had shown how to pin down orbits from the Doppler shift. In March 1958 their colleague McClure proposed turning it into a navigation system. The customer was the Navy, and specifically the Polaris program: ballistic missile submarines needed to know their exact position to aim their missiles. The system, called Transit, was serving the fleet by 1963. Satellite navigation was born to find submarines.

Today the descendant of that idea lives in every phone. And it depends on something that sounds like it belongs in a physics lecture rather than a map app: Einstein's discovery that time itself runs at different rates depending on how fast you move and how deep you sit in gravity.
GPS is a clock, not a map

Here's the core trick. Each GPS satellite carries atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts two things: what time it is aboard the satellite, and where the satellite is. Your receiver hears the signal and notes when it arrived. The difference between the send time and the arrival time, multiplied by the speed of light, is your distance from that satellite.

The catch is that light is ridiculously fast. It covers about 30 centimeters in a single nanosecond, a billionth of a second. A signal from a satellite overhead takes only around 67 thousandths of a second to reach you. So a timing error that seems laughably small becomes a big position error. Be off by one microsecond, a millionth of a second, and you've misjudged the distance by about 300 meters. Physicist Neil Ashby, writing about the system's physics, calculated that the satellite clocks must stay synchronized to within about 4 nanoseconds to get navigation errors under a meter.

items.label: Altitude of GPS satellites, circling Earth twice a day
Baseline layout: four satellites in each of six orbital planes
Operational satellites listed in the constellation (2017 count)

blocks.source: GPS.gov, Space Segment

blocks.text: The constellation is arranged so that at least four satellites are visible from nearly anywhere on Earth at any moment. Why four, and not three? That number is the most elegant part of the whole design.
Why you need four satellites

Suppose you know you're exactly 20,000 kilometers from satellite A. You could be anywhere on a giant sphere centered on it. Add satellite B, and you're on the circle where two spheres intersect. Add satellite C, and that circle gets cut down to two points, one of which is usually absurd, deep in space or inside the planet. So in a perfect world, three satellites would do.

But your phone doesn't have an atomic clock. It has a cheap quartz crystal that drifts. If your receiver's clock is off by even a millionth of a second, every distance it calculates is wrong by hundreds of meters, all in the same direction. The solution is beautiful: treat your clock error as one more unknown. Position needs three numbers (latitude, longitude, altitude) and the clock error makes four. Four unknowns need four equations, which means four satellites.

In practice the receiver doesn't solve this with a neat formula. It makes a guess at its position and clock error, predicts what the travel time from each satellite should be, compares that with what it measured, and adjusts the guess to shrink the mismatch. A few rounds of this and the answer settles. With more than four satellites in view, which is normal, it finds the position that best fits all the measurements at once, so one noisy signal can't drag the answer far off.

blocks.title: How your phone finds itself
items: Each satellite broadcasts its precise time and its orbital position
Your receiver records when each signal arrives by its own cheap clock
Travel time times the speed of light gives a rough distance, or pseudorange
With four or more satellites, it solves for position plus its own clock error
Extra satellites over-determine the answer and let it average out noise

blocks.text: That has a strange side effect. Once the receiver solves for its clock error, it knows the time almost as precisely as the atomic clocks in orbit. A cheap chip in your pocket becomes, in effect, a window onto some of the most precise timekeeping humans have built. Plenty of systems use GPS for exactly that, as a clock rather than a compass, to keep networks and equipment synchronized.
Einstein's tax
Now the relativity. Einstein's two theories make opposite predictions about the satellite clocks, and both matter.

**Special relativity** says moving clocks run slow. GPS satellites travel at several kilometers per second relative to the ground, so their clocks tick slightly slower than identical clocks on Earth. The effect costs them about 7 microseconds per day.

**General relativity** says clocks deeper in a gravitational field run slow, so clocks higher up run fast. You, on the surface, are deeper in Earth's gravity well than a satellite 20,200 kilometers up. That makes the satellite clocks tick faster than yours by about 45 microseconds per day. Gravity wins the tug-of-war.

Why would gravity change the speed of time? One way to picture it: light climbing out of a gravity well loses energy, which shows up as a lower frequency, like a clock that seems to tick more slowly when viewed from above. A clock on the ground, deep in the well, really does run slow compared to one in orbit. This isn't a quirk of the clocks' machinery. Any process, from an atomic transition to a heartbeat, would run at the same shifted rate. Time itself is what changes.

blocks.title: How relativity shifts a GPS satellite clock each day
blocks.note: Approximate values, compared with a clock at rest at sea level.
blocks.source: Pratap Misra, GPS World, 2023

blocks.text: Net result: each satellite clock runs about 38 microseconds a day fast. That sounds like nothing. Multiply it by the speed of light, though, and 38 microseconds equals about 11 kilometers of range. Ashby put it plainly in a 2002 *Physics Today* article: uncorrected clock errors building up over a single day would produce navigation errors of more than 11 kilometers. Within a week your map would put you in the wrong town. Within a month, in the wrong state.

Relativity isn't an exotic effect reserved for black holes and near-light-speed rockets. It's a line item in the engineering budget of a system you use every day. If GPS works, Einstein was right, and it's verified millions of times a second.

The fix is almost comically simple. Before launch, engineers deliberately set each satellite clock to tick slow. The standard GPS reference frequency is 10.23 megahertz; the satellite clocks are tuned to 10.22999999543 megahertz instead, so that once they're in orbit and relativity speeds them up, they match ground clocks. In Ashby's terms, it's a correction of about 4.46 parts in ten billion. A measurement made in orbit in 1977 came in at 4.425 parts in ten billion, close to the prediction.

There are subtler effects too. Satellite orbits aren't perfect circles, so each clock speeds up and slows down slightly as it swings closer to Earth and farther away, and receivers correct for that in software. Earth also rotates while a signal is in flight, so the receiver has moved a little by the time the signal arrives. Ashby estimated this rotation effect, called the **Sagnac effect**, at about 200 nanoseconds for a trip around the equator, which is far too large to ignore when a nanosecond is 30 centimeters.
How good it gets, and what breaks it

The U.S. government commits to keeping the error in the signal broadcast from space, called the **user range error**, at or below 2 meters 95% of the time. It actually does far better: on one day in April 2021, the global average was about 0.64 meters. That's not the same as how accurately your device knows where it is, because your receiver adds its own errors. GPS.gov puts typical smartphone accuracy at about 4.9 meters under open sky.

items.label: Committed signal-in-space error, 95% of the time
Measured signal error, global average, April 2021
Typical smartphone accuracy under open sky

blocks.source: GPS.gov, GPS Accuracy

blocks.text: Most of the gap between those numbers comes from the world around you. Buildings, bridges and trees block signals. Indoors or underground, the signals barely reach you at all. Worse is **multipath**: a signal bounces off a glass tower before reaching your phone, travels a longer path, and makes the satellite look farther away than it is. That's why your blue dot drifts across the street downtown. Less often, the culprits are radio interference, deliberate jamming, or major solar storms disturbing the upper atmosphere.

The atmosphere adds its own error. The **ionosphere**, a layer of charged particles high above the weather, slows radio signals by an amount that shifts with the time of day and with solar activity. Because that delay depends on the signal's frequency, satellites that broadcast on more than one frequency let a receiver compare the two and cancel most of it. That's one reason newer phones and receivers, which can listen on multiple frequencies, tend to hold a steadier fix.

For years, civilians also faced a deliberate handicap. The military intentionally degraded the public signal, a feature called **Selective Availability**, to keep the best accuracy for its own forces. In May 2000, President Clinton ordered it switched off, and in 2007 the government decided its next-generation GPS III satellites would be built without the feature at all. The location economy that followed, from ride-hailing to delivery apps to fitness trackers, grew on top of that decision.

blocks.text: The world runs on borrowed time

There's an irony in the story for anyone who serves on a submarine. Satellite navigation was invented for missile boats, yet a submerged boat can't use it, because GPS radio signals don't penetrate seawater. Down there, navigation falls back to inertial systems, which sense every acceleration and rotation and integrate them into a running position estimate. Those systems slowly drift, so sooner or later a boat needs an outside fix to reset the error. Even the best clock and the best gyro eventually need a reference beyond themselves.

Above the surface, the dependence runs the other way. So much now leans on GPS, for navigation and for timing, that losing it would ripple far beyond lost drivers. The signals arrive from orbit extremely faint, which makes them easy to drown out with a jammer or imitate with a fake transmitter. That's why militaries, including the Navy, still train to navigate without it, and why engineers keep looking for backups. A system that works perfectly almost all the time can quietly turn into a single point of failure.

That's the deeper idea hiding in GPS. Nothing in the system measures position directly. It measures time, compares time, and corrects time, and position falls out as a consequence. Every piece of it rests on the fact that time isn't the same everywhere: it runs faster on a satellite than on your wrist, and slower for things that move. An idea that sounded like philosophy when Einstein published it now gets checked automatically every time someone asks for directions.

It's also a lesson in what precision really costs. The difference between a working system and a useless one came down to 38 millionths of a second a day, an error nobody would ever notice on a wristwatch. In any complex system, the small, invisible drift is the dangerous one, because it compounds quietly while everything still looks fine. The engineers who built GPS didn't wait for the error to show up on a map. They predicted it, measured it and set the clocks wrong on purpose before launch, so that in orbit, they'd be right.

takeaways: GPS works by timing: your distance to each satellite is the signal's travel time multiplied by the speed of light.
You need four satellites, not three, because your receiver's cheap clock error is a fourth unknown.
Relativity makes satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day; uncorrected, that's over 11 km of error per day.
Engineers fix it by setting satellite clocks slightly slow before launch, at 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23.
Small, steady drift is the dangerous kind of error: predict it and correct it before it compounds.

title: The Gaming Chip That Ate the World
dek: GPUs were built to color millions of pixels sixty times a second. That turned out to be almost exactly the math modern AI runs on, and it reshaped the most valuable industry on the planet.

blocks.text: In 2012, a graduate student named Alex Krizhevsky, working with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto, entered a contest to see which computer program could best identify objects in photos. Their neural network had 60 million adjustable numbers and 650,000 artificial neurons. They trained it for five to six days on two consumer graphics cards, Nvidia GTX 580s with 3 gigabytes of memory each. The same kind of card people bought to play games.

The results weren't close. In the contest's main measure, their network got the right answer outside its top five guesses only 15.3 percent of the time. The second-best entry missed 26.2 percent. The network, later nicknamed AlexNet, is often credited with kicking off the modern deep learning boom. And it ran on hardware designed to draw explosions in video games.

That's not a coincidence or a historical footnote. It's the key to understanding why a company that made gaming cards became one of the most valuable businesses in the world, and why the graphics card in a gaming rig is a close cousin of the chips training today's AI. The story comes down to one question: what is a GPU actually good at?
Two ways to be fast

A CPU, the main processor in any computer, is built to finish one task as quickly as possible. That's called minimizing *latency*. To do it, each CPU core is loaded with clever machinery: big caches that keep data close by, circuits that predict which way the code will branch before it gets there, and logic that reorders instructions to avoid waiting. A modern CPU core is a brilliant generalist. It can run your operating system, a game's logic and a spreadsheet, jumping between wildly different instructions with ease.

A GPU, or graphics processing unit, is built for something else: *throughput*, getting the most total work done per second, even if any single piece takes a while. Instead of a few brilliant cores, it has thousands of simple ones. They give up most of the cleverness. What they can do is perform the same arithmetic on huge amounts of data at the same time.

Picture a machine shop. A CPU is a handful of master machinists, each able to build anything from a blueprint, fast. A GPU is a stadium full of people with calculators, each told to multiply two numbers and add a third, all at once. Hand the stadium a custom part to build and it's helpless. Hand it ten million identical multiplications and it finishes before the machinists have read the blueprint.

Why not just build a CPU with thousands of cores? Because cleverness costs. Every cache, branch predictor and reordering circuit takes up silicon and burns power, and a chip has a fixed budget of both. A CPU spends much of that budget making each core smart. A GPU spends it on raw arithmetic and accepts that each lane is simple. Neither design is better in general. Each is a bet about what kind of work is coming.

items.label: Cores in AMD's top 5th-gen EPYC server CPU (2024)
32-bit math cores in an Nvidia H100 GPU
Transistors on the H100

blocks.text: A fair warning about those numbers: a GPU core and a CPU core aren't the same kind of thing. A CPU core is a full, independent processor. A GPU core is closer to a single lane of arithmetic, grouped with dozens of others that all execute the same instruction together. The comparison is apples to orange slices. But the shape of the difference is real, and it decides which jobs each chip is good at.
Why pictures are parallel

GPUs took this shape because of what graphics demands. In a 2007 explainer, Nvidia researchers David Luebke and Greg Humphreys walked through the pipeline. A 3D scene is built from triangles. To draw a frame, the GPU moves every triangle into place, lights it, projects it onto the flat screen, figures out which pixels each triangle covers, and colors those pixels. Then it does the whole thing again, often 60 times a second, which leaves about 16 milliseconds per frame.

Here's the crucial property: each pixel can be computed independently of the others. The color of one pixel on the left side of the screen doesn't depend on a pixel on the right. Neither does each vertex of each triangle. That's what engineers call *embarrassingly parallel* work, and it's the ideal job for a stadium of calculators.

And what math is the stadium doing? Moving and rotating a triangle is a matrix multiplied by a vector. Lighting involves *dot products*, which means multiplying two lists of numbers pair by pair and adding up the results. Over decades, GPU makers poured their engineering into doing exactly those operations faster and in greater volume. By 2007, a GeForce 8800 had 128 programmable processors, and Luebke and Humphreys reported that GPU code often ran 5 to 20 times faster than optimized CPU code, with some algorithms beating it by more than 100 times.

blocks.text: A neural network is a pile of multiplications

Now look at what a neural network does. An artificial neuron takes a list of inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds them all up, and passes the total through a simple function that decides how strongly to fire. That multiply-and-add is a dot product, the same operation the GPU uses for lighting.

A *layer* of neurons is many dot products at once, which is exactly a matrix multiplied by a vector, the same math used to move triangles. Process a batch of images together and it becomes a matrix multiplied by a matrix. Stack dozens of layers and you have a deep network. Training it means running data forward through the layers, measuring how wrong the output was, and then running the error backward to adjust every weight, which again is mostly matrix multiplication.

blocks.title: What a network does with one batch of images
items: Turn each image into a long list of numbers, one per pixel channel.
Multiply that data by the first layer's weight matrix.
Apply a simple function to each result, then pass it to the next layer.
Repeat through every layer to get a guess for each image.
Compare guesses to the right answers and compute the error.
Run the error backward, again as matrix math, and nudge every weight.

blocks.text: In other words, the bulk of the work in deep learning is the same arithmetic graphics cards had spent decades optimizing, and each of those multiplications is independent of the others. The match was close to perfect. Researchers didn't need a new kind of chip. They needed a way to talk to the one already sitting in gaming PCs.
From shaders to CUDA

For years, scientists who wanted to use GPUs for non-graphics work had to disguise their problems as graphics, packing data into textures and pretending calculations were pixel colors. It worked, but it was miserable. In November 2006, Nvidia released CUDA, a platform that let programmers write ordinary C-style code for the GPU. Suddenly, a physicist or a machine learning researcher could treat the graphics card as a general-purpose parallel computer.

That bet looked odd for years. Nvidia was spending money on features most gamers never touched. But it meant that when researchers like Krizhevsky came along, the tools were waiting. AlexNet's code ran on CUDA. So did most of what followed, and the libraries, tutorials and habits of an entire research field grew up around it. Today that software ecosystem is arguably a bigger advantage for Nvidia than any single chip.

blocks.text: The real bottleneck is moving data

Here's something most people don't realize about modern chips: doing arithmetic is cheap. Getting the numbers to the arithmetic units is the hard part. A GPU with tens of thousands of lanes is useless if they sit idle waiting for data from memory. Engineers call this the *memory wall*, and a lot of GPU design is about climbing it.

The H100 uses *high-bandwidth memory*, stacks of memory chips mounted right next to the processor and wired to it with thousands of connections. Nvidia lists 80 gigabytes of it, moving data at 3.35 terabytes per second. That's enough to move the entire contents of a 1-terabyte drive in under a third of a second. Even so, feeding the chip is often the limit, which is why AI engineers obsess over squeezing models into less memory.

The second trick is *tensor cores*, specialized units that multiply small blocks of matrices in a single step instead of one number at a time. The third is lower precision. Graphics and science traditionally used 32-bit or 64-bit numbers. Neural networks turn out to work fine with 16-bit or even 8-bit numbers, which take less memory and less energy. Nvidia lists the H100 at 67 trillion operations per second for ordinary 32-bit math and 1,979 trillion for 16-bit tensor core math, though that headline figure assumes a trick for skipping zeros.

items.label: H100 memory bandwidth
H100 teraFLOPS: 32-bit regular vs 16-bit tensor core (with sparsity)
Maximum power for one H100 board

blocks.source: Nvidia H100 product specifications

blocks.text: There's also a physical ceiling on how big one chip can be. Lithography machines can only expose a limited area in one shot, called the *reticle limit*. Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs work around it by building two maximum-size dies and linking them at 10 terabytes per second so they behave like one GPU, for a total of 208 billion transistors. When you can't make the chip bigger, you make two and glue them together very, very fast.
The chip that ate the world

Once it became clear that bigger neural networks trained on more data kept getting better, demand for GPUs exploded. The research group Epoch AI estimates that the computing power used to train notable AI models has grown about 4.4 times per year since 2010, doubling roughly every six months. Nvidia's financial reports show what that looks like from the seller's side.

blocks.title: Nvidia data center revenue by fiscal year
blocks.note: Nvidia's fiscal year ends in late January, so FY2026 is mostly calendar 2025.
blocks.source: Nvidia quarterly and annual results press releases, 2022–2026

blocks.text: In fiscal 2026, Nvidia's data center business alone brought in $193.7 billion, out of total revenue of $215.9 billion. Four years earlier, the data center line was $10.6 billion. A company that most people knew for gaming cards became, in practice, an AI infrastructure company. Everything else, gaming included, now makes up only about a tenth of the company's sales.

It's not only training, either. Every time someone asks a chatbot a question, generates an image or gets a recommendation, a trained network runs forward through its layers. That step is called *inference*, and it is the same matrix math, repeated for every user, every second of the day. Training builds the model once. Inference runs it endlessly. Both run largely on GPUs or on chips built in their image.

The AI researcher Rich Sutton summed up the underlying pattern in a 2019 essay called *The Bitter Lesson*. Looking back over decades of AI research, he argued that clever approaches built on human knowledge kept losing to simpler methods that could soak up more computation. His essay is blunt about it.
General methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective.
blocks.by: Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 2019

blocks.text: Whether that holds forever is debated. Computing power is expensive, energy-hungry and running into physical limits of its own. But it explains why the industry treats GPUs like a strategic resource. If progress tracks computation, then whoever controls the chips controls the pace.

The biggest shifts often come from noticing that a tool built for one job is secretly perfect for another. Nobody designed GPUs for AI. Gamers paid for decades of development of the exact math machine AI needed.

Biologists have a word for this: *exaptation*, when a trait that evolved for one purpose gets drafted into a completely different one. Feathers probably started as insulation before they were used for flight. GPUs started as pixel painters before they became the engine of AI. The lesson travels well beyond chips. The most valuable skill isn't always inventing a new tool. Sometimes it's looking at a tool everyone takes for granted and recognizing what else it is.

The graphics card in a gaming PC uses the same basic architecture and the same CUDA programming model that trained AlexNet. With free tools, anyone curious can write code that runs on those thousands of lanes, train a small network, and watch the stadium of calculators do its work. The machine that renders the next match is, quietly, one of the most important computers ever designed.

takeaways: CPUs minimize latency with a few smart cores; GPUs maximize throughput with thousands of simple ones.
Graphics and neural networks both boil down to huge numbers of independent multiply-and-add operations.
CUDA, released in 2006, let researchers program GPUs directly, and AlexNet proved the payoff in 2012.
Modern AI chips are often limited by moving data, not by doing math; memory bandwidth and lower precision matter enormously.
Big breakthroughs often come from seeing a new use for an existing tool.

title: The Autocomplete That Learned Too Much
dek: Every chatbot answer is built one word-fragment at a time by a machine trained only to guess what comes next. The real question is what it had to learn to guess well.

blocks.text: Type a question into a chatbot and watch the answer come back. It doesn't arrive all at once. It streams in a few characters at a time, like someone typing on the other end. That stutter isn't a design flourish. It's a window into the machine: the model is literally producing its answer one small piece at a time, and every piece is a guess.

When OpenAI introduced GPT-2 in 2019, it boiled the whole training goal down to one line. The model was trained to “predict the next word, given all of the previous words.” That's it. No grammar rules, no built-in encyclopedia, no logic module. Everything a modern **large language model** (LLM) does, from writing code to explaining reactor physics, grows out of that one almost insultingly simple objective, repeated at enormous scale.
Which raises the real puzzle: how does next-word guessing turn into something that can debug your script or walk you through a circuit? To see it, you have to follow a sentence through the machine.
Step one: turning words into numbers

A neural network can only do arithmetic, so text has to become numbers first. The model's first move is to chop your input into **tokens**, chunks of text from a fixed vocabulary. A common word like “the” is usually a single token. A rarer word gets split into fragments, so “unbelievably” might become “un,” “believ” and “ably.” This is why models sometimes fumble at counting the letters in a word: they never see letters, only chunks.

Each token is then swapped for a long list of numbers called an **embedding**. Think of it as coordinates in a space with thousands of dimensions. In GPT-3, every token became a list of 12,288 numbers. Nobody hand-assigns those coordinates. They are learned during training, and they end up arranged so that tokens used in similar ways sit near each other. “Reactor” lands closer to “turbine” than to “sandwich,” not because anyone said so, but because of the company those words keep in billions of sentences.
Step two: attention, the trick that changed everything

For years, language models read text like a ticker tape: one word at a time, left to right, carrying a fading memory of what came before. Long sentences broke them. In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a cocky title, “Attention Is All You Need,” introducing the **transformer**. Its central idea was to let every token look directly at every other token in the passage and decide which ones matter to it.

Mechanically, it works like this. For each token, the model computes three vectors: a **query** (what am I looking for?), a **key** (what do I offer?) and a **value** (what information do I pass along if chosen?). Each token compares its query against every other token's key. Strong matches get high scores, the scores are squashed into weights that add up to one, and the token absorbs a weighted blend of everyone's values. After one round of attention, each token's numbers carry a bit of context from the whole passage.

Take the sentence “The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.” What does “it” mean? You know instantly: the trophy. In a transformer, the token “it” sends out its query, and a trained model weights “trophy” heavily, because big things not fitting into containers is how trophies and suitcases work. Change “big” to “small” and the right answer flips to the suitcase. Attention is the machinery that lets the model make that call.

blocks.title: What happens to your prompt
items: Your text is split into tokens, chunks from a fixed vocabulary
Each token becomes an embedding: a long list of learned numbers
Attention lets every token pull in context from every other token
Feed-forward layers transform each token's updated numbers
This repeats through dozens of stacked layers (96 in GPT-3)
The last layer gives a probability for every possible next token
One token is picked and appended, and the whole stack runs again

blocks.text: A transformer stacks this many times over. GPT-3 had 96 layers, each with 96 attention “heads” running side by side, so different heads can specialize: one tracking which noun a pronoun points to, another tracking open quote marks or unclosed brackets in code. The design also suited the hardware. Because all the tokens are processed at once instead of in sequence, transformers run well on GPUs, chips built to do thousands of multiplications in parallel. The original paper's base model trained in about 12 hours on eight GPUs. That efficiency is what made the next decade of scaling possible.

At the top of the stack, the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, converted into probabilities. After “The capital of France is,” almost all the probability piles onto “Paris.” The system then **samples** one token, appends it to the text, and runs the entire stack again to get the next one. A setting called **temperature** controls how adventurous that pick is: low temperature nearly always takes the top choice, high temperature gives long shots a chance. Every chatbot answer you have ever read was assembled this way, one draw at a time.

There's also a hard limit on how much the model can see at once, called the **context window**. GPT-3's was 2,048 tokens, roughly a few pages of text. Anything outside the window simply doesn't exist for the model; it has no memory between conversations unless the text is fed back in. When a long chat starts “forgetting” what you said at the beginning, that's usually the window, not a lapse in attention. Newer models have far larger windows, but the principle is the same: the model only knows what's in front of it plus what's baked into its parameters.
Step three: how 175 billion knobs get set

All of that machinery is defined by **parameters**, the numbers inside the model that decide how embeddings are formed, how queries and keys are computed, and how each layer transforms its input. Before training they are random, and the model outputs gibberish. Training is the process of nudging them, and the loop is brutally simple.

blocks.title: The training loop
items: Show a passage with the next token hidden
The model predicts probabilities for every token
Measure how wrong it was about the real next token
Backpropagation traces the error back to every parameter
Nudge every parameter slightly to shrink the error

blocks.text: The tracing step, **backpropagation**, is just the chain rule from calculus applied very carefully: it works out, for each of billions of parameters, which direction to move it so the right answer would have been a little more likely. Move them all a tiny bit, then repeat with the next chunk of text, trillions of times. This is **gradient descent**: walking downhill on a landscape of error, one small step at a time, without ever seeing the whole map.

Then comes scale. GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3, a year later, had 175 billion and was trained on 300 billion tokens, mostly filtered web pages plus books and Wikipedia. The industry assumption was that bigger was the main lever. In 2022, DeepMind ran a large set of training experiments and concluded the field had been following the wrong recipe.

blocks.title: Model size, billions of parameters
blocks.note: Chinchilla was a quarter of Gopher's size and beat it across a wide range of tests.
blocks.source: OpenAI, 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022

blocks.text: Their finding: for a fixed computing budget, model size and training data should grow together. Double the parameters, double the tokens. By that rule, giant models like DeepMind's own 280-billion-parameter Gopher were badly undertrained, all brain and not enough reading. To prove it, they trained Chinchilla, a quarter of Gopher's size, on 1.4 trillion tokens, about 20 tokens per parameter, using the same compute. It outperformed Gopher and GPT-3 across a large range of tasks.

blocks.title: Training data, billions of tokens
blocks.note: Llama 3's figure is reported as “over 15 trillion” tokens.
blocks.source: Brown et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Hugging Face, 2024

blocks.text: The industry took the lesson and then sprinted past it. Meta's Llama 3 models, released in 2024 at 8 and 70 billion parameters, were trained on more than 15 trillion tokens. For the 8-billion model, that's nearly 2,000 tokens per parameter, nearly a hundred times Chinchilla's ratio. The logic is economic: a model is trained once but run for millions of users, so a smaller model that has read far more is cheaper every time anyone asks it something.
From autocomplete to assistant

A model trained only on next-token prediction, called a **base model**, isn't an assistant. It's a document continuer. Ask it “How do I troubleshoot a ground fault?” and it might reply with three more questions, because on the internet, questions often show up in lists of questions. It has learned the shape of text, not the job of answering.

Turning it into an assistant takes a second phase. First, people write example conversations showing good answers, and the model is fine-tuned on them. Then comes **reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF): the model writes several answers, humans rank them, a separate model learns to predict those rankings, and the language model is tuned to produce answers that score well. In OpenAI's 2022 InstructGPT study, raters preferred answers from a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way over answers from the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. A model more than 100 times smaller won, because it had been taught what the job was.

blocks.title: Base model vs. tuned assistant

left.head: Base model
items: Trained only to continue text
Treats your question as the start of a document
Imitates whatever it's shown, good or bad
Knows a lot, but not what you want

right.head: Tuned assistant
items: Further trained on example conversations
Treats your message as a request to answer
Shaped by human rankings of better and worse answers
Same knowledge, aimed at being useful

blocks.text: Why it makes things up

The flaw everyone has met is **hallucination**: a fluent, confident, completely wrong answer. A citation to a paper that doesn't exist. A function that isn't in the library. Once you understand the training objective, this stops being mysterious. The model was never trained to say true things. It was trained to say likely things, and most of the time likely and true overlap. When they don't, nothing inside the model raises a flag.

A 2025 paper by Adam Kalai and colleagues at OpenAI and Georgia Tech sharpened this into two arguments. First, some facts are essentially arbitrary, like a particular person's birthday. If a fact shows up only once in the training data, there's no pattern to learn from, and the authors argue the error rate on that kind of fact should be at least as high as the share of such facts that appear just once. Second, the grading makes it worse. Most benchmarks award a point for a right answer and nothing for “I don't know,” so a model that always guesses scores at least as well as one that honestly admits uncertainty.

If you've ever bluffed a multiple-choice question, you've done what the model does. When a blank scores zero, guessing is the rational move. Treat a chatbot's confidence as a writing style, not as evidence.

The practical upshot: LLMs are strongest where you can check the output. Code runs or it doesn't. A math step can be verified. A summary can be compared against the document in front of you. They are weakest on obscure specifics, such as exact figures, names, citations and niche regulations, which are precisely the things that appear rarely in training data. Use one like a sharp shipmate who has read everything once and never admits when he's fuzzy: great for ideas, explanations and first drafts, never the final word on a value that matters.
Is it “just” autocomplete?

Critics like to say an LLM is “just predicting the next word,” as if that settled things. It doesn't, because it hides how hard the prediction can get. To predict the next line of a physics derivation, it helps to model the physics. To predict how a character in a novel responds, it helps to model what she wants. Nobody programmed those abilities in. Training simply rewards whatever internal machinery lowers prediction error, and over trillions of tokens, some fairly sophisticated machinery pays for itself.

Researchers have started looking at that machinery directly. In 2024, Anthropic reported extracting millions of internal **features** from one of its Claude models: recurring patterns of neuron activity that line up with human concepts. One responded to the Golden Gate Bridge whether it was named in English, mentioned in other languages or shown in a picture. When researchers artificially turned that feature up, the model began insisting it was the bridge. That isn't proof of understanding in the human sense, and whether these systems “know” anything is a genuinely open argument. But it shows the inside isn't a lookup table of stored phrases. It's a learned map of concepts, and parts of that map can be read.

Here's the reframe worth keeping. Nuke school drills into you the difference between someone who can recite a procedure and someone who understands the plant well enough to predict what happens next. A language model sits in a strange spot on that spectrum. It was only ever graded on prediction, and prediction at this scale pushed it to build something like understanding along the way: patchy, alien and sometimes confidently wrong. So the interesting question isn't whether it's “just” predicting. It's how much of what we call understanding is, underneath, very good prediction.

takeaways: An LLM writes one token at a time; every token is a weighted guess about what comes next.
Attention lets every word look at every other word, which is how a model resolves context like what “it” refers to.
Since Chinchilla, data matters as much as size: today's models read trillions of tokens.
Hallucinations follow from the objective. The model learned what's likely, not what's true, so verify specifics.
“Just predicting the next word” undersells it: predicting well forces a model to learn a lot about the world.
