title: The Banana Problem: Radiation Doses in Perspective
dek: A year standing watch on a nuclear sub can deliver less dose than one chest x-ray, while the biggest source in most American lives seeps up through the basement floor.

blocks.text: In 2025, the average person monitored for radiation aboard the Navy's nuclear-powered ships picked up about 6 millirem of occupational dose for the entire year. A single chest x-ray is about 10 millirem. A full-body CT scan is about 1,000. The average American, who has never stood a watch anywhere near a reactor, absorbs roughly 620 millirem every year just by breathing, eating, flying and going to the doctor.

Those numbers sound backwards to most people. The reactor is the scary thing, so it should carry the big dose. But radiation does not care about how frightening its source looks. It cares about energy deposited in tissue, and once you measure that honestly, the ranking of everyday risks gets rearranged in ways that are worth understanding, especially if you work around the stuff.
This is a tour of the dose ladder, from bananas to CT scanners, with real numbers and a frank look at what those numbers mean for your health.

items.label: Average yearly dose per person in the US (6.2 mSv)
Share of that average from medical procedures
Average 2025 occupational dose of Navy fleet personnel

blocks.source: NCRP Report 160 via US NRC and Bolus, J Nucl Med Technol, 2013; Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program report NT-26-2, 2026

blocks.text: Where the 620 comes from

The standard reference for American radiation exposure is NCRP Report No. 160, published in 2009 by the National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements using mostly 2006 data. It put the average yearly dose at 6.2 millisieverts, or 620 millirem. (One millisievert equals 100 millirem; the Navy and the NRC tend to talk in rem, most of the world in sieverts.) About half came from natural background and about half from human activity.

It helps to know what that unit is measuring. Effective dose is a bookkeeping tool. It starts with the energy radiation deposits in tissue, then weights it by the type of radiation and by how sensitive each organ is, so that a dose to the lungs and a dose to the whole body land on the same scale. It was built for protecting populations and setting limits, not for predicting what will happen to one particular person.

The natural half is dominated by one thing: radon. This colorless gas seeps out of soil and rock as uranium decays, collects in basements and poorly ventilated rooms, and is inhaled. NCRP puts the inhaled share at about 228 millirem a year, roughly three quarters of all natural exposure. Cosmic rays add about 33 millirem, the potassium-40 and other radionuclides in your own body add about 29, and the ground under your feet about 21.

Those are averages, and real lives vary a lot. Someone in Denver gets more cosmic radiation than someone at sea level, because a mile of thinner air overhead does less shielding. Radon swings far more, from house to house and county to county, depending on local geology and ventilation. It is not a harmless curiosity, either. The EPA ranks radon as the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States after smoking, responsible for an estimated 21,000 lung cancer deaths a year.

The human-made half is almost entirely medicine. The NRC notes that medical procedures account for about 96% of exposure from human-made sources. Consumer products, fallout and the entire nuclear power industry are rounding errors by comparison. The NRC caps the dose any member of the public may receive from a licensed facility at 100 millirem per year.

Here is the twist. In the early 1980s, the average American dose was about 3.6 millisieverts. By 2006 it had jumped to 6.2. Background radiation had not changed at all. Medical exposure went from about 15% of the total to 48%, driven by an explosion in CT scanning, which by itself accounted for about half of all medical dose. The country's radiation problem, to the extent it had one, was in the hospital, not the power plant.

That trend has since reversed. A 2020 follow-up study for NCRP by Fred Mettler and colleagues found that per-person medical dose fell from about 2.9 millisieverts in 2006 to 2.3 in 2016, even though the number of CT scans rose from 67 million to 84 million. Better machines and more careful dose settings did that. It is a good example of a technical community noticing a number creeping up and actually bending it back down.
The everyday ladder

Radiation doses span an enormous range, so it helps to split them into two ladders. The first covers the small stuff you encounter without thinking about it. The NRC lists a dental x-ray at about 1.5 millirem and a chest x-ray at about 10. The CDC estimates that a one-way flight across the United States delivers about 3.5 millirem of cosmic radiation, so two transcontinental trips roughly equal one chest x-ray. Natural radioactivity in food and water adds about 30 millirem over a year.

blocks.title: Small doses: everyday exposures
blocks.note: Banana value is the 'banana equivalent dose' of about 0.1 microsievert. Fleet value is occupational dose only, with background subtracted.
blocks.source: US NRC, Doses in Our Daily Lives; CDC, Radiation from Air Travel; University of Groningen; NNPP report NT-26-2

blocks.text: The second ladder starts where the first one ends. A head CT is about 200 millirem, a chest CT about 700, and a full-body CT about 1,000, according to the NRC's table. A nuclear medicine study averages around 400. One full-body scan delivers about as much dose as three years of everything nature throws at you. That is not a reason to refuse a scan your doctor thinks you need. It is a reason to ask whether a scan is needed, and to keep a rough mental count of how many you have had.

blocks.title: Big doses: medical imaging and limits
blocks.note: The NRC's occupational limit for adult radiation workers is 5,000 mrem (50 mSv) per year.
blocks.source: US NRC, Doses in Our Daily Lives and Man-Made Sources

blocks.text: Why the banana is a trick question

Bananas are the internet's favorite radiation unit. They contain potassium, a small fraction of which is radioactive potassium-40, and someone once worked out that eating one delivers about 0.1 microsievert, or 0.01 millirem. The 'banana equivalent dose' is a joke unit, but a useful one: it reminds people that radioactivity is everywhere, including inside them.

Here is the catch, and it is the most interesting part. The University of Groningen's radiation protection academy points out that eating extra bananas barely changes your actual dose, because your metabolism keeps total body potassium nearly constant. Eat more, and you excrete more. The potassium-40 dose you carry is set mainly by your body chemistry, not your fruit intake.

That small detail holds a bigger lesson. A dose figure is not a property of an object. It depends on what the radioactive material is, where it ends up, how long it stays and which tissues it reaches. Iodine-131 concentrates in the thyroid. Radon's decay products lodge in lung tissue. Cesium spreads through muscle and leaves over months. The same activity, measured in becquerels or curies, can mean very different doses depending on biology. That is why health physicists talk about pathways, not just sources.
Radiation is a quantity, not a quality. The useful question is never 'Is it radioactive?' Almost everything is. It is 'How much dose, to which tissue, over what time, in exchange for what benefit?'
What a dose actually costs

So what does any of this do to your odds of getting sick? The most widely cited answer comes from the National Academies' BEIR VII report from 2006. Its risk model predicts that if 100 people each received a single dose of 0.1 sievert (10 rem, or 10,000 millirem) above background, about one of them would develop cancer from it. For context, about 42 of those same 100 people would be expected to develop cancer from all other causes over their lifetimes.

BEIR VII then assumes that lower doses carry proportionally lower risk, so 1 rem would mean about one extra case per thousand people. This is the linear no-threshold model, or LNT, and it is where honest scientific argument begins. At doses below roughly 10 rem, the predicted effects are so small that no epidemiological study can cleanly detect them against the 42-in-100 baseline. LNT is an assumption that fits the high-dose data and is extended downward because it is cautious.

Some researchers argue that cells repair low-level damage well enough that small doses carry less risk than LNT predicts, or even none. Others argue that certain effects could be worse than linear. Large studies of nuclear workers and veterans who were exposed slowly over decades are under way precisely because this question is still open. Regulators keep using LNT because, for setting limits, erring on the cautious side is cheap. The fair summary is that low-dose risk is small, uncertain, and not zero by assumption.
The quietest radiation environment you have lived in

Now back to the sailors. The Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program publishes an annual report on occupational radiation exposure, and the 2026 edition contains some striking numbers. In 2025, fleet personnel averaged about 0.006 rem of occupational dose. Since 1954, the average yearly dose per person monitored aboard ships has been 0.058 rem, compared with about 0.3 rem a year that an average American gets from natural background. No program worker has exceeded 2 rem in any year since 1980, well below the 5 rem federal limit.

The report also makes a claim that surprises many people. For crew stationed outside the propulsion plant, total exposure at sea, including the reactor, is lower than what the public receives from natural background ashore. Seawater blocks cosmic radiation, and ship construction materials have low natural radioactivity. Operators actually pick up more dose in port, during maintenance and overhaul, than from running the plant underway.

The shielding design is deliberately conservative. According to the report, a person would have to spend more than 48 hours a day in a ship's living quarters to exceed exposure limits, which is a polite way of saying it cannot happen. Every rack, mess deck and passageway was laid out with that margin in mind.

For comparison, the same report notes that workers at the 95 commercial power reactors covered in its 2024 data averaged about 0.06 rem each. Across the roughly 156,000 officers and enlisted people trained to operate naval plants, average lifetime dose from that work is around 0.54 rem. That is less than one year of average American exposure from all sources.

blocks.title: Where the dose actually comes from

left.head: What people fear
items: Living near a nuclear power plant
Serving on a nuclear submarine
Eating bananas or Brazil nuts
Airport security scanners

right.head: What dominates real exposure
items: Radon gas in homes, about 228 mrem a year on average
CT scans, up to 1,000 mrem each
Cosmic rays, which rise with altitude and flight time
Natural radioactivity inside your own body

blocks.text: Thinking in doses

The practical value of all this is a habit of mind. When a headline says something is 'radioactive,' convert it to a dose and put it on the ladder. When a doctor suggests a CT, weigh it: the benefit of catching a problem is often far larger than a risk measured in fractions of a percent, but repeat scans add up. When you buy or rent a house, remember that radon is the largest single source of exposure for most Americans and is cheap to test. The EPA's suggested action level is 4 picocuries per liter of air.

For anyone working in the nuclear field, the deeper lesson is that the dosimeter on your belt is measuring a tiny slice of your lifetime exposure. The program behind it is designed so that slice stays small, through shielding, time limits, distance and monitoring. The tools are the same ones you learned early: time, distance and shielding. Halve the time and you halve the dose. Double your distance from a small source and the dose rate drops to roughly a quarter, the same inverse-square rule that governs light from a bulb. Put dense material in between and most gamma rays never reach you. Respect for radiation and fear of radiation are different things. Respect means knowing the numbers well enough to spot both carelessness and panic.

takeaways: The average American gets about 620 mrem (6.2 mSv) a year; about half is natural, mostly radon, and nearly half is medical.
Medical imaging drove US dose up from 3.6 mSv in the 1980s to 6.2 mSv in 2006; per-person medical dose then fell from 2.9 to 2.3 mSv by 2016.
A full-body CT (about 1,000 mrem) outweighs years of typical occupational dose for naval nuclear personnel.
BEIR VII estimates about 1 extra cancer per 100 people from 10 rem; below that, risk is extrapolated with the cautious linear no-threshold model and remains debated.
Ask 'how much dose, to which tissue, for what benefit?' and test your home for radon.

title: Small Reactors, Big Bets: Where a Navy Nuke Fits in Civilian Power
dek: Small modular reactors are finally getting construction permits, while federal forecasts still show operator jobs shrinking; here is how to read both, and what the civilian paths actually look like.

blocks.text: In September 2026, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued the Tennessee Valley Authority a licence to build a 300-megawatt reactor at Clinch River, near Oak Ridge, Tennessee. Six months earlier it had authorized TerraPower to build a sodium-cooled reactor in Kemmerer, Wyoming, the agency's first construction permit for a commercial non-light-water power reactor in more than 40 years. Dow Chemical's subsidiary is lined up behind them with four small gas-cooled units for a chemical plant on the Texas coast.

Read only those headlines and civilian nuclear power looks like it is about to boom. Now read a different source. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that employment of nuclear power reactor operators will shrink about 6% between 2025 and 2035, from roughly 5,200 jobs to 4,900. At the start of November 2026 the World Nuclear Association listed zero power reactors officially under construction in the United States.

Both pictures are true at once. For anyone weighing civilian nuclear work as a career, especially from the Navy's nuclear pipeline, the useful skill is learning to hold both in your head: real momentum, real risk, and a job market that rewards people who are licensed and qualified when the momentum turns into concrete.

items.label: Median annual wage, US nuclear power reactor operators, May 2025
Active NRC-licensed operators at US power reactors
Operable US power reactors in late 2026

blocks.source: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2026; US NRC Operator Licensing; World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the USA, 2026

blocks.text: What makes a reactor small

A small modular reactor, or SMR, is generally defined as one producing 300 megawatts of electricity or less. A typical large reactor produces around 1,000 megawatts or more. The smallest designs, under about 20 megawatts, are often called microreactors. The 'modular' part matters as much as the size. The idea is to build reactor modules in factories, ship them to sites and assemble them, the way aircraft are built in series rather than one at a time.

Under that label sits a zoo of technologies. Most near-term designs are simplified light-water reactors, close cousins of today's plants and of naval reactors, using familiar low-enriched fuel. Others are more radical: fast reactors cooled by liquid sodium or lead, high-temperature reactors cooled by helium gas, and reactors that use molten salt. The water-cooled designs carry the least technical risk. The exotic ones promise higher temperatures for industrial heat, longer fuel life or better use of uranium, in exchange for less operating history.

Developers also pitch safety benefits from smallness. A small core holds less decay heat and can often be cooled by natural circulation and passive systems, without pumps or operator action. That, in turn, may justify smaller emergency planning zones, which would let reactors sit closer to towns and factories. TVA's early site permit for Clinch River was written with the expectation that the emergency planning zone could extend only to the site boundary. Regulators decide these questions plant by plant, so the promise is real but not automatic.

This is a deliberate reversal of history. The World Nuclear Association notes that early power reactors in the 1950s and 1960s were small. From the 1970s, utilities pushed vendors to build bigger and bigger plants to spread fixed costs over more output, which is economies of scale. SMR developers are betting on economies of series instead: build many identical units, learn on each one, and drive the cost down the way manufacturing does.

blocks.title: Electrical output per reactor unit
blocks.note: Gross electrical output per unit as listed by the World Nuclear Association; several SMR plants combine multiple modules.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the USA, 2026

blocks.text: Small reactors are not a new idea to the military. The Army ran a program from 1954 to 1977 that built reactors for remote sites, including one at McMurdo Sound in Antarctica that generated 78 million kilowatt-hours between 1962 and 1972, and a floating plant on a converted Liberty ship in the Panama Canal Zone. And of course the Navy has operated compact, high-reliability reactors at sea for seven decades. Much of what SMR vendors advertise, such as small cores, long fuel cycles and passive safety, would sound familiar in a submarine engine room.

The military is coming back for more. In October 2025 the Army launched its Janus Program to put commercial microreactors on military installations, and in August 2026 it picked five developers. In October 2026 the Navy selected Radiant's 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor for Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, which would be the state's first power-producing reactor.
The scoreboard in late 2026

It is easy to lose track of who is actually building what, so here is the state of the leading US projects as of this writing. The common thread is that licensing, which used to be the bottleneck, has been moving faster than many expected. Construction and cost are now the real tests.

TerraPower's Natrium plant is a good example of where things stand. It is a 345-megawatt sodium-cooled fast reactor that runs on metallic high-assay fuel, sited near a coal plant in Wyoming. Non-nuclear construction began in April 2026, with the first safety-related concrete planned for 2027. Kairos Power, meanwhile, is building Hermes, a 35-megawatt-thermal test reactor cooled by molten fluoride salt in Oak Ridge, and expects construction to finish in 2028. Test reactors like Hermes produce no electricity for sale. Their job is to prove the technology and train the first people who will run it.

blocks.text: Alongside new builds, the industry is doing something nobody expected a decade ago: restarting closed plants. Holtec's Palisades plant in Michigan, shut in 2022, was authorized to receive fresh fuel in July 2025. Constellation is working to restart the undamaged unit at Three Mile Island, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, and NextEra is pursuing a restart of Duane Arnold in Iowa. The Department of Energy has also put $400 million each behind TVA's Clinch River project and Holtec's planned SMR-300s at Palisades.
Why the skeptics are not wrong

The cautionary tale is NuScale. It was the first SMR design to win NRC approval, and a group of Western municipal utilities planned a six-module plant at Idaho National Laboratory. By late 2022 the estimated price of its power had risen from about $55 per megawatt-hour to between $90 and $100, partly because of inflation in steel and construction. In November 2023 the project was cancelled. A good design and a licence were not enough without customers willing to pay first-of-a-kind prices.

Fuel is another constraint. More than half of SMR designs in development need high-assay low-enriched uranium, enriched to between 5% and 20% uranium-235. The World Nuclear Association notes that only Russia and China can produce it at scale today; the US company Centrus began producing small amounts from a demonstration cascade in October 2023. And economies of series only arrive once there is a series. The first few units of any design are almost always the most expensive.

That is why the BLS projection is not crazy. It is a projection for the occupation as it exists today, and it cannot count jobs at plants that have not been built. If even a fraction of the announced projects reach operation in the 2030s, each one will need its own trained, licensed crew. If they stall, the job market looks more like the BLS line. The honest planning stance is to be ready for the upside without betting your rent on it.

New reactors do not come with operators. Every NRC operating licence is tied to one specific facility, so each new plant must train and license its own crews before it can run. Experienced people who can pass that process will be the scarce input.
The civilian paths for a Navy nuke

The BLS notes that some nuclear power reactor operators gain their experience in related roles in the Navy. In practice, people leaving the naval program usually land in a few kinds of civilian jobs. Pay figures below are national medians from the BLS for May 2025; actual offers vary by region, plant, shift work and overtime, so treat them as rough benchmarks rather than promises.

blocks.text: Licensed operations is the path most people picture. You typically start as a non-licensed operator, sometimes called an equipment operator, working rounds in the plant while you complete the site's training program. When the plant certifies that you have met its training and experience requirements, it sponsors you for an NRC licence as a reactor operator (RO) or senior reactor operator (SRO). The requirements are set by the facility using industry guidelines from the National Academy for Nuclear Training, and some plants run classes that take experienced candidates directly to SRO.

blocks.title: How an NRC operator licence works
items: Get hired by a plant and complete its training program, often starting as a non-licensed operator
The plant certifies your training and experience on NRC Form 398 and sponsors your application
Pass a medical exam certifying you are fit to operate
RO candidates must score at least 80% on a 75-question written exam; SROs take 25 more questions and need 70% on that portion
Pass an operating test with a plant walkthrough and simulator scenarios
Hold a licence valid for that plant only, renewed every 6 years, with requalification and a medical exam every 2 years

blocks.text: Maintenance is the other big door, and it is the natural fit for an electrician. Plants employ electrical maintenance technicians who work on breakers, motors, switchgear, batteries and protective relays, and the BLS lists powerhouse, substation and relay repairers at a $103,020 median with about 20,900 jobs nationally. Those skills also transfer outside nuclear, to utilities, substations and large industrial sites. Radiation protection and chemistry technicians, grouped by the BLS as nuclear technicians, earn a $110,240 median.

There is also the grid side. Power distributors and dispatchers, the people in control centers who balance generation and load and route power across transmission networks, earned a $106,730 median in May 2025. Their work is a direct extension of what a ship's electrical division does on a smaller scale: keep frequency and voltage steady while generators and loads come and go. It is a path that does not depend on any particular reactor getting built.

Whichever door you choose, expect to be a student again. The BLS notes that power plant operators typically need several years of onsite training and experience to become fully competent, and that nuclear operator licences must be maintained through ongoing requalification exams. For people who got through nuke school, that rhythm of classroom, qualification cards and oral boards will feel familiar. The difference is that the plant, the procedures and the regulator are new.
What transfers and what does not

A Navy nuke leaves with things civilian plants value: deep theory training, years of watchstanding, comfort with procedures and formal communications, and the habits of a radiation worker. Those are hard to teach and slow to build, which is why the naval program has long been a feeder for the industry.

Some things do not transfer directly. Commercial plants run different designs, much larger and with different systems, and every licence is site-specific. The regulator is the NRC, not Naval Reactors, with its own rules and inspection culture. Plants are businesses that care about refueling outage schedules and electricity prices in a way a submarine never does. And an NRC licence takes real time and effort to earn, even for experienced candidates, because you have to learn a specific plant in depth.

A few practical moves make the transition easier. Keep copies of qualification records, watch hours and evaluations, because plants assess experience against written criteria. Talk to the command career counselor about transition programs and education benefits, and confirm the current rules, since they change. If a degree is on your horizon, know that technical degrees open doors to SRO and engineering roles later. And remember that the licensed operator path is not the only one: maintenance, radiation protection, training and grid operations all draw on the same core skills.

The deeper point is that the safety net is not a particular plant or a particular reactor design. It is a rare and portable ability: running high-consequence machinery by procedure, under pressure, without cutting corners. SMRs may or may not boom on schedule. People who can do that work well will be needed either way.

takeaways: SMRs are reactors of about 300 MWe or less, built to win on factory production and repetition rather than sheer size.
Licensing momentum is real in 2026 (Clinch River, Kemmerer, Long Mott), but cost and fuel supply remain the big risks, as NuScale's cancelled Idaho plant showed.
The BLS put the May 2025 median wage for nuclear reactor operators at $122,890, and still projects a 6% decline in those jobs by 2035.
NRC operator licences are tied to one plant, so every new reactor will need its own licensed crews.
Electrical maintenance, relay and substation work, radiation protection and grid operations are strong paths beside licensed operations.

title: Three Mile Island: The Light That Said Closed
dek: A stuck valve, an indicator that reported a command instead of a fact, and a crew doing exactly what it was trained to do melted half a reactor core in 1979.

blocks.text: At 4 a.m. on Wednesday, 28 March 1979, the control room of Three Mile Island unit 2, near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was quiet. The reactor was almost brand new, a 959-megawatt pressurized water reactor running at 97% power on the night shift. Within the next few hours, about 45% of its core would melt, and nobody in that room would realize it for a very long time.

Nothing exploded. No one was hurt. The radioactive release was tiny. And yet TMI-2 became the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear history and reshaped the industry more than any event before or since. The reason is uncomfortable: the operators were not reckless. They were careful, well-intentioned and following their training. The plant was lying to them, and their training made the lie convincing.
A minor trip, then a valve that stayed open

It started on the non-nuclear side. A mechanical or electrical failure stopped the main feedwater pumps that send water to the steam generators. With no feedwater, the steam generators could no longer pull heat out of the primary loop. The turbine tripped, and the reactor scrammed automatically, a shutdown that took about one second. So far this was a routine transient that plants were designed to ride out.

With heat removal suddenly reduced, the primary coolant heated up, expanded and pushed pressure up. As designed, the pilot-operated relief valve, or PORV, on top of the pressurizer popped open to bleed off the excess. About 10 seconds later, once pressure fell, it should have closed. It did not. It stuck open, and reactor coolant began pouring out as steam into a drain tank.

Here is the detail that turned a stuck valve into a meltdown. The control room had a light for the PORV, and that light showed the valve closed. But it was not wired to the valve's actual position. It only showed that a close signal had been sent to the valve's solenoid. The plant was reporting what it had been told to do, not what it had done. The crew had a small-break loss-of-coolant accident in progress and an instrument telling them, in effect, that there wasn't one.
Design rule written in molten fuel: an indicator should show the state of the equipment, not the command sent to it. If a light can be lit while the valve is open, sooner or later it will be.
Trained to do exactly the wrong thing

As coolant drained out, pressure fell and the high-pressure injection pumps started automatically, pumping emergency water into the primary system. This was the safety system doing its job. Then the operators made the decision that every investigation would circle back to: they throttled it back.

They had a reason. The pressurizer level, the water level in the tall tank that controls primary pressure, was rising. Their training told them that pressurizer level was the one dependable measure of how much water was in the system, and that they must never let the pressurizer fill solid with water, because then they could lose control of pressure and risk rupturing the system. A rising level looked like a system getting too full.

What was actually happening was the opposite. Steam escaping through the open valve at the top of the pressurizer was drawing water up into it, and steam pockets forming elsewhere in the primary system were pushing water into the pressurizer too. Level went up while the total inventory went down. There was no instrument to show the water level in the reactor vessel itself, because in normal operation the vessel is always completely full. So the crew assumed that a full pressurizer meant a covered core.

Without forced flow or enough makeup water, the core uncovers and overheats

blocks.text: Steam kept forming in the primary loop. Pumping a mix of steam and water made the big reactor coolant pumps vibrate violently, and to protect them the operators shut them down. That ended forced cooling of the core. The water level in the vessel kept dropping as coolant boiled away through the stuck valve, until the top of the core was uncovered and the fuel began to overheat. The zirconium cladding reacted with steam, producing hydrogen and releasing radioactive material into the coolant.
Nearly sixteen hours to restore cooling

At 6:22 a.m., about two hours and twenty minutes in, operators closed a block valve between the PORV and the pressurizer, and the coolant leak finally stopped. By then the damage was well under way, and steam and gases inside the system were blocking flow through the core. The rest of the day was a struggle to collapse those steam bubbles and get circulation back. In the afternoon, a sudden spike in containment pressure revealed that hydrogen had burned inside the reactor building. Not until 7:50 p.m. did the crew get one reactor coolant pump running again and restore forced cooling.

Think about what the crew was facing. Alarms were ringing and lights were flashing across the boards, and every individual reading had an innocent explanation. Pressurizer level high: too much water. Coolant pumps shaking: protect the pumps. Relief valve light: closed, so that leak was ruled out. Each clue was explained away by a mental model that was internally consistent and wrong. That is the signature of the hardest accidents to stop, the ones where nobody is panicking because everybody is confident.

The reactor reached cold shutdown, with natural circulation and water below 100 °C, only on 27 April, a month later. When engineers finally removed the vessel head in July 1984 and looked inside, they found that at least 45% of the core, about 62 tonnes, had melted, and 19 tonnes had flowed down into the bottom of the vessel. The steel vessel had held. So had the containment building.

blocks.text: The bubble, the panic and the dose

For the public, the worst days were Friday and Saturday, 30 and 31 March. A deliberate venting of radioactive gas produced a reading of 1,200 millirem directly above a plant stack. Through garbled phone calls between people who did not know the plant's status, officials came to believe it was an off-site reading. A hydrogen bubble had also collected at the top of the reactor vessel, and for a time NRC officials feared it could explode. It never could have; there was not enough oxygen in the system. But the fear drove a weekend exodus, and the communication failures became as famous as the meltdown.

The actual release was small. About 2 million people around the plant received an average dose of about 1 millirem above normal background, according to the NRC. A chest X-ray is about 6. The maximum possible dose to someone at the site boundary was under 100 millirem. The Pennsylvania Department of Health tracked more than 30,000 people living within five miles for 18 years and found no unusual health trends, and more than a dozen independent studies found no excess cancers.

The cleanup was its own engineering saga. Defueling did not even begin until October 1985, after years of preparation; crews on a platform over the open, flooded vessel fished out damaged fuel with long-handled tools, keeping it underwater the whole time. By 1990, 342 canisters of fuel and debris had gone to the Idaho National Laboratory. More than 2 million gallons of accident-generated water were processed and evaporated. About 1% of the fuel is still in the vessel, and final decommissioning of unit 2 is expected to run until about 2052.

blocks.title: TMI doses in context
blocks.note: The site-boundary figure is an upper bound; the true maximum was below it.
blocks.source: US NRC, Backgrounder on the Three Mile Island Accident

blocks.text: It had already happened once

The most haunting part of TMI is that it was a rerun. On 24 September 1977, at the Davis-Besse plant in Ohio, which also used a reactor from the same vendor, Babcock and Wilcox, a loss of feedwater led to a pressurizer relief valve sticking open. The operators throttled high-pressure injection when pressurizer level rose, for the same reason TMI's crew would. Shift supervisor Mike Derivan later wrote that for the first 20 minutes the two events were nearly identical. At Davis-Besse, he worked out what the plant was really doing and acted on it, and the event ended as a footnote instead of a disaster.

Derivan has argued that the TMI operators did what they were trained to do. In his account, the vendor's training stressed the rule for throttling injection so hard that failing to apply it could cost an operator a certification exam, while neither that vendor nor others in the industry correctly understood how a plant behaves when the leak is in the steam space at the top of the pressurizer. About a dozen operators at two plants, 18 months apart, made the same choice and believed it was correct. An engineer at the vendor raised concerns in a memo in November 1977, but the warning was soft and the lesson never reached TMI's control room.
What changed

TMI permanently changed how US reactors are run. Training shifted from picking an event-specific procedure out of a book to symptom-based procedures that walk operators through yes-or-no questions, starting with whether the core is covered, before they try to diagnose the specific fault. Full-scale control room simulators became central. Control rooms were redesigned around human factors, and requirements for relief valves, instrumentation and auxiliary feedwater were tightened. The NRC put at least two resident inspectors at every plant, required emergency plans tested with state and local agencies, and opened a 24-hour operations center.

The industry also policed itself. In 1979 utilities created the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, which set performance standards, shared operating experience across plants and, from 1985 through its National Academy for Nuclear Training, accredited training programs. The point of sharing was exactly the Davis-Besse lesson: one plant's near miss should become every plant's training scenario.

There was a price, too. Public confidence in nuclear power in the US dropped sharply after the accident, and TMI became a major reason that new reactor construction stalled through the 1980s and 1990s. An accident that injured no one ended up shaping the American energy mix for a generation, which says as much about communication and trust as it does about engineering.

Median US plant capability factor, 1980 vs after 2000
Cost of the nearly 12-year TMI-2 cleanup

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Three Mile Island Accident

blocks.text: The results showed up in the numbers. Significant events per reactor fell from 2.38 in 1985 to 0.10 by the end of 1997. Median capability factor rose from about 65% in 1980 to over 80% in 2000 and above 90% afterward. TMI-1, the undamaged twin, restarted in 1985 with revamped training, ran an uninterrupted 616 days in 1997 and stayed among the country's best performers until it closed in 2019 for economic reasons. In 2024 its owner announced plans to restart it under a power deal with Microsoft, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center. Cleaning up TMI-2 took nearly 12 years and about $973 million.

The deeper lesson is about what an operator can know. The TMI crew was not ignorant or lazy. They read their instruments correctly and applied their training faithfully, and the core melted anyway, because the instruments answered a different question than the one that mattered and the training rested on an incomplete model of the plant. The fix was not just better people. It was instruments that report reality, procedures built around protecting the core first, and a system that moves every near miss to every control room. For anyone who stands watch, the useful habit is simple: when the indications do not add up, ask what each one is actually measuring.

takeaways: The PORV light showed that a close signal was sent, not that the valve was closed; indicators must show actual state.
Operators throttled emergency injection because rising pressurizer level looked like overfilling; there was no vessel level gauge.
About 45% of the core melted, yet the vessel and containment held and the average public dose was about 1 millirem.
A nearly identical event at Davis-Besse in 1977 was a warning that never reached TMI's operators.
Symptom-based procedures, simulators, INPO and shared operating experience came out of TMI and drove big safety gains.

title: Ninety-Five Thousand Tonnes and Nowhere to Go
dek: America's spent nuclear fuel would fit on one football field and gets less dangerous every year, so why did Finland open the world's first permanent repository while the US pays billions to keep waiting?

blocks.text: In October 2026, the Finnish government granted an operating licence to a facility called Onkalo, a network of tunnels about 400 meters down in the granite bedrock at Olkiluoto on Finland's west coast. Once the national regulator finishes its final inspections, it will become the first place on Earth to permanently bury spent fuel from civilian power reactors.

The United States, which built the world's largest fleet of nuclear plants, has nothing comparable. Its roughly 95,000 tonnes of used fuel sits at current and former power plant sites, in steel-lined pools and in rows of concrete and steel casks on gravel pads. The federal government was legally obligated to start taking that fuel away in 1998. It never did, and taxpayers have paid more than $12 billion in court settlements to utilities as a result.

Nuclear waste is often described as an unsolved technical problem. The Finnish tunnels suggest otherwise. The more interesting story is why a problem that is physically small, well understood and shrinking with time has proved so hard to finish.

items.label: Used fuel from US power reactors as of 2026
Share of that fuel already in dry cask storage
Paid to utilities in settlements and judgments by Sept 2025

blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, US Nuclear Fuel Cycle, 2026 (citing IAEA and DOE)

blocks.text: How much is there, really?

Start with scale. The Department of Energy estimates that US reactors produce about 2,000 metric tons of spent fuel a year, while generating nearly a fifth of the country's electricity. By its count in 2022, all the commercial spent fuel produced since the 1950s, then about 90,000 metric tons, could be stacked on a single football field to a depth of less than 10 yards. That is decades of electricity for a large nation, in a volume smaller than many landfills take in a week.

Small does not mean centralized, though. The DOE counted spent fuel stored at more than 70 sites in 35 states, and roughly a quarter of those sites no longer have an operating reactor. At those 'orphaned' sites, a security force, monitoring staff and a fence now exist mainly to guard rows of casks on a concrete pad, at the expense of whoever owns them, until the federal government takes the fuel.

The fuel itself is not a glowing liquid. It is the same thing that went into the reactor: ceramic uranium oxide pellets sealed in metal tubes, bundled into assemblies several meters long. It comes out solid and stays solid. What changed inside the reactor is its composition. A small fraction of the uranium has split into fission products, many intensely radioactive, and some uranium-238 has absorbed neutrons to become plutonium and other heavy elements called actinides.

Globally, the World Nuclear Association cites IAEA estimates that about 430,000 tonnes of spent fuel have been produced since civilian nuclear power began, of which about 30% has been reprocessed. Around 263,000 tonnes sit in storage today, more than two thirds of it in pools.
Not all nuclear waste is the same waste

When people say 'nuclear waste' they usually picture spent fuel, but most radioactive waste by volume is far more mundane. Low-level waste includes gloves, rags, tools, filters and protective clothing with small amounts of mostly short-lived contamination. It does not need shielding to handle and goes to near-surface disposal sites. The US has several, in Texas, South Carolina, Utah, Tennessee and Washington.

Intermediate-level waste, such as used ion exchange resins, sludges and reactor components, needs some shielding. High-level waste is the material that is radioactive enough to generate significant heat: spent fuel declared as waste, or the concentrated residue from reprocessing it. The proportions are lopsided in a way that reframes the whole debate.

blocks.title: Radioactive waste: volume vs radioactivity
blocks.note: High-level waste is about 3% of the volume but about 95% of the radioactivity.
blocks.source: World Nuclear Association, Radioactive Waste Management, 2025

blocks.text: In other words, more than 90% of radioactive waste by volume already has working disposal routes around the world. The hard part is a small, dense, hot slice. That is good news in one sense: the problem is concentrated and therefore controllable. It is bad news in another, because concentrated hazards make the strongest political symbols.
The waste that cools itself

Here is the property that makes nuclear waste unlike almost any other hazardous material. It gets less dangerous on its own. Mercury, lead and arsenic stay toxic forever. Radioactive atoms decay, and the most intensely radioactive ones decay fastest. That is why freshly discharged fuel needs years in a pool, under several meters of circulating water, before it can move to dry storage.

The storage hardware is less exotic than people imagine. Spent fuel pools are typically 7 to 12 meters deep, with several meters of water above the racks, which are built with neutron absorbers. The water does double duty as coolant and shield. Once fuel has cooled for at least about five years, it can be loaded into a sealed steel canister holding up to roughly 40 assemblies in inert gas. The canister sits inside a concrete and steel module about 6 meters tall, cooled by nothing more than air rising through vents. There are no pumps to fail.

According to the World Nuclear Association, after about 40 to 50 years out of the reactor, the heat and radioactivity of spent fuel have fallen by more than 99%. The catch is the long tail. Some fission products and actinides last for thousands to hundreds of thousands of years. Without reprocessing, spent fuel takes on the order of 300,000 years to decay to the radioactivity of the uranium ore it came from. If uranium and plutonium are separated out and recycled, the remaining high-level waste gets there in about 9,000 years.

blocks.title: The life of a fuel assembly in the US today
items: Burns in the reactor core for several years, spending roughly 18 to 24 months between refuelings
Moves underwater to the spent fuel pool to shed its early, intense heat
After years of cooling, is sealed in a steel canister filled with inert gas
Canister goes into a concrete and steel cask, cooled by natural air flow
Waits on site for a federal repository or interim store that does not yet exist

blocks.text: Spent fuel is also not entirely spent. The DOE notes that more than 90% of its potential energy remains after about five years in a reactor. France, Russia and a few other countries reprocess fuel to recover uranium and plutonium for new fuel, which extracts some 25 to 30% more energy from the original ore and cuts high-level waste volume by about 85%, according to the World Nuclear Association. The United States does not currently do this commercially, mostly for reasons of cost and proliferation policy rather than physics.
The scariest part of the waste is also the shortest-lived part. Time is the main safety system, which is why the debate is really about institutions that last, not chemistry that fails.
The American stalemate

The US plan was set out clearly enough. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982 made the federal government responsible for permanently disposing of commercial spent fuel. Utilities would pay a fee of a tenth of a cent per kilowatt-hour into a Nuclear Waste Fund, and the DOE would start removing fuel from reactor sites by 1998. In 1987, Congress amended the law to name Yucca Mountain in Nevada as the sole initial repository site.

Nevada fought it from the start. The DOE submitted a licence application in 2008, the Obama administration moved to withdraw it soon after, and a federal appeals court ordered the NRC to resume its review in 2013. The NRC's staff finished the safety evaluation in 2015, but Congress has not funded construction and the project has been effectively frozen ever since. Meanwhile, utilities paid in about $24.6 billion in fees between 1983 and 2025, and the fund stood at $51.4 billion at the end of fiscal 2025, mostly unspent.

Because the government broke its contracts, utilities sued and won. By September 2025, the DOE reported $12.2 billion paid in settlements and judgments, with a further $38.6 to $44.3 billion in liabilities estimated to remain. Those payments come from a general taxpayer fund, not from the waste fund itself. Private companies tried to fill the gap with consolidated interim storage sites in Texas and New Mexico. Both were licensed by the NRC, then blocked by state opposition and a federal appeals court. The Supreme Court reversed that court ruling in June 2025 on procedural grounds, but the New Mexico developer wound up its project anyway that October.

Public opinion is not really the obstacle it is often assumed to be. A YouGov poll from April 2026, commissioned by a waste disposal company and reported by the World Nuclear Association, found 81% of Americans saying a permanent solution for used fuel should be a national priority. Wanting a solution and wanting it in your own state are different things, though, and the American system gives states many ways to say no.

blocks.text: How Finland got to yes

Finland's design, called KBS-3 after a Swedish concept, uses layered barriers. Spent fuel goes into heavy iron inserts inside thick copper canisters. The canisters are placed in holes drilled into the floors of tunnels about 400 meters deep, surrounded by bentonite clay that swells when wet and seals out water. The surrounding crystalline bedrock has been geologically quiet for an extremely long time.

Each barrier is meant to buy time independently. Copper corrodes extremely slowly in oxygen-free groundwater, and archaeologists have found ancient copper objects that survived thousands of years underground. The clay limits how fast water can reach the canister and how fast anything can leave it. The rock keeps groundwater flow slow and chemistry stable. Nobody has to maintain it once it is sealed, which is the point: the design does not depend on future governments staying competent.

The timeline was long but steady. Construction was licensed in November 2015. The operator, Posiva, applied for an operating licence in December 2021 and tested its encapsulation plant with dummy fuel. Finland's safety regulator, STUK, issued a favorable safety assessment in August 2026, and the government granted the licence that October. Sweden has picked its own site at Forsmark, and Canada selected a site in northwestern Ontario in November 2024. Natural analogues help make the case: the two-billion-year-old natural reactors at Oklo in Gabon show many fission products staying close to where they formed for geologic time.
What the problem actually is

Viewed from a submarine, the waste question can look oddly familiar. Naval spent fuel is shipped to a federal facility in Idaho, and the naval program has run for decades on a principle of total accountability for every source of radioactivity. The commercial side has its own track record: the DOE counts more than 2,500 cask shipments of spent fuel across the country over about 55 years without a radiological release. Dry casks on reactor sites have been a quiet success. None of this is the hard part.

The hard part is that a repository asks a society to make a promise lasting longer than any society has existed. Finland's answer is to design a system that keeps its promise without needing anyone to remember it. America's long stalemate shows what happens when the technical case is settled but trust is not. The fuel waits in casks, safe enough for now, while lawyers and legislators argue about where 'later' should be.

The best way to think about nuclear waste may be this: it is a small, well-characterized, slowly fading hazard attached to a very large political problem. Solving the first was an engineering task, and engineers largely have. Solving the second requires something harder to build than a tunnel in granite.

There are paths forward. The DOE has been exploring a consent-based process for siting interim storage, which flips the Yucca approach: find a willing community first, then build. Engineers are studying alternatives such as deep boreholes drilled kilometers into basement rock, an idea the National Academy of Sciences first evaluated in 1957. Some advanced reactor developers want to recycle used fuel into new fuel. Each option has costs and critics. What they share is the recognition that the bottleneck is no longer knowing how. It is agreeing where, who pays and who decides.

takeaways: The US holds about 95,000 tonnes of used fuel, all at current or former plant sites, with more than half already in dry casks.
High-level waste is about 3% of radioactive waste by volume but about 95% of its radioactivity; the rest already has disposal routes.
Spent fuel loses more than 99% of its heat and radioactivity in 40 to 50 years, but a long-lived tail lasts for millennia.
Missing the 1998 federal deadline has cost US taxpayers $12.2 billion in settlements so far, with tens of billions more expected.
Finland's Onkalo shows the technical problem is solvable; the remaining challenge is political trust over very long time spans.

title: Why Smart People Make Dumb Money Moves
dek: Investors routinely earn less than the very funds they own. Behavioral finance explains the gap, and why being clever doesn't close it.

blocks.text: Here is a strange fact about investing. Over the ten years that ended in December 2025, the average US mutual fund and ETF returned 9.9% a year, according to Morningstar. The average dollar that investors actually had in those same funds earned 8.7% a year. Same funds, same decade, same market. About an eighth of the return simply disappeared.

It didn't go to fees; those are already counted in the fund's return. It went to timing. People poured money in after funds had gone up and pulled it out after they'd gone down, which is exactly backward. Nobody forced them to. They did it to themselves, with good intentions and, often, after a lot of research.

That gap is the subject of behavioral finance, the study of why real people handle money differently from the rational calculators in economics textbooks. Its core lesson is uncomfortable for smart people in particular: intelligence doesn't protect you from these mistakes. Sometimes it makes them worse, because a sharp mind is very good at building convincing reasons for a bad move.
The gap between the fund and the person

Morningstar calls its annual study *Mind the Gap*. It compares a fund's official return, which assumes you bought at the start and held to the end, with the dollar-weighted return of all the money that actually flowed in and out. The 2026 edition found investors captured about 88% of what their funds earned. The missing 1.2 percentage points a year sounds small until you compound it over a working life.

Run the arithmetic. If those two rates held for 40 years, $10,000 growing at 9.9% a year would become about $436,000. At 8.7%, it would become about $281,000. That's not a real forecast, since nobody knows future returns, but it shows the scale: a slightly worse habit, repeated for decades, can cost a third of the final pile. The behavior gap isn't a rounding error. Over a career, it can be the single largest cost an investor pays.

The pattern inside the data is the interesting part. The gap was smallest in plain US stock funds, where investors kept about 97% of the return. It was larger in sector funds, the ones that bet on a single industry like tech or energy, and largest in so-called alternative funds. The more volatile the fund, the bigger the gap: the calmest fifth of funds lost 0.4 points a year to investor timing, while the most volatile fifth lost 2.1 points. Exciting funds attract exactly the kind of in-and-out trading that destroys returns.

blocks.title: Return lost to investor timing, by fund type
blocks.note: Gap between fund total return and investors' dollar-weighted return, 10 years to Dec. 31, 2025
blocks.source: Morningstar, Mind the Gap 2026

blocks.text: Think of a ranked game where the matchmaking punishes you every time you change your main. The players who pick something solid and stick with it climb. The ones who jump to whatever is trending after every patch end up always learning, never compounding. Markets behave much the same way, except the patch notes are headlines and the penalty is real money.
Overconfidence: the more you trade, the less you keep

In 2000, finance professors Brad Barber and Terrance Odean published a paper with a blunt title: *Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth*. They analyzed 66,465 households with accounts at a large discount broker from 1991 to 1996, a booming market. The average household turned over 75% of its stock portfolio every year. The households that traded the most earned 11.4% a year, while the market returned 17.9%. They weren't unlucky. Trading costs and poorly timed decisions ate the difference.

blocks.title: Annual returns, 1991–1996
blocks.source: Barber & Odean, Journal of Finance, 2000

blocks.text: Their explanation was overconfidence. Each trade is a bet that you know something the person on the other side doesn't. A year later the same researchers tested that idea by comparing men and women, since psychology research had found men tend to be more overconfident. Across more than 35,000 households, men traded 45% more than women and earned risk-adjusted returns 1.4 percentage points a year lower. Single men traded 67% more than single women, and the gap in returns grew to 2.3 points. More confidence, more trades, worse results.

Overconfidence isn't rare or limited to a reckless few. Ask a room of people whether they're above-average drivers and most of the hands go up, which can't be true of everyone. Investing works the same way. Almost everyone who buys an individual stock believes, at that moment, that they've spotted something the market missed.

Day trading is the extreme version. Economists Fernando Chague, Rodrigo De-Losso and Bruno Giovannetti studied every person who started day trading Brazilian equity futures between 2013 and 2015 and kept at it for at least 300 days. 97% of them lost money. Only 0.4% earned more than a bank teller's wage, which the authors pegged at about $54 a day. They found no evidence that people got better with practice. Their verdict was that day trading for a living is close to impossible for an individual competing against professional, high-speed firms.

items.label: Brazilian day traders who persisted 300+ days and lost money
Who earned more than a bank teller's wage (about $54 a day)

blocks.source: Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti, 2019

blocks.text: The cruel part is how markets give feedback. In most skills, practice gives clean signals: the shot hits or it doesn't. In trading, a bad decision can make money and a good one can lose it, and the noise can last for months. That's the perfect environment for overconfidence, because every lucky win feels like proof of skill.
Losses hurt more than gains feel good, mostly

In 1979, psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed *prospect theory*, one of whose central ideas is loss aversion: losing $100 feels worse than winning $100 feels good. A 2024 meta-analysis by Alexander Brown, Taisuke Imai, Ferdinand Vieider and Colin Camerer pooled 607 estimates from 150 studies and put the typical ratio at about 1.96. On average, a loss carried roughly twice the psychological weight of an equal gain.

It's worth knowing that not everyone agrees. In 2018, David Gal and Derek Rucker argued in a review that the evidence for loss aversion as a general rule is weaker than its fame suggests, and that losses only loom larger in certain situations. The honest summary is that the effect is real in many settings, especially when stakes are framed as losses, but it isn't a universal law of the mind.

Where loss aversion clearly shows up in money is the *disposition effect*. In a 1998 study of 10,000 brokerage accounts, Odean found that investors were much quicker to sell stocks that had gone up than stocks that had gone down. Selling a winner locks in a pleasant feeling. Selling a loser makes the loss official. So people hold the losers, hoping to get back to even, and sell the winners. Odean found the behavior wasn't justified by what the stocks did next, and it raised investors' taxes, since realizing gains triggers tax while realizing losses can reduce it.
The price you paid for something is a fact about your past, not about its future. The market doesn't know or care where you got in. Every hold decision is really a fresh buy decision.
Attention is a trade signal, for the other side

A newer finding involves apps. Barber, Odean and colleagues studied Robinhood, the commission-free app that made trading as easy as tapping a screen. Robinhood users did more *attention-induced* trading than other retail investors, piling into stocks that were in the news or topping the app's popularity lists. When Robinhood users bought a stock in a big surge, it tended to do badly afterward. For the most heavily bought stocks each day, returns over the next 20 days averaged 4.7% below what would be expected.

This is herding. When everyone is talking about something, it feels safer to join, because so many people can't all be wrong. In markets they often are, because by the time something is on everyone's feed, the price already reflects the excitement. You're not early. You're the liquidity that lets earlier buyers cash out.

Herding also explains why the average investor in the Morningstar data bought high and sold low. Rising prices create stories, stories create buyers, and buyers arrive late. Falling prices create fear, fear creates sellers, and they leave just before the recovery. None of this requires stupidity. It only requires being human in a crowd.

Social media adds fuel. A screenshot of someone's 400% gain spreads fast; the thousands of quiet losses don't get posted. So the picture you see of what other investors are doing is badly skewed toward winners, which makes the odds look better than they are. The same filter runs through gaming clips, startup stories and trading forums: you see the highlight reel and assume it's the average match.
Why being smart doesn't save you

These biases aren't a matter of IQ. Overconfidence often grows with knowledge, because learning a bit about a field makes you feel more in control than you are. People who are good at arguments are also good at arguing themselves into things. A clever person who has decided a stock is going up can find ten reasons to support it and dismiss the five reasons against.

Other habits make it worse. People overweight what they saw recently, so a year of rising prices feels like a permanent trend. Present bias, the tendency to grab rewards now and push costs onto future you, turns long-term saving into a constant uphill fight. And the urge to *do something* is powerful when markets move. Doing nothing feels passive and irresponsible, even when the data say it is usually the best move available.

There's also the way money gets mentally relabeled. Gains from a lucky trade often feel like *house money*, as if it isn't really yours yet, so it's easier to gamble with. A small loss on a bet often triggers the urge to win it back with a bigger bet. Both instincts make sense in the moment and both quietly raise the amount of risk you're taking, usually right after a streak, when your judgment feels sharpest and is actually least reliable.

The reframe is this: for an ordinary investor, the edge isn't information. Professionals with faster computers and better data are already on the other side of every trade you make. Your edge, if you have one, is behavior: patience, low costs, and the ability to sit still when other people can't. In this game, the player who does less often scores more.
Build the rules before you need them

The best defense against your own brain is deciding in advance, while you're calm, what you'll do when you aren't. This is the same logic as a pre-mission checklist or a casualty procedure. You don't want to invent a plan during the emergency. You want to execute one you already trust.

blocks.title: A behavior-proof investing setup
items: Automate contributions every payday so investing happens without a decision.
Pick a simple, diversified allocation once, and write down why you chose it.
Set a rule for when you'll change it, such as once a year or after a major life event, never after a headline.
Wait at least a few days before acting on any urge to buy or sell, and write down the reason first.
If you want to pick stocks or trade for fun, cap it at a small slice you can afford to lose.

blocks.text: Military life gives you one accidental advantage here. When you're underway with no internet, you can't check your portfolio, panic-sell during a crash or chase a stock your friends are hyping. Many investors would pay for that kind of forced patience. The trick is to bring the same habit back to shore, so that the boring automatic plan keeps running whether or not you're watching it.

For most sailors, the simplest version of this setup already exists. A Thrift Savings Plan lifecycle fund with automatic contributions is close to a behavior-proof portfolio by design: diversified, cheap, rebalanced for you, and deducted before the money ever hits your account. The main way to break it is to start tinkering, moving everything to the safest fund after a scary month or into stocks after a great one. The best thing most people can do with that account is set it correctly and then leave it alone.

Behavioral finance doesn't say people are hopeless with money. It says our mistakes are predictable, and predictable mistakes can be designed around. You can't stop the feelings. You can build a system where the feelings don't get a vote.

takeaways: Over ten years to 2025, investors earned 1.2 points a year less than the funds they owned, mostly from bad timing.
The households that traded most earned 11.4% a year while the market made 17.9%.
97% of Brazilian day traders who stuck with it for 300+ days lost money.
Losses tend to hurt about twice as much as equal gains feel good, which makes people hold losers and sell winners.
Your edge is behavior, not information: automate, write rules in advance, and trade less.

title: The Budget You Never Have to Look At
dek: Most budgets fail because they need willpower every single day. Military pay is predictable enough that you can make the right decisions once and let the system run itself.

blocks.text: Here's a pattern anyone who has done a long underway will recognize. For weeks there's nowhere to spend money: no stores, no restaurants, no delivery apps. Paychecks keep landing on the 1st and the 15th. Then the boat pulls in, and you're looking at the biggest bank balance you've ever had, plus a strong feeling that you've earned the right to enjoy it. A month later, a surprising amount of it is gone, and it's hard to say exactly where.

That isn't a character flaw. It's what happens when a pile of money meets a human brain that reads a balance as permission. The fix isn't more discipline. It's a system that makes the important decisions before the money ever reaches your checking account, so that what's left is genuinely yours to spend without guilt or spreadsheets.
Your paycheck is a budgeting cheat code

Most civilians your age deal with irregular hours, surprise rent increases and paychecks that change every week. Military pay is the opposite. It arrives on a fixed schedule, the amount barely changes from month to month, and the big increases are predictable: an across-the-board raise every January, a step up as your years of service grow, and a jump with each promotion. For 2026, the general raise was 3.8%, effective January 1.

blocks.title: E-5 monthly basic pay in 2026, by years of service
blocks.note: Basic pay only. Special pays, bonuses and allowances (BAH, BAS, sea and sub pay) come on top and vary.
blocks.source: 2026 military basic pay table, effective Jan 1, 2026 (NavyCS; Military.com)

blocks.text: That predictability is a gift, because the hardest part of saving is deciding how much, over and over. If you know roughly what's coming and when, you can decide once. Special and incentive pays such as sea pay, submarine duty pay and nuclear bonuses add to this but can change with assignments, so a smart default is to build your plan around basic pay and treat the extras as bonus fuel for savings.

Start by learning your real number, which is not the figure on a pay chart. Your Leave and Earnings Statement shows the path from gross pay to what actually lands in your account: federal and state income tax (depending on your state of legal residence), Social Security and Medicare, SGLI life insurance premiums, TSP contributions and any allotments, plus any tax-free allowances you receive, which are added on top. Plan around the net deposit for each payday, not the headline salary, and you'll avoid the common shock of a budget built on money that was never coming.
Why most budgets die in week three

The classic budget asks you to track every purchase, compare it with a category limit and adjust. It works for some people. For a lot of others it lasts a few weeks, because it turns every coffee and every game purchase into a small decision with a small dose of guilt. Decisions are tiring, and the tracking habit is usually the first to go when life gets busy, which on a boat is always.

Behavioral economist Richard Thaler, who later won a Nobel Prize, described a set of mental habits he called **mental accounting**. People don't treat money as one interchangeable pool. They sort it into labeled buckets in their heads, such as rent money, fun money or found money, and they spend differently depending on the label. That breaks the textbook rule that a dollar is a dollar, and it explains a lot: why a tax refund or a deployment balance feels easier to blow than the same amount earned week by week.

Mental accounting is usually described as a bias. You can turn it into a tool. If your brain is going to label money anyway, set up the labels on purpose, in separate accounts, so the default action is the one you'd choose on your best day.

The Defense Department's own data shows why this matters. In the 2022 Status of Forces Survey, 65% of active-duty members said they followed a monthly budget or spending plan. Yet 35% reported at least one financial challenge in the previous year, up from 25% in 2020, and the average score on a standard financial well-being scale fell from 61 to 55. Having a budget on paper and having a system that holds up under pressure are not the same thing.

items.label: Active-duty members who said they follow a monthly budget (2022)
Reported at least one financial challenge in the past year, up from 25% in 2020
Junior enlisted with no emergency savings

blocks.source: OUSD(P&R), Financial Literacy and Preparedness of Members of the Armed Forces: 2022 Status of Forces Survey (Dec 2023)

blocks.text: Pay yourself first, automatically

The alternative is sometimes called pay-yourself-first, or a reverse budget. Instead of tracking spending and saving whatever is left, you move savings out first and spend whatever is left. The only numbers you have to decide are a few percentages and fixed amounts. After that, the system enforces itself, because money you never see in checking is money you don't miss.

This works because defaults are powerful. When economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied a company that switched its retirement plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment, participation jumped dramatically, and many new hires simply stayed at whatever rate the company had set. Inertia, which normally works against saving, started working for it. A pay-yourself-first system borrows the same trick: make saving the thing that happens unless you actively stop it.

blocks.title: The one-afternoon setup
items: Set your TSP contribution, taken from pay before it reaches you; at least enough to get the full BRS match
Open a separate savings account at a different bank or credit union, so it isn't one tap away
Set up an allotment or automatic transfer that moves a fixed amount there every payday
Put fixed bills (phone, insurance, subscriptions) on autopay from one bills account
Whatever remains in checking is guilt-free spending money: no tracking required

blocks.text: The point of separate accounts is friction. Money in the same app as your debit card is easy to borrow from yourself "just this once." Money at a different institution takes a deliberate step to reach. That small hassle is exactly the kind of speed bump that protects you from a 0200 impulse purchase after a rough watch. Allotments, which take money directly from military pay before it hits your account, can be set up through myPay.

One more bucket is worth adding once the basics run: a sinking fund for expenses that are certain but irregular. Car insurance that bills every six months, flights home on leave, holiday gifts, a new phone every few years. None of these are emergencies, yet they wreck budgets because they show up as big one-time hits. Add up what they cost in a year, divide by 24 paydays, and transfer that amount automatically. When the bill comes, the money is already sitting there.

A rough sanity check many people use is the 50/30/20 rule, popularized by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi: about half of take-home pay to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings. For service members living in barracks or aboard ship, with housing and meals largely covered, "needs" can be far smaller than half. That's the real advantage of this stage of life. A savings rate well above 20% can be possible without feeling deprived, simply because the biggest expenses most adults face aren't on your bill yet.

blocks.title: Two kinds of budget

left.head: Tracking budget
items: Log every purchase
Dozens of small decisions a week
Breaks down when you're busy or tired
Saving is whatever happens to be left

right.head: Default budget
items: Set percentages once
A few decisions a year
Keeps running underway with no input
Saving happens first, automatically

blocks.text: The guilt-free part is not a throwaway line. A system that leaves you no room to enjoy money is a system you'll eventually abandon. The goal is to spend the leftover on what you actually care about, whether that's a better PC, gym gear, travel or nights out with friends, and to be ruthless only about the things you don't care about. Recurring charges are the usual leak: streaming services, game passes and app subscriptions that each feel small and together can add up to a real monthly bill. A quick scan of your statement twice a year, cancelling anything you didn't use, often frees more money than any amount of skipping coffee.
The homecoming problem

Underway life creates a specific risk: money accumulates while you can't spend it, then you come home to a large balance at the exact moment you most want to celebrate. Psychologically, that balance feels like a windfall, even though it's just normal pay that piled up. The mental-accounting brain files it under found money, and found money gets spent fast.

The defense is to decide what happens to that money before you pull in, while you're calm and far from any store. Pick a split ahead of time, for example a set share to savings or investing, a set share for a real celebration, and the rest left for normal life, and write it down. When you get back, you're executing a plan rather than making a decision while tired, excited and surrounded by people suggesting expensive ideas. The habits article on delay discounting explains why the version of you planning ahead makes better calls than the version standing at the checkout.

The same logic covers the other big money moment: the emergency. The 2022 survey found most active-duty members had some emergency savings, with an average of about 3.1 months of expenses, but about one in five junior enlisted members had none. Without that cushion, a broken phone or a surprise travel cost turns into a credit card balance or an expensive loan. A starter emergency fund is usually the first job of that separate savings account.
Spend your raises before you get them

The most painless savings increase is the one you commit to before the money arrives. Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built a program around this idea called Save More Tomorrow, in which employees agreed in advance to send part of each future raise into their retirement savings. Because their take-home pay never went down, it didn't feel like a sacrifice, and participants' savings rates climbed substantially over the following years.

Military pay makes this easy to copy, because you know your raises are coming. Each January, at each promotion and at each years-of-service step, bump your TSP or savings allotment by part of the increase before you get used to the bigger paycheck. Your spending money still rises, just a bit more slowly than your pay. Over a few years, that habit can quietly double your savings rate without a single month that feels tighter than the one before.

The flip side is lifestyle creep: letting every raise turn into a permanently higher cost of living. A bigger car payment or a pricier phone plan feels great for a few months, then becomes the new normal, and the extra pay is spoken for forever. Fixed monthly commitments are the hardest spending to undo, so they deserve the most thought. One-time splurges fade; recurring ones compound against you.
The five-minute check-in

A default system doesn't mean zero attention. It means very little attention, on a schedule. Once a month, read your Leave and Earnings Statement: confirm your TSP percentage, your allotments and that the entitlements you're supposed to get are actually there. Pay errors happen, and the LES is where you'll catch them. Then glance at your savings balance and make sure the transfers ran. That's it.

Then, once a year, do a slightly bigger review. January is a natural moment, since that's when the annual raise shows up on your LES. Ask three questions: did the automatic transfers actually happen all year, is the emergency fund where you want it, and how much of this year's raise should go to savings before you start spending it? Fifteen minutes, once a year, is enough to keep the whole machine pointed in the right direction.

Watch for the predators, too. Areas around bases have long attracted high-cost lenders, aggressive car dealers and "military discount" financing that is anything but a discount. Federal law, the Military Lending Act, limits the cost of many types of credit offered to service members, but it doesn't cover everything and it can't stop you from signing a bad deal. If an offer needs an answer today, the answer is no until you've talked to someone neutral.

Every command has access to free, unbiased financial help. Your command financial specialist and the personal financial managers at Fleet and Family Support can review a budget, check your LES and talk through big purchases. This article explains the mechanics; they can look at your actual numbers.

takeaways: A budget that relies on daily willpower usually breaks; one built on automatic defaults keeps running underway.
Pay yourself first: TSP, savings allotment and bills move automatically, and what's left is guilt-free.
Decide what happens to your post-underway balance before you pull in.
Commit part of every raise and promotion to savings before you get used to it.
Read your LES once a month; it's the only tracking you really need.
