title: The Best Thing Money Can Buy Is an Hour
dek: Most people use spare cash to get more stuff. Research led by Ashley Whillans suggests buying back time makes people happier, and almost nobody does it.

blocks.text: Picture two Saturdays. On the first, you spend $40 on something you can hold: a game, a hoodie, a new set of earbuds. On the second, you spend the same $40 to make a chore disappear. Maybe you pay for a laundry service, order dinner instead of shopping and cooking, or pay a neighbor's kid to deal with the car. Which Saturday leaves you happier by the evening?

Most people bet on the stuff. It's tangible, it lasts, and spending money on a chore feels slightly lazy, even a little embarrassing. A team of psychologists led by Ashley Whillans, then at Harvard Business School, ran almost exactly this experiment. The time-saving Saturday won. And the more interesting finding came next: when they asked people how they'd spend extra money, almost nobody chose to buy time, even very rich people who could easily afford it.

That gap, between what makes people happier and what they actually do with spare cash, says something important about how badly we keep score with money. We count every dollar. We almost never count the hours.
Two weekends, one experiment

The study, published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* in 2017, came in two parts. The first was a set of large surveys covering 6,271 adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands. People reported whether they regularly spent money to offload tasks they disliked, such as cleaning, cooking or errands, and how satisfied they were with their lives. Those who bought time this way reported higher life satisfaction. The pattern wasn't limited to the rich; the senior author, Elizabeth Dunn, stressed that the benefits of buying time aren't just for wealthy people.

Surveys can't tell you which way the arrow points, though. Maybe happier people are simply more likely to hire a cleaner. So the team added a field experiment. Sixty working adults received $40 on two separate weekends. On one, they had to spend it on something that saved them time. On the other, they had to buy a material thing for themselves. The order was randomized. At the end of each day, people reported their mood and how pressed for time they felt.

On the time-saving weekend, participants reported more positive feelings and less time stress than on the material weekend. The money was identical. The difference was what it bought. The researchers' explanation is simple: feeling short on time is a steady background stressor, and paying to remove one draining task shrinks it, which leaves more room for the rest of the day to feel good.

items.label: Adults surveyed in four countries; those who paid to offload disliked tasks reported higher life satisfaction
Share of 98 working adults who said they'd use a $40 windfall to save time
Share of about 850 millionaires who spent nothing to outsource tasks they disliked

blocks.source: Whillans et al., PNAS, 2017; University of British Columbia, 2017

blocks.text: Why almost nobody does it

Here's the puzzle. When the researchers asked 98 working adults how they would spend an unexpected $40, only 2% said they would use it to save time. In a separate survey of roughly 850 millionaires, almost half said they spent no money at all outsourcing tasks they disliked. These are people for whom a cleaner or a meal service is a rounding error, and many of them still mop their own floors and resent it.

A few forces seem to push in the same direction. Stuff is visible and lasting. A new monitor sits on your desk and reminds you that you own it; the two hours you didn't spend at the laundromat leave no trace. Time also feels strangely elastic. Next week always looks emptier than this week, so trading money for time feels unnecessary, because surely you'll have more time later. You won't. Next week fills up exactly like this one did.

There's an identity piece, too. Many people, especially those who grew up without much money, feel that paying someone to do something you *could* do yourself is wasteful or self-indulgent. That instinct is useful when money is tight. It becomes a blind spot once it isn't, because it treats your hours as worth nothing. Money gets a price tag and a budget. Time gets neither, so it gets spent carelessly.

Think about how this plays out in a game you care about. Nobody who plays seriously grinds a low-value activity for hours when a better route exists; they optimize for progress per minute without thinking twice. Yet the same person will happily spend a free afternoon doing errands that could have been batched, delivered or skipped, because real-life hours don't come with an efficiency readout. The tools for valuing time are already in your head. They just aren't pointed at your actual life.
You track your money to the dollar and your time not at all. That's why time leaks. Before buying anything, it's worth asking: does this give me hours back, or does it cost me hours later?
Time poverty is a real cost

Researchers call the feeling of having too much to do and not enough time to do it *time poverty*, and it has been linked to stress and lower well-being. The Whillans paper opens with an odd observation: as countries around the world have grown richer, people's sense of time scarcity has grown too. More money hasn't bought more breathing room. If anything, the hours of people whose time is worth more get claimed by more things.

Other studies point the same way. In 2016, Hal Hershfield, Cassie Mogilner and Hanna Barnea found that people who said they would choose more time over more money tended to be happier than people who chose money. In a 2019 preregistered study, Whillans and colleagues followed about 1,000 graduating university students. Those who valued time over money went on to pick more intrinsically rewarding activities and jobs, and were happier a year later, even after accounting for how happy they were to begin with.

Commuting is the cleanest real-world example. In a classic study of German workers, economists Alois Stutzer and Bruno Frey found that people with longer commutes reported systematically lower well-being, and that they were not making up for it with better pay or cheaper housing. Standard economics predicts people would only accept a longer commute if something compensated them for it. In their data, nothing did. They called it the commuting paradox. For anyone choosing between a cheap apartment far from base and a pricier one ten minutes away, that's worth knowing: the cheaper place may cost you an hour a day, every day.

There's an important twist. A 2021 paper by Marissa Sharif, Cassie Mogilner and Hal Hershfield, using data from 35,375 Americans, found that well-being rises with free time only up to a point. Too little discretionary time was linked to lower well-being through stress. But having a lot of free time was also linked to lower well-being, apparently because people felt unproductive. When those people spent their free time on something purposeful, the drop shrank. So the goal isn't maximum leisure. It's enough time, used on things that matter.
What actually counts as buying time

Not every purchase that claims to save time does. A food delivery that replaces an hour of shopping and cooking you dread buys time. A gadget that needs setting up, updating and fixing often costs time. A subscription you forget to cancel costs time and money. The test is whether the purchase removes a task you actively dislike, and whether the hour it frees goes to something you value more.

blocks.title: Buying time vs. looking like it

left.head: Usually buys time
items: Paying to skip a chore you dread, like laundry or deep cleaning
Living closer to work, even for a bit more rent
A direct flight instead of a cheaper one with a long layover
Buying a used tool once instead of borrowing it every time

right.head: Often costs time
items: Gadgets that need constant setup, updates and troubleshooting
Cheap things that break and must be replaced
Saving $10 by driving 30 minutes to another store
Freed-up hours that go straight to the phone

blocks.text: That last item matters. Whillans has described how modern time gets shredded into what she calls *time confetti*: small scraps of a few minutes, broken up by notifications and quick checks. Buying back an hour does little if the hour gets confettied into scrolling. The research finding is about time spent on rest, people and meaningful work, not about time in general.

The idea also has limits. If paying for a service leaves you anxious about rent, you've swapped one stressor for a bigger one. The studies found benefits across income levels, but nobody is arguing that a person with no cushion should hire a housekeeper. The principle is about where the next dollar of *discretionary* money goes, after the bills and the savings are handled.
A system for your own hours

Military life complicates this in useful ways. Underway, you can't buy time at all. The schedule is set, the chores are assigned, and no app delivers to a boat at depth. That makes in-port time more valuable, not less. A long duty rotation leaves only so many free days, and every one spent doing errands you hate is a day you didn't spend training, building something or seeing people.

Think about what a typical in-port week actually contains: duty days, qualifications, PT, the drive in, the laundry that piled up during the last underway, meals, a car that needs attention, and the errands you put off. Most of those are fixed. A few aren't. The ones that drain you most are rarely the longest; they're the ones that feel pointless, like waiting in line, cleaning up after a week of not cleaning, or doing paperwork you could have done in five minutes if it hadn't been buried. Those are the best candidates for spending a little money, or a little planning, to make them go away.

blocks.title: Run a simple time audit
items: List the recurring tasks in a normal in-port week and roughly how long each takes.
Mark the ones you actively dread, not just the ones that take long.
For each dreaded task, find the cheapest way to make it disappear or shrink.
Try one for a month and notice how your free days feel, not just how many hours you saved.
Decide in advance what the freed time is for, so it doesn't leak into scrolling.

blocks.text: A rough way to frame the trade: figure out what an hour of your after-tax pay is worth, then ask whether paying someone that much or less to take a dreaded hour off your hands feels like a good deal. It's not a precise formula, and it ignores the fact that your free hours are scarce in a way your work hours aren't. But it breaks the habit of treating your own time as free.

The biggest version of this idea is saving itself. Money in the bank is stored time. Six months of expenses saved means six months you could spend between jobs, in school, or building a business without panic. Seen this way, buying time and saving money aren't opposites. They're two versions of the same move: using money to get control over your hours instead of letting money control them.
What the evidence can and can't say

It's worth being honest about how solid this is. The field experiment that gives the causal evidence had 60 people, which is small, and it relied on self-reported mood. The large surveys are correlational, so they can't fully rule out that happier, more organized people just tend to hire help. Most samples come from wealthy Western countries. The effects are real but modest; buying a meal kit will not transform your life.

Still, the core point is hard to dismiss, and it has the advantage of being cheap to test. You don't need a peer-reviewed study to find out whether paying $20 to skip a chore you hate improves your Saturday. You can run that experiment on yourself next time you're in port, and keep the result.

A good way to run that test is to compare two in-port weekends, one where you outsource or skip a single dreaded chore and one where you don't, and simply notice how the evenings feel. Keep the experiment honest by spending the same amount either way. That's essentially the design of the study, shrunk to a sample size of one. It won't prove anything to a scientist. It might tell you something about yourself.

The deeper reframe is this: money is a tool for buying the life you want, and a life is made of hours. People who get that tend to spend differently. They worry less about owning the newest thing and more about whether their days feel like theirs.

takeaways: In a randomized field study, spending $40 to save time made people happier than spending $40 on stuff.
Almost nobody does it: 2% chose to buy time with a windfall, and about half of millionaires surveyed outsourced nothing they disliked.
Long commutes are linked to lower well-being that pay and cheaper housing don't make up for.
Buy time only with discretionary money, and decide what the freed hours are for.
Savings are stored time: every month of expenses saved is a month of freedom.

title: The Real Math of Retiring Early
dek: How soon you can stop working depends mostly on one number you control. The famous 4% rule behind it is shakier for long retirements than the internet admits.

blocks.text: Two people start working at 20. The first earns a big salary and saves 10% of it, like the standard advice says. The second earns half as much but lives on half of what comes in and invests the rest. Who can stop working first? It isn't close. Under one common set of assumptions, the high earner needs about 51 years. The saver needs about 17.

That result is the engine behind FIRE, short for Financial Independence, Retire Early, a movement that grew online through the 2010s with blogs, forums and a lot of spreadsheets. Its central claim sounds too simple to be true: how soon you can stop needing a paycheck depends far more on what fraction of your income you keep than on how much you earn.

The math is real. But the internet version usually leaves out the hard parts: where the famous 4% rule came from, why it gets shakier the earlier you retire, and why people who reach the finish line sometimes find it isn't what they wanted. This is the full picture, so you can decide what to take from it.
The one equation

Start with your *FI number*, the amount of invested money that could cover your yearly spending indefinitely. The FIRE rule of thumb is 25 times annual spending. If you spend $40,000 a year, the target is $1 million. The 25 comes from the 4% rule, which says you can withdraw 4% of a portfolio in the first year and raise that amount with inflation each year after. One divided by 0.04 is 25.

Now notice what your savings rate does. When you save more, two things happen at once. You put more money toward the goal each year, and you shrink the goal itself, because you've proven you can live on less. A person who lives on 90% of their income needs to replace 90% of it. A person who lives on 50% only needs to replace half. That double effect is why the curve below is so steep.

blocks.title: Years of work until financially independent, by savings rate
blocks.note: Assumes starting from $0, a 5% annual return after inflation, and retiring at 25x annual spending
blocks.source: Calculated using the assumptions in Mr. Money Mustache, The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Early Retirement, 2012

blocks.text: Income is missing from that chart on purpose. Under these assumptions, two people with the same savings rate reach independence in the same number of years whether they earn $40,000 or $400,000. Income still matters a great deal in practice, because it's far easier to save 50% of a large paycheck than of a small one. But the chart's point stands: lifestyle creep, the habit of spending every raise, quietly erases the advantage of earning more.

It also tells you where to look for savings. Daily coffee gets the attention, but the big levers are the few large, recurring costs: housing, vehicles and food. A cheaper car payment or a roommate changes your savings rate every single month without requiring willpower every single day. One good decision about a big fixed cost often beats a hundred small acts of self-denial.

Two assumptions in that math deserve suspicion. A 5% return after inflation is a reasonable long-run guess for a stock-heavy portfolio, not a promise; real returns have been much lower for a decade at a time. And the 4% withdrawal rule wasn't designed for early retirees at all.
Where 4% came from

In 1994, a financial planner named William Bengen tested withdrawal rates against historical US market returns. He asked a simple question: what's the highest starting withdrawal, adjusted for inflation each year, that would have survived every 30-year retirement in the record? His answer was roughly 4%. A few years later, a study by three professors at Trinity University reached similar conclusions, and the 4% rule became the most famous number in retirement planning.

The key words are *30-year*. Bengen was modeling a person retiring around 65. Also, 4% was the *worst case* in the historical record, not a typical outcome. In many historical periods, a retiree following it would have ended up with plenty left over. In the worst ones, such as retiring just before a long stretch of high inflation or a deep crash, it barely held.

Morningstar publishes an updated estimate every year using forward-looking assumptions about stock and bond returns. Its figure for a 30-year retirement with a 90% chance of not running out of money has bounced between 3.3% and 4.0% in recent years, moving mainly with its expectations for future stock and bond returns. Its 2025 estimate was 3.9%. The lesson isn't that one of these numbers is right. It's that the safe rate depends on conditions at the moment you retire, which you can't choose.

blocks.title: Morningstar's safe starting withdrawal rate, 30-year retirement
blocks.note: 90% probability of success, 30% to 50% stocks, excluding Social Security
blocks.source: Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income, 2025

blocks.text: The 4% rule is a historical worst case for a 30-year retirement. Retire at 40 and you might need your money to last 50 years or more, which is a different problem.
The 40-year problem

Karsten Jeske, an economist who writes the *Early Retirement Now* blog, ran one of the most detailed public studies of withdrawal rates for long retirements, using US market data going back to 1871. One example from his work captures the issue. With a portfolio split evenly between stocks and bonds, a 4% withdrawal survived about 95% of historical 30-year periods but only about 65% of 60-year periods. Stretching the timeline made failure roughly seven times more likely.

His conclusion for early retirees was that 3.5% is closer to the real safe number, possibly lower if stock prices are high when you retire. That sounds like a small tweak. It isn't. At 3.5%, the multiple rises from 25 times spending to about 28.6 times, so the $1 million target becomes about $1.14 million. At 3.25%, it becomes about $1.23 million.

The reason long retirements are fragile is *sequence-of-returns risk*. If the market drops hard in the first few years after you stop working, you're selling investments at low prices to pay your bills, and those shares are gone before the recovery. The same average return in a different order can leave you rich or broke. Over a 30-year retirement, a bad start can be survived. Over 50 years, it has more time to compound.

blocks.title: Two kinds of retirement

left.head: Traditional, at 65
items: About 30 years to fund
Social Security and Medicare arrive on schedule
4% has held up in the historical worst case
Little time for a bad start to compound

right.head: Early, at 40
items: 50 years or more to fund
Decades of health insurance to buy yourself
Safer to plan around 3.5% or less
A crash in year two can shape the next five decades

blocks.text: What the spreadsheet leaves out

Health insurance is the biggest blind spot. People who stop working before 65 lose employer coverage and aren't yet eligible for Medicare, so they pay for decades of coverage out of their portfolio. Kids, aging parents, a house that needs a roof, and the simple fact that spending is hard to predict thirty years out all push the real number higher.

The other blind spot is psychological. A 2021 study by Marissa Sharif, Cassie Mogilner and Hal Hershfield, drawing on data from 35,375 Americans, found that well-being rises with free time only to a point. Too little was linked to stress. But a lot of free time was also linked to lower well-being, because people felt unproductive. When people with abundant free time spent it on productive or purposeful activities, the downside shrank. The lesson for FIRE is clear: retiring *from* something is not the same as retiring *to* something.

There are practical snags too. Most retirement accounts, including the TSP, are built for people who stop working in their late 50s or 60s, and pulling money out early can trigger taxes and penalties unless you use one of the specific exceptions. Early retirees need a plan for how to reach their money in the gap years, which usually means some savings in regular taxable accounts as well. Inflation is another quiet threat: a budget that feels comfortable at 40 can feel tight at 70 if your personal costs rise faster than average.

Critics of the movement also point out that extreme frugality can become its own trap. Someone who spends a decade saying no to friends, travel and experiences to hit a number has traded away years that don't come back. The research on time and happiness suggests that money spent on relationships and on reducing daily stress pays real dividends. A plan that makes your twenties miserable to make your forties free is a trade worth questioning, not an automatic win.

That's why many people in the FIRE world don't actually stop working. They change the deal. *Barista FIRE* means covering part of your spending with a low-stress job. *Coast FIRE* means investing heavily early, then saving nothing more and letting compounding finish the job while you earn just enough to live. These versions are far more forgiving. Even a small income in the early years of retirement sharply reduces sequence-of-returns risk, because you sell fewer shares when prices are down.

Flexibility works the same way on the spending side. Retirees who are willing to trim their withdrawals for a year or two after a bad market can usually start with a higher rate than those who insist on a fixed, inflation-adjusted paycheck no matter what. The 4% rule assumes total rigidity. Real people rarely need to be that rigid, and the ability to adapt is worth a lot.

Here's the coast idea in numbers. Money growing at 5% a year after inflation roughly doubles every 14 years. If a 25-year-old had $100,000 invested and never added another dollar, at that rate it would be worth about $432,000 in today's money at 55. The earliest dollars do the heaviest lifting, which is the single most important point for someone in their early twenties.
The young-sailor version

A junior sailor has a few unusual advantages here. Housing and food are partly covered through allowances or provided outright. There's no commute while underway and few chances to spend. The Thrift Savings Plan comes with government matching, covered in detail in a separate article. And most importantly, a 20-year-old has the one ingredient no high earner can buy: decades of compounding ahead.

There's also a built-in version of early retirement in the military itself. Someone who serves 20 years can collect a lifetime, inflation-adjusted pension starting around age 40, along with military health coverage. Not everyone wants to stay that long, and that's a legitimate choice. But it's worth recognizing the pension for what it is in FIRE terms: a large, guaranteed income stream that would take a big portfolio to replicate.

For someone leaving after one enlistment, the most valuable FIRE lesson may not be early retirement at all. It's that a high savings rate during your twenties buys options in your thirties: the freedom to go to school full time, take a lower-paying job you love, or start a business without the pressure of needing it to pay rent in month three.

blocks.title: Find your own numbers
items: Track what you actually spend for three months, including irregular costs.
Multiply your yearly spending by 25 for a traditional target, or about 28 to 30 for an early one.
Calculate your savings rate: what you invest divided by your take-home pay.
Count your runway: how many months of expenses you could cover with no income.
Raise the savings rate by cutting big fixed costs before small daily ones.

blocks.text: Freedom is a spectrum

The most useful reframe from FIRE has nothing to do with retiring at 40. It's measuring wealth in time instead of dollars. Divide your savings by your monthly spending, and you get the number of months you could live without a paycheck. Three months means a job loss is a crisis. Two years means it's an opportunity. Ten years means work becomes optional.

Every month added to that number is a small piece of independence, and you don't have to reach the end to benefit. A person with a year of runway negotiates differently, takes smarter risks and tolerates a bad boss less. The finish line is optional. The direction is what changes your life.

The honest version of FIRE, then, is less a promise than a set of tools: know your spending, push your savings rate as high as you can sustain without hating your life, invest simply, and treat the 4% rule as a rough guide that gets less reliable the longer you need the money to last.

takeaways: Your savings rate, not your income, mostly decides how many years until you're financially independent.
The 4% rule came from 30-year retirements and was the historical worst case, not the typical outcome.
Early retirees face a longer horizon; 3.5% or less is a safer planning number.
Health insurance and purpose are the two biggest things FIRE spreadsheets leave out.
Measure wealth in months of runway; every month added is a piece of freedom.

title: The Business of Selling You a Business
dek: Dropshipping courses, done-for-you stores and crypto hype share one pattern: the steady money goes to whoever sells the dream. What FTC data and court cases show.

blocks.text: The pitch was polished. A company called Click Profit promised buyers a hands-off online store on Amazon, Walmart or TikTok, run by its own AI-powered system. Ads talked about six- to eight-figure incomes and the chance to sell the store later at a multiple. The price of entry was a management fee of at least $45,000, plus thousands more for inventory.

In March 2025, the Federal Trade Commission sued. According to the FTC's complaint, over a fifth of the Amazon stores earned nothing after fees, and another third made less than $2,500 in gross sales over their entire lifetime. Amazon blocked, suspended or terminated roughly 95% of them. Most buyers, the FTC alleged, lost everything they paid, and some were left with credit card debt and boxes of unsold products. These are allegations; a court decides the case. But the pattern is one the FTC has seen again and again.

This article is about that pattern, the business of selling people the dream of a business. It shows up in dropshipping courses, done-for-you Amazon stores, trading signal groups and crypto hype. Not everything in these worlds is a scam. But the reliable money is very often made by the person selling the dream, not the person buying it.
The scale of it

Each year the FTC publishes data from its Consumer Sentinel Network, a database of fraud reports from the public. For 2025, the FTC reported about 3 million fraud reports and $15.9 billion in reported losses. Investment scams were the largest category by far, at $7.9 billion. A year earlier, the totals were $12.5 billion lost, with investment scams at $5.7 billion and business and job opportunity scams at about $750 million.

Two things make these numbers worse than they look. First, they only count what people reported, and most fraud victims never report. Second, the share of reporters who actually lost money is rising: 38% in 2024, up from 27% the year before. Younger adults aren't immune. In the 2024 data, 44% of people in their twenties who reported fraud said they lost money.

Military consumers show up in the data too. In 2024, service members, veterans and their families filed 99,443 fraud reports with $584 million in losses. The median loss was $700. But in the investment category, the median loss was $10,000, and in business and job opportunities it was $2,800. These are the categories where people hand over real savings, not pocket change.

blocks.text: Selling the shovel

During the California Gold Rush, many of the people who reliably made money weren't miners. They were the merchants selling picks, pans and jeans to miners. The modern online version is the course. When someone with a rented sports car and a screenshot of a big sales day offers to teach you their system, it's worth asking a simple question: which business is actually making this person money, the store or the course?

The FTC's recent cases sketch a common shape. Ecommerce Empire Builders sold training programs costing nearly $2,000 and done-for-you online storefronts costing up to $35,000, promising profits of $10,000 a month. In May 2025, a court order permanently banned the company and its owner from selling business opportunities, with a $9.8 million judgment, partly suspended because they couldn't pay. In June 2025, the FTC announced a settlement banning the operators of Ascend Ecom, which it said had taken at least $25 million from consumers with promises that AI-powered tools would bring in thousands of dollars a month in passive income.

Several of these operations also tried to stop customers from complaining. The FTC said Click Profit cited a non-disparagement clause to threaten people who complained, and the Ascend and Empire orders specifically banned contract terms that keep consumers from posting reviews or reporting problems. When a business needs to legally prevent you from describing your experience, that tells you something about the experience.

blocks.title: The guru funnel
items: Free video showing a lifestyle and big sales screenshots
Cheap course or community that teaches the basics
Expensive coaching, mastermind or done-for-you store
Poor results blamed on your effort or mindset
Pitch for the next, more advanced tier

blocks.text: Notice how the loop protects the seller. If you fail, the problem was your execution, so the solution is more coaching. The model works for the seller regardless of whether anyone downstream makes money. That is the core tell of a get-rich-quick product: the seller's income doesn't depend on the buyer's success.

It's also worth knowing how to read the proof. A screenshot of a $50,000 month usually shows revenue, the total money customers paid, not profit. Take out the product cost, ad spend, fees and refunds and the real number can be small or negative. And the people posting screenshots are a filtered group: the few who did well, plus the ones paid to say so. You never see the thousands who tried quietly and stopped.

None of this is a judgment on the people who buy in. These pitches are designed for ambitious people who want more than a paycheck, who are willing to work and who are tired of being told to be patient. That's exactly why they work. The target isn't the lazy or the foolish. It's the hungry.
Dropshipping, honestly

Dropshipping itself is a real, legal business model. You run an online store, a customer orders, and a supplier ships the product directly to them. You never touch inventory. Some people do build profitable businesses this way. The question isn't whether it's possible. It's whether the version being sold to beginners makes sense.

Here's the problem in plain terms. If you can set up a store selling a product from a supplier in an afternoon, so can thousands of other people, often selling the identical item. There's no barrier to entry, which means there's no protection from competition. The only way to win is to find customers more cheaply than everyone else, which usually means paid ads, which means your profit is decided by an auction you don't control.

Run some made-up but realistic-looking arithmetic. Say you sell a gadget for $30 that costs you $10 including shipping. That looks like a $20 profit. Now subtract the payment processing fee, the store platform's monthly cost, and refunds from customers annoyed by slow shipping. Then subtract the ad spend needed to get each sale. If it takes $15 of ads to land one $30 order, most of your margin is gone before you've paid yourself anything. Courses tend to show revenue screenshots. The number that decides everything is ad cost per sale, and it rarely appears in the highlight reel.

You'll often see claims like "90% of dropshippers fail." Be skeptical of those too. There's no reliable public dataset on dropshipping success rates, and many of the statistics floating around trace back to companies selling apps or courses. The honest answer is that nobody outside the platforms knows the real number. What the FTC cases do show is what happens in the worst version: stores that never open, stores suspended by the platform, and buyers who end up in debt.

There's also platform risk. A store that lives on Amazon, Shopify or TikTok exists by permission. One policy change, one complaint pattern or one automated review can freeze the account and the money in it. The Click Profit allegation that about 95% of stores were blocked, suspended or terminated is an extreme case, but the underlying risk applies to anyone building on someone else's platform. If you do want to try dropshipping, do it with a small budget you're prepared to lose, treat it as paid lessons in marketing, and never pay someone tens of thousands of dollars to do it for you.
A business that anyone can start in an afternoon is a business anyone can copy in an afternoon. Ask what makes yours hard to copy. If the answer is nothing, you're competing on ad spend alone.
Crypto: hype as a business model

Crypto has its own version of the shovel problem. Researchers at the Bank for International Settlements studied crypto exchange app use in 95 countries from 2015 to 2022. They estimated that between 73% and 81% of retail investors had likely lost money on their initial bitcoin investment. The reason was timing: app downloads surged when prices were rising, so most people arrived after the run-up, just in time for the fall.

Then there are outright scams. Investment fraud was the FTC's largest loss category in both 2024 and 2025, and in 2024 the losses paid through bank transfers or cryptocurrency exceeded losses through all other payment methods combined. A common pattern starts with a friendly stranger on social media or a dating app, slowly builds trust, then introduces a "platform" that shows impressive fake gains until the victim tries to withdraw. Crypto payments are hard to reverse, which is exactly why scammers prefer them.

Influencer coins and pump-and-dump schemes follow the same shovel logic as the courses. Early insiders buy cheap, hype the coin to their audience, and sell into the wave of late buyers they created. The audience provides the exit.

A few habits filter out most of this. Real investments don't guarantee high returns, because nothing that can rise a lot is free of the risk of falling a lot. Real brokers and advisers can be looked up on FINRA's free BrokerCheck tool. Real platforms let you withdraw your money without a surprise fee or a sudden "tax" to unlock it. And no legitimate opportunity requires you to decide before you've had time to sleep on it. Urgency is a tactic, not a feature.
Red flags and the honest alternative

items: Promises of passive, guaranteed or effortless income.
"AI does everything" or "fully automated" claims.
Income screenshots without full costs, refunds and ad spend.
The seller makes most of their money teaching the method, not using it.
Pressure: limited spots, countdown timers, "price goes up tonight."
Encouragement to use credit cards, loans or retirement money to pay.
Contracts that bar you from complaining or posting reviews.
Payment requested in crypto, gift cards or wire transfers.

blocks.text: The FTC's Business Opportunity Rule requires sellers of many money-making opportunities to give buyers a short disclosure document before they pay, and to have written evidence for any earnings claims they make. If a seller dodges that question, or the earnings claims can't be backed up, walk away. And if you've been hit, report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; those reports are exactly the data that builds the cases above.

None of this means building a business is a bad idea. It means the real version looks different. Real small businesses usually start slow and cheap: a few hundred dollars, not tens of thousands. They sell something with an edge, such as a skill, an audience, a product you made, or knowledge of a niche others don't have. They test demand before scaling. A Roblox game, a YouTube channel or a small online store built around something you know well all fit that mold. The skills involved, like marketing, writing, building and analyzing data, compound over years.

blocks.text: The most useful question to carry around is simple: who is making money here, and from whom? If the honest answer is that the money comes from people like you buying the program, then you're not the business owner. You're the customer, and the product is hope.

In FTC cases, done-for-you store schemes charged up to tens of thousands and most buyers lost money.
Dropshipping is legal but easy to copy; ad cost per sale decides profit, and courses rarely show it.
An estimated 73% to 81% of retail bitcoin app investors likely lost money, mostly by arriving late.
Always ask: is the seller's income coming from the business or from selling it to you?

title: Two GI Bills and One Decision Not to Rush
dek: The Montgomery and Post-9/11 GI Bills pay for school in completely different ways, and court rulings in 2024 and 2025 changed the rules for people who have both. The rules as of November 2026.

blocks.text: Thirty-six months at the current full-time Montgomery GI Bill rate comes to $93,636. That's real money, and it's only one of the two education programs many sailors can draw on. Yet plenty of people spend more time comparing phones than figuring out how their GI Bill actually works.

A common belief goes something like this: the Montgomery GI Bill covers about three years of college plus housing. That sentence mixes up two different programs. The Montgomery GI Bill sends you a flat monthly check and leaves the rest to you. The Post-9/11 GI Bill pays the school directly and adds a separate housing allowance. Which one is better depends on where and how you study, and a Supreme Court case in 2024, followed by a second court ruling in 2025, changed the rules for many people who have both.

These are the rules as published on VA.gov as of November 2026. Benefits law and VA policy change. Confirm everything with the VA and your base education office before making a decision. This is general information, not financial or legal advice.
Two different machines

The Montgomery GI Bill for active duty, known as Chapter 30 or MGIB-AD, is the one you pay into. If you entered active duty after June 30, 1985, and didn't opt out, $100 a month was taken from your pay for your first 12 months, $1,200 in total. To use it, you generally need an honorable discharge, a high school diploma or equivalent, and enough continuous service, typically three years, or two if that was your enlistment agreement. Most people get up to 36 months of benefits, and you usually have 10 years after leaving the service to use them.

MGIB-AD pays a fixed monthly rate directly to you. For October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027, the full-time rate for someone with at least three years of continuous active duty is $2,601 a month. Three-quarter-time students get $1,950.75 and half-time students get $1,300.50. Out of that check, you pay your own tuition, books and rent. The rate goes up most years; the same full-time rate was $2,358 in 2023–24 and $2,438 in 2024–25.

items.label: MGIB-AD full-time monthly rate, 3+ years of service (Oct. 1, 2026 to Sept. 30, 2027)
Full-time rate with 2 to 3 years of service
What you paid in: $100 a month for 12 months

blocks.source: US Department of Veterans Affairs, VA.gov, 2026

blocks.text: The Post-9/11 GI Bill, Chapter 33, works differently. You don't pay into it. Anyone with at least 90 days of active duty after September 10, 2001, qualifies for some level of benefit, and the percentage rises with service time. At 100%, it covers full in-state tuition and fees at public schools, paid straight to the school. Private and foreign schools are capped; for August 1, 2026, through July 31, 2027, the cap is $30,908.34 a year.

On top of tuition, Post-9/11 pays a monthly housing allowance when you attend more than half time. For in-person classes, it's based on the military housing allowance for an E-5 with dependents at your school's location, so it's much larger in expensive cities. For fully online students, it's half the national average, up to $1,198 a month. There's also up to $1,000 a year for books and supplies. Benefits don't expire for anyone whose service ended on or after January 1, 2013, and with Defense Department approval, service members can transfer some or all of the benefit to a spouse or child.

Two smaller details matter at the edges. Benefits are counted in months of entitlement, so going full time burns them faster than part time but also pays the full rate. And for private schools that cost more than the yearly cap, the Yellow Ribbon Program lets participating schools cover part of the gap, with the VA matching their contribution, for students at the 100% benefit level. Not every school participates, and those that do often limit the number of spots.

blocks.title: Post-9/11 GI Bill benefit level by active-duty service
blocks.note: Service on or after Sept. 11, 2001. Some other paths, such as a Purple Heart, also qualify for 100%.
blocks.source: VA.gov, Post-9/11 GI Bill rates, effective Aug. 1, 2026

blocks.text: Where each one wins

blocks.title: The two GI Bills side by side

left.head: Montgomery (Chapter 30)
items: You paid $1,200 to join
Flat monthly check paid to you
You cover tuition, books and rent from it
Usually must be used within 10 years of leaving

right.head: Post-9/11 (Chapter 33)
items: No buy-in
Tuition paid to the school, plus housing and books
Housing tied to E-5 BAH where you study
No expiration for service ending in 2013 or later

blocks.text: For many people attending in person, especially at a public school in a high-cost area, Post-9/11 is the bigger package. It covers the tuition outright and then pays a housing allowance on top, which in an expensive city can be large. That's where the "college plus housing" idea comes from. It describes Post-9/11, not Montgomery.

Montgomery can come out ahead when tuition is low. Because it pays the same flat amount no matter what the school charges, a cheap community college or low-cost program leaves more of the check in your pocket. Online study is a good test case. Under Post-9/11, a fully online student gets tuition covered plus up to $1,198 a month for housing. Under Montgomery, the same student gets $2,601 a month and pays tuition out of it. On those numbers alone, Montgomery leaves more cash whenever monthly tuition is under about $1,400. That's rough arithmetic, not a verdict; the real comparison depends on your enrollment, your benefit percentage, breaks between terms and the specific school.

The VA's online GI Bill Comparison Tool runs these calculations for a specific school and situation. It's worth using before you choose, because the gap between the two programs can be thousands of dollars a year in either direction.

It also helps to know that the GI Bill isn't only for four-year degrees. According to the VA, the benefits can pay for non-college degree programs, apprenticeships and on-the-job training, flight training, and licensing and certification tests. For a sailor planning to move into civilian nuclear power, skilled trades or technical work, those uses can be more valuable than a degree program, and the right program choice can look different for each one. A flat Montgomery check during a paid apprenticeship works very differently from a Post-9/11 housing allowance tied to a campus.
What Rudisill changed

For years, people eligible for both programs faced a hard choice. To use Post-9/11, you generally had to give up Montgomery, and your Post-9/11 benefit was capped at whatever Montgomery time you had left. Older VA material says that choice can't be changed once made.

Then an Army veteran named James Rudisill, who had served multiple separate periods of active duty, challenged that limit. On April 16, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled in *Rudisill v. McDonough* that veterans with separate periods of service qualifying for each program may use both, up to a combined 48 months. In 2025, the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims went further in *Perkins v. Collins*, holding that a veteran with a single obligated period of service may also qualify for both, if that period is long enough and contains qualifying time for each program.

blocks.title: How the GI Bill rules got here
items: The original GI Bill helps World War II veterans attend college
Montgomery GI Bill begins for those entering active duty after June 30
Congress creates the Post-9/11 GI Bill
Forever GI Bill removes the time limit for service ending in 2013 or later
Apr 2024
Supreme Court decides Rudisill v. McDonough
Perkins v. Collins extends the idea to some single periods of service
Mar 2026
VA says veterans no longer need to request a Rudisill review
Oct 2026
Current MGIB-AD rates take effect

blocks.text: According to the VA's Rudisill page, last updated in October 2026, people eligible under these decisions no longer have to give up Montgomery to use Post-9/11, Post-9/11 is no longer capped at your remaining Montgomery time, and people who previously gave up Montgomery can revoke that choice. The overall limit across programs is still 48 months. The VA says it is automatically reviewing the files of about 1.04 million affected veterans rather than requiring them to apply.

The VA's Montgomery page adds a useful line: if you served 56 months or more on active duty, you may qualify for up to 48 months combined across both programs. With less than 56 months, you can generally use only one benefit, with Post-9/11 capped at 36 months. Nuclear-field sailors usually sign up for six years, which is longer than 56 months. That doesn't guarantee anything. How your months are counted toward each program is a VA decision, and the details are new enough that it's worth getting a written answer.

Why does an extra 12 months matter? A typical bachelor's degree takes about four academic years of roughly nine months each, which is about 36 months of benefits. A 48-month limit can stretch to cover a full degree with room for a graduate certificate, part of a master's, or a summer of extra courses. For someone starting from scratch, a year of paid school is a serious difference.

It's also a reminder that VA's own pages don't always agree. The older comparison chart on the VA site, last updated in 2025, still says the choice between programs cannot be changed, while the newer Rudisill page says earlier waivers can now be revoked. When official sources conflict, the newest specific guidance usually reflects current policy, but that's exactly the kind of thing to confirm with a person, not a webpage.

One more detail: if you relinquish Montgomery, use Post-9/11 and have less than 56 months of active duty, the VA refunds part or all of your $1,200 contribution. And if you paid into the optional $600 Montgomery buy-up program, which increases Montgomery payments, that money does nothing for you under Post-9/11.
Using it while you're still in

While you're on active duty, both programs pay less. Montgomery pays the monthly rate or your actual tuition and fees, whichever is lower. Post-9/11 pays no housing allowance to active-duty members. In other words, the most valuable parts of each benefit are designed for after you leave.

That's why most service members take classes on active duty through Tuition Assistance, a separate military program that pays for courses without touching your GI Bill entitlement. There's also a Tuition Assistance Top-Up option that uses your GI Bill to cover what Tuition Assistance doesn't, but it spends GI Bill months to do it. The months are the scarce resource, so it's worth thinking twice before using them on courses that Tuition Assistance could mostly cover.

If you ever want to transfer Post-9/11 benefits to a future spouse or child, timing matters. A transfer generally has to be requested while you're still serving, and it usually comes with an additional service obligation. Leave first, and that door typically closes. It's a decision to make deliberately before separating, not to discover afterward.

For someone who spends long stretches underway, the practical window for classes is usually shore duty or the time between deployments. A few online courses through Tuition Assistance, finished before leaving the service, can mean starting school as a civilian with credits already banked and the full GI Bill still intact.
What to check before you choose

blocks.title: Before you use either benefit
items: Confirm on your pay records that the $1,200 Montgomery contribution was actually taken.
Visit your base education office or Navy College office and ask about Tuition Assistance first.
Check your eligibility and remaining entitlement on VA.gov.
Run your target schools through the VA's GI Bill Comparison Tool under both programs.
Ask the VA in writing whether Rudisill or Perkins applies to your service history.
Don't give up Montgomery or make an election until you're about to enroll and understand the trade.

blocks.text: Be careful with schools, too. Because GI Bill money is reliable, some schools recruit veterans aggressively, with fast enrollment, glossy promises about careers and pressure to sign up before you've compared options. The VA's comparison tool shows whether a school follows its Principles of Excellence program, which commits schools to things like clear cost information and no high-pressure recruiting, and flags cautionary information about schools. A school that pushes you to decide this week is a school to slow down with.

The bigger point is about attitude. Many people treat the GI Bill as a vague promise that school will be paid for someday. It's better understood as a large, specific asset with rules, deadlines and trade-offs, worth tens of thousands of dollars, sometimes much more. Assets like that deserve a plan.

Rules may have changed by the time you read this, and your situation has details no article can see. Before you decide, confirm the current rules with the VA, at VA.gov or by phone at 1-800-698-2411, and with your base education office.

takeaways: Montgomery pays a flat monthly check to you; Post-9/11 pays the school plus housing and books.
As of Oct. 1, 2026, the full-time Montgomery rate is $2,601 a month for 3+ years of service.
Post-9/11 usually wins for in-person school in high-cost areas; Montgomery can win when tuition is low.
Rudisill (2024) and Perkins (2025) let some people use both, up to 48 months combined.
Use Tuition Assistance on active duty, and confirm everything with the VA and your education office.

title: Does Money Buy Happiness? The Rivals Who Settled It Together
dek: One famous study said happiness stops rising at $75,000. Another said it never stops. Then the authors teamed up, and the answer turned out to depend on who you are.

blocks.text: In 2010, two Nobel-winning economists published a short paper with a number that escaped into the wild. Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton reported that Americans' day-to-day happiness rose with income, but only up to about $75,000 a year. After that, the line went flat. The figure spread everywhere: in articles, in talks, and famously in 2015, when a Seattle CEO cited it while raising his company's minimum salary to $70,000.

Eleven years later, a younger researcher named Matthew Killingsworth looked at a much bigger pile of real-time data and found no plateau at all. Happiness kept climbing with income, well past $75,000. Two credible studies, two opposite answers. What happened next is rarer in science than it should be: the rivals sat down together, with a neutral referee, to figure out who was right. The answer is more interesting than either original claim, and it says a lot about what money actually does for people.
Two kinds of happiness

The first step is to notice that "happiness" means two different things. One is how you feel in the moments of your life: whether this afternoon was pleasant, stressful, boring or fun. Researchers call this emotional or experienced well-being. The other is how you judge your life when you step back and think about it, often measured by asking people to rate their life on a ladder from worst possible to best possible. That's life evaluation.

These two don't always move together. Someone grinding through a hard but meaningful stretch, like nuke school or a demanding deployment, might rate their life highly while feeling pretty rough most hours of the day. Someone drifting through easy, pleasant days might feel fine moment to moment and still rate their life as going nowhere. Any honest answer about money has to say which kind of happiness it means.
The $75,000 plateau

Kahneman and Deaton analyzed more than 450,000 responses to a daily Gallup survey of US residents. For life evaluation, the pattern was simple: the more money people had, the better they rated their lives, with no sign of stopping. For emotional well-being, measured by asking whether people had felt things like enjoyment, stress or sadness the previous day, the picture was different. It rose with income, then stopped improving at around $75,000 a year.

They also found that low income made life's other blows hurt more. Divorce, illness and loneliness were associated with more emotional pain among people with less money. And they noted that for everyday emotions, other factors, such as health, caregiving, loneliness and smoking, were relatively stronger predictors than income. Their summary was memorable: high income buys life satisfaction but not happiness.

One detail people often forget: that $75,000 figure was in 2008 and 2009 dollars. Adjusted with the Consumer Price Index, it's roughly $118,000 in late-2026 prices. Even if the plateau were real, it would sit far higher than the number still quoted online.

items.label: Gallup survey responses in Kahneman & Deaton (2010)
Real-time happiness reports in Killingsworth (2021), from 33,391 employed US adults

blocks.source: Kahneman & Deaton, PNAS, 2010; Killingsworth, PNAS, 2021

blocks.text: The challenger

Killingsworth used a different method. Through a smartphone app, people were pinged at random moments and asked how they felt right then, on a continuous scale from very bad to very good. Over time, he collected 1,725,994 of these reports from 33,391 employed US adults. Instead of yes-or-no questions about yesterday, he had fine-grained snapshots of the moment.

His result, published in 2021: both kinds of well-being rose steadily with income, and the slope was just as steep for higher earners as for lower earners. There was no sign of a plateau at $75,000. Higher incomes went with more positive feelings, such as confidence and interest, and fewer negative ones, such as sadness and boredom.

There's a key detail in how both studies measured income: they used its logarithm. In plain terms, that means what matters is the *percentage* change, not the dollar amount. Going from $40,000 to $80,000 is a doubling, and so is going from $80,000 to $160,000. In Killingsworth's data, each doubling bought roughly the same bump in happiness. So an extra $10,000 matters enormously to someone earning $30,000, and barely registers for someone earning $300,000. Money kept mattering, but each additional dollar mattered less.

Money and happiness follow a curve of doublings, not dollars. A raise that doubles your income changes a lot; the same dollar raise later in life changes much less. That's diminishing returns, not a hard ceiling.
The adversarial collaboration

Instead of trading rebuttals for a decade, Killingsworth and Kahneman did something unusual. They agreed to an adversarial collaboration, a joint project between researchers who disagree, with psychologist Barbara Mellers as arbiter. They reanalyzed Killingsworth's data, looking not just at the average person but at people across the range of happiness, from the least happy to the most.

The answer, published in 2023, reconciled both papers. For the least happy fifth or so of people, happiness rose with income up to about $100,000 and then flattened, just as Kahneman and Deaton had described. For everyone else, happiness kept rising with income, and for the happiest people it rose even faster at higher incomes. The overall average looked like a smooth climb because these different patterns blended together.

Think about what that split implies. If you're broadly doing okay, more income tends to keep adding something, whether that's more comfort, more experiences or simply less friction. If you're deeply unhappy because of grief, illness, loneliness or depression, money helps up to the point where basic stresses are handled, and then it stops reaching the real problem. Same paycheck, different curve, because the sources of unhappiness are different. That's why one-size-fits-all claims about money and happiness kept failing.

blocks.title: How fast happiness rose with income above $100k, by happiness level
blocks.note: Regression slope of happiness on log income above $100,000. The three lowest groups were not statistically different from zero.
blocks.source: Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, PNAS, 2023 (Table 1)

blocks.text: Why did the 2010 study miss this? The authors concluded its yes-or-no questions about yesterday's emotions could tell unhappy people apart but couldn't distinguish degrees of happiness. Once someone was doing reasonably well, the measure had nowhere higher to go. In effect, Kahneman and Deaton had measured unhappiness, and what they found was real: money reduces misery up to a point, and beyond that point, for the most unhappy people, their remaining problems aren't the kind more income fixes.

The process itself is worth a moment. Kahneman, who died in 2024, spent years promoting adversarial collaboration as a better way to settle scientific fights than dueling papers. The usual pattern in research is that each side digs in, picks at the other's methods and talks past them. Here, a famous senior scientist agreed to test whether his own best-known finding had been misread, and published the answer. Being willing to be wrong in public is rarer than being smart, and it's how a field actually gets closer to the truth.

It's an honest, almost humble conclusion, and the authors said so. Both original studies relied on standard practices, such as assuming everyone follows the same curve, that turned out to hide what was going on.
What money actually buys

Killingsworth's 2021 data also offered clues about why income and well-being move together. People were asked how much they felt in control of their lives. Statistically, that sense of control accounted for about 74% of the link between income and moment-to-moment happiness. Financial insecurity, measured by trouble paying regular bills, accounted for about 38%. The overlap is the point: a big part of what money provides is the feeling that life isn't pushing you around.

items.label: Share of the income–happiness link accounted for by feeling in control of your life
Share accounted for by financial insecurity (trouble paying bills)

blocks.source: Killingsworth, PNAS, 2021

blocks.text: Two other findings are worth sitting with. First, higher earners reported feeling *more* pressed for time, not less, so a bigger paycheck didn't automatically buy breathing room. Second, people who strongly equated money with success were less happy on average, and there was no income level at which that belief went with feeling better. Simply thinking money was important wasn't linked to being happier or unhappier overall. Valuing money for what it does seemed harmless. Treating it as a scoreboard did not.

How you spend may matter too. In a well-known 2008 study, psychologist Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues found that spending money on other people was linked to greater happiness than spending on yourself, including in an experiment where people were randomly assigned to spend a small sum on themselves or on someone else. Research on spending to buy back time, such as paying to skip chores you hate, points in a similar direction. These lines of research come from smaller studies than the income work and deserve more caution, but they suggest that how money is used matters, not just how much there is.
What the debate doesn't settle

All of this is correlational. Richer people are happier on average, but that doesn't prove the money made them happier. Healthier, more energetic or more optimistic people might earn more in the first place. In a published commentary, psychologists Julia Rohrer and Sebastian Wenz argued that the 2023 paper leaned on causal assumptions the data couldn't support. Both data sets come from the United States, and Killingsworth's included only employed adults. And in Kahneman and Deaton's data, health and loneliness predicted daily emotions more strongly than income did.

blocks.title: Myth vs. what the research shows

left.head: Popular version
items: Happiness stops at $75k
Money doesn't buy happiness
More money fixes everything

right.head: Closer to the evidence
items: No universal plateau; it depends on the person
On average, more income goes with more well-being, by doublings
For the unhappiest people, gains fade past about $100k

blocks.text: None of this makes the question pointless. It makes it more precise. Instead of asking whether money buys happiness, the better questions are which problems money can solve for you, how much it takes to solve them, and what you're trading away to get it, whether that's time, health or relationships.

For someone at the start of a career, the most useful takeaway might be about the shape of the curve. The steepest happiness gains in the data come from escaping money stress and gaining a sense of control. You don't need a huge salary for that. You need a cushion that turns emergencies into inconveniences, no debt that dictates your choices, and enough saved that a bad job or a bad boss isn't a trap. Savings, seen this way, are not just future money. They are present-day freedom.

The doubling rule has a practical edge, too. Early in a working life, income can double in just a few years through promotions, new qualifications or a jump into a better-paid civilian field, and those doublings are exactly where the research finds the biggest changes in how people feel. Later on, doubling a large income is much harder and, by the same curve, buys no more than the early doublings did. That's an argument for investing heavily in skills and earning power while you're young, and for not assuming that the next raise will feel as big as the last one.

There's also the problem of adjustment. People get used to new levels of comfort surprisingly fast, so a lifestyle that felt like a reward one year becomes the baseline the next. That's part of why spending every raise on upgrades can leave people no happier than before, while the same money set aside to build security keeps paying off in the form of options. A habit of saving doesn't just buy a future. It quietly buys a feeling of control today, which is the very thing the data links most closely to income and happiness.

And the warning is just as clear: if more money isn't fixing what's making you unhappy, more money probably won't. The researchers' own conclusion was that for the least happy people, beyond a certain income, the remaining miseries come from places a paycheck doesn't reach.

takeaways: Money and happiness move together by doublings: each extra dollar matters less as income rises.
The famous $75,000 plateau holds only for the least happy fifth of people, and at about $100,000 in the 2023 reanalysis.
A big part of money's link to happiness is a sense of control and freedom from bill stress.
Treating money as a scoreboard is linked to lower well-being at every income.
The evidence is correlational; health and relationships still matter more than income.

title: The Boring Machine That Turned $100 Into a Million
dek: Compound growth and index funds are the least exciting idea in finance and the one with the best track record. The math is easy. Sitting still is the hard part.

blocks.text: Picture someone in January 1928 putting $100 into the biggest companies in America and then doing nothing for the rest of their life. No trading, no watching the news, no clever moves. Just reinvesting the dividends and leaving it alone. By the end of 2025, according to the long-running dataset kept by NYU finance professor Aswath Damodaran, that $100 would have grown to about **$1.16 million**.

The same $100 parked in three-month Treasury bills, about the safest thing you can own, would have grown to roughly $2,600. Nobody in this thought experiment picked a hot stock or dodged a crash. They simply owned the whole market and gave it time. That is the entire idea behind index investing, and it's worth understanding properly, because the same forces that make it work are the ones that make most people quit before it pays off.

items.label: $100 in the S&P 500 from 1928 to 2025, dividends reinvested (before inflation)
The same $100 in 3-month Treasury bills
Average yearly S&P 500 return, 1928–2025 (compounded)

blocks.source: Damodaran, NYU Stern, Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills (2026 update)

blocks.text: Growth on top of growth

Compounding just means your returns start earning returns of their own. In the early years it's almost invisible: a 10% gain on $1,000 is $100, which is nice but changes nothing. The action lives at the far end of the curve, where a single year's growth can be bigger than everything you originally put in. Human intuition is built for straight lines, which is why this curve keeps surprising people (the Math section digs into why).

Here's the version that should change how a 20-year-old thinks about money. Using Damodaran's actual year-by-year S&P 500 returns, imagine someone who invested $1,200 at the start of every year, about $100 a month, from 1986 through 2025. Over 40 years they put in $48,000. They ended with roughly **$766,000**. Someone who did exactly the same thing but started ten years later, in 1996, put in $36,000 and finished with about $240,000.

blocks.title: $1,200 a year into the S&P 500, value at end of 2025
blocks.note: Total put in: $48k, $36k and $24k. Nominal dollars, before fees and taxes.
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern historical returns (data through 2025)

blocks.text: The late starter contributed only $12,000 less but ended with less than a third as much. Those first ten years of deposits weren't powerful because they were large. They were powerful because they had the longest runway. A dollar invested at 20 can end up doing more work than several dollars invested at 40.

Look closely at the late part of that 40-year run and the curve becomes obvious. In 2024 alone, the 1986 starter's account grew by about $129,000, more than two and a half times everything they had contributed in four decades. Two years earlier, in 2022, the same account dropped by about $90,000 in a single year. Both numbers come from the same source: once a balance is large, the market's ordinary swings move more money in a year than your paycheck ever could. That's the payoff of compounding, and it's also why the late years feel so volatile.

There's a useful way to think about the two phases. Early on, your deposits do the heavy lifting: in the first few years of that 1986 run, the yearly $1,200 was usually bigger than the market's gain. By the mid-1990s that flipped, and the account was growing by more in a typical year than the owner was putting in. Saving is what builds the base; time is what turns it into an engine. Neither works without the other.

One more honest adjustment: these are nominal dollars. Prices rose a lot between 1928 and 2025, so that $1.16 million buys far less than it sounds. Damodaran's figures put the inflation-adjusted value at about $61,000 in 1928 dollars, an average real gain of roughly 6.8% a year. That's less dramatic, but it's still more than a 600-fold increase in buying power over one long lifetime. Cash in a drawer over the same period lost most of its value.
You don't control the market's return. You do control your start date and your consistency, and over long periods those two inputs matter more than almost anything else you can choose.
What an index fund actually is

A stock is a slice of one company. An index is just a list, like the S&P 500, which tracks around 500 large US companies weighted by their size. An index fund buys everything on that list in the same proportions, so its return is the market's return minus a small fee. No star manager, no research team, no bets on which company wins next year.

The S&P 500 isn't the only index. Total-market funds add thousands of smaller US companies, international funds hold companies in other countries, and bond index funds do the same trick with loans to governments and corporations. The principle is identical every time: don't try to find the winners inside a category, just own the category cheaply. How much to hold in stocks versus bonds mostly depends on when you'll need the money, since money you need in two years shouldn't be riding on a market that can drop a third in one.

That sounds like settling for average. It isn't, for a reason the Nobel-winning economist William Sharpe laid out in a two-page 1991 paper called "The Arithmetic of Active Management." Before costs, the average actively managed dollar has to earn the market's return, because all investors together *are* the market. Active management costs more to run. So after costs, the average active dollar has to trail the average index dollar. It's not a theory about markets; it's arithmetic.

The scoreboard agrees. S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes a regular report called SPIVA that compares professionally managed funds with their benchmarks. Over the 15 years ending in 2024, about 90% of actively managed US large-company funds trailed the S&P 500. And 2025 was another rough year for stock pickers: according to the year-end 2025 SPIVA report, 79% of active large-cap funds lagged the index.

blocks.title: Active US large-cap funds that trailed the S&P 500
blocks.note: Periods ending December 2024.
blocks.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2024

blocks.text: Why owning everything beats owning a few things

There's a second, stranger reason to own the whole haystack instead of hunting for needles. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder studied every US common stock in the CRSP database back to 1926 and found that the majority of individual stocks, over their lifetimes, did worse than one-month Treasury bills. The entire net gain of the US stock market came from the best-performing 4% of companies. The rest, taken together, roughly matched T-bills.

Think about what that means for a stock picker. Market returns are driven by a small number of huge winners that are hard to spot in advance. If you own five or ten stocks, the most likely outcome is that you miss most of them. An index fund guarantees you own the few that end up mattering, because it owns all of them. It's like a loot table where almost all the value sits in a handful of rare drops: the only way to be sure you get them is to open every box.

The few managers who do beat the market in one stretch rarely keep doing it in the next, which is why the losing share tends to stay high or climb as the time window gets longer. Picking the fund that will win the next 15 years is just as hard as picking the stock.
The silent leak

Fees look harmless because they're quoted as tiny percentages. According to the Investment Company Institute, the average actively managed US stock mutual fund charged 0.64% a year in 2025, while the average index stock mutual fund charged 0.05%. The Thrift Savings Plan, the retirement plan for the military and federal workers, reported net expenses of about 0.034% for 2025, or 34 cents a year for every $1,000.

items.label: Average active stock mutual fund expense ratio, 2025
Average index stock mutual fund, 2025
TSP net expense ratio, 2025

blocks.source: ICI, Trends in the Expenses and Fees of Funds, 2025 (March 2026); FRTIB administrative expense review (January 2026)

blocks.text: Half a percent sounds like rounding error until you remember that fees compound too, just in the wrong direction. A fee is charged on your whole balance every year, including all the growth you've piled up. With an assumed 7% yearly return, shaving 0.6 percentage points off every year leaves a 40-year balance about a fifth smaller. You never get a bill for it. The money just quietly isn't there.
The part that's actually hard

If this were easy, everyone would be rich. The math is easy. Living through it is not. In Damodaran's data, the S&P 500 lost money in 26 of the 98 years from 1928 to 2025. It fell almost 44% in 1931 and about 37% in 2008. Anyone who invested at the start of 2000 was still behind ten years later, after two crashes, with nothing to show for a decade of patience.

But watch what happens as the holding period stretches. Using the same data, every 20-year stretch since 1928 ended with a gain, even after adjusting for inflation. The odds of losing money shrink quickly with time, because the good years get more chances to outweigh the bad ones.

blocks.title: How often the S&P 500 lost money, by holding period
blocks.note: Share of rolling periods from 1928 to 2025 with a negative total return (dividends reinvested, before inflation).
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern historical returns (data through 2025)

blocks.text: That chart is the whole strategy in one picture. The risk in stocks is real, but it's mostly short-term risk. The bigger danger is selling during a crash, which turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss and often means missing the rebound. The year after the 2008 collapse, the S&P 500 returned about 26%, while the news still felt like the end of the world.

Could you just dodge the crashes? It's the obvious question, and the answer is that almost nobody does it reliably. To win by timing, you have to be right twice: when to get out and when to get back in. Rebounds often start while things still look terrible, so the person waiting for good news to buy back in usually pays a higher price than the person who never left. A plan that requires you to predict the future isn't a plan.

There's an honest caveat. The US market of the last century is one of history's great success stories, and it's where these numbers come from. Not every market was so kind: Japan's stock market took more than three decades to get back to its 1989 peak. Past returns are a record, not a promise. That's one reason many investors also hold international stocks and bonds, and why nobody can tell you what the next 40 years will return.
Boring on purpose

blocks.title: Two ways to invest

left.head: Picking and timing
items: Feels skilled and active
Higher fees, more trading costs and taxes
Needs you to be right again and again
Most professionals trail the index over 15 years

right.head: Owning the index
items: Feels like doing nothing
Fees close to zero
Needs only time and patience
Gets the market's return, by design

blocks.text: The reason this approach is so hard to follow is that it gives your brain nothing to do. Games, social feeds and trading apps are all built on tight feedback: you act, something happens, you get a hit. Index investing pays you for *not* acting. The winning behavior is to set up automatic contributions, choose something broad and cheap, and then mostly ignore it, especially on the days the headlines are screaming.

For service members, a simple version of this already exists. The TSP's C Fund tracks the S&P 500, and its Lifecycle (L) Funds mix stocks and bonds automatically based on when you expect to need the money. Contributions come out of your pay before you ever see them. The companion article on the TSP and the Blended Retirement System covers the matching money and the rules. None of this is a recommendation of a particular fund; it's a description of how the tools work.

blocks.title: The boring system
items: Pick a contribution rate and have it taken from every paycheck automatically
Use a broad, low-cost index fund instead of a handful of individual stocks
Raise the rate whenever your pay goes up, before you get used to the bigger check
Check in once or twice a year, not daily
When the market crashes, change nothing and keep buying on schedule

blocks.text: Life on a submarine is oddly well suited to this. You can't refresh a stock app from a watch station. You can't panic-sell in the middle of a long underway. Weeks go by, contributions keep landing, and the market does whatever it does without your help. A lot of investors on land would do better with that kind of enforced distance.

This is how the mechanics work, based on historical data, not personal financial advice. Your timeline and situation matter. Before changing anything, talk to your command financial specialist or the personal financial counselors at Fleet and Family Support.

takeaways: Starting early beats investing more later: the first dollars get the most years to compound.
An index fund owns the whole market; after fees, most professional stock pickers trail it over long periods.
Fees compound against you, so fractions of a percent matter over decades.
US stocks often lose money in a single year but never lost over any 20-year stretch from 1928 to 2025. That's history, not a guarantee.
The hard part is behavior: automate it, then leave it alone, especially during crashes.
