title: The Leak in Every Savings Account
dek: Inflation is a tax nobody votes on and nobody sends you a bill for. Here's what it is, why it spiked after 2021, and why the money that feels safest is the money guaranteed to shrink.

blocks.text: In June 2022, the price of the typical basket of things Americans buy was 9.1% higher than a year earlier. That was the fastest yearly increase since November 1981, before most of today's sailors' parents had finished school. Gas, groceries, rent and used cars all jumped at once, and for a while it felt like every receipt was a small shock.

But the dramatic year isn't the most important part of the story. The quieter part is what happens in ordinary years. By the government's own price index, a $100 bill tucked in a drawer in January 2000 now buys roughly what $50 bought back then. Nobody took the money. Nothing went wrong. Prices just kept rising a little at a time, and the bill stayed $100.

items.label: Yearly rise in consumer prices, June 2022: the highest since 1981
What $100 from January 2000 is worth in buying power (September 2026)

blocks.source: BLS CPI-U (series CUUR0000SA0 / CPIAUCNS) via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: What inflation actually measures

Inflation is a rise in the general level of prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what each dollar can buy. It isn't about one item getting expensive; a bad orange harvest raises orange prices without being inflation. It's about the overall cost of living drifting upward across thousands of goods and services at once.

The number you hear in the news usually comes from the Consumer Price Index, published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Government data collectors track the prices of a large, weighted basket of goods and services that urban households buy, from rent and car insurance to haircuts and coffee, and compare the cost of that basket over time. The Federal Reserve prefers a similar measure, the price index for personal consumption expenditures, and aims for inflation of 2% a year on that measure over the long run.

Two things are worth knowing about any index like this. First, it's an average, and your personal inflation rate depends on what you actually buy. Someone who lives aboard ship and doesn't pay rent barely feels rising housing costs, while someone with a long commute feels every gas spike. Second, a target of 2% means the plan is for prices to keep rising, slowly and predictably. Stable prices, in central-bank language, still means your cash loses a little every year.

Measuring this is harder than it sounds. Products change: a phone that costs the same as five years ago is a much better phone, and the index tries to adjust for that. People also switch to cheaper options when prices rise. Critics on one side argue the official numbers understate what families feel; a government-appointed commission in the 1990s concluded the opposite, that the CPI was overstating inflation at the time, and the method was revised. Neither camp thinks the index is perfect, but it's the best common yardstick there is.
Why prices rise

Economists group the causes into a few families. **Demand-pull** inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, so sellers can raise prices. **Cost-push** inflation happens when it suddenly costs more to make things, such as when energy prices spike, and producers pass that on. And **expectations** matter: if everyone expects prices to rise, workers ask for bigger raises and businesses raise prices preemptively, which helps make the prediction come true.

The 2021–2022 surge had all three. Supply chains snarled during the pandemic, demand rebounded strongly as economies reopened, supported by relief spending and very low interest rates, and energy and food prices spiked after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Economists still argue about how much each factor mattered. The Federal Reserve responded by raising interest rates sharply in 2022 and 2023, making borrowing more expensive to cool demand, and yearly inflation fell back to around 3% by mid-2023.

blocks.title: How much prices rose over the previous 12 months, each June
blocks.note: Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, not seasonally adjusted.
blocks.source: BLS CPI-U (series CUUR0000SA0 / CPIAUCNS) via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: Notice that the line never goes back down to where it started. Inflation falling from 9% to 3% doesn't mean prices fell. It means they rose more slowly. The higher prices from 2021 and 2022 are baked in, and yearly inflation picked up again in spring 2026, reaching 4.2% in May. That's the uncomfortable truth about price levels: they tend to ratchet in one direction.
The math of slow erosion

A handy shortcut called the rule of 72 tells you how long it takes for something growing at a steady rate to double: divide 72 by the rate. At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years. At 6%, about 12. For a 20-year-old, that means the cost of living could plausibly double before age 45 even if inflation stays fairly tame. A retirement plan that ignores that is planning to retire poorer than it thinks.

This is why any long-range money number should come with a question attached: in whose dollars? A retirement calculator promising a million dollars in 45 years sounds enormous, but at 3% inflation a future million buys roughly what a quarter of a million buys today. Good calculators let you show results in today's dollars. If one doesn't, mentally cut big long-term numbers down to size before getting excited, or worried, about them.

Over the long run, US inflation has averaged about 3% a year since 1928, according to the CPI figures in NYU professor Aswath Damodaran's historical dataset. That small-sounding number, compounded over 98 years, means the price level rose almost nineteenfold. A dollar kept in cash since 1928 kept its face value and lost about 95% of its buying power.

Falling prices aren't the cure, by the way. Prices fell sharply from 1930 to 1932, by more than 6% in 1930 and roughly 9 to 10% in each of the next two years, during the Great Depression. When people expect prices to fall, they put off spending and borrowing, businesses cut jobs, and debts become harder to repay. That's one reason central banks aim for low, steady inflation rather than zero.

Inflation also plays tricks on perception. Psychologists Eldar Shafir and Amos Tversky and economist Peter Diamond studied what they called **money illusion**: the tendency to think in face-value dollars instead of buying power. In scenarios they posed, people often judged a worker who got a bigger raise in a high-inflation year as happier than one who got a smaller raise with no inflation, even when the second worker was better off in real terms. Bigger numbers feel like progress. Your brain sees the raise and doesn't do the subtraction.

The subtraction is simple once you know to do it. What you really earn on savings is the interest rate minus inflation, called the real return. A savings account paying 4% in a year of 3% inflation leaves you about 1% richer in buying power. One paying 0.5% in the same year leaves you about 2.5% poorer, even though the balance went up. The statement shows growth either way; only one of them is real.
Winners and losers

Inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. People holding cash or money owed to them at a fixed rate lose, because they get repaid in cheaper dollars. People who owe money at a fixed rate quietly gain, because their payment stays the same while their pay and prices rise. That's part of why a fixed-rate mortgage can be a good deal in inflationary years, and why a variable-rate credit card balance is the opposite: card rates tend to rise along with interest rates.

People on fixed incomes, like retirees with pensions that aren't adjusted for prices, get squeezed the hardest. That's why it matters that military retired pay and Social Security include cost-of-living adjustments tied to inflation. Workers are somewhere in between: wages do tend to catch up, but usually after prices have already moved, which is exactly what the military pay data shows.
Safe isn't the same as safe

This is where inflation flips the usual idea of risk. Cash feels safe because its number never goes down. But measured in what it can buy, cash is the one asset that is guaranteed to lose over time. Investments that bounce around from year to year have, historically, been the ones that outran rising prices. The chart below uses Damodaran's data to show average yearly returns after inflation from 1928 through 2025.

blocks.title: Average yearly return after inflation, 1928–2025
blocks.note: Compounded annual real returns; stock returns include reinvested dividends.
blocks.source: Calculated from Damodaran, NYU Stern, Historical Returns (2026 update)

blocks.text: Short-term Treasury bills, the classic safe asset, barely stayed ahead of inflation over that span. Bonds did a little better. Stocks, with all their crashes, grew buying power by almost 7% a year on average. That doesn't make stocks right for every dollar. Money you'll need soon shouldn't be exposed to a market that can fall by a third in a bad year. But it does mean that keeping long-term money in cash isn't the cautious choice it looks like. It's a slow, guaranteed loss traded for the comfort of a number that never drops.

Every pile of money has a job and a timeline. Money for emergencies and near-term plans needs to be stable and easy to reach. Money for 10, 20 or 40 years from now has to beat inflation, or it's shrinking while you sleep.
Your paycheck versus prices

Military basic pay has its own built-in inflation defense. By law, the annual raise is tied to the Employment Cost Index, a measure of how fast private-sector wages are growing, unless the President or Congress sets a different number. In practice, that means raises follow wages, which tend to follow prices with a lag.

blocks.title: Annual military basic pay raise
blocks.note: Across-the-board raise each January. In 2025, junior enlisted also received an extra targeted raise from April 1.
blocks.source: Congressional Research Service, Defense Primer: Military Pay Raise (IF10260), Jan 2026

blocks.text: That lag showed up clearly in the inflation spike. The across-the-board raises from 2021 through 2025 add up, compounded, to about 21.6%. Over roughly the same stretch, from December 2020 to December 2025, consumer prices rose about 24.4%. The bigger raises of 2023 and 2024 were partly catch-up, and the targeted 2025 increase for junior enlisted helped those ranks further. But for a member whose pay rose only by the general raise, the paycheck lost a little ground to prices over those five years.

items.label: Military basic pay, general raises 2021–2025 combined
Consumer prices, December 2020 to December 2025

blocks.source: CRS IF10260 (Jan 2026); BLS CPI-U via FRED; calculated

blocks.text: The real lesson is that annual raises mostly just keep you in place. Actual gains in buying power come from promotions, years-of-service steps, new skills and, over time, from owning assets that grow faster than prices. That's true in uniform and it will be just as true in a civilian career.
Living with a leaky bucket

blocks.title: Protecting money from inflation
items: Keep an emergency fund in an insured savings account that pays interest, so it loses less to inflation than cash at zero
Don't hold large piles of idle cash for years without a specific purpose
Invest long-term money in diversified assets that have historically outpaced inflation
Commit part of every raise to savings, so savings grow at least as fast as your pay
Watch your own lifestyle inflation; it's the part of the cost of living you control

blocks.text: There's also a quieter form of inflation that has nothing to do with the CPI: the gradual rise in what you consider normal. Better phone, bigger subscription bundle, more takeout. Each upgrade feels small and permanent at once. Economists measure the national price level, but your personal cost of living is mostly set by your own choices, and it's the only part of the problem you fully control.

The deeper reframe is this: inflation means that doing nothing with money is itself a decision, and usually a losing one. Leaving savings in a zero-interest account isn't neutral. It's a bet that the next 20 years will have no inflation, a bet that history says almost never wins. Understanding that doesn't require predicting the economy. It just requires noticing that the bucket has a small hole in it and deciding what to do about it.

This explains how inflation works, not what to do with your specific money. For a personal plan, including where to keep an emergency fund and how to invest, talk to your command financial specialist or Fleet and Family Support's personal financial managers.

takeaways: Inflation is a falling value of money: $100 from January 2000 buys about what $50 did then.
When inflation cools, prices still rise, just more slowly. They rarely go back down.
Cash is the only asset guaranteed to lose buying power; over 1928–2025, US stocks gained about 6.8% a year after inflation.
Military raises track wages with a lag; real gains come from promotions, skills and investing.
Doing nothing with money is a decision, and usually a losing one.

title: The Retirement Deal Most Sailors Don't Understand
dek: Under the Blended Retirement System, the government matches part of what you save, but only if you know the rules. How the TSP and BRS work, as of 2026.

blocks.text: In 2022 the Defense Department asked thousands of active-duty members a basic question about how their own retirement system works. Among junior enlisted members, only 41% got it right. Across all ranks it was 48%. Those numbers come from the Pentagon's annual report to Congress on the financial literacy of the force, based on the 2022 Status of Forces Survey.

That's a strange gap, because the Blended Retirement System is one of the few places in life where someone will hand you free money for doing something that's good for you anyway. The catch is that the free money has conditions, deadlines and a couple of traps. This is a plain-language tour of how it works under the rules in effect in 2026. Rules change, so treat this as a map, then confirm the details for your own situation with your command financial specialist or the personal financial counselors at Fleet and Family Support.

items.label: Junior enlisted who answered the BRS knowledge question correctly (2022)
All active-duty members who answered it correctly

blocks.source: OUSD(P&R), Financial Literacy and Preparedness of Members of the Armed Forces: 2022 Status of Forces Survey (Dec 2023)

blocks.text: From all-or-nothing to portable

For decades, military retirement worked like a cliff. Under the legacy "High-36" system, serve 20 years and you earned a pension for life: 2.5% of your average highest 36 months of basic pay for every year served, so 50% at 20 years. Leave at year 12 and you walked away with no retirement benefit at all. Since the large majority of people who join leave long before 20 years, most of the force was serving under a retirement plan they would never collect.

The Blended Retirement System, which took effect on January 1, 2018, kept a pension but made it smaller and added a savings account that goes with you whenever you leave. Everyone who first entered service on or after that date is automatically in BRS. Members already serving with fewer than 12 years had the option to switch during 2018. If you enlisted any time after 2017, this is your system.

items: **A smaller pension at 20 years:** 2.0% of your highest-36-month average basic pay per year served, instead of 2.5%.
**TSP contributions from the government:** an automatic 1% of basic pay plus matching of up to 4% more.
**Continuation pay:** a one-time mid-career bonus for agreeing to serve four more years.
**A lump-sum option at retirement:** trade part of your early pension checks for cash up front.

blocks.text: The TSP piece is the one that matters for almost everyone, because it pays out whether or not you ever reach 20. The Thrift Savings Plan is the government's version of a civilian 401(k): an investment account inside your name, funded from your paycheck, with the government adding money on top.
The free money, exactly

Here are the rules, as published by the TSP and the Defense Department. About 60 days after you enter service, the government starts putting 1% of your basic pay into your TSP every pay period, even if you contribute nothing. That 1% vests, meaning it becomes permanently yours, once you have two years of service. After your second full year, the government also starts matching what you put in: dollar for dollar on the first 3% of basic pay, then 50 cents per dollar on the next 2%. Matching money is yours immediately.

Add it up and the math is simple. Put in 5% of basic pay and the government puts in 5% too: the automatic 1% plus a 4% match. Put in more than 5% and there's no extra match, though the extra savings still count. Put in less and you leave part of the match unclaimed. Both the automatic and matching contributions stop after 26 years of service.

blocks.title: What the government adds, by what you contribute
blocks.note: After two years of service. Before then, only the automatic 1% applies.
blocks.source: TSP booklet TSPBK34; Air Force benefits BRS fact sheet (reviewed Jan 2026)

blocks.text: Since October 1, 2020, new members are automatically enrolled to contribute 5% of basic pay, up from 3% before that date. That default was chosen on purpose: it's exactly the amount that captures the full match. If you never touched your TSP election, you're probably at 5% already. If you lowered it or stopped it to free up cash, you may be turning down part of your pay.

The choice of default isn't a small detail. In a well-known 2001 study, economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea tracked a large company that switched its 401(k) from opt-in to automatic enrollment. Participation rose sharply, and many new employees simply kept whatever contribution rate and fund the company had pre-selected, even though few people had picked that combination when they had to choose it themselves. People treat the default as advice. The military's 5% default is a good one, but it's still worth deciding on purpose rather than by inertia, especially as your pay grows.

To make that concrete, take an E-5 with more than three years of service. Under the 2026 pay table, monthly basic pay is about $3,776. Contributing 5% means roughly $189 a month comes out of the paycheck, and the government adds another $189. Over a year that's about $2,266 from the sailor and about $2,266 from the government, a little over $4,500 going to work. Contribute nothing, and the government's share drops to the automatic 1%, about $38 a month.

The match is effectively an instant 100% return on the first 3% of basic pay you contribute and 50% on the next 2%. No stock, fund or side hustle reliably offers that. Whatever else you decide, understand what you give up by contributing less than 5%.
Where the money actually goes

Contributions don't just sit there; they buy into one or more TSP funds. The G Fund holds special government securities and can't lose value, but it grows slowly. The F Fund holds bonds. The C Fund tracks the S&P 500, the S Fund holds smaller US companies, and the I Fund holds international stocks. The Lifecycle, or L, Funds are pre-built mixes of the other five, set to a target year. If you were auto-enrolled and never chose, your money goes into the L Fund matched to your age, which starts out heavy on stocks and shifts toward safer assets as that date approaches.

The TSP is also unusually cheap. Its board reported net expenses of about 0.034% for 2025, meaning roughly 34 cents a year on every $1,000. Most retail mutual funds charge many times that. Low costs matter because fees, like returns, compound over decades. The companion article on index funds and compounding explains why that matters more than it sounds.
Traditional or Roth

Every dollar you contribute goes in one of two tax doors. **Traditional** contributions come out before federal income tax, which lowers your taxable pay now, but you pay tax on the money and its growth when you withdraw it in retirement. **Roth** contributions come out after tax, so they don't lower today's bill, but qualified withdrawals, including all the growth, come out tax-free later. To qualify, at least five years must have passed since your first Roth contribution and you generally need to be 59½ or older.

The usual way people reason about it: if you expect to be in a higher tax bracket later than you are now, paying the tax now (Roth) tends to look better. Young enlisted members often have relatively low taxable income, partly because allowances such as BAH and BAS aren't taxed. That's not a rule, just the logic. You can split contributions between both, and it's worth running your numbers with a financial counselor rather than guessing.

There's one military-specific wrinkle. Pay earned in a designated combat zone is tax-exempt, and TSP contributions from that pay follow special rules. Traditional contributions from tax-exempt pay don't count against the normal yearly limit, though they do count against a larger overall cap. If you ever earn combat-zone pay, ask finance how it interacts with your TSP.
Limits, cliffs and traps

For 2026, the IRS caps your own traditional plus Roth contributions at $24,500, with a total limit of $72,000 including tax-exempt and government contributions. Few junior sailors will hit that, but anyone who does should know about the front-loading trap. The TSP warns that if you max out early in the year, your contributions stop, and the government's matching stops with them for the rest of the year. Spreading contributions across every pay period keeps the match flowing.

items: **The two-year cliff:** leave service before two years and the automatic 1% contributions are forfeited. Your own money and any matching stay yours.

**The 90-day exit:** members who were auto-enrolled can ask for a refund of their own automatic contributions within 90 days of the first one. The government's automatic 1% stays in the account; matching on the refunded money is forfeited.
**Cashing out early:** money pulled out before retirement age usually means income tax plus, in most cases, an extra 10% early-withdrawal tax. That can wipe out years of growth.
**Pay raises:** your contribution is a percentage, so it rises automatically with promotions and annual raises, like the 3.8% raise on January 1, 2026.

blocks.text: When you leave the military, the TSP comes with you. You can leave the money in the plan, keep investing it at the same low cost, or roll it into another retirement account. What you can't do is keep receiving government contributions once you're out.
The pension still matters

blocks.title: BRS milestones for someone who joined after 2017
items: ~Day 60
Auto-enrolled at 5%; government's automatic 1% begins
2 years
Automatic 1% vests; matching begins
7–12 years
Continuation pay window, for a four-year commitment
20 years
Pension: 2.0% × years served × high-36 average basic pay
26 years
Automatic and matching contributions end
Retirement
Option to take 25% or 50% of early pension value as a lump sum

blocks.text: For those who do stay 20, the pension is still the biggest single asset in the package: a monthly payment for life, adjusted for inflation. Under BRS, 20 years earns 40% of the high-36 average instead of the legacy 50%. Continuation pay is a mid-career offer between roughly the 7th and 12th year of service in exchange for four more years. For 2026, the published active-duty amount is 2.5 times monthly basic pay, though the timing and amount can vary by service and year. At retirement, you can choose to receive a lump sum of 25% or 50% of the pension's discounted value, in exchange for smaller monthly checks until full Social Security retirement age, usually 67, when the full pension resumes.

The lump sum is a classic test of how people value now versus later. Because the government calculates it with a discount rate, the cash up front is generally worth less than the monthly payments you give up. It can still make sense for some people. It's the kind of decision worth making slowly, with real numbers in front of you.
The real point of BRS

The deeper change in BRS is philosophical. The old system rewarded only the minority who stayed for a full career. The new one assumes, realistically, that most people serve for a while and then do something else, and it makes sure they leave with something. A sailor who serves six years, contributes 5% throughout and lets it sit invested could walk out with a meaningful head start on retirement, money that under the old system simply wouldn't exist.

That shifts responsibility, too. A pension needs nothing from you except time. The TSP needs you to contribute, pick sensible funds, and not raid it the first time you change jobs. The system gives you the tools; the 41% question is whether people know they're holding them.

Check your Leave and Earnings Statement for your TSP contribution percentage and the government contribution lines. If anything looks off, or you're not sure which BRS rules apply to you, ask your command financial specialist or base finance office. These are the 2026 rules; Congress and the TSP can and do change them.

takeaways: If you joined after 2017, you're in BRS: a smaller pension plus government TSP contributions you keep even if you leave before 20.
Contributing 5% of basic pay captures the full match; the government then adds 5% as well.
The automatic 1% vests at two years; matching starts after two years and is yours immediately.
Don't front-load to the yearly limit, or you lose matching for the rest of the year.
Rules change: confirm yours on your LES and with a command financial specialist.

title: The Thousand People Who Pay the Rent
dek: Kevin Kelly's famous napkin math says a creator needs only 1,000 true fans to make a living. The math is right. What it quietly assumes is where the real lessons are.

blocks.text: A thousand people is not many. It is a mid-sized high school, a few crews' worth of a big ship, the attendance at a minor league ballgame on a slow night. In 2008 the writer Kevin Kelly, a founding editor of Wired, argued that this is roughly how many people a creator needs to make a living. Not a million followers. Not a viral hit. A thousand people who care enough to pay.

His math fit on a napkin. If each of those thousand true fans spends about $100 a year on your work, you earn about $100,000 a year. The essay, called 1,000 True Fans, has been passed around ever since by musicians, writers, podcasters, game makers and YouTubers, often as a kind of permission slip: you do not have to be famous, you just have to matter a lot to a few people.
The arithmetic is not the interesting part. The interesting part is what each number in that equation is hiding, and what happens when you look at a real platform's data instead of a napkin.
What Kelly actually claimed

Kelly defined a true fan narrowly. It is someone who will buy anything you make: drive a long way to see you, preorder the deluxe edition, buy the version they already own because it has a new cover. He imagined them at the center of a set of rings. Around the true fans sit many more casual fans who buy now and then, and around them, a much larger crowd who know your name. The true fans are the ones who reliably pay.

He set the price at about $100 a year because that is roughly a day's wages for many people, an amount a devoted fan can spend without much pain. And he attached two conditions that tend to get dropped when the idea is retold. First, the creator has to make enough new work each year to give fans something to spend $100 on. Second, the creator needs a direct relationship with those fans, so that the money flows to the creator instead of mostly to a label, publisher or store in between.

It helps to remember when this was written. Kickstarter did not launch until 2009 and Patreon until 2013. Kelly was describing a world that was only starting to exist, in which the internet would let small creators reach small audiences directly. Much of what he predicted arrived. Some of it arrived in a shape he did not expect.
The number that moves is the price

In 2020 the investor Li Jin, then at the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, wrote a response called 1,000 True Fans? Try 100. Her point was that the $100 assumption was the weakest part of the napkin. If a creator can offer something worth $1,000 a year to the right person, 100 fans produce the same $100,000. She pointed to course platforms where individual creators had earned six figures from a few dozen students.

blocks.title: Fans needed for $100,000 a year
blocks.note: Simple division of $100,000 by yearly spend per fan; before any platform fees, taxes or costs.
blocks.source: Kelly, The Technium, 2008; Jin, a16z, 2020

blocks.text: One example from her essay: an art advisor who sold a course on Teachable earned about $110,000 from 76 students, an average of more than $1,400 each. Those were not casual buyers. They were people paying for a specific result they badly wanted. That is the real shift in Jin's version. A fan at $10 a year is supporting you. A fan at $1,000 a year is buying a transformation, and expects one.

items.label: Earned by one Teachable creator from a single course
Students who paid for it, about $1,440 each on average

blocks.source: Li Jin, 1,000 True Fans? Try 100, a16z, 2020

blocks.text: Jin's other observation was that fans do not all have to pay the same amount. She pointed to a podcast on Patreon with tiers running from $5 a month up to $500, a top tier priced a hundred times the bottom one. The many people at the low end keep the lights on and feel included. The handful at the top, who want access and recognition, can account for a surprising share of the total. Free-to-play games discovered the same pattern long ago, which is why a game can be free for almost everyone and still make money.

The chart above makes one thing obvious. The difference between needing 10,000 fans and needing 100 is entirely about what you offer each one. Most new creators spend all their energy on the left side of the equation, getting more people, and almost none on the right side, giving each person something worth more.
A viewer is not a fan, and neither is a subscriber

Here is where platforms complicate the napkin. On YouTube, subscriber counts feel like a measure of fans. They are not even close. In September 2026, Todd Beaupré, who runs YouTube's growth and discovery team, said in an interview that the click rate from the subscriber row on the home page is often around 10 percent or less, even for a channel's best videos. Nine in ten subscribers who are shown a new upload pass on it, and YouTube considers that normal.

Roblox shows the same gap from the spending side. In its annual report for 2025, Roblox said it averaged 127 million daily active users, while about 1.8 million people paid for something on a typical day. On average, those paying users spent a little over $10 on the days they paid. Divide the two figures and roughly 1 or 2 percent of the people in the building on any given day are the ones paying the rent.

items.label: Average daily active users on Roblox in 2025
Average daily unique paying users
Average daily spend per paying user

blocks.source: Roblox Corporation, Form 10-K for fiscal 2025

blocks.text: That is not a Roblox quirk. It is the shape of almost every audience. A large crowd watches. A smaller group engages. A very small group pays, and an even smaller group would follow you anywhere. Kelly's rings are real; they are just much steeper than most people expect when they start.

blocks.title: The fan ladder, from widest to narrowest
items: Strangers who see a thumbnail or a game icon
Viewers or players who try one thing
Regulars who come back without being reminded
Buyers who have paid you at least once
True fans who would buy almost anything you make

blocks.text: What the napkin leaves out

The most pointed critique came from Dave Karpf, a political scientist who studies digital media. Writing in 2022, he argued that the essay leaned on a hopeful idea from the 2000s, that the internet would let niche work be found as easily as hits. In practice, recommendation systems tend to funnel attention toward what is already popular. Being one click away from a hit is not the same as being found.

He also pointed out that platforms take cuts, so the direct relationship is rarely direct. Roblox keeps 30 percent of a game pass sale before a developer can cash out. App stores take their share of purchases on phones. And $100,000 of revenue is not $100,000 of income. As Karpf notes, a self-employed American pays roughly 15 percent in Social Security and Medicare tax on earnings, covering both the worker's and the employer's share, and buys their own health insurance, equipment and software on top of that.

blocks.title: The napkin vs. the spreadsheet

left.head: Napkin version
items: You sell to fans directly
Fans find you because the internet is flat
Every dollar spent reaches you

right.head: What actually happens
items: A few percent of an audience ever pays
Platforms sit between you and the fan
Algorithms concentrate attention on hits
Fees, taxes and costs come off the top

blocks.text: Karpf's sharpest point is that the model favors creators whose fans have money to spare. A thousand true fans of a niche finance newsletter can pay far more than a thousand true fans of a game aimed at twelve-year-olds, whose spending depends on a parent's card. That is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to think hard about who your audience is and what they can actually afford.
What a true fan of a game or a gaming channel buys

For a small studio or channel, the useful question is not how to get 1,000 fans. It is what a true fan of this specific thing would want to buy that a casual viewer would not. For a Roblox game, the answer is mostly inside the game: passes and items that make the experience better for people who already love it, private servers to play with friends, early access to new levels. For a gaming channel, it might be memberships, a Discord where the creator actually shows up, or eventually something more valuable, like coaching or a course for people trying to fix the same problem the channel documents.

Notice that none of those work until people care. A game pass in a game nobody returns to sells nothing. A membership on a channel nobody watches twice has no members. This is the quiet message under Kelly's essay. The money is downstream of a relationship, and relationships are built with consistency and trust, one returning viewer or player at a time. (The articles on retention and on a channel's first 1,000 subscribers come at the same truth from other directions.)

It also helps to be honest about time. Kelly's thousand fans are usually the residue of years of steady work, not the output of one good month. If a channel posts once a week and each video converts a handful of strangers into regulars, and a small fraction of regulars eventually become buyers, the curve is slow at first and then compounds. Most people quit during the slow part, when the numbers feel like they mean nothing. They do mean something; they are just measuring the wrong ring.

A better scoreboard for the first year is a short list of depth numbers. How many players came back the next day and the next week? How many viewers watched a second video? How many people joined a Discord and actually talked? Those numbers are small and unglamorous, and they are the best early predictor of whether a true-fan base is forming.
A useful test for any new project: can you name ten real people who would be disappointed if it disappeared? If not, work on that before working on monetization.
Depth beats breadth, at first

The lasting value of 1,000 True Fans is not the number. It is the direction of attention. Most creators measure breadth, because breadth is what dashboards show: views, impressions, subscribers, visits. Kelly's essay asks you to measure depth instead: how many people come back, how many would pay, how many would tell a friend without being asked.

Depth is also the part a small builder can control. You cannot make an algorithm favor you, and you cannot make a game go viral. You can make something a small group of people genuinely loves, show up for them on a schedule, and give them ways to support you that feel worth the money. If that group reaches a few hundred or a thousand, Kelly's napkin starts to look less like a fantasy and more like a plan. If it never does, no amount of reach would have saved it.

There is one more reason depth matters for a two-person project in particular. A small, devoted group gives you something a big, shallow audience cannot: honest feedback from people who want you to succeed. They will tell you which update they loved and which level they hated, test things early, and forgive a rough patch. For builders who can only work in the gaps between other duties, that kind of group is not just a revenue source. It is the reason the project keeps going when motivation dips, because someone is waiting for the next thing.

Kelly was right that a thousand is not many. He was perhaps too hopeful about how easy they are to find. The reframe worth keeping is that you are not looking for an audience. You are looking for your people, and they are worth more than the crowd around them.

takeaways: Kelly's math: 1,000 fans spending $100 a year is $100,000 in revenue, before fees, taxes and costs.
The lever most creators ignore is value per fan; 100 people paying $1,000 equals 1,000 paying $100.
Subscribers and players are not fans. On big platforms only a few percent of an audience pays.
Platforms sit between you and fans and concentrate attention on hits; plan for that, do not wish it away.
Measure depth (returners, buyers, people who would miss you) before breadth.

title: The Open Kitchen
dek: When a cafeteria let diners and cooks see each other, quality ratings jumped about 22 percent. Building in public works for similar reasons, but one well-known study warns that announcing your plans can quietly replace doing them.

blocks.text: Picture a cafeteria where diners order food and cooks make it behind a wall. Neither side ever sees the other. Researchers from Harvard Business School and University College London tried a simple change in a field experiment: they used video screens so that diners could watch the cooks, and cooks could watch the diners. The food, the recipes and the staff stayed the same.

Customer ratings of quality went up by about 22 percent, and the time it took to get food out fell by about 19 percent. Lab experiments in the same project explained why. When customers could see the work, they perceived more effort and valued the service more. When cooks could see the people they were feeding, they felt more appreciated, found the work more meaningful and tried harder. Visibility changed both sides.

items.label: Customer-reported quality after cooks and diners could see each other
Time to serve the same food

blocks.source: Buell, Kim & Tsay, Harvard Business School working paper 14-115, 2014

blocks.text: That cafeteria is a small model of something many creators and indie developers now do on purpose: building in public. Instead of working in silence and revealing a finished product, they share the process as they go. Weekly devlogs, revenue screenshots, clips of broken prototypes, threads about what failed. It can work remarkably well. It can also quietly sabotage the very work it is supposed to promote. The research explains both.
Why seeing the work raises its value

The cafeteria study built on earlier work by Ryan Buell and Michael Norton, who named something they called the *labor illusion*. In experiments with simulated travel and dating websites, people often preferred a site that made them wait while showing them the work it was doing, step by step, over a site that returned identical results instantly. Seeing effort made people value the result more and feel a kind of reciprocity toward whoever did the work.

A related effect works on the people who take part. In 2012, Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely described the *IKEA effect*: people value things they helped build more than identical things they did not, whether it is flat-pack furniture, origami or Lego. There was an important condition. The boost only appeared when the building was completed. When people failed to finish, or their creation was taken apart, the extra love disappeared.

Building in public taps both effects. Followers who watch the process see the effort behind the result, so they value it more. Followers who vote on a feature, report a bug or suggest a name feel a small sense of ownership, so they care whether it succeeds. That is a different mechanism from the one in the article on journey videos, where audiences root for a person getting better at a skill. Here, the product itself becomes more valuable because people watched it being made and had a hand in it.
Building in public turns spectators into stakeholders. People care most about the things they watched being made, and most of all about the things they helped make.
Transparency as a magnet

Openness can also attract people directly. In December 2013, the social media software company Buffer, then a team of about 15, published every employee's salary along with the formula used to set it. It was an unusual move at the time. In the 30 days before the post, Buffer received 1,263 job applications. In the month after, it received 2,886, more than double.

blocks.title: Buffer job applications around its open-salary post
blocks.note: One company and one month. A striking example, not a controlled experiment.
blocks.source: Quartz, January 2014

blocks.text: Part of what happened is self-selection. A public salary formula tells job seekers exactly what kind of company Buffer was, so the people who valued that kind of openness raced to apply, and the ones who would have hated it stayed away. Building in public works the same way for products. Every honest post is a filter: it pulls in the people who like how you think and quietly turns away the ones who never would have stuck around.

Games offer a longer example. Factorio, a factory-building game, began in 2012 as a two-person project in the Czech Republic. Its developers ran a crowdfunding campaign in 2013 and started a weekly blog called Factorio Friday Facts, writing in detail about features in progress, technical problems, design arguments and office news. They kept posting nearly every week for years, through Steam early access in 2016 and the full release in 2020. The studio grew to about 30 people, and by its own count the game has sold more than 3.5 million copies.

blocks.title: Factorio: building in public for most of a decade
items: Development starts as a two-person garage project
Crowdfunding campaign; weekly Friday Facts blog begins
Launches on Steam while still in development
Version 1.0 released
Later
More than 3.5 million copies sold, team of about 30

blocks.text: It would be wrong to say the blog made the game. Factorio succeeded because it is excellent, and plenty of devlogs go unread. But the blog built something that ads cannot buy: an audience that understood the game's design, trusted its developers and felt they had followed it from the start. The work earned the attention. The openness kept it.
The trap: announcing can replace doing

Here is the part building-in-public evangelists rarely mention. In 2009, Peter Gollwitzer and colleagues published four experiments in *Psychological Science* on what happens when other people notice your plans. They studied identity goals, like a law student intending to read legal journals to become a good lawyer. When participants' intentions were acknowledged by someone else, they acted on them *less*: they worked on the goal for less time over the following week and jumped on fewer chances to act in the lab.

The explanation is called symbolic self-completion. Telling people "I'm becoming a game developer" and having them notice gives you a premature sense of already being one. The social reward for the identity arrives before the work does, and the drive to earn it weakens. The effect showed up mainly in people who were strongly committed to the goal, which is exactly who builds in public. These were small experiments and deserve more replication, but the mechanism will feel familiar to anyone who has announced a project and then never touched it again.

blocks.title: Two kinds of public posts

left.head: Announcing
items: "I'm going to build a huge RPG"
Shares plans and identity
Likes arrive before the work
Can replace effort

right.head: Showing
items: "Here's the jump physics I fixed this week"
Shares finished pieces of work
Feedback arrives on something real
Requires effort to post

blocks.text: The practical fix follows directly. Post artifacts, not intentions. A clip of a mechanic that now works, a before-and-after of a map, a chart of what changed when you tweaked something, a bug you finally killed. Each of those required work before it could be shared, so the social reward is tied to progress instead of to promises. It also lines up with the IKEA finding: completed pieces build attachment, while abandoned announcements build nothing.

There is a related trap in the numbers. Once posts get likes, it is tempting to optimize the posts instead of the product, which is Goodhart's law in creator form: when a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring what you cared about. A good check is to ask, once a week, whether the thing you are building got better. If the audience grew and the product did not, the balance is off.
What to share, and what it costs

Not all openness is the same. Roughly, builders share three kinds of things: the process (how something is being made), the product (what it looks like right now) and the numbers (players, revenue, costs). Each has a different payoff and a different price.

Process is the safest and often the most interesting. Explaining why you changed the jump arc, or how you fixed a physics bug, is useful to other builders and shows players that someone thoughtful is behind the game. It also forces you to understand your own decisions well enough to explain them, which is the same reason teaching something is a good way to learn it.

Product updates are the most direct marketing. A short clip of a new feature is something people can react to, share and remember. It is also how building in public feeds the first-hundred-players problem from the article on the first hundred customers: every post is a chance for the right person to say "I want to try that," and every follower is a candidate for the next playtest.

Numbers are the most powerful and the most double-edged. Sharing real revenue or player counts builds unusual trust, because so much of the internet is inflated screenshots. But numbers also tell competitors exactly which niche is profitable, and they put emotional pressure on you when the line goes down. Plenty of builders who shared every month's revenue stopped once growth stalled, which is its own signal to followers. A middle path is to share direction and lessons, such as "retention doubled after we shortened the tutorial," without publishing every figure.

A useful way to think about all three is that building in public should create accountability for output, not applause for identity. Telling the internet you are a game developer does little. Committing to show a playable change every week puts a small, real deadline on your calendar. The research on public intentions has not settled exactly where that line falls, so treat this as a sensible reading rather than a proven rule, and pay attention to how it works for you.
The fear of looking bad

The biggest reason people do not build in public is not strategy. It is the fear of looking incompetent. Research from the University of Mannheim suggests that fear is distorted. In seven studies published in 2018, Bruk and colleagues found that people judge their own moments of vulnerability, like admitting a mistake or asking for help, much more harshly than they judge the same moments in others. Observers tend to judge the same vulnerability more positively, focusing on what it says about honesty rather than on what went wrong. The researchers called it the *beautiful mess effect*.

That matches what tends to happen with devlogs. Honest posts about what broke often draw more support than polished announcements, because they are interesting and relatable. It ties into the spotlight effect, covered in its own article: people notice your flaws much less than you think, and are kinder about them than you expect.

There are real things to keep private, though. Clones are a genuine risk on platforms where games are easy to copy. The article on moats covers which advantages actually protect a small team, and a mechanic is rarely one of them, which is an argument for sharing the journey rather than hiding it. Money details between partners, personal information and anything about other people deserve care. And for anyone in the military, operational security outranks every growth tactic. Ship movements, schedules and locations never belong in a devlog, and your command's social media guidance is the rule to follow.
A routine that survives a deployment

Building in public sounds like it requires being online constantly. It does not. The most durable examples, like Factorio's Friday Facts, were weekly rhythms built around real progress, not hourly posting. A cadence you can keep matters more than volume, and long stretches offline can actually produce the best material, because you come back with a pile of finished work to show.

For a two-person team, it also helps to split the job. One partner can own the weekly post while the other keeps building, then swap. That way the public side never eats all of one person's limited free time, and both stay close enough to the audience to hear what players are saying.

blocks.title: A sustainable building-in-public routine
items: Keep a private log of what you built, broke and learned, even when you cannot post.
Once a week or once a port visit, turn the log into one post showing a finished piece of work.
Show the problem and the fix, not just the result. The struggle is what people follow.
Ask one specific question per post, like which of two thumbnails or jump arcs feels better.
Share numbers you are comfortable with, and decide in advance what stays private.
Check monthly: did the product improve, or only the posts?

blocks.text: Back in that cafeteria, the cooks did not start performing for the cameras. They started caring more about the food, because they could see who was eating it. That is the best version of building in public. Not a marketing campaign wrapped around the work, but a window that makes the work better, the builders more motivated and the audience more invested. Use it to show what you have done, not what you plan to do, and it can be one of the few marketing tools that actually improves the product.

takeaways: Seeing effort makes people value the result more, and taking part makes them care whether it succeeds.
Post artifacts, not intentions. Announcing goals can give a premature sense of achievement.
Your audience judges your mistakes far more kindly than you do.
A steady weekly rhythm beats constant posting, and works even with long offline stretches.
Decide in advance what stays private, and never let a devlog break operational security.

title: The Store That Runs Itself Does Not Exist
dek: Online shopping is now 17 percent of US retail, and nearly one in five online purchases gets sent back. Before opening a dropshipping store, walk a single order through the real math.

blocks.text: The ad usually looks the same. Someone young stands next to a rented sports car, scrolls through a dashboard full of green numbers and explains that their online store runs itself. They never touch the products. A supplier ships everything. Artificial intelligence picks what to sell. For a few thousand dollars, their course or done-for-you service will set one up for you too.

In 2024 and 2025, the US Federal Trade Commission sued several companies that sold exactly that dream. One, which marketed itself as FBA Machine and Passive Scaling, promised income from automated, AI-powered Amazon stores and, according to the FTC, cost its clients more than $15 million. About 14 percent of the stores it set up made no sales at all, and more than three-quarters brought in $60,000 or less in total sales, before any costs. Another, Ascend Ecom, was accused of taking at least $25 million from customers. In a third case, the FTC said the AI technology a company advertised simply did not exist.

None of that means online selling is a scam. It is one of the biggest and fastest-growing parts of the economy. It means the version sold in ads, where the store runs itself and the money is passive, is not the version that exists. If you want to sell physical products online someday, the most valuable thing you can do is walk a single order through the real math, including the parts the ads skip: ad costs, returns and the rules of moving goods across borders.

items.label: Client losses the FTC attributed to the FBA Machine scheme
Consumer losses alleged against Ascend Ecom

blocks.source: American Bar Association Antitrust Law Section, summary of FTC cases

blocks.text: The market is real

Start with what is true. According to the US Census Bureau, American e-commerce sales reached about $340 billion in the second quarter of 2026, adjusted for seasonal swings. That was 17.1 percent of all retail sales, and 12.2 percent more than a year earlier. Online shopping is not a fad, and the tools to start a store, from website builders to payment processing to print-on-demand suppliers, have never been cheaper or easier.

items.label: US e-commerce sales, Q2 2026 (seasonally adjusted)
Share of all US retail sales made online
Growth from Q2 2025

blocks.source: US Census Bureau, Quarterly E-Commerce Report, August 2026

blocks.text: It is worth reading that number the other way around, too. After decades of growth, more than four out of five retail dollars in the US are still spent somewhere other than an online store. E-commerce is growing steadily, not swallowing everything overnight. A small store is competing for a slice of a big but crowded market.

But the same ease is the trap. When anyone can open a store in an afternoon, everyone does. The barrier to entry that protects a business, whether a skill, a brand, a relationship or a product nobody else has, is exactly what a turnkey store lacks. The question is never whether people buy things online. It is why they would buy this thing from you.
What dropshipping actually is

Dropshipping is a simple arrangement. You run the storefront and the marketing. When a customer orders, you pass the order to a supplier, often overseas, who ships the product directly to the customer. You never hold inventory, which is the appeal: no warehouse, no upfront stock, little money at risk on unsold goods.

Look at what you do and do not control, though. You own the customer relationship, so every late package, broken item and angry email is yours to handle. But you do not control the product's quality, the packaging, the shipping time or whether the supplier runs out of stock. And because the same products are available to anyone through the same supplier catalogs, a competitor can list the identical item tomorrow, often at a lower price. When the product is the same for everyone, the only thing left to compete on is marketing, and marketing costs money.

Product research is the other hidden grind. Experienced sellers describe testing product after product, most of which never sell well enough to cover their ads. Each test costs real money in ad spend, and the winners attract copycats quickly. That cycle of testing, finding a winner and watching it get copied is the real job behind the "passive" label, and it is why stores built only on trending products tend to have short lives.

blocks.title: The pitch versus the job

left.head: What the ads promise
items: Passive income
AI picks winning products
No inventory, no risk
Scale fast with ads

right.head: What the work involves
items: Daily customer service and refunds
Testing products that mostly fail
Supplier delays and quality you can't check
Ad costs that rise as you compete for buyers

blocks.text: Walk one order through the math

Here is a made-up but realistic-shaped example, so you can see where the money goes. These are not industry averages; they are round numbers to show the structure. Plug in real quotes before trusting any version of this.

Suppose you sell a gadget for $30. The supplier charges you $9 for it and $5 to ship it to the customer, so $16 is left. The payment processor takes a few percent plus a small fixed fee on every card transaction, and your store platform and apps charge monthly fees, so call it $14 left after a share of those. Now the big one: what did it cost to get this buyer? If you found them through social media ads and it took $15 of ad spend per purchase, you just lost a dollar on the sale. And you have not yet paid for returns, refunds for packages that never arrived, or your own time.

That ad cost is not a scare number. Customer acquisition cost routinely exceeds what a first purchase earns. Dropbox, one of the most successful software companies of its era, found in its early days that paid search cost $233 to $388 to win a customer for a $99 product, as described in the article on the first hundred customers. Real stores survive that math in only a few ways: customers who buy again, higher prices backed by a brand people trust, products with much fatter margins, or free attention from content and word of mouth. Unit economics, the per-customer version of this math, is the subject the rest of the business library keeps coming back to for a reason.

blocks.title: Where a $30 sale goes in the example
items: Customer pays $30.
Supplier: product cost and shipping take about half.
Payment processing and store software take a few more dollars.
Advertising to find this buyer can take everything that is left, or more.
Returns, lost packages and refunds come out of whatever survives.
Your time is paid last, if at all.

blocks.text: A store is not profitable because its products sell. It is profitable if what is left after product, shipping, fees, ads and returns is more than zero, and keeps being more than zero as you grow.
The returns nobody budgets for

Returns are the cost that new sellers forget. In its 2025 report with Happy Returns, the National Retail Federation estimated that US shoppers would return about $850 billion worth of merchandise that year. That is 15.8 percent of all retail sales. For online purchases the rate was higher, 19.3 percent, meaning close to one in five things bought online was sent back. Retailers also estimated that about 9 percent of all returns were fraudulent, such as empty boxes or counterfeit items sent back in place of the real thing.

blocks.title: Share of US retail sales returned, 2025
blocks.note: Holiday figure is retailers' expectation for the season.
blocks.source: National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, October 2025

blocks.text: Shoppers also expect returns to be easy. In the same survey of 2,006 consumers, 82 percent said free returns were a major factor in deciding where to buy, and 71 percent said one bad return experience made them less likely to shop with that retailer again. Shoppers aged 18 to 30 made an average of 7.7 online returns in the previous year, more than any other generation.

For a dropshipper, every one of those numbers lands harder. A big retailer can resell returned stock or send it back through its own warehouse. A small store selling products shipped from another continent usually cannot: shipping a $9 item back overseas costs more than it is worth. So the realistic options are to refund and let the customer keep it, or refuse and risk a dispute, a bad review and a chargeback. Either way, the cost comes out of a margin that was already thin.
The rule change that broke a business model

For years, one quiet rule made cheap cross-border dropshipping work. Under the US *de minimis* exemption, packages worth $800 or less could generally enter the country without duties. That let products ship one at a time straight from overseas factories to American doorsteps with no import tax. Whole business models, including many dropshipping stores and some of the biggest discount shopping apps, were built on it.

Then the rule went away. Duty-free treatment for low-value packages from China was cut off first, and on August 29, 2025, an executive order suspended de minimis treatment for shipments from every country. Low-value parcels now face duties. In February 2026, after the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs that the original suspension relied on, a new executive order kept the suspension in place, according to the trade law firm Sandler, Travis and Rosenberg.

The specific rules will keep shifting, so check current ones before acting on any of this. The bigger lesson is about risk. A business whose profit depends on a single rule, a single supplier, a single ad platform or a single marketplace can be wiped out by a decision made in a meeting it was never invited to. That is the same platform risk described in the article on building on rented land, applied to shipping containers instead of game platforms.
What actually works, and what you already have

People do build durable online stores, but they rarely look like the ads. They tend to share a few traits: a product that is meaningfully different or hard to copy, a brand or community people trust, customers who come back, and a founder who knows the niche personally. Many start by selling to people like themselves, which is how they find products and words that land. Plenty also hold inventory, because controlling quality and shipping speed is worth the risk.

Before buying a course or a done-for-you store, a few tests separate opportunity from sales pitch. Does the seller earn more from teaching the business than from running it? Are earnings claims backed by documents or by screenshots? Is anything described as automated or AI-powered actually explained? The FTC cases above mostly involved promises of passive, automated income, and the money section of this library covers why get-rich-quick offers keep finding buyers.

Here is the reframe worth keeping. For a creator building a Roblox game, the most attractive e-commerce business might be the one you are already working on. A game pass is a digital product with no supplier, no shipping, no customs forms and no returns of physical goods. Delivering it to one more buyer costs essentially nothing. Roblox takes a large cut, as the article on Roblox developer earnings explains, but the platform also handles payments, delivery and much of the discovery. Measured by the order walk-through above, that is a remarkably clean business: most of the costs that sink small online stores simply do not exist.

There is also a practical constraint that no course mentions: a physical store needs someone to answer it. Orders get stuck, addresses are wrong, packages vanish, customers want to know where their item is today. A store left unattended for weeks collects refund requests, chargebacks and one-star reviews. For anyone whose job takes them offline for long stretches, that alone rules out running a store solo. A game that keeps working while you are away, with payments and delivery handled by the platform, fits that life far better.

Physical e-commerce can still be a great goal, especially paired with an audience you have built yourself. A creator with a loyal following can sell merchandise or a product their fans actually want, with far lower ad costs than a stranger running a store from a supplier catalog. Build the audience and the skills first, and you get to choose the product later. Start with the store, and you are renting attention at whatever price the ad auction sets.

takeaways: E-commerce is big and growing, but an easy-to-start store has no protection from competitors.
Walk one order through the math: product, shipping, fees, ad cost per buyer and returns. Many stores lose money per sale.
Close to 1 in 5 online purchases is returned. For overseas-shipped goods, returns usually mean refunds you cannot recover.
A business that depends on one rule, platform or supplier can be erased by a single decision. The end of de minimis proved it.
Digital products, like game passes, avoid most of the costs that sink small physical stores.

title: The First Hundred Are Carried by Hand
dek: Airbnb was earning $200 a week when its founders flew to New York with a rented camera. Early marketing is less about reach than about being specific, being memorable and doing the work that doesn't scale.

blocks.text: In 2009, Airbnb was close to dying. The site had listings, a working product and three founders who believed in it, and revenue had been stuck at about $200 a week for months. Joe Gebbia, one of the founders, scrolled through the New York listings and noticed something embarrassing: the photos were terrible. Dim phone shots, cluttered rooms, pictures lifted from classified ads. Nobody could tell what they would actually be sleeping in.

Paul Graham, who was running the startup accelerator Y Combinator, suggested a fix that sounded almost silly for a tech company. Fly to New York. Rent a camera. Knock on hosts' doors and take better pictures yourselves. They did, with no spreadsheet proving it would work. Weekly revenue doubled to about $400, the first real improvement in eight months.

Four hundred dollars a week is not a business. But the story holds the whole logic of early marketing in miniature. The founders did not buy ads or hire an agency. They found the specific thing stopping people from saying yes, fixed it by hand, and talked to customers face to face while doing it. That is what getting the first hundred customers usually looks like: slow, manual, a little humbling, and far more educational than any launch campaign.

items.label: Airbnb's weekly revenue in 2009, flat for months
Weekly revenue after the founders reshot New York listings by hand

blocks.source: First Round Review interview with Joe Gebbia

blocks.text: Marketing is a fight for a few seconds of attention

Strip away the jargon and marketing has three jobs. The right people have to notice you exist. They have to understand, quickly, what you are and why it is for them. And they have to remember you later, when they are actually ready to play, buy or subscribe. Most beginners obsess over the first job and neglect the other two, which is why a viral post can bring a spike of visitors who leave and never come back.

Remembering is where repetition comes in. In 1968, the psychologist Robert Zajonc showed that people tend to like nonsense words, symbols and faces more simply because they have seen them more often, an effect he called *mere exposure*. It is one of the oldest findings in social psychology, and it is why brands put the same logo, colors and name everywhere for decades.

The modern picture is more careful. A 2017 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin* by Richard Montoya and colleagues pooled 268 exposure curves from 81 articles and found that liking rises with repetition and then turns back down, an inverted U. Familiarity helps until it becomes boredom or irritation. For a small creator, the practical reading is that consistency builds recognition, but spamming the same clip into every Discord server does not make people like you more. It makes them mute you.

The bigger lesson is that you cannot buy attention cheaply at the start. Dropbox found this the hard way. Before it became a household name, the company tried paid search ads. In founder Drew Houston's own 2010 slides, the cost of acquiring each customer through search ran from about $233 to $388, for a product that sold for $99. Every paying user lost the company money. Houston labeled the experiment, bluntly, a failure.

blocks.title: Dropbox's early paid search math
blocks.note: When it costs more to win a customer than the customer pays, more ads only lose money faster.
blocks.source: Drew Houston, 'Dropbox: Startup Lessons Learned', 2010

blocks.text: Positioning: the sentence that sorts people

Before you can win attention, you need to know what you want people to notice. That is positioning: deciding what you are, who you are for and what you should be compared to. Positioning consultant April Dunford, author of *Obviously Awesome*, built a career on the observation that many good products fail because customers file them in the wrong mental drawer. A product described as "another project management app" is judged against giants. The same product described as a tool built specifically for, say, video editors working with clients gets judged on a smaller field where it can win.

Positioning matters even more on a crowded platform. A Roblox player scrolling the front page gives each thumbnail and title a second or two. "Obby" tells them almost nothing, since there are thousands of obbies. A sharper frame tells them what the first minute will feel like and why it is different from the last ten games they tried. The goal is not to sound clever. It is to make the right player think, instantly, "that's my kind of game", and the wrong player scroll past without wasting either of your time.

blocks.title: Two ways to describe the same game

left.head: Vague
items: A fun obby with lots of levels
For everyone
Competes with every obby on Roblox
Players cannot predict the first minute

right.head: Positioned
items: A launcher game where each jump sends you farther than the last
For players who love numbers going up and big fails
Compared with a handful of launcher games, not all obbies
The thumbnail promises the core feeling

blocks.text: On a platform, the name, icon and thumbnail are the positioning. They are the only parts most people ever see. That is why it is worth testing a few versions with real players before launch: show three thumbnails to ten people who fit your target and ask which game they would click and what they expect it to be. If their answers do not match what the game actually is, the problem is not the art. It is the promise.

A useful test: try finishing the sentence "It's like ___, but ___." If you cannot fill both blanks with something specific, the people you are trying to reach cannot either. And notice that good positioning excludes people on purpose. Trying to appeal to everyone usually means nobody feels it was made for them.
Do things that don't scale

In a 2013 essay titled "Do Things That Don't Scale", Paul Graham argued that almost every startup has to recruit its first users by hand. Founders tend to wait for users to arrive on their own, and they almost never do. His examples are deliberately unglamorous. Stripe's founders, instead of sending a sign-up link, would ask an interested developer to hand over their laptop and set up the payment system for them on the spot. Graham's partners nicknamed it the Collison installation, after the two brothers who founded the company.

Pinterest's Ben Silbermann noticed that many early users cared about design, so he went to a conference for design bloggers and recruited people in person. Facebook started at a single university, then a few more, so that each small community hit critical mass before the next one opened. The pattern is the same each time: pick a narrow group, reach them personally, and make them very happy before worrying about reaching everyone else.

Graham also points out why tiny numbers are not as pathetic as they feel. If you start with 100 users and grow 10 percent a week, you have roughly 14,000 after a year and about 2 million after two. The hard part is not getting big. It is getting the first group of people who care enough to stick around and tell others. That group is also your best source of information about what to fix. (The separate article on the lean startup covers how to treat early users as experiments, not just numbers.)

Founders resist this advice because it feels like a waste. Why spend an afternoon on one user when the goal is thousands? Graham's answer is that the founders have little to lose at the start, and that the habit of delighting individual customers scales better than people expect. There is also a quieter benefit. When you onboard people personally, you see the exact moment their face goes blank, the button they cannot find, the rule they did not understand. No analytics dashboard shows you that as clearly as watching one confused person.

Narrow also beats broad for a reason covered in the article on 1,000 true fans: a hundred people who love something will carry it further than a thousand who think it is fine. Love produces word of mouth, return visits and forgiveness for rough edges. Mild approval produces a polite thumbs up and then nothing.
The first hundred customers are not a marketing problem to be solved with reach. They are a research project. Every one you recruit by hand tells you something an ad never will.
Turn customers into the channel

What finally worked for Dropbox was not more ads. It was its own users. In 2010 the company offered free storage to both the person who sent an invite and the friend who signed up. According to Houston's slides, that two-sided reward permanently raised sign-ups by 60 percent. By April 2010, users were sending about 2.8 million referral invites a month, and referrals accounted for roughly 35 percent of daily sign-ups, with shared folders and other built-in sharing adding about 20 percent more. The company went from 100,000 registered users in September 2008 to 4 million by January 2010.

The key detail is that the referral reward made the product itself better. More storage was the thing users already wanted, and shared folders only worked if your friends had accounts too. Marketing that is built into how the product is used beats marketing bolted on afterward. Games have an obvious version of this: features that are more fun with a friend, moments that beg to be clipped, and rewards that make inviting someone feel like helping them rather than spamming them.

That connects to a point made in the article on why distribution beats product: on Roblox, how players behave in your game drives how often the platform recommends it. A friend who joins because they were invited, and then stays, is worth far more than a stranger who bounces in thirty seconds. A small, loyal starting group sends the algorithm better signals than a big crowd that leaves.
A first-hundred plan for a small team

For two people building a game in their spare time, the first hundred players are within reach without spending money, as long as you treat it as a deliberate project instead of hoping launch day takes care of it. Here is one way to break it down.

blocks.title: Getting the first hundred players by hand
items: Write the one-sentence position: what it is, who it is for, what it is like but better.
List 20 real people who fit that description, by name if you can: friends, cousins, people in Discords you already belong to.
Invite them one at a time with a personal message, and watch at least a few of them play, live or on a recording.
Fix the biggest thing that made people quit, the way Airbnb fixed its photos, before inviting anyone new.
Ask the players who stayed where people like them hang out, then go there and show up as a person, not an ad.
Add one reason to bring a friend that makes the game better for both players.
Only when people return on their own, test small paid promotion and measure what each player actually costs.

blocks.text: Keep one simple record as you go: for each new player, where did they come from? A personal invite, a clip, a Discord post, a friend who was already playing. After a few dozen players, a pattern almost always shows up, and it is usually not the channel you expected. That record tells you where to spend your next scarce hour.

Notice what is missing: ad budgets, logos, a launch trailer. Those can come later. The early goal is to learn which sentence makes the right people lean in, which part of the experience makes them leave, and what makes the ones who stay tell a friend. Unit costs and lifetime value matter eventually, and paid ads can work once you know those numbers, but spending before you know them is how Dropbox lost money on every search customer.

Long stretches of time away from a keyboard actually suit this approach better than you might expect. You cannot run a daily social media machine from a place with no internet. You can, however, collect a handful of player recordings before you leave, study them offline, and come back with a short list of fixes and a short list of people to personally invite. Small, specific, by hand.
The reframe

Most people imagine marketing as a megaphone: the louder you shout, the more you sell. The early evidence points the other way. Airbnb doubled its revenue by taking photos. Stripe grew by installing its software on strangers' laptops. Dropbox grew when it stopped paying for attention and started rewarding users who brought friends.

At the start, marketing looks less like a megaphone and more like a conversation with a few dozen people who might care. If you can make those people genuinely happy, and understand exactly why, you have something worth amplifying. If you cannot, no amount of amplification will save it. So the real question for any new project is not "How do I reach a million people?" It is "Who are the first twenty, and what would make them tell someone?"

takeaways: Marketing has three jobs: get noticed, be understood fast, and be remembered. Beginners usually only work on the first.
Positioning decides who you are compared with. A narrow, specific frame beats trying to appeal to everyone.
Recruit the first users by hand and watch them closely. They are a research project, not a number.
The best growth is built into the product, like Dropbox's referral storage, not bolted on afterward.
Do not pay for attention until you know what a customer is worth. Dropbox paid up to $388 to win a $99 customer.
