title: The Video That Was the Product
dek: Dropbox tested its idea with a three-minute screencast before the software worked for the public. The lean startup turned that trick into a method, and the best evidence for it comes from an experiment that treated founders like scientists.

blocks.text: Building a file-syncing service that actually works across every kind of computer is brutally hard. Drew Houston, the founder of Dropbox, knew that years of engineering stood between him and a product anyone could use. So before finishing it, he made a short demo video showing how it would work, packed it with in-jokes for the tech crowd on the news site Digg, and posted it. According to Houston, the beta waiting list jumped from 5,000 people to 75,000 overnight.

Eric Ries, who told the story in a 2011 guest post on TechCrunch, drew the lesson in one line: in that case, the video was the minimum viable product. Nobody could use it. Nobody could buy it. But it answered the question that mattered most at that stage, which was whether enough people wanted this thing to justify the years of work. The answer came back in a day.

items.label: Dropbox beta waiting list before the demo video
Waiting list the next day, per Drew Houston

blocks.source: Eric Ries, TechCrunch, October 2011

blocks.text: That is the core of what became known as the lean startup, the method Ries laid out in his 2011 book of the same name. It is often summarized as ship fast. A better summary is: figure out what you most need to learn, and find the cheapest way to learn it. (The separate article on shipping early covers why version one should embarrass you. This one is about what version one is for.)
A startup is an experiment

Ries's central claim is that a startup is not a small version of a big company. A big company executes a known plan to serve known customers. A startup is searching for a plan, under so much uncertainty that most of its early guesses about customers, pricing and features will be wrong. He built on the work of Steve Blank, a serial founder and teacher whose customer development approach insisted that founders get out of the building and talk to real customers before scaling anything.

Blank put the distinction neatly: a startup is a temporary organization whose job is to search for a business model that can repeat and grow, while an established company's job is to execute one it already has. The tools that serve execution, such as detailed plans, fixed deadlines and feature roadmaps, can actively mislead during the search, because they reward doing the plan rather than finding out whether the plan is right.

Under that kind of uncertainty, Ries argued, the unit of progress is not code written or features shipped. It is what he called validated learning: something you now know about customers that you did not know before, backed by evidence from their behavior rather than your hopes. A team can work flat out for a year, ship a polished product and have learned almost nothing, because it never put a risky assumption in front of real people.

He knew this from experience. His earlier company, IMVU, spent months building a 3D chat product as an add-on to existing instant messaging networks, on the theory that people would not want to switch networks. When real users finally tried it, the theory fell apart; they were happy to use a new, standalone network and were reluctant to invite their existing friends into something odd. Months of careful engineering had gone into supporting an assumption that a cheap test would have broken in days.

blocks.title: Build, measure, learn
items: Ideas: state the riskiest assumption as a testable guess
Build: make the smallest thing that can test it
Measure: watch what real people actually do
Learn: decide to persevere, change course, or stop

blocks.text: The loop runs backward from how it is drawn. You start by deciding what you need to learn, then what you would have to measure to learn it, and only then what you need to build to get that measurement. Most builders run it the other way: build what seems cool, see what happens, and try to learn something from the result.
An MVP is an experiment, not a small product

The phrase minimum viable product has been stretched so far it now often just means a rough first version. Ries meant something sharper: the version of a product that lets a team learn the most about customers with the least effort. The emphasis is on learning, and the minimum refers to effort, not quality.

blocks.title: Two ways to read 'minimum viable product'

left.head: MVP as a small product
items: Build fewer features, but build them
Ship when it feels sort of ready
Success means people use it
Next step: add more features

right.head: MVP as an experiment
items: Build only what tests one assumption
Ship when it can answer the question
Success means you learned something true
Next step: test the next riskiest assumption

blocks.text: Seen that way, an MVP can be almost anything. A video, a landing page with a sign-up button, a version where humans quietly do by hand what software will eventually automate. For a game, it might be a single level that contains only the core loop, played by twenty strangers, with nothing else built around it. The question is not whether the thing is good. It is whether it can tell you what you need to know.

Ries also warned about the numbers people use to fool themselves, which he called vanity metrics. Total sign-ups, total visits and total views only ever go up, so they always feel like progress. What matters are actionable metrics: numbers tied to a specific change that tell you whether that change worked. For a Roblox game, total visits is a vanity metric. The share of new players who return the next day, measured before and after an update, is an actionable one.
What the evidence says

For years the lean startup was mostly supported by stories, and stories select for winners. Nobody writes up the startups that ran perfect experiments and still died. So it matters that someone tested a version of the idea properly.

In a randomized controlled trial published in Management Science in 2020, Arnaldo Camuffo and colleagues worked with 116 early-stage Italian startups and tracked them at 16 points over about a year. Both groups got ten sessions of training on getting feedback from the market. But one group was taught to work like scientists: to build a theory of why their idea would succeed, turn it into explicit hypotheses, and run rigorous tests. The control group was left to judge its ideas by intuition.

items.label: Startups randomly assigned in the trial
Training sessions given to both groups
Tracking period, with 16 data points per startup

blocks.source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella & Spina, Management Science, 2020

blocks.text: The founders who behaved like scientists performed better, were more likely to pivot to a different idea, and were no more likely to drop out early. The authors' explanation is about precision. Testing hypotheses made founders less likely to keep chasing ideas that only looked good, and more likely to spot ideas that looked weak but were actually promising. It is one study, in one country, with fairly small firms, so it is not the final word. But it is a real experiment, and it points the same way as the method.

Notice what the trial did not test. It did not compare launching fast against launching slow. It compared thinking clearly about assumptions against going with your gut. That distinction matters, because the most serious critique of the lean startup is about speed.
The critique: false starts

Tom Eisenmann, a Harvard Business School professor, studied failed ventures for his 2021 book Why Startups Fail. One pattern he named was the false start: founders who took launch fast and fail fast so literally that they rushed out a product without first doing basic research on what customers needed. When it flopped, they had learned only that this particular version did not work, not why. Then they repeated the process, burning time and money on a series of half-informed guesses.

Eisenmann's point is not that the lean startup is wrong, but that it is often read as permission to skip thinking. The cheapest test of an idea is frequently not a product at all. It is a conversation with ten potential users, a look at what similar products already do, or a careful list of what has to be true for the idea to work. Building an MVP is the second-cheapest test, not the first.

Before building anything, write down the one assumption that would kill the project if it were false. Then ask what the cheapest possible test of that assumption is. It is usually smaller than a prototype.

There is a second limit worth knowing, and it matters for games in particular. Some products only reveal their value when they are reasonably finished. A gray-box prototype can make a good mechanic look dull, because so much of what makes a game satisfying comes from feedback, sound, animation and the feeling of control. (The article on game feel covers why.) A team that tests a rough build, sees flat reactions and kills the idea may have thrown away something that only needed a little juice.

The answer is not to skip testing but to test the right layer. A core loop can be tested with placeholder art as long as the moment-to-moment feel is roughly there; a story or a world usually cannot be tested that way at all. Part of the skill is knowing which of your assumptions a cheap test can actually answer, and which ones need a more complete build before the data means anything. Lean thinking says to spend the least effort that gives a trustworthy answer. Sometimes the least effort is still a real chunk of work.

Finally, experiments only help if someone is willing to read them honestly. Every builder is tempted to explain away a bad result: the testers were the wrong people, the timing was off, the next update will fix it. Sometimes that is true. The discipline the lean method asks for is to write those excuses down before the test, so that you cannot invent them afterward.
Lean for a two-person game and a new channel

For a small team working in stolen hours, this method is less a business philosophy than a survival skill. Time is the scarcest resource, and the most expensive mistake is spending months polishing something built on an untested guess. The lean move is to name the guess out loud and test it before it costs much.

For a Roblox game, the riskiest assumption is almost always whether the core loop is fun on its own, before any progression, cosmetics or story. That can be tested with one rough level, a few friends of friends, and the game's own retention numbers. If people do not come back to the bare loop, more features will not save it. (The articles on retention and on deciding with data go deeper into what to measure.)

For a YouTube channel, the risky assumptions are about the audience and the promise. Does anyone want this particular angle? Does this packaging make the promise clear? Those can be tested with a handful of videos made quickly, each built around a single question, rather than with one perfect launch video that took two months. Each upload is a small experiment; the analytics are the lab results.

blocks.title: A lean cycle you can run in a month of spare evenings
items: Write the project's riskiest assumption as a single sentence.
Decide what result would prove it wrong, before you test it.
Build the smallest thing that could produce that result.
Put it in front of real players or viewers, not just friends.
Read the numbers that tie to the assumption, not the vanity totals.
Decide: keep going, change direction, or stop and start the next idea.

blocks.text: The hardest step is the last one. Ries called it the choice to pivot or persevere, and it requires something founders rarely have: a willingness to be wrong in public, even if the public is only your brother. Deciding in advance what result would change your mind makes that easier, because the decision was made by a calmer version of you before the result arrived.

Houston's video worked because it was aimed at a question, not at an audience. He did not need applause. He needed to know whether to spend the next several years building Dropbox. The real lesson of the lean startup is to keep asking which question you are trying to answer, and to refuse to build anything bigger than the answer requires.

takeaways: An MVP is the cheapest experiment that tests your riskiest assumption, not a small version of the final product.
Measure actionable metrics tied to a specific change, such as next-day return rate, not ever-rising totals.
A 2020 randomized trial of 116 startups found founders taught to test hypotheses like scientists did better and pivoted more.
Fail fast is not a license to skip thinking; talking to users is often a cheaper test than building anything.
Decide in advance what result would make you change course.

title: Whoever Speaks First
dek: In study after study, the first number on the table drags the final deal toward it. Six decades of negotiation research explain when to use that, how to defend against it, and why so many people never ask at all.

blocks.text: Two people sit across a table, one playing a buyer and one a seller in a simulated business deal. They have the same information sheet, the same deadline and the same instructions. The only difference between pairs is who speaks first. In a series of experiments published in 2001, the psychologists Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler found that this one detail decided a great deal. Whichever side made the first offer, buyer or seller, tended to walk away with the better deal, and the first offer was a strong predictor of the final price.

It sounds like a trick. It is closer to a law of how minds handle uncertainty. When nobody knows exactly what something is worth, the first concrete number becomes the reference point that everything else is measured against. Negotiation research has spent six decades mapping when that works, when it backfires and how to defend against it. Most people never use any of it, because most people never negotiate at all.

That is a costly habit. In a study of newly hired employees across many industries, Michelle Marks of George Mason University and Crystal Harold of Temple University found that those who negotiated their starting salary raised it by about $5,000 on average, and more than half of the negotiators also won something extra, like vacation time. The researchers projected that, with 5 percent yearly raises compounding on top, a $5,000 higher start could add up to more than $600,000 over a 40-year career.

items.label: Average starting-salary gain for new hires who negotiated
Of negotiators also won a non-salary benefit

blocks.source: Marks & Harold, Journal of Organizational Behavior, 2011 (via George Mason University)

blocks.text: How strong is the anchor?

A single study can mislead, so the useful question is what happens when you pool many. In 2006, Dan Orr and Chris Guthrie ran a meta-analysis of anchoring in negotiation studies, combining 19 effect sizes from 16 articles. They found a correlation of about 0.5 between the opening anchor and the final outcome. Put plainly, roughly a quarter of the variation in where deals landed was associated with where the first number was set. For social science, that is a big effect.

Two details from that analysis are more interesting than the headline. The anchor's pull was weaker for people with real professional experience, though only a few studies included them, so that finding is tentative. And it shrank as negotiators had more information. When people knew little about the other side, the correlation was about 0.54. With moderate information it was 0.47, and with lots of information it fell to 0.38.

blocks.title: How much the opening anchor tracks the final deal
blocks.note: Higher numbers mean final deals follow the first offer more closely. Information and experience weaken the pull.
blocks.source: Orr & Guthrie, Ohio State Journal on Dispute Resolution, 2006

blocks.text: That pattern is the whole game in miniature. An anchor is powerful exactly to the degree that the person hearing it is unsure what the thing is worth. Homework is the antidote. So if you know more about the market than the other side does, it usually pays to speak first. If you know less, your priority is to find out more before any number gets said.
Defending against someone else's number

Galinsky and Mussweiler's study had a second, more hopeful finding. The first-mover advantage disappeared when the person receiving the offer deliberately focused on information that contradicted it. In separate experiments, thinking about the other side's alternatives, thinking about the other side's bottom line, or simply focusing on one's own target price all cancelled out the anchor's effect. This worked both face to face and over email.

That is the scientific case for the oldest advice in negotiation: know your alternatives before you sit down. In their 1981 book *Getting to Yes*, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project called it your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If the deal on the table is worse than your BATNA, you walk. If you have not worked out your BATNA, you have no way to know when an offer is bad, and the other side's anchor fills the gap.

What if you do not have a strong alternative? A 2018 set of studies by Michael Schaerer, Martin Schweinsberg and Roderick Swaab found that simply imagining a strong alternative helped people with weak positions negotiate more ambitiously and reach more profitable deals, mainly because it raised their aspirations and their first offers. But the effect had limits. It stopped helping when the imaginer did not make the first offer or when the other side was doing the same thing, and it backfired when the two positions were very hard to reconcile. Imagination can lift your aim, not change reality.

Put those findings together and you get a simple script for the moment someone else names a number first. Do not treat their number as the starting point for haggling. Pause, bring your own target back to mind, and answer with your own number and the reason behind it, as though their figure had never been said. Then shift the conversation to the evidence: comparable prices, results, alternatives. The anchor loses its grip when the discussion is about reasons instead of about the distance between two figures.

The same logic answers the dreaded question in job interviews, "What salary are you looking for?" If you have done your research and know the market range, giving a specific, reasoned number near the top of it is often the stronger move. If you genuinely do not know, the smarter play is to ask what range they have budgeted for the role, and to treat the answer as information rather than as a ceiling.

blocks.title: A one-page prep sheet before any negotiation
items: Research the market: what do similar jobs, items or deals actually go for?
Write down your target, the ambitious but defensible result you are aiming for.
Write down your walk-away point and your best alternative if there is no deal.
Guess the other side's alternatives and bottom line. What happens to them if you say no?
List the issues beyond price: timing, extras, responsibilities, flexibility.
Decide whether you know enough to make the first offer, and prepare a reason for it.

blocks.text: The shape of a good first offer

A 2026 review by Loschelder and Petrowsky of Leuphana University sums up the trade-off. First offers can anchor outcomes in your favor, but an offer that is too aggressive can alienate the other side, raise the chance of no deal at all and leave a bad taste even if you win. The advantage is strongest when the offer is shaped well, and four features keep coming up: precision, framing, ranges and rationales.

Precision is the most surprising. In studies with 1,254 participants, Malia Mason, Daniel Ames and colleagues at Columbia Business School found that a precise opening number, like $5,015, made recipients assume the person knew the item's value well, so they answered with more conciliatory counteroffers than they did after a round number like $5,000. In a real-world check, only about 2 percent of home listings they looked at used precise prices. Most people round, and rounding signals a guess.

Ranges can work too, with care. Ames and Mason found that some range offers, such as asking for $7,200 to $7,600 for a car, got better terms without hurting the relationship, because the listener takes both ends as clues about your real bottom line and an extreme counter starts to feel rude. Ranges that are too wide or too extreme lose that benefit. And a rationale helps any number: an offer tied to a reason, such as comparable sales or measured results, invites a discussion about the reason instead of a flat no.
A good first offer is ambitious, specific and explained. An outrageous one is not an anchor. It is an insult, and the research says insults raise the odds that nobody gets anything.
The pie is usually not fixed

Everything so far treats negotiation as a tug-of-war over one number. Many real negotiations are not like that, and assuming they are is one of the most common mistakes people make. In a review of 32 experiments, the negotiation researchers Thompson and Hrebec described what they called the lose-lose effect: two sides often share an interest without realizing it, and they settle on a deal that is worse for both than one that was easily available.

Negotiation teachers love a simple story to illustrate this. Two siblings fight over one orange and eventually split it down the middle. One then squeezes her half for juice and throws away the peel. The other grates his half's peel for baking and throws away the fruit. Each could have had twice as much if either had asked the other one question: what do you want it for?

blocks.title: Two ways to negotiate the same deal

left.head: Fighting over positions
items: I want 60 percent
Each concession is a loss
Hide your priorities
Split the difference at the end

right.head: Trading on interests
items: Why does each side want what it wants?
Trade things you value less for things you value more
Share priorities selectively to find trades
Add issues so both sides can win something

blocks.text: This matters for anyone building something with a partner. Two brothers splitting the work on a Roblox game are not really negotiating over one number. One might care more about creative control of the map, the other about the code or the money. Treating every disagreement as a split-the-difference fight leaves value on the table. (The separate article on partner roles covers why those conversations are worth having before money arrives.) The negotiation research adds how: ask about interests first, then trade.
Who asks, and who pays for asking

If negotiation pays, why do so many people skip it? Part of the answer is that asking feels risky, and for some people it really is riskier. A 2015 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin* by Jens Mazei and colleagues pooled 123 effect sizes from nearly 11,000 people and found that men, on average, got somewhat better economic outcomes than women. But the gap depended heavily on context. It shrank when negotiators had experience, when they knew the bargaining range and when they were negotiating on behalf of someone else, and it even reversed in the conditions least stacked against women. A 2026 review by the same research group concludes that gaps in outcomes persist in some situations, while the gap in willingness to start negotiating has largely narrowed.

Social class shows a similar pattern. In a 2026 paper in *PNAS*, researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, MIT and Stanford studied more than 10,000 people across four studies and found that people from lower-class backgrounds were less likely to start negotiations, partly because they felt less powerful and feared backlash. In a fifth experiment with HR professionals, that fear turned out to be partly justified: the identical request drew more backlash when it came from a lower-class candidate. The authors call it a double bind. Staying quiet keeps you behind, and asking carries a higher social price.

The common thread in both lines of research is that information and practice shrink the gaps. Knowing the market range, having done it before and having a clear reason to ask all made a difference. Those are things you can build on purpose.

For anyone in the military, this is a skill that may need deliberate practice. Military pay is set by tables, not bargaining, so years can pass without ever negotiating a salary. That changes the moment you look at civilian jobs. A nuclear-trained technician with real plant experience walking into a utility hiring process has market information to gather, alternatives to line up and a precise, reasoned number to prepare. The first civilian offer is an anchor too.
How sure is the science?

One honest caveat. Much of negotiation research comes from simulated negotiations, often between students with play money. A 2026 analysis of 50 recent negotiation studies by Joachim Hüffmeier and colleagues found that independent replications and other transparency practices are still uncommon in the field, especially in specialty journals. The first-offer effect has been found many times by many labs, which is reassuring, but exact numbers like a correlation of 0.5 should be read as rough guides, not physical constants.

Still, the practical message is unusually consistent across studies. Do the homework, because information weakens anchors. Know your alternative, because it tells you when to walk. Make a specific, reasoned first offer when you know the market. Look for trades instead of only splitting differences. And above all, ask. The research is clearest on one point: the deal you never negotiate is the one that is guaranteed not to get better.

takeaways: First offers anchor outcomes, especially when the other side is unsure what things are worth.
Defend against an anchor by focusing on your target, your alternatives and the other side's alternatives.
Make first offers specific and explained. Precise numbers and reasoned ranges outperform round guesses.
Look for trades on what each side cares about most. Many deals that look like tug-of-war are not.
Information and practice shrink negotiation gaps. Prepare like it is an exam, then actually ask.

title: The Number That Arrives First
dek: Students bid triple for the same keyboard because of their Social Security numbers. Pricing psychology is real, but smaller and stranger than its reputation, and Roblox's own data says most creators charge too much.

blocks.text: In a marketing class at MIT, students were shown a handful of ordinary products: a cordless keyboard, a bottle of wine, a box of chocolates. Before bidding on each one, they were asked to write down the last two digits of their Social Security number and say whether they would pay that many dollars for it. The number was meaningless. Everyone knew it was meaningless. It still bent their bids.

Students whose numbers ended between 80 and 99 bid an average of $56 for the keyboard. Students whose numbers ended between 1 and 20 bid $16. Across the products, the high-number group's bids ran roughly 216 to 346 percent higher. The economist Dan Ariely, who ran the study with George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec, used it to make a provocative claim: people often do not know what things are worth, so they grab whatever number is nearby and adjust from there.

items.label: Average keyboard bid, Social Security digits 80 to 99
Average keyboard bid, Social Security digits 1 to 20

blocks.source: Ariely, Loewenstein & Prelec, 'Coherent Arbitrariness', QJE 2003; Ariely, HuffPost, 2008

blocks.text: That idea, that value is partly invented on the spot, sits under almost every pricing trick you have seen: the crossed-out "was" price, the $9.99 tag, the three-tier menu with one option nobody buys. Some of these effects are among the most solid findings in behavioral science. Others are much smaller and shakier than their reputation. And for someone selling game passes on Roblox, the most useful pricing evidence available turns out to come from Roblox itself.
The anchor drops first

The classic demonstration came from Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in 1974. They spun a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, then asked people what percentage of United Nations member countries were in Africa. People who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25 percent. People who saw 65 said 45 percent. A random number, visibly produced by a wheel, moved a factual guess by twenty points.

This is anchoring: the first number you encounter becomes the starting point, and people adjust away from it, but not far enough. Unlike many famous psychology results, the basic effect has held up well. When the Many Labs project re-ran classic experiments across dozens of labs in 2014, anchoring was among the effects that replicated most strongly.

The size of the effect in real purchases is another matter. In 2014, the economists Zacharias Maniadis, Fabio Tufano and John List re-tested anchoring on valuations and found weaker effects than the original studies, and they used the episode to warn that a single striking result is a poor guide to how big an effect really is. There is a further reason for caution with this particular body of work. In 2021, a separate 2012 paper co-authored by Ariely was retracted after investigators found that some of its data had been fabricated. Ariely denied fabricating it, and the anchoring findings rest on many other labs too, but it is a reminder that the most quotable numbers deserve the most skepticism.

In practice, sellers use anchors constantly. A store shows the expensive model first. A software page lists the enterprise plan beside the basic one. A sale tag shows a crossed-out higher price. The last one has legal limits: the US Federal Trade Commission's long-standing guides on deceptive pricing say a "former price" has to be one the item was genuinely offered at, not a number invented to make the discount look bigger. An honest anchor is a real comparison. A fake one is a lie with a price tag.
Anchoring is real and robust. What is not settled is how much it moves money in a real market where people can compare prices, read reviews and walk away.
The decoy nobody is meant to buy

The second famous trick works on choice rather than price. In 1982, Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto showed that adding a clearly inferior third option can shift people toward the option it most resembles. They called it the attraction effect. Marketers call it the decoy.

The best-known illustration comes from Ariely's book *Predictably Irrational*. He described an old subscription offer from *The Economist*: web only for $59, print only for $125, or print and web together for $125. Nobody sane picks print only when print plus web costs the same. But in his classroom test, its presence seemed to matter. With all three options, 16 percent of students chose web only and 84 percent chose the bundle. With the useless print-only option removed, 68 percent chose web only and just 32 percent took the bundle.

blocks.title: Share choosing the $125 bundle
blocks.note: A classroom demonstration with students, not a market test. Treat it as an illustration of the idea.
blocks.source: Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational, 2008

blocks.text: That demo is vivid, but it was a classroom poll, not a field experiment with real money. And the academic picture has grown more complicated. In 2014, Shane Frederick, Leonard Lee and Ernest Baskin argued in the *Journal of Marketing Research* that the attraction effect mostly appears when products are reduced to tidy numbers on a page. When people actually taste a drink, or see hotel rooms in photos, the effect tends to vanish. Huber and his colleagues replied that the effect is real but only under specific conditions: the two main options have to be close, the decoy has to be obviously worse, and the comparison has to be easy to see.

That is a useful correction. A decoy works best on a confusing menu of numbers, when the buyer cannot easily judge quality. It works worst on things people can experience directly. A game pass that players can see in action is closer to the hotel photo than to the spreadsheet.
Why $9.99 still works

Then there is the oldest trick of all, the price ending in 9. It sounds too silly to matter: $2.99 versus $3.00 is a one-cent difference. But in 2005, Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz showed through five experiments that people really do perceive $2.99 as meaningfully cheaper than $3.00, and only when the leftmost digit changes. $2.99 versus $3.00 triggers it. $2.79 versus $2.80 does not. They call it the left-digit effect. We read numbers left to right, and the first digit gets most of our attention.

Field evidence backs this up. Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester ran three experiments with a mail-order clothing retailer, printing different versions of the same catalog with different prices for the same items. A price ending in $9 increased demand in all three tests. The boost was larger for new items, which customers had no prior price for, and weaker when items were already marked with a "Sale" sign.

That pattern reveals what is really going on. A 9-ending is partly a signal. It says "this is a deal" to someone who does not know what the item should cost. When customers already know the price, or already see a sale tag, the signal adds less. That is also why many premium brands avoid 9s entirely: they do not want to look like a discount.

Virtual currencies add one more layer. On Roblox, players see prices in Robux, not dollars, so the anchors that matter are other Robux prices: what the last game charged for a similar pass, what a skin costs in the avatar shop. Few players convert back to dollars in their heads. That makes the left-digit effect and familiar price points inside the game's own currency more relevant than any rule about $9.99.
More choices, fewer buyers? Not so fast

You may have heard of the jam study. In 2000, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth in a grocery store and found that a display of 24 jams attracted more browsers but led to fewer purchases than a display of 6. It became the founding story of "choice overload" and has been quoted in countless pricing pages to justify cutting options.

The follow-up research is much less dramatic. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd pooled 50 experiments with more than 5,000 participants and found an average effect of virtually zero. Some studies found that more options hurt, others found they helped, and nobody could pin down reliable conditions for when overload kicks in. The honest takeaway is not "always offer three options." It is that the menu matters, but no magic number works everywhere, and you have to test yours.

blocks.title: Pricing claims versus the evidence

left.head: What the blogs say
items: Anchors can triple what people pay
Always add a decoy tier
Three options is the magic number
Psychological prices are a growth hack

right.head: What the research shows
items: Anchors are robust, but real-market effects are smaller
Decoys work mainly on abstract, numeric menus
Choice overload averages out to about zero
Real tests typically find single-digit gains

blocks.text: What a real pricing lab found

Here is the part most pricing blogs cannot offer: results from a platform running experiments on millions of real purchases. In October 2024, Roblox launched Price Optimization, a tool that tests different prices for a game's items and passes on small groups of players for two weeks and recommends the best one. Its announcement contained a blunt line for creators: most of them unknowingly price their in-game items too high, and in many cases the fix would be to cut prices.

In April 2025 Roblox added regional pricing, which automatically lowers prices in countries where Robux are expensive relative to local incomes. In June 2026 it folded both into one system called Managed Pricing and published results. Among the top 2,500 games, those using regional pricing saw an average 4 to 10 percent increase in overall Robux spending, 1 to 6 percent more players and playtime, and 43 to 52 percent more pass purchases in the discounted regions. Creators using price optimization saw average earnings growth of 4 percent.

blocks.title: Roblox regional pricing results, top 2,500 games, 2025
blocks.note: Low and high ends of the ranges Roblox reported. Pass purchases were measured in the discounted regions. Averages, not guarantees.
blocks.source: Roblox Developer Forum, Managed Pricing announcement, June 2026

blocks.text: Four percent sounds small next to the $56-versus-$16 keyboard. That is the point. When real buyers can compare, wait and walk away, good pricing usually adds single-digit percentages, not miracles. The dramatic lab effects shrink in the wild. And the biggest gain on Roblox did not come from a psychological trick at all. It came from lowering prices for players who could not afford them, which brought in buyers who had been priced out entirely.

This connects to the economics covered in the separate article on Roblox developer earnings. Because a creator keeps only a slice of each Robux spent, and because a digital pass costs nothing to deliver to one more player, selling twice as many passes at a lower price is often better than selling a few at a high one. Volume is cheap to serve when the product is code.
A pricing playbook for a game pass
Put the research together and a sensible approach emerges. It uses the real effects lightly, ignores the hype and leans on testing.

blocks.title: Pricing your first passes
items: Look at what similar games charge for similar passes. That is the anchor players already carry.
Show the most valuable pass first, so cheaper ones look reasonable next to it, but make sure it is genuinely worth its price.
Keep the menu short and clearly different: each option should do a different job for a different player.
Price for volume at launch. A digital pass costs nothing to deliver, and Roblox's data says most creators start too high.
Turn on regional pricing and price testing once you have enough buyers, and let real behavior pick the number.
Change one thing at a time and watch revenue per player, not just sales count.

blocks.text: Anchoring also explains why your launch price matters more than later ones. The first price your early players see becomes their reference point. Lowering it later feels like a gift; raising it feels like a betrayal, even if the new price is fair. If you are unsure, it is usually easier to start a little low and add value, or create a new premium pass, than to push an existing price up on the players who know what it used to cost.

One warning sits on top of all of this. Tricks that make players feel cheated, like fake "was" prices or decoys that only exist to confuse, may win a sale and lose a player. Your audience on Roblox is young and talks to each other constantly, so trust is a pricing asset too. The anchoring research says first impressions of value stick. That cuts both ways: a pass that feels like a rip-off anchors how players see everything else in your game.

The deeper lesson from the Social Security experiment is not that people are easy to fool. It is that value is uncertain, and people reach for whatever reference point is nearby. Your job as a seller is to give them an honest one: a clear comparison, a fair price, a product that obviously earns it. Then test, because the market's answer is worth more than any psychology blog's.

takeaways: Anchoring is one of psychology's most robust effects: the first number people see shapes what they think is fair.
Decoys and choice-overload effects are real only under narrow conditions. Do not build a strategy on them.
A 9-ending signals a deal. It helps most when buyers do not already know the price.
In real markets, good pricing usually adds single-digit percentages. Roblox's price optimization averaged 4 percent.
For digital goods with near-zero delivery cost, test lower prices before higher ones.

title: Follow the Robux: Where a Player's Dollar Actually Goes
dek: Roblox paid its creators about $1.5 billion in 2025, and the typical creator who cashed out got a few hundred dollars a year. Tracing a single dollar through the system explains both numbers.

blocks.text: Two numbers from Roblox's own reports sit next to each other uneasily. In 2025, according to the company's annual filing, creators earned about $1.5 billion through its Developer Exchange program, up from about $923 million the year before. And in the twelve months that ended in December 2024, the median creator in that program received $1,575.

Both numbers are true at once, and the gap between them is the whole story of Roblox as a business for small developers. There is a lot of money moving through the platform, it is growing fast, and almost all of it lands on a small number of games. To see why, it helps to follow one dollar from a player's parent's card to a developer's bank account and count what happens along the way.

items.label: Earned by Roblox creators through DevEx in 2025
The same figure for 2024
Median yearly payout to a DevEx creator (12 months to Dec 2024)

blocks.source: Roblox Form 10-K for fiscal 2025; Roblox Annual Economic Impact Report, 2025

blocks.text: Following one dollar

Start with the purchase. Players buy Robux in bundles, and the price per Robux depends on the bundle and how it is bought. Roblox's annual report puts the average selling price in 2025 at about one cent per Robux. So, roughly, a dollar of real money becomes 100 Robux in a player's account.

Next, the player spends those Robux in your game, say on a game pass. Roblox's filing says that when creators sell their own items inside their own experiences, they receive 70 percent of the Robux and the platform keeps 30 percent. Of the 100 Robux, 70 land in your account as what Roblox calls earned Robux.

Finally, you cash out through the Developer Exchange, usually shortened to DevEx. Since September 5, 2025, the standard rate has been $0.0038 per earned Robux, up from $0.0035 before that. Seventy Robux times $0.0038 is about 27 cents. That is the core fact of Roblox economics for a small developer: of each dollar a player spends in your game, roughly a quarter reaches you, before any taxes.

blocks.title: Cash to the developer per $1 a player spends
blocks.note: Assumes Robux bought at the 2025 average of about $0.01 each and the 70% creator share on in-game sales. Real bundle prices vary.
blocks.source: Roblox Form 10-K FY2025; Roblox DevEx documentation, 2026

blocks.text: Where does the rest go? The 30 percent fee pays for the platform itself: servers, moderation, payments, discovery. Purchases made on phones also pass through app stores, which take a cut of their own before Roblox sees the money. And the gap between what Robux cost players and what Roblox pays to buy them back is how the company funds everything else. None of that is hidden, but it rarely appears in the stories about teenage developers buying houses.
Rule of thumb: under the standard rate, a game keeps roughly a quarter of what its players spend. A game pass priced at 100 Robux is worth about 27 cents to its creator, not a dollar.
The 18+ rate, and who it is really for

On April 30, 2026, Roblox announced a higher exchange rate for a specific slice of spending, starting June 8. The DevEx documentation now lists a rate of $0.0054 per earned Robux, about 42 percent above the standard rate. It applies only to certain purchases, namely developer products, passes, subscriptions and private servers, made by players in the United States who have been verified as 18 or older through facial age estimation or a government ID, in eligible games. The announcement tied eligibility to games using the R15 avatar type.

The company was open about the motive. It said its U.S. users aged 18 to 34 were growing by more than half year over year and spent about 50 percent more than under-18 players, while flagging that those figures were early estimates. In plain terms, Roblox is paying developers more to build games that adults want, because adults have their own money.

For most small games, the honest reading is that this rate will cover a minority of revenue at best. A casual obby whose players skew young will see most of its earnings at the standard rate, and every Robux that was earned before September 5, 2025 still cashes out at the old $0.0035 rate first. The higher rate is a signal about where the platform wants to grow, not a raise for everyone. It is worth knowing about when choosing what to build next, and not worth counting on when estimating what the current game will earn.
A power law, not a ladder

Roblox's 2025 economic impact report gives a rare look at how earnings are spread among developers. In 2024, the top 10 developers averaged $33.9 million each. The top 100 averaged $6 million. The top 1,000 averaged $820,000. The median DevEx creator, the one in the exact middle of the more than 24,500 creators in the program, got $1,575. A footnote says some of these figures were measured in Robux spent, so treat them as approximate, but the shape is unmistakable.

blocks.title: Average yearly earnings by developer rank, 2024
blocks.note: The median bar is too small to see. That is the point. Roblox notes some figures are measured in Robux spent.
blocks.source: Roblox Annual Economic Impact Report, September 2025

blocks.text: This is what a power law looks like. It is not a ladder where each rung is a bit higher than the last; it is a cliff. And remember that the median here is the median of people who already qualified to cash out, which requires at least 30,000 earned Robux. The many developers who never reach that threshold are not in the sample at all.

The cliff should change how a small team thinks about success. If the distribution were a ladder, steady effort would produce steady income. On a cliff, most of the return goes to games that break out, and breaking out depends on things like retention and the ability to ship updates fast enough to ride a trend. (The articles on retention and on shipping early cover those levers in depth, and the one on platform risk covers what happens when Roblox changes the rules.)
Designing for the few who pay

The power law exists inside each game too. Using the filing's figures, only about 1.4 percent of Roblox's daily users paid for anything on an average day in 2025. Those who did spent a little over $10 on average. So a game's income does not come from everyone spending a little. It comes from a small group spending a meaningful amount, supported by a much larger group who play for free and make the game feel alive.

That has a design consequence that is easy to get wrong. The free players are not freeloaders; they are the crowd, the competition, the friends who get invited, and the reason a paying player bothers to show off a rare trail or a flashy effect. A game that squeezes them with constant purchase prompts or walls them out of the fun tends to shrink, and a shrinking game earns less from its payers too. The healthier pattern is to sell things that make a game the player already loves feel better, faster or more personal, and to leave the core loop open.

A useful exercise is to imagine the player most likely to spend real money in your game and ask what they would happily pay for that a casual player would not miss. Often the answers are cosmetic flair, convenience, a private server to play with friends, or a way to support the creators they like. Rarely is the answer a paywall in front of the fun. The 18+ rate pushes in the same direction from the other side: Roblox is signaling that it wants games adults enjoy enough to spend on, which means games with depth, not just games with more store buttons.

There is also a timing lesson. Monetization added to a game nobody returns to does almost nothing, because the people who would eventually pay never stick around long enough to want anything. The order that works is retention first, then a small number of well-made things to buy, then more of whatever the data says players actually value.
What it takes to cash out

The Developer Exchange has a short list of requirements. You must be at least 13, have a verified email on your Roblox account, hold at least 30,000 earned Robux, have a DevEx portal account, and have a tax form on file: a W-9 for U.S. taxpayers or a W-8 for everyone else. You can cash out once per calendar month. At the standard rate, the 30,000-Robux minimum is worth $114.

items: Counts as earned: in-game sales of passes, developer products and subscriptions, paid access and private servers, Creator Store and Marketplace sales, Creator Rewards, and legitimate group payouts.
Does not count: Robux you bought, monthly subscription grants, trading or reselling items, Robux transferred or gifted to you, or anything from content that was moderated.
Older balances: Robux earned before September 5, 2025 cash out at $0.0035 and must be cashed out before newer Robux.

blocks.text: Work the minimum backward and it gets concrete. To earn 30,000 Robux at a 70 percent share, players must spend about 43,000 Robux in your game, which at the 2025 average price is roughly $430 of real money. That is the first real milestone for a new game: not a million visits, but a few hundred dollars of player spending that adds up to your first cash-out of a bit over a hundred dollars.

Two practical cautions apply to anyone in the military. The tax form is there because this is taxable income, so keep records and talk to a tax preparer or the free tax help offered on base. And service members are generally expected to follow their command's rules on outside work and business activity, so ask your chain of command or legal office what applies before money starts flowing.
Running your own numbers

The useful formula is simple. Daily players, times the share who pay, times what they spend, times 0.7 for the platform fee, times the exchange rate. Every term except the last two is something your game controls through design, and every one of them shows up in Roblox's own analytics dashboard once the game has players.

For a sense of the ceiling, Roblox's filing says the platform averaged about 15 cents of player spending per daily user per day in 2025, and roughly 1.8 million of its 127 million daily users paid for something on a typical day. Those averages include avatar shopping and the biggest hit games, so a typical small game will earn well below them per player. Even at the platform average, 1,000 daily players would generate about $150 a day of spending and around $40 a day for the developer. Use that as an upper bound for daydreams, and your own dashboard as the real answer.

blocks.title: Estimating what your game earns
items: Pull average daily active users from your analytics.
Find the share of players who buy anything, and what they spend on average.
Multiply to get daily player spending in Robux.
Multiply by 0.7 for your share, then by $0.0038 for dollars.
Compare that to the 30,000-Robux minimum to see how long until a first cash-out.

blocks.text: The economics are not a reason to quit. They are a reason to aim carefully. Roblox gives two people with no studio, no publisher and no budget access to an audience of well over a hundred million daily players, and it pays real money when a game works. What it does not do is pay much for a game that is merely fine. The money follows players who come back, and players come back to games that are built around one strong idea and keep getting better.

So the question for a two-person team is not whether Roblox pays fairly in the abstract. It is whether this particular game can find a group of players who return every week and care enough to spend. Answer that with real data from a released version, and the DevEx math becomes a simple multiplication instead of a hope.

takeaways: Of each dollar a player spends in your game, about 27 cents reaches you at the standard DevEx rate of $0.0038.
The $0.0054 rate covers only qualifying purchases by age-verified U.S. adults in eligible games; most young-audience games will earn mostly at the standard rate.
Earnings follow a power law: top-10 developers averaged $33.9M in 2024, while the median DevEx creator got $1,575.
Your first milestone is 30,000 earned Robux ($114), which takes roughly $430 of player spending.
DevEx income is taxable, and military members should check outside-work rules with their command.

title: Cause of Death: Ran Out of Money
dek: Ask founders why their company died and the top answer is cash. That is like a coroner writing 'heart stopped.' The data on business failure gets far more useful once you separate the symptom from the disease.

blocks.text: Every coroner knows that a heart stopping is not a cause of death. It is what death looks like at the end. The useful question is always what came before: the blocked artery, the infection, the fall. Business failure has the same problem. When the research firm CB Insights read through 111 startup post-mortems written by founders and investors, the most common reason given for failure was running out of cash or failing to raise more. Of course it was. That is what failure looks like at the end.

The interesting part of failure is upstream. And the first thing to clear away is a number almost everyone has heard, that nine out of ten startups fail. It is repeated so often it sounds like a law of nature. The official data says something different, and more interesting.
The real survival curve

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks every private-sector business establishment, from law firms to food trucks, through its Business Employment Dynamics program. In January 2024 it published the fate of every establishment that opened in March 2013. A year later, about 80 percent were still operating. After five years, about half. After ten years, just over a third.

blocks.title: Share of U.S. establishments born in 2013 still operating
blocks.note: Covers all private-sector establishments, not only tech startups. Closing is not always failing.
blocks.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, TED, January 2024

blocks.text: Two things stand out. First, the curve is steepest at the start. About one in five businesses is gone within a year, and the losses slow down every year after that. In the first year, about one in five closed. Between years nine and ten, fewer than one in twelve of the remaining survivors did. Getting through the first couple of years is the hardest part by far.

Second, these numbers include businesses that closed for reasons that are not failures at all. Owners retire, sell, move or simply decide they want a different life. Venture-backed tech startups are a different population with different math, aiming for huge outcomes and accepting that most will not get there. So the honest summary is not that 90 percent of businesses fail. It is that about half of new establishments in the U.S. are still around after five years, and the danger is concentrated early.
Survival risk is front-loaded. Whatever you are building, the first year or two is where most projects die, which is exactly when motivation is easiest to lose and evidence is hardest to read.
What founders say killed them

The CB Insights analysis, published in 2021, is the most widely cited look at why startups say they failed. Founders could name several reasons, so the percentages add up to well over 100. Running out of cash led the list at 38 percent, followed closely by no market need at 35 percent. Then came being outcompeted, a flawed business model, and regulatory trouble.

blocks.title: Reasons cited in 111 startup post-mortems
blocks.note: Multiple reasons per startup, so totals exceed 100%. Self-reported by founders and investors.
blocks.source: CB Insights, 2021, via SmartCompany

blocks.text: Treat this list with care. These are post-mortems people chose to write and publish, mostly from tech startups. Founders are also not neutral judges of their own failure; blaming the market or a competitor is easier than blaming your own decisions. And 111 stories is a small sample. The value of the list is not its precision. It is the pattern it reveals once you read it as a chain instead of a menu.

There is a deeper bias hiding in all failure research, and it runs in both directions. During the Second World War, the statistician Abraham Wald was asked where to add armor to bombers, based on where returning planes had bullet holes. His insight was that the holes on returning planes showed where a plane could be hit and survive. The armor belonged where the returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there never came back.

Startup stories have the same shape. The success stories everyone hears, the teenager whose game exploded or the channel that blew up after one video, are the planes that came back. Thousands of projects that did the same things and vanished left no story behind. And the failure stories that do get written skew toward founders articulate and secure enough to publish one. Neither set is a fair sample. The safest lessons are the ones that show up in both: build something specific people want, keep the team aligned, and do not run out of the resource your project actually runs on.
Reading the list as a chain

Running out of cash is rarely an independent event. Money runs out because revenue never arrived, and revenue never arrived because not enough people wanted the product at a price that worked. Read that way, no market need, a flawed business model, bad pricing and running out of cash are often the same story told at different stages: the first is the disease, the last is the death certificate.

blocks.title: How most failures actually unfold
items: A team builds something based on an untested belief about what people want.
Real users show up in smaller numbers than hoped, or do not come back.
The team adds features, spends on marketing, or lowers prices to compensate.
Costs keep running while revenue stays flat.
Cash or motivation runs out, and that gets recorded as the cause.

blocks.text: This is why the second item on the list, no market need, deserves more attention than the first. It is the one founders can actually do something about early, cheaply, before much money is at stake. The lean startup method, covered in its own article, is essentially a toolkit for catching this disease before it reaches the bloodstream.

For a side project, the chain has a twist. A game built by two people with day jobs has almost no burn rate, so it cannot literally run out of cash. It runs out of something else: hours, energy, belief. Burnout sits at the bottom of the CB Insights list at 5 percent, but for part-time builders it is the equivalent of the top line. When a side project has no players, the founders quietly stop opening the editor, and the project dies without anyone writing a post-mortem. (The articles on building on the side and on finishing one project take this problem head-on.)
Six ways good ideas die

Tom Eisenmann, a Harvard Business School professor, spent years studying failed ventures for his 2021 book Why Startups Fail. He was especially interested in startups that looked promising, with smart founders and decent ideas, and still collapsed. He sorted the deaths into patterns, which are more useful than the CB Insights list because they describe mistakes rather than outcomes.

items: **Bad bedfellows:** a good idea sunk by the wrong partners, team, or investors.
**False starts:** launching fast without first researching what customers need, then cycling through uninformed guesses.
**False promises:** early adopters love the product, the team scales, and mainstream customers turn out not to care.
**Speed traps:** growing faster than the business can support, until the cracks break it.
**Help wanted:** a fast-scaling company runs short of the money or people it needs at a critical moment.
**Cascading miracles:** a vision so big that too many things all have to go right at once.

blocks.text: Two of these matter most for a small builder. False promises are a trap for game makers in particular: the first players of a new game are often friends, fellow developers, or enthusiasts who will forgive anything. Their enthusiasm can be real and still say little about whether ordinary players will stick around. The fix is to find out early how strangers behave.

Bad bedfellows is the other. Eisenmann found that a good idea is not enough if the people around it are mismatched, and CB Insights' list shows team problems and disharmony appearing again and again. For two brothers building a game, the risk is not that one of you is a bad person. It is unclear roles, unspoken expectations about effort, and no agreed way to make decisions. (The article on partner roles covers this in detail.)
Who actually succeeds

If failure has patterns, so does success, and one of the best-documented findings cuts against the stereotype of the hoodie-wearing twenty-two-year-old. Pierre Azoulay and colleagues combined U.S. Census Bureau data on businesses, workers and owners to study millions of startups across the whole country, not just the famous ones. In a 2020 paper in American Economic Review: Insights, they found that the most successful founders tend to be middle-aged.

items.label: Average founder age of the 1-in-1,000 fastest-growing new U.S. firms

blocks.source: Azoulay, Jones, Kim & Miranda, AER: Insights, 2020

blocks.text: Their strongest predictor of success was not youth or genius but prior experience in the same industry. Founders who had worked in a field knew its customers, its suppliers and its hidden problems. They had, in effect, done years of free market research before starting.

It is worth being precise about what this does and does not say. It is an average, and plenty of young founders build great companies. It also does not mean age itself causes success. The likelier story is that age is a stand-in for what accumulates with it: industry knowledge, savings, contacts, judgment about people, and a track record that makes others willing to take a chance on you. Those can be built at any age, but they cannot be skipped.

For someone who is twenty and wants to own a business eventually, this is a more encouraging finding than it sounds. It means that the years spent learning a trade, a system, or an industry are not a detour from entrepreneurship. They are often the raw material for it. A nuclear-trained electrician understands power systems, maintenance, technical training and rigid procedure from the inside. Someone with ten years in gaming and content knows that world's players better than most outsiders ever will. Experience is the moat that founders often do not realize they are digging.
A pre-mortem for your own project

The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a simple exercise he called the pre-mortem. Before a project starts, the team imagines that it is a year in the future and the project has failed. Each person writes down why. Because the failure is treated as having already happened, people stop defending the plan and start explaining its death, and they surface risks they would not have raised in a normal planning meeting.

Applied to a small game or channel, the exercise takes fifteen minutes. Imagine it is next year and the project is dead. Did players never come back after their first session? Did the two of you stop agreeing on what to build? Did the project grow too big to finish in the time you actually have? Did the person doing most of the work burn out? Each answer points to a check you can run this month rather than discovering it in a year.

blocks.title: A fifteen-minute pre-mortem
items: Imagine it is a year from now and the project has quietly died.
Each partner writes, alone, the three most likely reasons it died.
Compare lists and circle the reasons that appear on both.
For each circled reason, name the earliest sign you would see.
Agree on one cheap check for each sign, and put a date on it.

blocks.text: The pre-mortem works best when it is honest about the one resource a side project lives on. For a funded startup that resource is cash, and the founders watch the bank balance every week. For a part-time project, it is the hours the builders are actually willing to put in. Watching that number, and noticing early when it starts to slide, is the side-project version of watching the runway.

The data on business failure is less frightening than the folklore and more useful. Most new businesses do not vanish in year one; half of them make it five years. The ones that die usually die of something upstream of money, most often building something too few people wanted, or of problems between the people building it. Both can be spotted early by anyone willing to look. Cash running out is just the last thing that happens.

takeaways: About half of new U.S. establishments survive five years; the 'nine in ten fail' line is folklore, but risk is front-loaded.
Running out of cash is usually the final symptom; no market need is the disease that most often causes it.
For side projects, the equivalent of cash is time and motivation; projects without users die quietly when builders stop showing up.
Prior industry experience is one of the best predictors of founder success; the fastest-growing firms have founders averaging 45.
Run a pre-mortem: imagine the project failed, list why, then check for the early signs now.

title: The Algorithm Doesn't Watch Your Video. It Watches the Viewer.
dek: In 2012 YouTube made a change that cost it a fifth of its views overnight, and kept it. What the company has actually said about its recommendation system since then is less mysterious, and more useful, than the myths creators trade.

blocks.text: In 2012, engineers at YouTube flipped a switch and watched views fall by about 20 percent almost immediately. For most companies that would be a crisis and a rollback by lunch. YouTube left the change in place. The company later described this moment itself, in a 2021 post by Cristos Goodrow, its vice president of engineering, as the point where it stopped treating a click as proof that a viewer was happy.

That small piece of history is a better guide to the algorithm than most of the theories passed around creator forums. It shows what the system was built to want, and what it was willing to give up to get it. A new channel that understands that one trade has a clearer picture than a channel that has memorized a hundred tips.

This article sticks to what YouTube has said on the record: its engineering blog, its public How YouTube Works pages, and interviews its growth team has given on Creator Insider, the company's own channel for creators. Those are the claims of an interested party, and they should be read that way. But they are the closest thing to a primary source anyone outside the company has.
From popularity to clicks to something harder

YouTube's account of its own history runs in clear steps. When recommendations began in 2008, the system mostly ranked videos by popularity and dumped the winners into a trending list. Everyone saw roughly the same thing. That works when a site is small and fails when it holds billions of videos aimed at very different people.

Next came clicks. By 2011, according to Goodrow's post, the team had concluded that clicks were a poor signal, because people often clicked on videos that turned out not to be what they expected. A misleading thumbnail could win the click and lose the viewer. So in 2012 the system began counting watch time, and that is when views dropped by a fifth: fewer people were tricked into starting videos they did not want.

Watch time had its own flaw. A person can sit through something and feel worse for it, or leave a video playing while doing something else. So YouTube added surveys. Some viewers are asked to rate a video from one to five stars, and only time spent on videos rated four or five counts toward what the company calls valued watchtime. Because almost nobody answers surveys, a machine learning model predicts how everyone else would have answered.

blocks.title: What YouTube says it has optimized for
items: Recommendations begin; videos ranked largely by popularity
Team concludes clicks are an unreliable signal of what viewers want
Watch time added as a signal; views drop about 20% at once
Later
Viewer surveys feed 'valued watchtime'; a model predicts answers for everyone else
Borderline content demoted in recommendations

blocks.text: Notice the direction of travel. Each step moved away from something easy to count and toward something closer to the viewer's actual experience. That does not make the system benevolent. It makes it a machine that keeps trying to measure satisfaction, because a satisfied viewer comes back tomorrow. (The general version of this, and its downsides, is covered in the article on recommendation algorithms.)
Pull, not push

The most common mental picture among creators is of YouTube as a distributor. You upload, the algorithm decides whether to push your video out, and if it likes you it pushes harder. Todd Beaupré, who leads YouTube's growth and discovery team, has said repeatedly that this is backwards.

In his description, recommendations are built at the moment a person opens the app. The system looks at that one viewer, their history and what similar viewers enjoyed, and pulls from the whole library the videos most likely to satisfy them right now. Your video is not being pushed. It is a candidate, competing in millions of tiny private auctions, one per viewer per session. Notifications are the main exception, for people who asked for them.

That reframe dissolves several popular fears. Beaupré has said the discovery system mostly judges individual videos rather than channel averages, so one weak upload does not doom the next one. He has denied that there is a penalty box for channels that take breaks, saying the system tries not to lean on historical data that does not predict how a new video will do. And because recommendations are not limited to recent uploads, an old video can find a second life when interest in its topic returns.

blocks.title: Creator folklore vs. YouTube's stated position

left.head: What creators often believe
items: YouTube pushes videos out to audiences
A bad video hurts the whole channel
Taking a break gets you punished
A video that flops in 48 hours is dead
Subscribers will see and watch everything

right.head: What YouTube staff have said
items: Each viewer's feed is pulled together when they open the app
Discovery judges mostly video by video
No penalty box; old data is down-weighted if it is not predictive
Old videos can be recommended again when interest returns
Most subscribers skip most uploads, and that is normal

blocks.text: Be fair to the skeptics, though. These reassurances come with no published data, and creators in the comments under these interviews regularly report experiences that do not match them. The honest position is that YouTube's description is probably true on average and may not feel true for any one channel in any one month.
What it is actually predicting

Goodrow's post says the system learns from more than 80 billion signals. The ones the company names are ordinary: clicks, watch time, survey answers, shares, likes and dislikes, plus the history a viewer has chosen to keep. The important detail is the one people skip. YouTube says there is no fixed formula. How much each signal matters changes from viewer to viewer, and Beaupré has added that the weights shift by time and device as well.

items.label: Signals YouTube says its recommendation system learns from
Immediate drop in views when watch time was added in 2012
Typical click rate from the subscriber row, per YouTube's growth lead

blocks.source: Goodrow, YouTube Official Blog, 2021; Beaupré on Creator Insider, Sept 2026

blocks.text: A 2016 paper by three Google engineers gives a rough picture of the plumbing behind those claims. The system works in two stages. A first network narrows a library of millions of videos down to a few hundred candidates that might suit a given viewer. A second network then scores and ranks those candidates in detail. The paper is a decade old and the models have changed many times since, but the shape is a good mental model: first a coarse question about whether a video belongs in this person's world at all, then a fine question about whether it is the best choice right now.

That shape explains why topic clarity matters so much for a small channel. A video that does not obviously belong to any recognizable interest has a hard time even making the first cut. A video that clearly belongs to one, say aim training for players returning to tactical shooters, at least gets into the pool where the finer judgment happens.

This is why asking which metric the algorithm rewards is the wrong question. Click-through rate matters only as one clue about whether a particular viewer wanted a particular video. A high click rate followed by people bailing in the first minute is a strong clue that the promise was false. A modest click rate with long, satisfied viewing is a clue that the video is right for a narrower group, and the system will go looking for more people like them. (The articles on thumbnails and on retention graphs dig into those two clues.)

There is a useful way to compress all of this. The algorithm does not watch your video. It cannot judge your editing or your jokes. It watches viewers, and it tries to predict which of them will be glad they spent their time on you. Everything a creator can do to grow on YouTube reduces to two moves: be clear about who the video is for, and then make those people glad they clicked.
Your subscribers are not your audience

In a Creator Insider interview in September 2026, Beaupré offered a number that surprises most new creators. Across uploads, he said, the click rate from the subscriber row on the home page is often around 10 percent or less. Even on a channel's best videos, the large majority of subscribed viewers who see the video do not choose to watch it. He called that normal: people who like a channel do not want every single thing it makes.

This matters because creators tend to treat subscribers as a mailing list. They are not. A subscription is one weak signal among many that a viewer might like your next video. The system still asks the question fresh for each upload and each person: of everyone who subscribed, who is likely to want this one? A video can underperform with subscribers and still do well with strangers, because, according to Beaupré, the system learns about those two groups separately.

For a brand new channel there is even less to go on. With no viewing history attached to the channel, Beaupré has said, early distribution leans on matching the topic of the video to viewers who like that topic. If no interested audience shows up, impressions stop. That is not punishment. It is the system running out of reasons to believe anyone wants the video.

A small channel's real problem is rarely being suppressed. It is being ambiguous. If the title, thumbnail and first thirty seconds do not make clear who the video is for, the system has nobody to test it on.
The part that is not about engagement

It would be easy to read all this as a pure engagement machine. YouTube's own history says otherwise. Goodrow's post lists a series of interventions that override what viewers would have clicked: classifiers that kept racy or violent videos out of recommendations from 2011, the demotion of sensational tabloid content in 2015, and in 2019 the demotion of what the company calls borderline content, videos that come close to breaking its rules without quite doing so.

YouTube reported that the 2019 change cut watch time of borderline content that came from recommendations to non-subscribers in the United States by 70 percent. The post adds that responsibility signals can outrank engagement signals. In other words, there is an editorial layer sitting on top of the prediction layer, and it reflects decisions made by people about what the platform wants to be associated with.

For a gaming channel this is mostly background, but not entirely. Shock titles, fake drama and rage bait sit in exactly the zone where a click can be cheap and a recommendation can be withheld. The pattern from 2012 repeats: the system is built to stop rewarding things that win attention without earning satisfaction, and it keeps getting better at spotting them.
Using this without being used by it

The deepest lesson in YouTube's account is that the company has been fighting Goodhart's law for over a decade. Every time a number became the target, creators learned to game it, and the number stopped meaning what it used to. Clicks, then watch time, then surveys. A creator who chases whatever metric is fashionable this year is running the same race the engineers are trying to make unwinnable.

The alternative is almost boring. Pick viewers you understand, because you are one of them. Make a specific promise in the packaging. Keep that promise fast, and give people a reason to feel the time was well spent. For a channel about rebuilding aim after years away from games, the viewer is easy to picture: someone who also drifted away and wonders whether they can come back. Every upload can be checked against that one person.

blocks.title: A pre-upload check based on what YouTube says it measures
items: Name the viewer: who, specifically, should want this video?
Read the title and thumbnail as that viewer. Is the promise clear in two seconds?
Check that the first 30 seconds start delivering on that promise.
Ask whether that viewer would rate it four or five stars, not just finish it.
After upload, judge it over weeks, not hours; old videos can still be found.

blocks.text: None of this guarantees growth, and YouTube's statements are not neutral science. They are a company describing its product in the most flattering honest terms it can manage. But they line up with the one thing the company proved it believed back in 2012, when it gave up a fifth of its views. The system wants viewers who are glad they came. Build for those people, and you are working with the machine instead of guessing at it.

takeaways: YouTube moved from popularity to clicks to watch time to surveys; each step tried to measure satisfaction more honestly.
Recommendations are pulled for each viewer when they open the app; your video is a candidate, not a package being pushed.
There is no fixed formula. Signal weights vary by viewer, time and device, so chasing one metric misses the point.
Most subscribers skip most uploads. Treat each video as a fresh pitch to a specific viewer.
Clarity about who a video is for is the most useful thing a small channel can control.
