title: Two Drivers, One Child
dek: We say people should only be judged for what they control. Then we judge them for outcomes all the time. Moral luck is the philosophical puzzle hiding in every courtroom, every chain of command and every regret.

blocks.text: Two friends leave the same party at midnight. Each has had the same four beers over the same few hours. Each feels fine, and each makes the same bad decision to drive home. Their routes are equally long and equally dark. The first one pulls into his driveway, goes to bed and wakes up with a mild headache. The second one rounds a corner at the exact moment a child chases a ball into the street.

The first driver, if he is ever caught, gets a fine and a suspended license. The second goes to prison for years and carries what happened for the rest of his life. Almost everyone thinks that is how it should be. Now try to say what the second driver did that the first didn't. Same choice, same carelessness, same state of mind. The only difference was a child and a ball, and neither driver controlled those.
This is the problem of *moral luck*. Once you see it, you start finding it everywhere: in courtrooms, in hospitals, in the chain of command and in the private way you judge yourself.
The principle we all believe

Most people, if asked in the abstract, agree with something philosophers call the Control Principle: you should only be judged for what was under your control. If someone steps on your foot because they were shoved, you don't blame them. The 18th-century philosopher Immanuel Kant pushed this to its limit. A good will, he wrote, would shine like a jewel by its own light even if bad luck kept it from accomplishing anything at all. What counts morally is what you meant and what you chose, not how the dice landed.

In 1976 the British philosopher Bernard Williams coined the term moral luck, and in 1979 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel published a famous essay with the same title. Together they showed that the Control Principle, which feels obviously true, collides with almost every actual judgment we make. Williams later admitted he had meant the phrase to sound like a contradiction. Luck is the thing that's supposed to be outside morality. Yet it seems to be everywhere inside it.
Nagel's move was to show that if you apply the Control Principle consistently, it eats everything. Strip away every factor you didn't control, and there may be nothing left to judge at all.

blocks.title: Nagel's four kinds of moral luck
items: Resultant luck: how your actions turn out. The two drunk drivers.
Circumstantial luck: the situations you happen to face. Who gets tested by a war, a temptation or an emergency.
Constitutive luck: the temperament and character you were born or raised with. A short fuse, natural courage, empathy.
Causal luck: everything that caused you to be who you are and choose what you chose, which raises the free will problem.

blocks.text: Luck in results, circumstances and character

Resultant luck is the most obvious. In most U.S. courts, attempted murder carries a lighter sentence than murder, even if the would-be killer did everything possible and the gun simply jammed. A careless surgeon whose patient happens to recover gets no lawsuit, while an equally careless one whose patient dies may lose her career. Williams's own example was a painter, loosely based on Paul Gauguin, who abandons his family to pursue his art in the South Pacific. Whether he was justified, Williams argued, depends partly on whether he becomes a great painter, which he cannot know when he leaves.

Circumstantial luck is subtler and more disturbing. Nagel pointed out that ordinary citizens of Nazi Germany had the chance to behave heroically or terribly, and many failed. Someone with exactly the same character who happened to move to Argentina before the war never faced the test. We condemn the first person and not the second, though the only difference may be geography.

Constitutive luck goes deeper still. Some people are born with an easy temperament and find patience natural. Others have a quick temper they fight against every day. If the second person snaps once in a hard moment, we blame them, even though they didn't choose the temper they were working with.
And causal luck, the last kind, asks whether anything you do was ever really up to you, given everything that shaped you. That question opens straight into the free will debate.
The numbers behind the two drivers

The drunk driving case is not just a thought experiment. In a large national survey, the CDC asked American adults how many times in the past 30 days they had driven when they had perhaps had too much to drink. Scaling up the answers, researchers estimated about 147 million such episodes in 2018. That same year, about 10,511 people died in crashes involving an alcohol-impaired driver.

items.label: Self-reported alcohol-impaired driving episodes by U.S. adults, 2018
Deaths in U.S. alcohol-impaired-driving crashes, 2018
Deaths in such crashes in 2023, about 30% of all U.S. traffic deaths

blocks.source: Barry et al., Injury Prevention, 2022 (CDC BRFSS data); NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts, 2025

blocks.text: Put those numbers side by side and you get something like one death for every 14,000 self-reported episodes. That calculation is rough, since the survey and the crash data measure different things, and impaired drivers injure far more people than they kill. But the shape is clear. The overwhelming majority of people who make the same dangerous choice get home, and a small number become killers. Society treats those two groups completely differently.

Is that fair? The case that it is: the person who killed someone really did cause a death, and that is a fact about the world, not just about his mind. The case that it isn't: the lucky driver was exactly as reckless, and what he deserves shouldn't depend on whether a child happened to be on the corner. Notice that both answers feel right. That is what makes this a real puzzle and not a trick.
What people actually think

Psychologists have tested these intuitions directly. In a 2008 study, the Harvard psychologist Fiery Cushman found that people judge whether an action was *wrong* mainly by the person's intentions and beliefs, but when deciding how much to *blame* or *punish*, they also weigh what actually happened. Two different processes seem to be running at once: one that asks what was in the person's head, and one that starts from the harm and looks for whoever caused it.

In 2019 the philosophers Markus Kneer and Edouard Machery ran a set of experiments with a twist. When people saw the lucky and unlucky driver side by side, the large majority judged them equally blameworthy and their actions equally wrong. Moral luck seemed to vanish. But when each person saw only one version of the story, outcome mattered again, and the unlucky agent got more blame. That extra blame seemed to come from people assuming the unlucky driver must have been more careless, reasoning backward from the harm. Punishment judgments, interestingly, were more tied to outcomes than judgments of wrongness or blame, as if punishment runs on a different track.

That finding suggests a reading of moral luck that is less mysterious. Maybe we don't really believe outcomes change what someone deserves. Maybe outcomes are evidence. In real life, we rarely know exactly how careful someone was, so a disaster nudges us to assume they cut more corners. Sometimes that inference is right. Sometimes it's just the luck talking.
The skeptic's bullet

If you side with the Control Principle all the way, you have to accept some strange consequences. The lucky drunk driver is exactly as blameworthy as the one who killed a child. That sounds fair at first, until you notice what it implies: either we should be far harsher on the thousands of drunk drivers who got home, or far gentler on the one who didn't.

Circumstantial luck makes it stranger. Some philosophers argue that the counterpart who moved to Argentina deserves the same judgment as the Nazi sympathizer who stayed, because he would have done the same things. Others soften this: maybe he deserves the same, but we can never know what someone would have done, so we are only entitled to judge actual deeds. Either way, you end up saying that a quiet, harmless retiree may be as bad as a war criminal. Most people find that hard to accept, which is a sign of how deeply outcomes are woven into how we think about character.

Push further and the Control Principle seems to swallow the self. Your temperament came from genes and upbringing. Your choices came from your temperament and your circumstances. If nothing outside your control can count, it's unclear what is left that is really yours. This is why Nagel thought the problem might have no solution, only an uneasy truce between a principle we can't give up and judgments we can't stop making.
Command, accountability and bad seas

Military culture lives inside this puzzle. On January 8, 2005, the attack submarine USS *San Francisco* was running submerged at 525 feet about 360 miles southeast of Guam when she slammed into an undersea mountain that was not on the chart her crew was using. Machinist's Mate Second Class Joseph Ashley, 24, died of his injuries, and 97 crew members were hurt. The commanding officer, Commander Kevin Mooney, was relieved of command and reprimanded, and six other sailors were disciplined.

It was not pure bad luck. The Navy's investigation found that other charts showed a possible navigation hazard nearby, and concluded that with proper procedures and prudent navigation the grounding could have been avoided or made less severe. But here is the moral-luck question: how many other watch teams, on other boats, on other nights, have cut a similar corner and never hit anything? Their commanding officers kept their careers. The difference was a mountain.

The Navy's answer is that the captain is responsible for everything that happens on the ship, full stop. Philosophically, that is a deliberate embrace of resultant luck. Practically, it may be wise. Leaders who know they will own every outcome have a powerful reason to sweat the details, and crews benefit when nobody can hide behind "it wasn't my fault." Accountability can be a tool for making good behavior more likely, rather than a precise measurement of anyone's inner worth.

blocks.title: Should outcomes change blame?

left.head: Yes, results matter
items: You really did cause the harm
Owning outcomes makes people more careful
Law can't punish what happened only in someone's head
Feeling worse when you caused harm seems healthy

right.head: No, only choices matter
items: The lucky driver was just as reckless
Nobody controls where the child runs
Judging by outcomes rewards luck, not character
It risks punishing people for chance

blocks.text: Living with it

Williams offered one of the most humane ideas in this debate. He described a truck driver who, through no fault at all, hits a child who runs into the road. A bystander might feel sorry. The driver feels something different, which Williams called agent-regret: the particular weight of having been the one whose action caused the harm. We would think something was off about the driver if he simply shrugged and said it wasn't his fault, even though it wasn't. Owning outcomes you didn't fully control seems to be part of being a person in the world rather than a mind floating above it.

So maybe the answer is not to choose between the Control Principle and our everyday judgments, but to use each where it belongs. When judging others, lean on the Control Principle. The person who caused a disaster may not be worse than you, and the person who never got caught may not be better. When judging yourself, lean toward ownership. Treat your near misses as if they had happened, because the only thing separating them from disasters was luck you didn't earn.

You can practice this in small places. In a ranked match, a teammate who takes a smart fight and loses it to a lucky spray gets flamed, while one who makes a reckless push and wins it gets praised. Good teams learn to review the decision, not the result. The same goes for a watch turnover, a business bet or a hard conversation. Ask what the person knew, what they chose and what a careful person would have done. Then let the dice be dice.
A near miss is a free lesson. The choice was the same as the one that ends in disaster; only the outcome was lucky. Treat it with the seriousness of the disaster you avoided.

Some questions to carry with you. Think of the worst thing you ever did that turned out fine. Would you judge yourself differently if it hadn't? Think of someone you've blamed harshly. How much of what you blamed them for was choice, and how much was where they happened to be standing? And if your character itself was shaped by luck, by parents, temperament and the situations you were handed, what exactly is the self that gets the credit or the blame?

takeaways: Moral luck: we say people should only be judged for what they control, yet routinely judge them by outcomes they didn't control.
Nagel's four kinds: luck in results, in circumstances, in character and in the causes behind your choices.
Experiments suggest people judge lucky and unlucky agents equally when comparing side by side, but punishment still tracks outcomes.
Judge others mostly by their choices; judge yourself by owning outcomes, including the near misses.
Strict accountability for outcomes, like a captain's, can be a useful tool even if it isn't a perfect measure of character.

title: One Box or Two?
dek: A simple choice between two boxes has split philosophers, decision theorists and AI researchers for more than fifty years. Decide what you'd do before you read the arguments.

blocks.text: You are led into a room with two boxes on a table. Box A is clear, and you can see $1,000 inside. Box B is opaque. You're told it holds either $1 million or nothing. You can take both boxes, or you can take only Box B. That's the whole choice.

Here is the catch. Yesterday, before you arrived, a Predictor decided what to put in Box B. The Predictor has studied you closely: your history, your habits, your brain, whatever it needs. If it predicted you would take only Box B, it put $1 million inside. If it predicted you would take both, it left Box B empty.
The Predictor has played this game with thousands of people before you and has been right almost every time. The money is already in place or it isn't. Nothing you do now can change it.

Before reading on, actually decide. One box or two? Most people find the answer obvious within a few seconds. The trouble, as you're about to see, is that the people who find the opposite answer obvious are just as smart and just as sure.

blocks.title: Newcomb's problem
items: Box A is transparent and holds $1,000.
Box B is opaque and holds either $1,000,000 or nothing.
Yesterday a highly accurate Predictor guessed your choice.
If it predicted you'd take only B, it put $1,000,000 in B. If it predicted both, B is empty.
Now you choose: Box B alone, or both boxes.

blocks.text: A puzzle that splits people in half

The puzzle was invented around 1960 by William Newcomb, a physicist at the Lawrence Livermore lab in California. He never published it. The philosopher Robert Nozick heard it secondhand and wrote it up in 1969, giving it Newcomb's name. Nozick reported something odd that has held true ever since: he had put the problem to many people, almost everyone thought the right answer was perfectly clear, and they split almost evenly over which answer that was. Many on each side thought the other side was being silly.

Surveys have backed him up. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey of professional philosophers, among the 1,071 who said they were familiar enough with the problem to answer, about 39 percent favored two boxes and about 31 percent favored one box, with the rest choosing other answers or undecided. When the mathematician and writer Alex Bellos put the question to readers of *The Guardian* in 2016, more than 31,000 people voted, and one-boxers narrowly won.

blocks.title: One box or two? Who chose what
blocks.note: Philosophers: 2020 survey, those who endorsed a single answer, N = 1,071. Readers: online poll, 31,854 votes, two options only.
blocks.source: Bourget and Chalmers, PhilPapers Survey 2020; Alex Bellos, The Guardian, 2016

blocks.text: The earlier 2009 version of the survey found a similar tilt, with 31 percent of faculty respondents favoring two boxes and 21 percent favoring one, though that count included many people who said they weren't familiar with the problem. In both surveys two-boxing came out ahead among philosophers, while the big public poll leaned the other way. That gap alone should make you curious.
The case for one box

The one-boxer's argument is simple: look at who walks away rich. The Predictor is almost never wrong. So the people who take one box almost always find $1 million inside. The people who take both boxes almost always find Box B empty and leave with $1,000. If you watched a thousand people play, the one-boxers would be millionaires and the two-boxers would have enough for a nice weekend. Why would you want to be in the second group?

You can put this in expected-value terms. If the Predictor is right with probability *p*, then taking one box is worth *p* times $1 million on average. Taking both is worth $1,000 plus the chance the Predictor got you wrong, times $1 million. The one-box option wins whenever the Predictor is right more than about 50.05 percent of the time. Even a predictor barely better than a coin flip makes one-boxing the better bet, by this way of counting.

blocks.title: Calculated: average gain from taking one box instead of two
blocks.note: Uses evidential expected value. Two-boxers reject this way of calculating.
blocks.source: Calculated from the payoffs in the problem: gain = (2p - 1) x $1,000,000 - $1,000

blocks.text: The philosopher David Lewis, himself a two-boxer, gave this argument its famous nickname in a 1981 paper titled "Why Ain'cha Rich?" It is the taunt a one-boxer throws: if you're so rational, where's your money? Lewis's answer, as we'll see, was that the game is rigged against rational people. To one-boxers, that sounds like a very elaborate way of losing.
The case for two boxes

The two-boxer's argument is just as simple, and to many people it is airtight. The Predictor made its decision yesterday. The money is either in Box B right now or it isn't. Your choice cannot reach back in time and change what is in a box.

So consider both possibilities. If Box B has $1 million, taking both gets you $1,001,000 instead of $1,000,000. If Box B is empty, taking both gets you $1,000 instead of nothing. Whatever is in the box, taking both gives you $1,000 more.

Decision theorists call this a dominance argument: one option is better in every possible state of the world, so you should take it. Here is a vivid way to feel its force. Imagine a friend standing behind the table who can see into Box B. Whatever she sees, she would urge you to take both boxes, because whatever is there, the extra $1,000 is free money. If you know for certain what an informed friend would advise, shouldn't you follow it?

The two-boxer's diagnosis of the expected-value chart is that it confuses evidence with cause. Choosing one box is good *news*, because it suggests you're the kind of person the Predictor rewarded. But it doesn't *cause* the money to be there. That distinction is the heart of what philosophers call causal decision theory: choose the action that brings about the best results, not the action whose choice would be the best sign. A rival view, evidential decision theory, says choose the action that would be the best evidence of good outcomes, and it recommends one box.

And the taunt about money? Lewis's reply was that the game is built to pay people for being irrational. To see the point, imagine a billionaire who hands out cash to anyone who sincerely believes the Earth is flat. Flat-earthers would walk away richer, but that wouldn't make flat-earthism the rational belief. In the same way, two-boxers say, the Predictor rewards a disposition, and the rational choice in the room is still to take the extra $1,000 that is sitting right there.

blocks.title: The two arguments

left.head: One box
items: The Predictor is almost always right
One-boxers walk away with $1 million
Choosing one box is strong evidence B is full
Expected value favors one box

right.head: Two boxes
items: The money is already there or not
Taking both adds $1,000 either way
Your choice can't cause past events
A friend who could see inside would say take both

blocks.text: Why it won't stay settled

A good test for causal versus evidential reasoning is a variation sometimes called the smoking lesion. Suppose smoking itself is harmless, but a gene causes both a craving to smoke and cancer. Choosing to smoke would be bad news, since it suggests you have the gene, but it would not cause anything. Most decision theorists agree you should go ahead and smoke if you enjoy it. Evidential reasoning seems to get this case wrong, which pushes many philosophers toward causal reasoning and two boxes.

But one-boxers have a strong reply. In Newcomb's problem, the thing the Predictor tracks is not some gene that happens to be correlated with your choice. It is your decision-making itself. The Predictor is, in effect, running a model of you. If that model is accurate, then you are not choosing in isolation; you are choosing for both yourself and the copy of you inside the Predictor's head. Decide to take two boxes and the model took two boxes yesterday.

This line of thinking has become serious work in AI research. In 2017 Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares proposed what they called functional decision theory, which says you should treat your decision as the output of a procedure that may be running in more than one place, including inside anyone who can accurately predict you. That matters for artificial agents, which could be copied, simulated or have their code read by other agents. For a program that knows another system can inspect its source code, Newcomb's problem stops being a fantasy and becomes an engineering question.

There is also the free will angle. If a Predictor could reliably forecast your choice, does that mean your choice was settled before you made it? Some people refuse the setup entirely: such a Predictor is impossible, they say, so the puzzle tells us nothing. Others reply that it doesn't need to be perfect. Humans predict each other's choices better than chance all the time, and as the chart shows, better than chance is all it takes for the arguments to collide.
Try these variations on yourself. Each one is designed to break one of the two arguments, and noticing which ones bother you tells you which principle you actually trust.

items: **Glass boxes.** Both boxes are transparent and you can see $1 million sitting in Box B. Do you still leave the $1,000 on the table? A committed one-boxer arguably should, since the Predictor filled B because it foresaw that.

**The twin.** You play a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself, raised identically and placed in an identical room. Should you cooperate, knowing your twin will reason exactly as you do?
**The weak Predictor.** The Predictor is a psychologist who is right 60 percent of the time. Does your answer change? If it does, at what accuracy did it flip, and why there?

**Precommitment.** The night before, you could sign a binding contract to take one box. Almost everyone would sign. If signing is smart the night before, why does taking one box become dumb the next morning?

blocks.text: Newcomb problems in real life

You face weak versions of this puzzle all the time, because other people are predictors. Consider a hiring manager deciding whether to give you responsibility, a friend deciding whether to trust you with a secret, or a teammate deciding whether to rely on you in a clutch moment. They are predicting what kind of person you are from everything you've done. By the time a particular moment arrives, their prediction is already made, and one selfish move might win you a little more. But if you are the kind of person who would make that move, they probably already saw it coming.

The philosopher Derek Parfit described a version that makes the point sharply. You're stranded in a desert. A driver who is very good at reading faces offers to take you to town if, and only if, you will sincerely pay him a good sum once you get there. Once you arrive, paying gains you nothing. A purely causal reasoner knows this, so he can't sincerely promise, the driver reads it on his face, and he dies in the desert. Sometimes the best thing to be is a person who keeps commitments even when breaking them would pay.

Nuclear deterrence has the same strange structure, which matters to anyone who has served on a submarine. A ballistic missile submarine's deterrent works because an adversary predicts that an attack would be answered. Yet once an attack had happened, retaliating would not undo it. Deterrence depends on being reliably the kind of side that would follow through, decided long in advance. Strategists have argued about the paradox in that for decades, and it is Newcomb's problem with the highest stakes imaginable.

Your own future self is a predictor too. When you set a rule like no phone after lights out, or a fixed number of sets you finish no matter how you feel, the rule only works if your future self can count on present you to honor it. Each time you break it "just this once," you teach yourself that your commitments are negotiable, and the next prediction gets worse. Being reliable to yourself is a Newcomb strategy.

Many of life's biggest payoffs are decided by predictions others made about you before the moment of choice. The cheapest way to be predicted as trustworthy is to actually be the kind of person who is.
So, one box or two? Sit with a few questions before you settle it.

If you'd take both, would you also refuse to pay the driver in the desert? If you'd take one, can you say what your choice actually changes? And if the Predictor were not a mysterious being but an algorithm that has watched every choice you've ever made online, would your answer be different? Many philosophers have changed their minds about this puzzle. That alone suggests it's worth changing yours at least once.

takeaways: Newcomb's problem pits two strong principles against each other: maximize expected value, or take the option that's better no matter what.
In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, about 39% of philosophers chose two boxes and 31% one box; Guardian readers leaned one box.
Two-boxers say your choice can't cause the past; one-boxers point out that one-boxers walk away rich.
The puzzle matters for AI agents that can be copied, simulated or have their code inspected.
In real life, people predict you; being reliably trustworthy is often worth more than any single selfish win.

title: The View That Changes People
dek: Astronauts keep coming home saying that seeing Earth from space rewired something in them. What is the overview effect, how solid is the evidence, and can you get any of it without leaving the planet?

blocks.text: On December 24, 1968, three men in a cramped capsule were on their fourth orbit of the Moon when the commander, Frank Borman, rolled the spacecraft. Out the window, rising over the gray, cratered horizon, came the Earth: a small blue and white half-disk hanging in total black. Bill Anders grabbed a camera loaded with black-and-white film, then scrambled for color. The shot he took, later named *Earthrise*, became one of the most reproduced photographs ever made. It is often credited with helping fuel the modern environmental movement; the first Earth Day was held sixteen months later.

Apollo 8 had flown a quarter of a million miles to study the Moon. What the crew and the world remembered most was the view of home. Over the following decades, astronaut after astronaut reported something similar: a shift in how they saw the planet, borders, conflict and their own place in it. In 1987 the writer Frank White gave it a name, *the overview effect*.

The idea is beautiful and a little too tidy, which is exactly why it is worth examining. Does seeing Earth from space really change people? Or is it a story that astronauts, space agencies and the rest of us want to be true?

blocks.title: Seeing ourselves from outside
items: Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human to orbit Earth
Apollo 8 crew photograph Earthrise from lunar orbit
Apollo 14's Edgar Mitchell describes a sudden sense of connection on the way home
Apollo 17 takes the Blue Marble, a fully lit Earth
Frank White's book names the overview effect
Voyager 1 photographs Earth as a pale blue dot from about 3.7 billion miles
First survey study of positive effects of spaceflight on astronauts
William Shatner, 90, flies to space and reports grief, not joy

blocks.text: What astronauts describe

The accounts share a recognizable set of themes. The planet looks astonishingly beautiful and alive against a background of black that is described as deeper than any night on Earth. The atmosphere, which feels limitless from the ground, looks like a thin blue line hugging the curve of the planet, about as thick as the skin on an apple. National borders, which people die over, are invisible. Many describe a sudden, physical sense that everyone on that ball is in the same small boat.

For some, the shift went deep. Edgar Mitchell, the sixth man to walk on the Moon, said that on the trip home from Apollo 14 in 1971 he was flooded with a feeling of connection to everything he could see. He spent much of the rest of his life on questions of consciousness and founded a research institute devoted to them. Other astronauts came home and turned to environmental causes, peace work or art. The ISS astronaut Ron Garan wrote a book arguing that seeing Earth from orbit should change how we solve problems on the ground.

Frank White, who coined the term, has argued that the effect is not just a nice feeling but a cognitive shift: once you have seen the whole system at a glance, it becomes harder to think of it as separate pieces. His theory went further, suggesting that as more people go to space the effect could change human culture itself. That is a big claim, and it is where the skeptic's ears should perk up.

Here is one way to test it. Billions of people have now seen Earthrise, the Blue Marble and live video from the space station. If looking at the whole planet were enough to dissolve borders, the photographs should have done some of that work by now, and the evidence that they have is weak at best. Maybe a picture is not the view. Maybe the effect needs the whole package: the danger of the ride, the weeks of isolation, the silence, the body floating at the window. Or maybe it is rarer and more personal than the legend suggests.
What the research actually shows

For a phenomenon this famous, the scientific evidence is thin, mostly because so few people have gone to space. According to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, only about 570 people had flown above 100 kilometers by 2021, when the dataset ends. Commercial flights have added more since, but the whole group would still fit inside one large high school. Studying it is like trying to understand a disease from a handful of patients who also happen to be famous.

blocks.title: People who have ever been to space
blocks.note: First flight above 100 km counted once per person. Commercial flights after 2020 have added more.
blocks.source: CSIS Aerospace Security Project, via Our World in Data, 2022

blocks.text: The first systematic attempt to measure the effect came in 2006. Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco sent an anonymous questionnaire to 175 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown at least once. Thirty-nine returned it. Every single respondent reported a positive reaction to being in space, and the strongest feelings concerned the Earth's beauty and fragility. They also described lasting changes in attitudes and behavior. Interestingly, the respondents seemed to fall into two groups, one with intense changes and one with milder ones, and the pattern didn't depend on how many missions they had flown or how long they had been up.

items.label: Astronauts and cosmonauts who returned the 2006 survey
Respondents reporting a positive reaction to being in space

blocks.source: Ihle, Ritsher and Kanas, Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine, 2006

blocks.text: In 2016 a team led by David Yaden at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed astronauts' own descriptions of seeing Earth and found recurring themes of unity, vastness and connectedness. They argued the overview effect is best understood as an especially intense form of two experiences psychologists already study: *awe* and *self-transcendence*, the feeling that the boundaries of the self have softened and you are part of something larger.

Seen this way, the classic features of the overview effect make sense. Awe happens when something is too big for the mental boxes you normally use. From orbit, the box labeled "countries" stops matching what your eyes report, because there are no lines down there. The box labeled "the sky" turns out to be a film thinner than the distance you might drive to work. The mind has to rebuild its model on the spot, and the rebuilt model has fewer walls in it.

That framing connects the overview effect to a much bigger body of research. In 2003 the psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt defined awe as the response to something so vast that it doesn't fit your existing mental frameworks and forces you to update them. In a set of five studies with more than 2,000 people, Paul Piff and colleagues found that inducing awe, including by having people stand in a grove of towering trees, made them more generous and helpful and less entitled, partly by making them feel smaller. Space may be the most extreme awe trigger humans have ever found.
The skeptic's case

Now the pushback, and there is a lot of it. Start with the 2006 survey. Only 39 of 175 astronauts responded, about 22 percent. People who had a profound experience are far more likely to fill out a questionnaire about profound experiences. Astronauts who felt nothing special may simply have tossed it. A 100 percent positive rate from a self-selected fifth of the population tells you the effect is real for some people, not how common it is.

Second, astronauts are not random people. They are selected, trained and, for decades, were public representatives of national space programs. Telling an inspiring story about the fragile blue planet is part of the job, and once the overview effect had a name, everyone flying knew they were supposed to feel it. Expectation shapes experience. That doesn't make the feeling fake, but it makes it hard to separate the view from the script.

Third, the reaction isn't always uplifting. When William Shatner, the actor who played Captain Kirk, flew to the edge of space in October 2021 at age 90, he came back visibly shaken. He later wrote that he had expected a sense of connection, but what hit him was grief: the cold, empty black of space felt like death, and the Earth below looked painfully fragile. It is a reminder that awe and dread sit close together: the same vastness that makes one person feel connected can make another feel exposed.

There is also a measurement problem: nobody has tracked astronauts before and after flight in a careful, systematic way. Almost everything we know comes from what people said afterward, sometimes decades later, in interviews and memoirs. Memory edits itself to fit a good story, and few stories are better than coming back from orbit transformed. To really know whether spaceflight changes values, you would want to measure the same people before launch and long after landing, and compare them with similar people who trained but didn't fly.

Finally, attempts to recreate the effect on the ground have produced modest results. Virtual reality versions have been studied, and a 2024 pair of experiments in Amsterdam tested whether a VR trip to orbit made people behave more sustainably. A 7-minute version had no effect on donations to an environmental group. A 15-minute, more immersive version nudged feelings of connection to nature and donations upward, but not by a statistically significant amount, and it had no effect on how much meat and dairy people ate over the following week. Feeling moved is one thing. Changing behavior is another.

blocks.title: Two readings of the overview effect

left.head: A real cognitive shift
items: Consistent themes across countries and decades
Every survey respondent reported positive effects
Fits well-studied research on awe
Some astronauts changed careers and causes

right.head: Partly a story we tell
items: Tiny, self-selected samples
Astronauts know the script before they fly
Reactions vary, including grief
VR versions barely move behavior

blocks.text: The view from inside a hull

There is a mirror image of the overview effect that matters for people who live sealed away from the sky. The psychiatrist Nick Kanas, one of the authors of the 2006 survey, has written about what he calls the Earth-disconnect phenomenon for future Mars crews. From Mars, Earth will be just a bright dot, and a message home and its reply can take up to 44 minutes. If seeing Earth is a source of awe and grounding, losing sight of it may feed isolation and loneliness. He suggests telescopes or VR views of Earth as countermeasures.

Astronauts themselves seem to know this. When a seven-window dome called the Cupola was added to the International Space Station in 2010, it quickly became one of the crew's favorite places to spend free time, photographing and simply watching the planet roll by. On a mission measured in months, the view is not a luxury. It is part of how people stay sane.

A submarine is a purer version of that disconnect: no window at all, for weeks or months. Nobody has studied whether the absence of sky affects submariners the way Kanas worries it may affect Mars crews, so it would be wrong to claim it does. But the research on awe suggests a practical idea. Awe doesn't require orbit. Vast things do the work: a night sky far from city lights, open ocean, a mountain, an old forest, even a really good documentary on a small screen. When you finally get to stand under an open sky again, it may be worth doing it on purpose.
You can't buy a ride to orbit, but you can practice the overview move: zoom out on purpose. Picture your problem from the next room, the next town, the next decade. Most things shrink.
An overview you can carry

In 1990, at the request of the astronomer Carl Sagan, the Voyager 1 probe turned its camera back toward home from about 3.7 billion miles away. Earth showed up as a single pale speck in a beam of scattered sunlight, less than a pixel wide. Sagan spent years afterward pointing out that every war, every empire, every person anyone had ever loved, had happened on that dot. You don't need to fly to feel the sting of that picture.

Whether or not the overview effect turns out to be as powerful as its fans believe, it raises a question that applies to everyone: how much of what feels huge in your life only feels that way because you are standing too close to it? Watch-bill drama, a bad ranked game, an argument in a group chat, a number on a scale. None of these are nothing. But from far enough away, they take their true size.

Questions to sit with. If you could see the whole Earth for ten minutes, what do you think you would feel, and what does that guess say about you? If the effect is real, why does it so rarely last in people who only see photographs of it? And if awe can make people more generous and less self-focused, why do most of us spend so many hours staring at screens built to make us feel the opposite?

takeaways: The overview effect is the shift in perspective many astronauts report after seeing Earth whole from space.
Evidence is real but thin: one survey got replies from 39 of 175 astronauts, all positive, and that sample is self-selected.
Researchers frame it as an intense form of awe, an emotion that in studies can make people feel smaller and act more generously.
Not everyone reacts the same way; some, like William Shatner, felt grief, and VR versions barely change behavior.
You can borrow the move on Earth: seek out vast things and zoom out on purpose.

title: Are You Someone's Simulation?
dek: In 2003 an Oxford philosopher argued that one of three strange things has to be true, and the third is that you are almost certainly living inside a computer.

blocks.text: Minecraft players have built working computers out of redstone. Not mods, not plugins: actual processors made from in-game blocks, with memory and logic gates, slow and enormous, running simple programs inside a world that is itself a program running on a real machine. A computer inside a game inside a computer. Nobody inside that redstone CPU knows it's nested two layers deep, because there is nobody inside it. Yet.

Now push the idea forward a few centuries. Suppose game engines keep improving the way they have since Pong, and someday someone can simulate not just blocks and physics but brains, neuron by neuron, well enough that the simulated people think and feel. Then ask the uncomfortable question. If that day comes, and someone runs a lot of those worlds, how would anyone inside one of them know?

In 2003 the philosopher Nick Bostrom, then at Oxford, turned that late-night dorm question into a tight argument, published in *The Philosophical Quarterly*. It doesn't claim we live in a simulation. It claims something sneakier: that if you accept a few reasonable-sounding premises, you're forced to pick one of three surprising conclusions. And the third one is that you are almost certainly a simulated person.
Three doors, pick one

Bostrom calls the worlds in question *ancestor simulations*: detailed simulations of an earlier era of a civilization's history, run by its far-future descendants, which he calls posthumans. Then he says at least one of these must be true. First, almost every civilization at our stage goes extinct before it gets the technology to run such simulations. Second, almost no civilization that does get the technology has any interest in running many of them. Third, we are almost certainly living in one.

The logic is a counting argument. If even a small fraction of advanced civilizations run lots of ancestor simulations, then simulated minds will vastly outnumber original, biological ones. One real history, thousands or millions of copies. If you have no special evidence about which kind of mind you are, the honest bet is that you're one of the many, not the one. Bostrom calls this the *bland indifference principle*: if most observers with experiences like yours are simulated, your credence that you are simulated should match that fraction.

blocks.title: The simulation argument in five moves
items: Minds can, in principle, run on computers, not just on biological brains.
A technologically mature civilization would have enormous computing power to spare.
So it could run huge numbers of detailed simulations of its own past, cheaply.
If any meaningful fraction of civilizations did this, simulated minds would massively outnumber real ones.
Therefore: either almost no one gets there, almost no one bothers, or you are probably simulated.

blocks.text: The key word is *either*. Bostrom isn't selling door three. In the paper he says that, given how ignorant we are, it seems sensible to spread your belief roughly evenly across all three.

Each door is unsettling in its own way. Door one says humanity probably doesn't make it. Door two says every advanced civilization, without exception, loses interest in something we would find irresistible. Door three says the world around you is software.
Is that even possible?

The argument only works if the computing is affordable, so Bostrom ran rough numbers. He used two estimates of the processing it takes to match a human brain, one based on how much computation it takes to copy what the retina does, the other on synapse counts and firing rates. Then he multiplied out a full human history: about 100 billion people, living about 50 years each. He also cited estimates of what a computer the mass of a planet could do using nanotechnology designs already sketched on paper.

items.label: Operations per second Bostrom estimated a human brain performs
Operations to simulate the mental history of all humans who ever lived
Operations per second cited for one planet-sized computer

blocks.source: Bostrom, The Philosophical Quarterly, 2003

blocks.text: Put those together and the conclusion is startling. By his figures, one planet-mass computer could run the entire mental history of humanity using less than a millionth of its processing power for a single second. A civilization that could build many such machines wouldn't need to make sacrifices to run simulations. It could run them the way you leave a game server up overnight.

Notice the trick that keeps the cost down. The simulation doesn't need to model every atom in the universe. It only needs to model what its inhabitants actually look at, in the detail they look at it, the same way a game engine doesn't render the room behind you. Distant stars can be cheap points of light until someone builds a telescope. If a scientist zooms in on something, the system fills in detail on demand. As anyone who has written game code knows, that's just good optimization.

People sometimes point to quantum mechanics as a clue here, since particles seem not to have definite properties until they are measured. It sounds like rendering on demand. Physicists mostly treat that as a loose analogy, not evidence. Quantum theory makes the same predictions whether or not anyone is running it on a server, so the resemblance tells you more about how game-like our intuitions are than about what the universe is.
The strongest pushback

A lot of smart people find the argument clever but not convincing, and their objections are worth taking seriously. The deepest one goes straight at premise one. Bostrom assumes that a simulated brain would actually be conscious, that experience comes from the right kind of information processing, whatever it runs on. That is exactly the question nobody has answered. If consciousness needs biology, or something else computers lack, then simulated people would be empty puppets, and you, who definitely experience things, couldn't be one of them.

A second objection attacks the counting. In 2020 the Columbia astronomer David Kipping ran a Bayesian analysis of the argument. His point was that we don't know whether such simulations are even technically possible, and that uncertainty has to be counted alongside the huge number of possible simulated worlds. Once he did that, the probability that we are simulated came out below 50 percent, approaching 50 only in the limit of infinitely many simulations. The quantum-computing researchers Alexandre Bibeau-Delisle and Gilles Brassard reached a similar verdict the same year, arguing the odds are unlikely to be as high as earlier claims suggested, especially if simulations have to run simulations of their own.

A third objection is that the whole thing smuggles in assumptions about what posthumans would want. We have no idea what a mind a million years ahead of us values. Maybe running billions of suffering ancestors for fun would be considered monstrous. Maybe it's illegal. Maybe it's just boring, like asking an adult to keep playing with a toy they outgrew. Door two might be the boring, correct answer.

Then there's the falsifiability problem. A good scientific claim makes predictions that could prove it wrong. In 2012 three physicists, Silas Beane, Zohreh Davoudi and Martin Savage, tried to do exactly that. They imagined a simulation built on a cubic grid, like the lattices physicists already use to simulate the strong nuclear force, and asked what tell-tale signs that would leave. Their answer: the very highest-energy cosmic rays might show a subtle preference for certain directions, lining up with the grid. It's a long shot, but it turned a philosophy question into something a detector could, in principle, test.

blocks.title: Should you take it seriously?

left.head: Reasons to
items: The math of the counting step is simple and hard to dodge
Simulation power has grown relentlessly since the 1970s
A simulation only has to render what its inhabitants observe
It rests on premises many scientists already accept

right.head: Reasons to doubt
items: Nobody knows if simulated brains would be conscious
Bayesian analyses put the odds below 50 percent
We can't guess what posthumans would want
Hard to test, and so far no physics anomaly points to it

blocks.text: The twist: you can move the odds

Here is the part of the argument that gets under your skin. Suppose humanity, or some company, actually builds a convincing ancestor simulation full of conscious people. That would knock out doors one and two in one move: we'd have proof that civilizations can reach the tech and that at least one wants to use it. Kipping makes the same point. If we ever start producing such simulations ourselves, the odds that we are sims jump sharply.

Bostrom's paper ends on a related twist. Unless we are already living in a simulation, he notes, our descendants will almost certainly never run one. The two facts are chained together. Which means the people most excited about building the ultimate simulation are also, in a strange way, the people working hardest to prove they're probably inside one.

It gets stranger. Bostrom points out that computers can be stacked, the way a virtual machine runs inside your desktop. If our simulators can be simulated too, reality could have many levels, each one running on the one below. But every level costs the level beneath it, and a simulated civilization that grows powerful enough to start running its own simulations would get expensive fast. Bostrom notes, almost in passing, that this gives our hypothetical operators a reason to shut a simulation down right around the time its people are about to become posthuman.

If you build games, this has an odd ring to it. Every NPC you script lives in a world with rules you chose, physics you tuned, and corners you never bothered to render. Right now they're simple state machines with no inner life. But the direction of travel is clear. Characters in games are getting smarter every year, and some already chat back using language models. At what point would you owe them anything?

Flip the question around and it becomes a mirror. If we are someone's simulation, we would hope our creators cared whether we suffered, didn't delete us on a whim, and didn't run a few billion copies of history's worst years for entertainment. Whatever rules you would want them to follow are a decent first draft of the rules we should follow if we ever create minds of our own. The simulation argument, oddly, ends up being an ethics question about the future of game design.

blocks.title: The long history of doubting reality
items: c. 300s BCE
Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, then wonders if he's a butterfly dreaming he is a man
c. 375 BCE
Plato's cave: prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for the whole of reality
Descartes imagines an evil demon feeding him a false world
Hilary Putnam's brain in a vat on a scientist's lab bench
The Matrix brings the idea to the mainstream
Bostrom's simulation argument appears in The Philosophical Quarterly
Beane, Davoudi and Savage propose a physics test
David Chalmers argues in Reality+ that virtual worlds can be genuinely real

blocks.text: Would it even matter?

Say door three is right. Does anything change? The philosopher David Chalmers, who has spent decades on consciousness, argues in his 2022 book *Reality+* that the answer is less than you'd think. His view is that a simulated world isn't fake.

It's made of digital processes instead of whatever the base level is made of, but the tables still hold your weight, the people are still people, and the causes and effects are all still there. Physics already says your desk is mostly empty space and quantum fields. Finding out those fields are running on someone else's hardware adds one more layer underneath, not a lie on top.

On that view, your effort in the gym still built muscle, the reactor plant you learned still behaves exactly as the books said, and the people you love are still conscious beings who love you back. What would change is cosmic context. There'd be a creator, though possibly a bored grad student rather than a god, and the universe might have an off switch. The economist Robin Hanson once half-jokingly suggested that if we're simulated, we should try to be interesting so nobody shuts the simulation down.

There's also a deeper lesson hiding here, and it doesn't depend on the answer. The argument shows how a few modest-looking assumptions, chained together, can force you somewhere wild. That's a skill worth having. Whenever a conclusion feels crazy, look for the premise doing the heavy lifting. In Bostrom's case it's the idea that a mind is just information processing, which is the very question the hard problem of consciousness says we can't yet settle.

Thought experiment to sit with: you're offered proof, today, that this world is a simulation. List three things you would do differently tomorrow. If the list is short, the question matters less than it feels. If it's long, ask why those things depend on what the universe is made of.

Most people who try that exercise find their list is short. They'd still want to see their family, finish what they started, and get better at what they care about. That might be the most useful answer the simulation argument gives: whatever the substrate, the life is still the one you're living, and it still counts.

takeaways: Bostrom's argument is a trilemma: civilizations die out, don't bother, or we're probably simulated. He spread his own belief roughly evenly across all three.
Its weakest link is the assumption that a simulated brain would be conscious, which nobody has proven.
Bayesian reanalyses put the odds of being simulated below 50 percent, not near certainty.
If we ever build conscious simulations ourselves, the odds that we are simulated jump.
Even if it's true, a simulated world can still be real in the ways that matter: effort, skills and people still count.

title: The Side Project That Ate the Day Job
dek: Minecraft started as a programmer's after-hours experiment. The research on side ventures says keeping the day job is not a lack of nerve. The hard part is making a few hours a week add up.

blocks.text: In May 2009, a Swedish programmer posted a short clip of a blocky cave game he had been tinkering with. He called it Cave Game. He had a real job at a photo software company, and the game was something he worked on around it. People started paying for early access. He kept the job. Only in 2010, once the money from those early sales was beating his salary, did he quit to work on it full time. The programmer was Markus Persson, and the game became Minecraft.

The usual story about building something is a story of leaping: quit the job, burn the boats, go all in. Persson's story is the quieter one. He did not leap. He built on the side until the side project proved it could carry him, and then he stepped across. That quieter path turns out to be the one the evidence favors, and it is the only path open to someone whose day job is a submarine.

Notice one more thing about the Minecraft story. Persson did not build in secret and reveal a finished game. He posted footage within days of starting and shared builds on an indie developer forum, and early players followed along as it grew. Building on the side and building in public fit together well: when you can only work a few hours a week, letting people watch the progress turns small steps into something that also attracts an audience.
Keeping the day job is a strategy, not a weakness

In 2014, management researchers Joseph Raffiee and Jie Feng asked a simple question: do people who start businesses while still employed do better or worse than people who quit first? They used a long-running U.S. government survey that has followed about 12,700 Americans since 1979, and looked at business starts from 1994 to 2008.

The people who kept their jobs while starting, whom the researchers called hybrid entrepreneurs, had a 33 percent lower rate of exiting their new business than those who jumped straight from a paycheck into full-time self-employment. Keeping the job did not signal weak commitment. It bought time to learn whether the idea worked before betting everything on it.

items.label: Lower rate of exiting the business for founders who kept their day job at first
People followed in the U.S. survey the study drew on
Years of business starts analyzed

blocks.source: Raffiee & Feng, Academy of Management Journal, 2014

blocks.text: A fair caveat: this is an observational study. People who choose the hybrid route may simply be more careful or less risk-hungry, and that could explain part of the gap. But the logic holds either way. A paycheck lets you make decisions based on what the project needs instead of what next month's rent needs. That freedom is worth more than the extra hours a full-time founder gets.

For a sailor, this reframes the situation. Ships, watches and duty days do eat time. But a steady paycheck, no debt and a career path with a civilian safety net are exactly the conditions under which experiments are cheap. The constraint is hours, not survival. That is a much better problem to have.
Your schedule is more optimistic than you are

The first enemy of a side project is not laziness. It is bad estimating. In a classic 1994 study, psychologist Roger Buehler and colleagues asked senior psychology students to predict when they would finish their honors theses. They also asked for a best-case guess and a worst-case guess, the date if everything went as badly as it could.

blocks.title: Thesis completion: estimates vs reality
blocks.note: On average, the students took longer than even their worst-case guess. Only about 30% finished by their predicted date.
blocks.source: Buehler, Griffin & Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994

blocks.text: Look at the last two bars. The average student took longer than their own *worst-case* scenario. This is the planning fallacy, and it gets worse, not better, for part-time work. A full-time builder who loses a day loses a fifth of a week. A part-time builder who loses a weekend to duty or a long underway loses everything that week had.

The fix the research points to is to stop estimating from the inside, picturing the steps going smoothly, and start estimating from the outside: how long did similar things *actually* take before? If the last few game ideas each died after a couple of months, that is your base rate. Plan the next one assuming the same pull, and build the plan to survive it. A practical rule: whatever your estimate, cut the scope until the estimate is half of the time you really have.
If a plan only works when nothing goes wrong, it is not a plan. It is a best-case guess, and the data says reality usually lands past the worst case.

Cutting scope is where most side projects are actually won or lost. For a launcher obby, that might mean one world instead of three, a handful of upgrades instead of a full tree, and no trading system until people are clearly coming back. Every feature that does not make the first version fun is a feature that makes it later. Later is the most dangerous word for a part-time builder, because every extra month is another month for life to interrupt.
The real tax is restarting

Programmer and investor Paul Graham wrote an influential essay about two kinds of schedules. Managers live in one-hour blocks, and an extra meeting costs them one hour. Makers need long stretches, often half a day, because building requires loading a whole problem into your head before you can do anything useful. A single interruption can wreck a maker's afternoon.

Side builders live in the worst version of this. Their sessions are short and scattered, so a large share of each session goes to remembering where they left off: which script was broken, what the next level needed, what the partner changed. If it takes 30 minutes to get your head back into the project and you only have 60, half your time is gone before you start.

That means the most valuable habit for a side project is not working longer. It is making restarts cheap. Ernest Hemingway famously advised stopping a writing session while you still know what comes next, so the next day starts with momentum instead of a blank page. Builders can do the same thing on purpose.

blocks.title: The parking routine: last five minutes of every session
items: Stop in the middle of something easy, not at the end of something hard.
Write one line: what you were doing and what is broken right now.
Write the very next action, small enough to start in two minutes.
Note anything you need from your partner, so it can happen while you are away.
Save, commit or back up, so the next session starts from a known state.

blocks.text: This feels too small to matter. It is not. The first ten minutes of a session decide whether it becomes productive or turns into scrolling. A clear next action is the difference between "open Studio and fix the jump pad" and "open Studio and figure out what I was doing."
Why small wins keep you going

The second enemy is motivation fade. Harvard researcher Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer collected about 12,000 daily diary entries from 238 professionals across seven companies, each tracked for the length of a project. They wanted to know what separated people's best workdays from their worst.

The answer was almost embarrassingly simple. On the best days, the single most prominent event was making progress on meaningful work, even small progress. On the worst days, it was setbacks. They called this the progress principle. Feeling that you moved forward fuels the motivation to keep moving.

For a side project, this is a design requirement. If every session ends with "still not done" on a giant task, motivation drains. If tasks are cut small enough that most sessions end with something visibly working, a new obstacle, a fixed bug, a rough level, the project feeds itself. That is the same reason the parking routine ends with a tiny next step: it guarantees the next session starts with a quick win.

blocks.title: Two ways to build on the side

left.head: Waiting for big sessions
items: "I'll work on it when I have a free weekend"
Tasks sized like "build the level system"
Each restart takes half an hour
Long gaps kill momentum and the project fades

right.head: Small reps, cheap restarts
items: Short sessions on a fixed rhythm
Tasks sized to finish in one sitting
A parked next step makes restarts take minutes
Visible progress most sessions keeps motivation up

blocks.text: There is a related trap worth naming: confusing activity with progress. Watching tutorials, tweaking settings, rearranging a task list and redesigning the logo all feel productive, and all of them give you a little of the progress feeling without moving the project. A useful test at the end of a session is whether a player would notice what you did. If the answer keeps being no, the sessions are being spent on comfort work.

The same principle explains why fixed rhythms beat bursts of inspiration. Two or three sessions a week, at roughly the same times, mean the project never goes cold long enough for the restart cost to balloon. A burst of twelve hours one weekend followed by three weeks of nothing feels heroic but often produces less, because each return starts from zero.
Async: building with someone who is awake when you are not

Building with a partner while one of you disappears for weeks without reliable internet sounds like a dealbreaker. It is actually a known problem with a known shape. Remote teams across time zones solve it with asynchronous work: decisions and progress live in writing, so nobody has to be online at the same time.

The trick is splitting work by what needs a connection. Live operations, like publishing updates, answering players and posting clips, belong to whoever is on shore. Deep work that can be done offline belongs to whoever is underway: game design documents, level layouts sketched on paper, upgrade tables and pricing math, video scripts, lists of bugs and ideas to test. A deployment is not dead time for a project if the offline work is planned before it starts.

items: Before going underway: agree on one goal for the period and who owns which pieces.
Underway: work only on things that need no internet, and keep a running log of decisions and questions.
On return: hand over the log in one sitting, then merge, test and ship together.
Always: one shared written list of what is being built now, next and later, so nothing lives only in one person's head.

blocks.text: This also keeps the partnership healthy. Most friction between co-builders comes from surprise: one person changes something big while the other is away. Writing things down and agreeing on owners before a long absence prevents most of that.

Be realistic about energy, too. After a long watch or a duty day, deep design work may be out of reach, and forcing it usually produces work you redo later. Keep two kinds of tasks on the list: thinking tasks for when you are fresh, like designing a new mechanic, and low-energy tasks for when you are tired, like naming upgrades, cleaning up a bug list or sorting clips. Matching the task to the energy you actually have means a tired evening still moves the project a little, instead of becoming a reason to skip it entirely.
A few hours, every week, for a long time

Put the evidence together and a clear strategy appears. Keep the stable job; it makes experiments cheap. Distrust your schedule, and cut scope until the plan has room for duty days and surprises. Make every restart cheap with a parked next step. Size tasks so most sessions end with a small win. Split work with your partner by what needs a connection, and write everything down.

None of this needs a tracking spreadsheet or an elaborate system. It needs a rhythm: a few fixed sessions a week, each one starting with a written next step and ending with one. Minecraft did not need its creator to quit his job to get started. It needed him to keep coming back to it. The question to ask about a side project is not "How much time do I have?" It is "How little does it take for me to pick this back up?" Get that number close to zero, and a few hours a week compound into something real.

takeaways: Founders who kept their day jobs at first exited their businesses about a third less often; a paycheck makes experiments cheap.
People routinely blow past even their worst-case estimates, so cut scope until the plan fits half your real time.
The hidden cost of side projects is restarting; end every session with a written next step.
Small visible progress is the strongest daily motivator, so size tasks to finish in one sitting.
With a partner, split work by what needs internet: offline design underway, live operations on shore.
