title: Have the Hard Conversation Before You Need It
dek: Partnerships rarely die from bad ideas. They die from the conversations two people skipped at the start, and the research says friends and family skip them most.

blocks.text: In 2010, two brothers from Regina, Saskatchewan, started making a video game on the side. Chad and Jared Moldenhauer both had full-time jobs, so the game began as a weekend project with a team of three. It had an absurdly ambitious art style: every frame hand-drawn to look like a 1930s cartoon. They called it *Cuphead*.

When they finally showed it publicly in 2014 and then let people play it in 2015, the reaction was huge, and so was the criticism: the game was only boss fights, and players wanted more. The brothers faced the kind of decision that ends partnerships. Expanding the game meant years more work. Doing it properly meant quitting their jobs and remortgaging their homes. They made the call together, took the risk, and *Cuphead* came out in 2017 and went on to sell millions of copies.

blocks.title: Two brothers, one very risky game
items: Chad and Jared Moldenhauer start Cuphead as a side project while working full time
The game is unveiled publicly for the first time
Players can try it; the boss-only design is criticized
The brothers expand the scope, quit their jobs and remortgage their homes
Cuphead releases and goes on to sell millions of copies

blocks.text: Stories like this get told as stories about talent and passion. But look at what the studio said about how it worked. New ideas had to be approved by everyone on the team, and the debates over them could get heated. They had a rule for deciding, and they used it on the biggest bet of their lives. That is the less glamorous half of every successful partnership, and it is the half most partners skip.
What 10,000 founders reveal

Noam Wasserman, then a professor at Harvard Business School, spent about a decade studying nearly 4,000 startups and 10,000 founders for his book *The Founder's Dilemmas*. His central finding is that the decisions that sink new ventures are often made in the first days, when everyone is excited and nobody wants to spoil the mood.

The clearest example is how founders split ownership. Wasserman found that most teams settle it almost immediately, and that a third simply split everything equally. A related study he co-wrote with Thomas Hellmann, covering 1,476 founders in 511 ventures, found that equal splits were linked to lower valuations when the companies later raised money, especially in teams that agreed on the split in under a day. The founders who brought more to the table, such as the original idea, previous experience or their own money, gave up an estimated 10% of the company by accepting an equal split, according to the researchers' model.

items.label: Founding teams that settled equity in their first month
Teams that split ownership exactly equally
Estimated share of the company a stronger founder forgoes by accepting an equal split

blocks.source: Wasserman, The Founder's Dilemmas (HBS Working Knowledge, 2012); Hellmann & Wasserman, NBER, 2011

blocks.text: The lesson is not that equal splits are wrong. For two people contributing similar work, equal may be exactly right. The lesson is that a split decided in a rush, to avoid an awkward conversation, tends to stop matching reality later. And when ownership stops matching who is doing the work, resentment grows quietly until it does not stay quiet.

Why do so many teams rush? Hellmann and Wasserman's explanation is simple: negotiating is uncomfortable and costly, so many founders accept an equal split rather than pay the price of an honest conversation about who is bringing what. In other words, the 50-50 split is often not a decision at all. It is a way of avoiding one.

Wasserman has also been widely quoted as saying that about 65% of high-potential startups fail because of conflict among co-founders. Treat that number with care: it gets repeated far more often than it gets explained, so think of it as a strong signal rather than a precise measurement. But the direction matches everything else in his research. People problems kill more ventures than product problems.
Why family makes it harder, not easier

Here is the counterintuitive part. Wasserman found that teams made of friends and family were among the most fragile, not the most stable. The reason is not that relatives are worse partners. It is that they are more likely to avoid tough conversations to protect the relationship.
Strangers who start a company together have to write things down because they do not trust each other yet. Brothers assume they will figure it out.

blocks.title: Partnering with family: the trade

left.head: What you get for free
items: Trust from day one
Fast, honest communication
Shared history and humor
Someone who will not just vanish

right.head: What you risk
items: Skipping the awkward money talk
Unclear roles because 'we'll figure it out'
Old family dynamics showing up in decisions
A failed project hurting the relationship

blocks.text: Old dynamics matter more than people admit. An older sibling may expect to have the final word without either of you noticing. A younger one may defer on things they actually know better, then resent it later. None of this is anyone's fault, which is exactly why it is worth naming out loud. The goal is to make sure the partnership runs on the roles you chose, not the ones you inherited.

The stakes are also different. If two strangers fall out over a failed game, they lose a project. If two brothers fall out, they risk every holiday for the next decade. That is a reason to be *more* formal with family, not less.
Rich or king: know what each of you wants

Wasserman's most famous idea is that founders face a choice between being *rich* and being *king*. Rich means maximizing the value of what you build, which often means bringing in partners, money or a bigger studio and giving up some control. King means keeping control of the decisions, even if the thing you build stays smaller. His research suggests you usually cannot fully have both, and the founders who get hurt are the ones who never decided which they wanted.

This is not a theoretical question on Roblox. *Grow a Garden* began as one teenager's project; when it was still small, he sold a share to an established studio, which brought in weekly updates and a team. By the studio's account, the original creator kept a stake and still contributes and suggests updates.

That was a rich choice, and it worked spectacularly. Another creator in the same position might have refused, preferring to keep full control. Neither is wrong. What would be wrong is two partners discovering they want opposite things on the day a studio sends an offer.
How to disagree without damage

Even with clear roles, you will disagree, and that is healthy. Two people who never argue about a game are usually not thinking hard enough about it. The goal is not fewer disagreements. It is disagreements that end in a decision instead of a grudge.

A few habits make a big difference. Before arguing against your partner's idea, explain it back in your own words until they agree you understood it. That one step removes a surprising number of fights, because many arguments turn out to be two people defending different versions of the same idea. Argue about the game, never about who is smarter or who works harder.

Give a design debate a time limit, then decide using your agreed rule. And once a decision is made, both of you commit to it fully, even the person who lost the argument. Amazon built a leadership principle around this idea: disagree openly, then commit. A half-hearted version of a plan, built by a partner who is quietly hoping it fails, is the worst of both worlds.

Finally, go back and check. When an update ships, look at what players actually did and talk honestly about who called it right. Over time, you learn which of you has better instincts in which areas, and the roles can shift to match. The data becomes the neutral third partner that neither of you has to argue with.
Split roles, not just revenue

Most partners talk about money and never talk about decisions. But day to day, decisions cause far more friction than money. Who decides whether the launcher upgrade costs 50 coins or 80? Who decides whether to start a second game? What happens when you both feel strongly and disagree?

A simple structure works well for two-person teams. Give each person clear ownership of specific areas, such as one owning scripting and systems while the other owns building, art and the store page. In your own area, you make the final call after hearing the other person out. A short list of big decisions, like starting a new project, selling a share, spending real money or changing the revenue split, requires both of you to say yes. And when you are stuck on a design argument, you agree in advance to settle it the way good studios do: build the cheapest version of both ideas and let players decide.

blocks.title: A one-page partnership agreement
items: Roles: who owns which areas, and who makes the final call in each.
Big decisions: the short list that needs both partners to agree.
Tie-breaks: test both options with players, or alternate who decides.
Money: who owns the group, how revenue is split, and when you will revisit it.
Goals: rich or king, and what offer you would actually accept.
Exit: what happens to the game and the money if one person stops working on it.

blocks.text: Writing it down is the point. A one-page document you both agree to on a calm day is worth more than a hundred conversations remembered differently by each of you during a fight.

Clear ownership pays off in a less obvious way, too: it lets work continue when one partner disappears for a while. When one of you is away for weeks with no connection, a team where every decision needs both people simply stops. A team where each person owns an area keeps moving.

Leave a short written handoff before going dark: what you finished, what is next, and which decisions the other person can make without you. Keep a simple decision log, a running list of what you agreed and why, so nobody has to rely on memory when you reconnect. These habits feel like overhead for a two-person team. In practice, they are what make a part-time partnership work at all.
A written agreement is not a sign of distrust. It is shared memory. Six months from now, both of you will remember the original deal slightly differently, and the paper will not.
The money mechanics on Roblox

On Roblox, the practical version of ownership is usually a *group*. A game owned by a group can automatically split its earnings with recurring percentage payouts to members, set per game or across the whole group. That makes revenue sharing easy. It also means whoever owns the group, or holds the permission to manage payouts, controls the money and can change the split. Roblox's documentation is blunt about what happens if things go wrong: it says it cannot help arbitrate or resolve disagreements inside a group.

The per-game setting is more useful than it looks. Because splits can be set game by game, partners do not need one split for everything forever. A game you built together can be split one way, and a smaller project that one person builds mostly alone can be split another. That flexibility only helps if you use it deliberately, so add a line to your agreement about how new projects inside the group will be divided before anyone starts building them. The worst time to negotiate the split on a game is after it starts earning.

So decide, in writing, who owns the group and what the split is. Startups solve a version of this problem with *vesting*, where founders earn their ownership over time, often over four years with nothing earned until the first year is complete. The point is that if one founder leaves early, they do not walk away with a large share of something the other person keeps building.

A two-person game team does not need legal paperwork to borrow the idea. You can simply agree that the split will be reviewed every few months against who is actually doing the work, and that someone who stops contributing stops earning new shares. Once real money is involved, talk to a lawyer. If either of you serves in the military, also check your command's rules on outside business activity before income starts flowing.
The cheapest fight you will ever have

Every partnership has hard conversations. The only choice is when. Have them early, when the game earns nothing and nobody is hurt, and they cost an awkward evening. Have them late, when there is real money, years of work and two different memories of what was promised, and they can cost the project and the relationship.

That is the reframe worth keeping. A written agreement between brothers is not a sign that you do not trust each other. It is the thing that lets you *keep* trusting each other when the stakes go up. The Moldenhauers bet their homes on a game and stayed partners. Their talent made *Cuphead* good. Their way of deciding together is what let them survive making it.

takeaways: Decide equity, roles and decision rules on purpose, not in a rush to avoid awkwardness.
Family partnerships need more structure, not less, because the relationship is at stake.
Know whether each of you wants to be rich or king before an offer arrives.
Give each partner clear areas to own; reserve a short list of big decisions for both.
On Roblox, the group owner controls payouts, so put ownership and splits in writing.

title: You Are Building on Rented Land
dek: Roblox and YouTube give a small builder reach no one could buy. They also set the rules, the payout rate and who is allowed in, and they can change all three overnight.

blocks.text: In September 2023, thousands of game developers woke up to news that their engine maker wanted a new cut. Unity, the engine behind a huge share of indie and mobile games, announced a Runtime Fee: a charge tied to how many times a game was installed, set to begin in January. Developers were furious, partly because of the money and partly because of the principle. They had picked Unity years earlier under one set of terms. Now the terms were changing under games they had already built.

Unity backed down in stages. Within weeks it narrowed the fee so it would not apply to existing games and would only hit paid tiers. On September 12, 2024, a year after the uproar, a new CEO cancelled it for game developers entirely and went back to subscription pricing, with price rises for the paid plans. But for a year, every studio built on Unity learned something uncomfortable: the ground under their business belonged to someone else.

That is platform risk. If you build a Roblox game and a YouTube channel, you are building on two of the most generous platforms that have ever existed for small creators. You are also building on land you do not own. Neither fact cancels the other.
The landlord always writes the lease

Platforms make a trade with builders. They bring the audience, the payments, the hosting and the discovery. In return, they set the rules and keep the right to change them. When interests line up, it is a fantastic deal. When they diverge, the platform wins, because it owns the lease.

Zynga, the company behind FarmVille, is the classic case. Around 2011, roughly 90 percent or more of its revenue was generated on Facebook, and Zynga alone accounted for $445 million, about 12 percent of Facebook's revenue that year. Even so, Facebook began requiring Zynga to pay its 30 percent fee on purchases through Facebook's own currency, which squeezed Zynga's profits and pushed it to try to diversify. The biggest tenant in the building still paid the rent the landlord set.

Size does not protect you either. In August 2020, Epic Games added its own payment option to Fortnite on iPhone to get around Apple's cut, and Apple pulled Fortnite from the App Store. It took a long legal fight and court orders against Apple's fees before Fortnite returned to the U.S. App Store on May 20, 2025, nearly five years later. One of the richest game companies in the world could not simply negotiate its way back.

blocks.title: When the platform changed the deal
items: Jan 2018
YouTube raises the bar for ad money to 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours.
Aug 2020
Apple removes Fortnite from the App Store over payments.
Sep 2023
Unity announces a per-install Runtime Fee.
Aug 2024
Turkey blocks access to Roblox.
Sep 2024
Unity cancels the Runtime Fee for games.
May 2025
Fortnite returns to the U.S. App Store.
Sep 2025
Roblox raises its standard DevEx cash-out rate.

blocks.text: What changing the rules looks like on YouTube

YouTube's version arrived on January 16, 2018. Until then, a channel could earn ad money after 10,000 lifetime views. Overnight, the requirement became 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 hours of watch time in the past year, and existing channels below that line were reviewed and dropped from the program. YouTube said the change would affect a significant number of channels.

Why would a platform squeeze the people who fill it with content? Usually because someone more important to its business needs something. In 2018, the change came as YouTube worked to win back advertisers who had been burned by ads appearing next to objectionable videos. Raising the bar gave YouTube more control over which channels could carry ads. Small creators were not the target; they were simply in the way. That is the normal shape of platform risk: decisions made for the platform's biggest customers, felt hardest by its smallest suppliers.

items.label: Affected channels that had earned under $100 in the past year
Affected channels that had earned under $2.50 in the past month

blocks.source: YouTube, via 9to5Google, January 2018

blocks.text: Those numbers cut both ways. They show YouTube was right that most affected channels were earning almost nothing, so the money lost was small. They also show who absorbs rule changes: the smallest creators, who have the least voice and the fewest alternatives. If you are just starting, you are in that group. The rules will be written with someone else in mind, and you will adapt to them.

Rules are not the only lever. YouTube's own product chief said in 2018 that about 70 percent of watch time came from recommendations. Any change in how that system weighs videos can move a small channel's views far more than anything the creator does that week. No contract guarantees you a share of it.

Discovery itself can shift. Roblox's own documentation lists changes to its algorithm as one of the reasons a game's Home impressions can rise or fall, alongside the developer's own updates and seasonal traffic. A game can lose a chunk of its players in a week without its creators changing a single line of code. If you ever see that happen, it is worth checking for announcements before assuming the game suddenly got worse.
The fine print on Roblox

Roblox controls every part of the money pipeline for its developers. Players buy Robux from Roblox. Developers earn Robux. Developers who qualify can convert earned Robux to real dollars through the Developer Exchange, known as DevEx, at a rate Roblox sets. Roblox's own documentation says the exchange rate is subject to change, that Roblox decides at its discretion what counts as earned Robux, and that it can reject requests.

The rate has moved, and in this case in developers' favor. Before September 5, 2025, the standard rate was $0.0035 per earned Robux. It is now $0.0038, and a higher rate of $0.0054 applies to some purchases made by U.S. players who are verified as 18 or older. Robux earned before the change still cash out at the old rate.

blocks.title: What 30,000 earned Robux pays out through DevEx
blocks.note: 30,000 is the minimum to cash out. The 18+ rate applies only to certain purchases by age-verified U.S. adults; that bar is calculated from Roblox's published $0.0054 rate.
blocks.source: Roblox Creator Hub, Developer Exchange documentation, 2025

blocks.text: The lesson is not that Roblox is stingy. It is that every number in that chart is a policy, and policies move. The newest one rewards games that attract verified adults, which tells you where Roblox wants developers to point their work. A platform's incentives quietly steer what gets built on it.

Rule changes are also openings for anyone paying attention. When a platform shifts its incentives, builders who adapt early tend to find less competition for the new thing being rewarded. A developer who reads Roblox's announcements and asks what the platform is trying to encourage will usually spot those shifts months before someone who only notices when their numbers change. Reading the landlord's plans is not paranoia. It is market research.

Eligibility is also a rule set. To cash out, you need to be at least 13, hold at least 30,000 earned Robux, have a verified email and tax forms on file, and stay in full compliance with Roblox's Terms of Use and Community Standards. Breaking the rules can mean suspension from DevEx. For a game made by two people, that means the account and group that own the game are business assets, and a careless mistake by either person is a risk to both.

Then there is access itself. Turkey blocked Roblox in August 2024 over child safety concerns. Several countries followed in 2025 and early 2026, including Qatar, Iraq and Egypt, while others such as Kuwait and Russia blocked it and later restored access with conditions like disabled chat. If a big share of your players lives in one country, a government decision you never saw coming can erase them in a day.
Rented versus owned

None of this means you should avoid platforms. At your stage, that would be a bad idea. Building your own game launcher or video site would be slower, more expensive and almost certainly reach nobody. Roblox and YouTube are the right places to start. The goal is not to leave rented land. It is to know which of your assets are rented and to build some that are owned.

blocks.title: What you build on a platform vs what goes with you

left.head: Rented (the platform can change it)
items: Your place in recommendations
The payout rate and eligibility rules
Your subscriber count and channel
Access in each country
The Robux balance before it is cashed out

right.head: Owned (goes with you anywhere)
items: Your skills: scripting, design, editing
Design docs, source files and art you made
Your reputation and name as a builder
Direct ways to reach fans, like an email list
Cash already paid out and saved

blocks.text: Look at the right column. Almost everything on it is either knowledge or a direct relationship. Those survive a policy change. A builder who has shipped three Roblox games has skills that transfer to any engine. A creator who has learned to edit and tell stories can move to another video platform. A team with a few hundred players who chose to hear from them directly can announce the next game no matter what an algorithm decides.

Be careful about what counts as owned. A Discord server is extremely useful, but it is also another platform with its own rules. An email list is about as close to owned as a small creator gets, because the addresses travel with you. The honest version is that nothing online is fully owned. The point is not to have zero dependence. It is to not have *one* dependence.
Concentration is the number to watch

The simplest way to measure platform risk is one question: if this platform disappeared or changed its rules tomorrow, what share of my income and audience would go with it? For Zynga, the honest answer was about 90 percent. That is what made Facebook's decisions so painful. The risk was not that Facebook existed; it was that almost everything ran through it.

For a beginner, the answer will be close to 100 percent, and that is fine. A first game on Roblox and a first channel on YouTube should be fully committed to their platforms, because splitting attention across five platforms before anything works is a much bigger risk than any policy change. Concentration becomes dangerous as the stakes grow: when the income starts paying real bills, when a team depends on it, when it becomes the business you plan to leave the Navy for. That is the point to start deliberately building the owned column, not before.
Early on, concentration is focus. Later, the same concentration is fragility. The skill is noticing when one has turned into the other.
A platform-risk checklist for a two-person studio

blocks.title: Protecting what you build
items: Read the rules that pay you: Roblox's Terms of Use, Community Standards and DevEx terms, and YouTube's monetization policies.
Stay clearly inside the lines; avoid gray-area tactics like misleading titles or copied assets that could put the account at risk.
Keep backups of place files, scripts and art outside the platform, so a lost account is not a lost game.
Put ownership in writing: which group owns the game, who controls it and how payouts are split.
Give fans a way to follow you that you control, and invite them to it from inside the game and videos.
Watch where your players come from and avoid depending on a single country, source or feature.

blocks.text: Money also deserves a rule. Robux sitting in a balance is a promise from Roblox, not dollars in a bank. Rates and eligibility can change, so once a game earns past the cash-out minimum, it is reasonable to turn platform money into real money on a regular schedule. Taxes apply to DevEx income; if it gets meaningful, check with a tax professional or the base legal or finance office.

One more habit costs nothing: keep a short record of the rules you are relying on and check it when you come back from time away. Coming home from a long underway to find that a policy changed weeks ago is a real risk when you cannot check announcements regularly. A partner on shore who reads platform news and passes along anything important is worth a lot here.
The portable asset is you

The deepest protection from platform risk is not a contract or a backup drive. It is the builder. Unity developers who knew their craft could switch engines if they had to. Small YouTubers who lost ad revenue in 2018 still had the skills and viewers they needed to cross the new bar and earn it back.

So use the platforms fully, follow their rules carefully and enjoy the reach they give you. Just never confuse renting with owning. Every game you finish, every video you edit, every player who chooses to follow you directly is something no landlord can take back. Build those on purpose, and a rule change becomes a setback instead of an ending.

takeaways: Platforms give reach in exchange for control: they set the rules, payout rates and access, and can change them.
Even giants like Zynga and Epic could not escape platform decisions, and the smallest creators absorb rule changes first.
Roblox's DevEx rate, eligibility and country access are all policies; read them, follow them and expect them to move.
Skills, source files, reputation and direct contact with fans are the assets that survive any policy change.
Back up your work, put game ownership in writing, and turn platform balances into real money regularly.

title: The Leaky Bucket: Why Retention Decides Everything
dek: One of the most successful game studios on Earth cancelled a game that had already earned close to a million dollars. The reason comes down to three numbers: D1, D7 and D30.

blocks.text: In March 2020, Supercell, the Finnish studio behind *Clash of Clans* and *Brawl Stars*, put a new puzzle game called *Hay Day Pop* into soft launch, a limited release in a few countries. By the time it was eight months old it had reportedly brought in close to a million dollars. Then Supercell shut it down. The company's explanation was short: the game did not meet its standards for itself or for its players.

Killing a game that makes money sounds insane until you understand what Supercell is actually measuring. A soft launch is not mainly a test of whether a game earns. It is a test of whether players *stay*. Studios like Supercell are hunting for games people will play for years, and early revenue from players who are already drifting away is a warning, not a win.

In 2016, a Supercell developer described the company as a long-time serial killer of its own games. Of its ten most recent projects at the time, seven had been killed as prototypes and two in soft launch. Only one, *Clash Royale*, shipped worldwide.
For a small team, this is the most important idea in game strategy. How many people *try* your game mostly measures your marketing and luck. How many come *back* measures the game itself.
How a serial killer of games decides

Supercell's record shows the method in action. Games are built by small teams, released quietly to a few countries, and watched closely. If players do not stick around in the way the studio believes a long-lasting hit requires, the game dies, even after a year or more of work and sometimes after it has earned real money. *Smash Land* was built by a team of about five people over ten months, failed to hit its beta targets, and was cancelled after the team concluded it was not a game people would play for years. Reporting on later cancellations points the same way: games shut down for not meeting the studio's bar rather than for losing money.

blocks.title: Some of the games Supercell killed
items: Smash Land: soft launched in April, discontinued later that year after its beta
Rush Wars: closed about three months into its beta
Hay Day Pop: shut in November despite nearly $1M in soft-launch revenue
Everdale: shutdown announced in October after an open beta
Floodrush: killed about three months after entering beta
Clash Mini: development ended in March, folded into Clash Royale

blocks.text: Supercell rarely publishes the exact numbers behind these calls, so be careful about claiming any single metric killed any single game. But the pattern is clear. The studio decides early, using how players behave, long before it would show up as a revenue problem.
The bucket with a hole in it
Picture your player base as a bucket. New players pour in from the top: recommendations, search, friends, a YouTuber's video. Players leak out of holes in the bottom every day.
The level in the bucket, your daily active players, depends on both. If the holes are big, pouring faster barely helps. You can double your traffic and watch it drain away within a week.

On Roblox, the holes do something worse: they also shrink the tap. Roblox's documentation describes its Recommended for You system as one that tests a game on small groups of players and expands to more similar players if they engage and keep coming back. Among the signals it lists as most important are play-through rate, first-play bounce rate, playtime per user, and *play days per user* on day 1, days 2 to 7, and days 8 to 28. So poor retention costs you twice. You lose the players you have, and the algorithm sends you fewer new ones.

blocks.title: Why retention compounds on Roblox
items: New players arrive from recommendations
They return, or they leak away
Roblox measures returns and playtime per player
Strong signals bring more new players
Weak signals shrink the flow

blocks.text: Two details from the same documentation are worth knowing. Playtime counts for at most 60 minutes per user per game per day, so one obsessive player cannot fake a good game. And the signals are averaged per player rather than totaled, which means a small game with loyal players is not automatically buried by a giant one.
What D1, D7 and D30 actually measure

Retention numbers are always about a *cohort*: the group of players who first played on a given day. Roblox defines day-1 retention as the share of that group who came back the next day, with day 7 and day 30 measuring returns after a week and a month. That is classic retention: did they show up on that specific day? Some analytics tools also report rolling retention, which counts anyone who returned on that day or later, so always check which kind you are looking at before comparing numbers.
Each checkpoint tests a different part of your game. Roblox's own retention guide lays this out clearly, and it maps neatly onto how designers think about player journeys.

blocks.title: What each checkpoint is really testing
items: Day 0
The first session: did the first five minutes deliver fun fast?
Day 1
Core loop and first-time experience: is the basic action worth repeating?
Day 7
Progression: are there short and long goals worth coming back for?
Day 30
Long-term content: updates, social systems, events, and an endgame

blocks.text: The guide's advice for day 1 is to keep the core loop clear and fun, use a brief tutorial, and get players to the fun ideally in five minutes or less. For day 7, it points to goals, variety and difficulty pacing. For day 30, it suggests smaller updates every two to four weeks, bigger features every two to three months, and social mechanics like trading, guilds, competition and leaderboards. That sequence also tells you what order to build things in. There is no point designing a 30-day endgame for a game that loses most players overnight.
What good looks like, and why benchmarks are slippery

Everyone wants a target number. Here is the honest answer: it depends heavily on genre, platform and where your players come from, and Roblox does not publish platform-wide averages. What we do have is solid data from mobile games. GameAnalytics, which collects data from thousands of games through its analytics tools, publishes yearly benchmarks. Its report on 2025 shows how brutal the curve is.

items.label: Median mobile game's day-7 retention in 2025
Day-7 retention needed to reach the top 10%
Day-7 retention typical of the top 1%

blocks.source: GameAnalytics, 2026 Mobile and PC Gaming Benchmarks (2025 data)

blocks.text: The same report puts the median mobile game's day-30 retention below 1%. Read that again: for a typical mobile game, fewer than one in a hundred new players is still around a month later. The gap between an average game and a great one is not a little better. At day 7, the top 1% keeps several times as many players as the median.

Do not copy these numbers as Roblox targets. Mobile players often arrive through paid ads, a very different crowd from players who click a thumbnail on Roblox's home page, and an obby, a tycoon and a social hangout naturally retain differently. Roblox's answer is to show each creator a benchmark band built from similar experiences in the same genre, running from the 50th to the 90th percentile, right in the analytics dashboard.

More recently it added the option to view retention by acquisition source, so you can separate players who came from recommendations from those who came from search or friends. The most useful comparison is usually not against anyone else, though. It is against your own last update.
How to read your own curve

Retention curves almost always fall steeply and then flatten. The shape of the fall tells you where the hole is. A cliff between day 0 and day 1 means the first session is not landing: players are confused, bored, or not reaching the fun fast enough. A decent day 1 followed by a collapse by day 7 means the core action is fun but there is nothing to work toward. A healthy day 7 that fades by day 30 means you need content, events or social reasons to stay.

blocks.title: Where the hole is, and what to fix

left.head: What the curve shows
items: Big drop before day 1
OK day 1, collapse by day 7
OK day 7, fade by day 30
Curve flattens at a stable level

right.head: Where to look first
items: First five minutes and tutorial
Goals, upgrades, progression pacing
Updates, events, social systems
You have a core audience: grow it

blocks.text: That last row is the one to hunt for. When a curve flattens, it means some group of players has decided your game is part of their routine. Investors in apps and games often treat a flattening curve as the first real sign of a product people want, because it shows that the leak stops somewhere. A small flattening at 5% is worth more than a huge spike that keeps falling to zero.

Two warnings help you read the data honestly. First, cohorts change for reasons that have nothing to do with your design. Roblox's guide notes that a dip after a big influx of new players is typical and temporary, because a crowd brought in by a viral moment is less committed than players who found you organically. Second, small games have small cohorts, and small numbers bounce around. Look at several days or a full week of cohorts before deciding an update worked or failed.

A third trap is traffic mix. If a big YouTuber sends you thousands of curious viewers, or a sponsored ad brings a wave of people who would never normally pick your genre, your overall retention can drop even though nothing about the game got worse. That is why Roblox's October 2025 analytics update, which lets creators split D1, D7 and D30 by acquisition source, is so useful: it lets you check whether a change came from the game or from the crowd.
Retention for a two-person team

This is where the Supercell lesson becomes practical. You do not need to kill your game the way Supercell does. You need to make decisions based on what players do, not on how the game feels to the people who built it. Builders are the worst possible playtesters: they know where everything is, they love the ideas, and they never get bored of the thing they made.

The funnel is where small teams get the most value. Roblox's retention guide recommends tracking how many players complete each step of the first-time experience and fixing the large drop-offs. For an obby or launcher game, that might be the share of new players who finish the first stage, buy their first upgrade, and reach the third stage. If half of all new players never make it past the first jump, no amount of late-game content will help. That one number tells you exactly where to spend your next free evening.

blocks.title: A simple retention routine
items: Before launch, decide which number matters most right now. Early on, it is almost always day 1.
Track the first-session funnel: how many players finish each tutorial step and reach the first upgrade.
Ship one focused fix per update, aimed at the biggest drop-off you can see.
Compare the cohorts that joined after the update with the ones before it, over a full week.
Only once day 1 is healthy, shift attention to day 7 progression, then to day 30 content.

blocks.text: It also helps to borrow one more habit from Supercell: decide in advance what result would make you change course. Before a launch or a big update, write down the day-1 number that would count as success, the number that would mean keep fixing, and the number that would mean the core idea itself is not working. Choose these against your genre benchmark band, not against mobile charts or a viral hit. When the data arrives, you will be reading it against a plan you made with a clear head instead of arguing about it with hope or frustration in the room. For two partners, this also prevents the most common fight in small studios: one person seeing a disaster and the other seeing a promising start in exactly the same chart.

Notice what is not on that list: monetization. It is tempting to add game passes and shops early, especially once you know how Roblox payouts work. But money comes from players who stay. A game with strong retention and weak monetization can be fixed with a shop. A game with strong early monetization and weak retention is *Hay Day Pop*, earning money from a bucket that is quietly draining.

The same thinking applies to a YouTube channel. Views on a video are like installs: they measure packaging and luck. Whether people watch to the end, and whether they come back for the next upload, measures whether the channel itself is any good. A creator obsessing over view counts while ignoring returning viewers is pouring water into a leaky bucket.
The honest review

Here is the reframe worth carrying. Retention is the most honest review your game will ever get. Players do not have to write a word. They simply come back, or they do not, and the number does not care how hard you worked, how cool the idea is or how much your friends liked the trailer.

That can sound harsh, but it is actually freeing. You no longer have to guess whether the game is good or argue about it with your partner late at night. You can ask the players, every single day, and they will answer with the most reliable signal there is: their time. The studios that win are not the ones with the best ideas. They are the ones who listen to that answer fastest.

takeaways: Installs measure your marketing; returning players measure your game.
On Roblox, weak retention costs you twice: you lose players and get fewer recommendations.
Day 1 tests the first session, day 7 tests progression, day 30 tests long-term content. Fix them in that order.
Benchmarks vary hugely by genre and traffic source; compare against similar games and your own last update.
Look for the curve to flatten. A small loyal core beats a big spike that drains away.

title: The Garden That Took Three Days
dek: One of the most-played games in history began as something a teenager threw together in a few days. The lesson is not luck. It is how fast you start learning.

blocks.text: On March 26, 2025, a 16-year-old Roblox developer going by BMWLux published a simple farming game. You planted seeds, waited, harvested, sold, bought better seeds. By the account of the studio that later joined the project, the original version took a few days to build. Nobody would have called it polished. A few weeks later it had around 500 people playing at once and somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 daily players: a solid little hit, nothing historic.

Then a studio called Splitting Point bought a share and did one thing relentlessly: it updated the game every week. Within about two weeks of their involvement, concurrent players hit roughly 100,000. Within about a month, a million. By late June, *Grow a Garden* had more than 21 million people playing at the same time, a figure the Associated Press reported as a record for any video game, beating the previous Fortnite high.

blocks.title: Grow a Garden peak concurrent players, 2025
blocks.note: Each record landed on an update or event day. The May 18 figure is approximate.
blocks.source: Wikipedia, Grow a Garden (compiling Roblox and press reports), 2026

blocks.text: It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this. The lesson is not that rushed games win. Thousands of quick Roblox games go nowhere, and you only hear about the ones that exploded, which is survivorship bias in its purest form. The real lesson is about *sequence*.

The game got in front of players first and got good second, in public, one weekly update at a time. Every record in the chart above was set on an update or event day. The team was not guessing what players wanted. It was shipping, watching and shipping again.

Weekly updates also do something subtler than add content. Each one is a reason for lapsed players to come back, a fresh event for YouTubers to cover, and a small experiment the team can read in the next day's numbers. A game that updates every week gets fifty chances a year to learn what works. A game that waits for one big launch gets one. Even if the weekly team is only slightly smarter per decision, it gets to make so many more decisions that it pulls away.
You are worse at predicting players than you think

Why does shipping early beat polishing in private? Because almost nobody can predict what users will like, including professionals with enormous amounts of data. Ronny Kohavi, who ran Microsoft's experimentation platform, published a striking number in 2009. When Microsoft tested ideas in controlled experiments, ideas that someone had thought were worth building, only about a third improved the metric they were designed to improve. The rest did nothing or made things worse.

items.label: Microsoft ideas that improved the key metric they targeted when tested
Tested ideas that had no effect or hurt the metric

blocks.source: Kohavi et al., Online Experimentation at Microsoft, 2009

blocks.text: The same paper collects similar admissions from elsewhere: a Netflix figure that most of what the company tries turns out to be wrong, a lender's analyst who could guess test outcomes only about a third of the time. These are teams whose entire job is understanding users. If they are wrong two times out of three, two brothers designing a game at a kitchen table are not going to do better by thinking harder.

Once you accept that, the math of shipping changes. Every week you spend polishing an unreleased feature is a week spent betting on a guess that is probably wrong. Shipping early does not make your guesses better. It makes them *cheaper*, because you find out which ones are wrong before you have stacked a month of work on top of them.
Why builders hide their work
If shipping early is so clearly better, why does almost everyone delay? Mostly because of how it feels. Unreleased work is safe. As long as nobody has played your game, it might still be brilliant.
The moment it goes public, it becomes a specific thing with specific flaws, and some stranger can tell you it is bad. Polishing in private is often not perfectionism. It is protection.

Two facts make that protection less necessary than it feels. First, research on the spotlight effect suggests people notice our flaws far less than we expect; most players who bounce off an early version will not remember it existed.

Second, on a platform like Roblox, a game is not a fixed object. You can change it tonight. The first version of a live game is less like a final exam and more like the first draft of an essay that the whole class helps you edit. The risk of looking rough for a few weeks is small. The risk of spending a year building the wrong thing is large.

The same logic applies to a YouTube channel. Your first ten videos are your version 1. They will be worse than your fiftieth, and that is exactly why they need to exist: each upload teaches you something about hooks, pacing and thumbnails that no amount of planning can. Creators who wait until they feel ready often never upload at all.
Embarrassing is not the same as broken

LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman has a famous line, roughly: if the first version of your product does not embarrass you, you launched too late. It is good advice that is easy to misread. Embarrassing means *small*: placeholder art, one map, three upgrades, no trading system yet. It does not mean *broken*: crashes, a confusing first minute, a core loop that is not actually fun.

Roblox's own documentation draws the line clearly, even if it does not use those words. Its retention guide says the core loop and first-time experience drive whether players return the next day, and suggests getting players to the fun ideally in five minutes or less. Its discovery guide lists first-play bounce, players leaving within the first 60 seconds or within one to three minutes, among the most important signals its recommendation system watches. Rough edges are forgivable. A boring or confusing first minute is not.

blocks.title: What version 1 can and cannot get away with

left.head: Embarrassing: ship it
items: Placeholder or simple art
One map or one world
A handful of upgrades
No trading, guilds or events yet
A plain thumbnail you will redo

right.head: Broken: fix it first
items: Crashes or bad lag
Players unsure what to do
Core loop that is not fun yet
Progress that does not save
No reward in the first minutes

blocks.text: For a launcher-style obby, that might mean one world, one strong jump that feels great, a clear upgrade path for the first ten minutes, and nothing else. If the jump is fun and the first upgrade feels rewarding, players will forgive everything missing. If the jump feels floaty, no amount of extra worlds will save it, and you want to discover that in week three, not month eight.
Many cheap versions beat one perfect one

A small Stanford study adds an interesting twist on why iteration works. In 2010, Steven Dow and colleagues had 33 novice designers create web banner ads. Everyone made five drafts and got expert-style feedback, but one group made drafts in parallel, three at once and then two more, while the other group worked on one draft at a time. The final ads ran as a real campaign on a social network, so the researchers could measure what actual people clicked on.

blocks.title: Clicks per million ad views
blocks.note: Small study (33 novice designers). Parallel ads also got higher expert ratings.
blocks.source: Dow et al., ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 2010

blocks.text: The parallel group's ads got more clicks, higher expert ratings and longer visits from the people who clicked. The parallel designers also gained more confidence in their own design ability. It is one small study, so treat it as a clue rather than a law. But it points the same direction as everything else here: you learn more by putting several rough options in front of reality than by perfecting one in your head. For a game, that can be as simple as building two versions of the starting area and watching which one keeps playtesters around longer.

Notice that both groups in the study iterated five times before finishing. Neither group had the option of one perfect attempt, and that is the deeper point. The quality came from the loop of making, getting feedback and making again. A team that runs that loop ten times in the time another team runs it twice will usually win, even if the second team is more talented.
How Roblox actually tests your game

Shipping early matters even more on a platform that is itself running experiments on you. Roblox describes its Recommended for You system as a cycle of exploring and expanding. It shows a game to a small group of users who might like it. If that group engages, comes back and spends, it shows the game to more people like them. If they bounce, the expansion stalls.

blocks.title: The explore-and-expand loop
items: Roblox shows your game to a small group
Players engage, return or bounce
Signals are measured per player
Good signals: shown to more similar players
You update, and the loop runs again

blocks.text: One detail in the documentation is worth noticing. Roblox says the ranking signals are measured on players who arrived through the recommendation feed, averaged per player. In other words, the algorithm forms its opinion from strangers. That gives you a strong reason to put your game in front of strangers you can actually watch, such as a few people in a Discord or a playtest with friends of friends, before the algorithm's strangers arrive. Watching five real people play for ten minutes will tell you more than another month of building alone.

A few unglamorous details also matter from day one. Roblox's documentation says a game needs a custom thumbnail to receive impressions from homepage recommendations, and warns that misleading titles or images that do not match the game can reduce exposure. So version 1 can be small, but its front door has to be honest and present. A rough game with a clear, accurate thumbnail gets tested. A rough game with no thumbnail may barely get seen.

Once the game is live, resist the urge to treat the first week's numbers as a verdict. Early groups of players are small, so the numbers jump around, and a single YouTuber visit or a weekend can swing them. Read them as directions, not grades.

The questions that matter early are simple: do new players get through the first five minutes, where exactly do they quit, and does anyone come back the next day? Those three answers tell you what to fix in the next update. Shipping early is not a license to abandon a game the first time the chart dips. It is a way to find out which part of the game to fix while the fixing is still cheap.
A shipping rhythm for a part-time team
Speed for a part-time team does not mean working faster. It means shortening the time between an idea and finding out whether it worked. Here is a rhythm that fits a few hours a week.

blocks.title: From idea to evidence, on repeat
items: Build version 0 in a few weekends: one core loop and a first five minutes that feels good.
Watch at least five people who are not you play it. Say nothing and take notes on where they get stuck.
Fix the biggest confusion, then publish. Do not wait for the features list to be complete.
Before each update, write down what you expect it to change, in one sentence.
Ship on a fixed rhythm. Roblox suggests smaller updates every two to four weeks.
Compare the result to your prediction, keep what worked, and cut what did not.

blocks.text: The written prediction is the step people skip, and it is the one that turns shipping into learning. Without it, every update feels like it went fine. With it, you start to notice how often your guesses miss, which is exactly the humility Kohavi's numbers suggest you need. If one partner is going to be unreachable for weeks, build updates in batches ahead of time so the other can release them on schedule. A rhythm that keeps running while you are away is worth more than a burst of work followed by silence.

There is a real cost to all this. Shipping early means strangers will see your worst work. Some will leave bad comments. A few will be right. That sting is the price of information, and it is far cheaper than the alternative: discovering after a year of private work that the thing you loved does not hold anyone's attention.
Shipping is where building starts

Most people treat release as the end of making a game. The *Grow a Garden* story suggests the opposite. The version that a teenager built in a few days was the beginning, the first question asked out loud. The game that broke records was the answer to hundreds of questions asked one update at a time.
That is the reframe worth keeping. Version 1 is not your best shot at success. It is your first chance to stop guessing. The embarrassment fades fast, and the learning compounds.
The builders who win are rarely the ones with the best first draft. They are the ones who got to their tenth draft while everyone else was still polishing their first.

takeaways: Ship small, not broken: rough art is forgivable, a confusing first minute is not.
Even expert teams find that most of their ideas fail when tested, so make guesses cheap.
Watch real strangers play before the algorithm's strangers judge your game.
Write a one-sentence prediction before every update and check it afterward.
Release is not the finish line; it is the first time you stop guessing.

title: How Adults Actually Get Good at New Things
dek: Kids are not better learners at almost everything. Adults have different strengths and different traps, and knowing them can save months when you learn to code, build a game or pick up a trade.

blocks.text: In 2018 Joshua Hartshorne, Joshua Tenenbaum and Steven Pinker published a study built on an online grammar quiz that went viral. Almost 670,000 people took it, native and non-native English speakers who had started learning at every age from birth to adulthood. With that much data, the researchers could finally separate how old someone was when they started from how long they had been learning.

Their answer was a sharp deadline. The ability to learn the grammar of a new language to a native-like level stayed strong until about 17.4 years old, then declined steadily. People who started later could still become very good, but rarely indistinguishable from native speakers. Headlines turned it into a gloomy message: after your teens, the window closes.

items.label: English speakers in the grammar-learning dataset
Age when grammar-learning ability began to decline

blocks.source: Hartshorne, Tenenbaum & Pinker, Cognition, 2018

blocks.text: But that finding is about one very specific thing: absorbing the grammar of a language well enough to pass as native. Nobody has found a comparable deadline for learning to program, wire a panel, design a game level or run a reactor plant. Those skills are built mostly on knowledge and practice, and knowledge is something adults keep accumulating for decades.
Different abilities peak at different ages

A 2015 study by Hartshorne and Laura Germine, using data from 48,537 people tested online plus standard IQ and memory test norms, found that there is no single peak age for the mind. Some abilities, like raw processing speed, peak around the end of high school and then slowly decline. Others, including some kinds of memory, hold steady into the 30s. Still others, like vocabulary, keep rising into the 40s and beyond.

At 20 you are close to the top on speed and memory and still climbing on knowledge. Adults of any age also bring things children lack: the ability to plan their own learning, to notice when they are confused, to connect new material to a big store of existing knowledge, and to choose goals that matter to them. Those are not small advantages. They are, in large part, what learning is made of.

That does not mean age is irrelevant. If your goal is to speak a new language with fully native-like grammar, starting young helps a great deal, and the 2018 data show it. Raw speed does slowly decline, which matters in a few fields like competitive gaming at the very top. But for most technical skills, the kind that pay a salary or build a business, starting at 20, 30 or 40 mostly means starting with more background knowledge to hang new learning on, not less ability to learn it.

The adult disadvantages are mostly practical and emotional, not biological. Less free time. Jobs and watch bills that eat focus. And a stronger fear of looking bad, which leads many adults to avoid exactly the struggle that learning requires, or to retreat into activities that feel like progress without being progress.

The most common version of that retreat, for people learning to code, has a name among programmers: tutorial hell. You watch a tutorial, type along, and the thing works. It feels like learning. Then you open a blank file to build something of your own and realize you cannot start. Following along kept the instructor's working memory in charge of every decision, so yours never had to make one. The fix is uncomfortable but simple: spend far less time following and far more time building, even badly.
The shape of a learning curve

Any skill you practice tends to follow the same basic curve: fast improvement at first, then slower and slower gains. For decades psychologists described this as a power law of practice. In 2000 Andrew Heathcote, Scott Brown and Douglas Mewhort reanalyzed 7,910 individual learning series from 475 people and found something subtle. For individuals, improvement was better described by an exponential curve; the familiar power-law shape mostly appeared when many people's data were averaged together.

The technical detail matters less than the practical one. Early gains come quickly because there is so much low-hanging fruit: basic syntax, the main controls, the layout of a system. Then progress flattens, and it is easy to read the flattening as hitting your limit. Usually it means the easy gains are used up and the practice has to change, with harder problems, new feedback, a focus on specific weaknesses, before the next round of improvement.

Because plateaus are partly an illusion of attention, it helps to look back rather than only forward. Every few weeks, write one line about something you can do now that you could not do before: a script you wrote without help, a system you can now draw cold. Progress in the middle of a curve is slow enough to be invisible day to day and obvious over a month.

blocks.title: The three classic stages of skill learning
items: Cognitive: you think through every step and make lots of errors. Explanations and examples matter most here.
Associative: steps start linking together. Errors drop, and practice with fast feedback matters most.
Autonomous: the skill runs with little conscious effort, freeing your mind for strategy and new problems.

blocks.text: That three-stage model goes back to Paul Fitts and Michael Posner in the 1960s, and it holds up well as a rough map. Learning to write code in a new language, troubleshoot a circuit or move fluidly in a game all start with slow, effortful, error-filled thinking and end, if you keep at it, with something closer to instinct. Knowing which stage you are in tells you what kind of help to look for.
Practice the real thing

One of the most consistent findings in learning research is that skills transfer much less than people hope. In a 2023 review, Fernand Gobet and Giovanni Sala looked at meta-analyses of brain-training games, chess instruction, music lessons and working memory training, all of which had been promoted as ways to sharpen general thinking. Their conclusion was blunt: the overall effect on unrelated abilities was essentially zero. People get better at what they practice, and not much else.

Near transfer, between closely related skills, is real. A second programming language is much easier than the first because loops, variables and functions carry over. Troubleshooting one electrical system teaches habits that help on the next. But no general mental exercise will make you better at Luau except writing Luau, and no amount of puzzle apps will substitute for drawing a system from memory.

Realistic conditions matter too. A watchstander has to respond correctly while tired, interrupted and under time pressure, not while fresh and sitting with a book. A programmer has to debug code they did not write. A tradesperson has to work in awkward spaces with the wrong lighting. The closer your practice gets to those conditions, the less the skill falls apart when it counts.
The fastest route to a skill is to practice the skill itself, in conditions as close to the real thing as you can manage, as early as you can manage. Everything else is warm-up.
Struggle first or learn first?

There is a genuine debate about whether beginners should be shown how to do something first or should wrestle with a problem before being taught. Cognitive load research shows that complete beginners learn more from studying worked examples than from flailing at problems on their own. On the other hand, a 2021 meta-analysis by Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur of 53 studies found that having students attempt a problem *before* instruction produced better learning than instruction first, with a moderate effect size of 0.36, larger when the struggle phase was carefully designed. Notably, the advantage reversed for young children and for general skills.

items.label: Benefit of trying a problem before instruction, across 53 studies
When the struggle phase was carefully designed

blocks.source: Sinha & Kapur, Review of Educational Research, 2021

blocks.text: Part of the difference also comes down to who is doing the designing. In the productive failure studies, a teacher chose problems that were hard but approachable and then followed up with a clear explanation that built on the students' attempts. When you are teaching yourself, nobody is doing that for you. Struggle without a planned follow-up is just being stuck.

These findings fit together better than they first appear. A short, focused attempt at a problem shows you what you do not know and makes the explanation that follows land harder. Hours of unguided flailing, by contrast, mostly produce frustration. A good pattern for an adult learner is a brief honest attempt, then a clear worked example or explanation, then practice on your own.
Feedback that helps, and feedback that hurts

Feedback is the engine of skill learning, but it is not automatically good. In 1996 Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi analyzed 607 effect sizes from studies of feedback interventions covering more than 23,000 observations. On average, feedback improved performance by a moderate amount. But in more than a third of cases, it made performance *worse*.

items.label: Average effect of feedback on performance
Feedback interventions that lowered performance

blocks.source: Kluger & DeNisi, Psychological Bulletin, 1996

blocks.text: Their explanation was that feedback works when it keeps your attention on the task, what to change and how, and backfires when it pulls attention toward yourself, your worth, your status, how you compare. A comment like "your loop runs one time too many because of the condition on line 12" helps. A comment like "you are not really a coder" does not, and neither does the voice in your own head saying it. The best feedback sources for a self-taught adult are impersonal and fast: code that runs or crashes, a test you pass or fail, a playtester who gets stuck at the same spot every time.

When you do ask people for feedback, ask narrow questions. "Is this good?" invites vague reassurance or vague criticism. "Is there a simpler way to handle this event?" or "What would you check first in this casualty?" gets an answer you can act on. Experienced people are usually generous with specific questions, because they are easy to answer and show you have already done the work.
A plan for learning something new
Put it together, and a practical approach for learning to code, build games or pick up a trade looks something like this.

blocks.title: Learning a skill as an adult
items: Pick a small, concrete project that requires the skill, like one working mechanic in a game.
Try it briefly on your own to find out what you do not know.
Study a worked example of something similar and explain each step to yourself.
Rebuild it from memory, then change one thing at a time.
Get fast, impersonal feedback from errors, tests and playtesters.
When progress stalls, change the practice: a harder problem, a new weakness, a different feedback source.

blocks.text: Applied to a Roblox game, that might mean choosing one feature, say a checkpoint system, rather than following a long tutorial series. Try to build it, get stuck, look at how someone else did it, rebuild it without looking, then extend it. For a trade, it means getting your hands on real equipment as early as possible and asking experienced people to watch you work, rather than reading about it for months. For quals, it means walking spaces and talking through systems out loud, not just reading the books.

Two more things multiply everything above. Spread your practice out: several short sessions across a week beat one long one for almost any skill, and a night of sleep between sessions helps lock in what you practiced. And keep the project small enough to finish. A finished small game teaches more than an abandoned big one, because the last ten percent, the bugs, the polish, the edge cases, is where much of the real skill lives.

The adults who stall are rarely the ones who lack ability. They are the ones who spend months in comfortable, passive learning, watching videos, copying code, rereading notes, because it feels safe, and who quit at the first plateau because they read it as a verdict. The research says something more encouraging: the curve flattens for everyone, the window for most skills never closes, and the biggest advantage an adult has is the ability to notice what is not working and change it.

takeaways: The famous age-17 deadline is about native-like grammar, not about coding, game design or technical trades.
Different abilities peak at different ages; knowledge keeps growing for decades.
Plateaus are normal. They usually mean the practice needs to change, not that you have hit your limit.
Skills transfer narrowly: practice the actual thing, early and in realistic conditions.
Seek fast, impersonal feedback about the task, and ignore feedback about whether you are "a natural".
