title: The Brain Myths Smart People Believe
dek: Learning styles, the unused 90 percent, left-brained versus right-brained: why these ideas feel true, what the evidence says, and what they cost you.

blocks.text: Quick quiz. True or false: people learn better when information is presented in their preferred learning style, such as visual, auditory or hands-on. True or false: we use only about 10 percent of our brains. True or false: some people are left-brained and logical while others are right-brained and creative.

If you answered true to any of them, you have a lot of company. In a 2017 survey led by Kelly Macdonald of more than 3,000 members of the public, 93 percent agreed with the learning-styles statement. So did 76 percent of educators and, remarkably, 78 percent of people with substantial training in neuroscience. All three statements are false, or at least false in the way most people mean them.

These are called neuromyths: beliefs about the brain that sound scientific, spread through classrooms and corporate training, and do not survive contact with the evidence. They are worth understanding for a practical reason. Each one quietly shapes how people decide to study, and each one points in the wrong direction.

blocks.title: Share of the public endorsing common neuromyths
blocks.note: Survey of 3,045 adults. Endorsement was lower but still common among educators and people with neuroscience training.
blocks.source: Macdonald et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2017

blocks.text: Why smart people fall for them

You might assume that the more someone knows about the brain, the less likely they are to believe nonsense about it. A 2012 study by Sanne Dekker and colleagues found the opposite. They surveyed 242 teachers in the UK and the Netherlands, all interested in applying brain science to education. On average the teachers believed about half of the neuromyths presented to them. And teachers with more general knowledge about the brain were more likely, not less, to endorse the myths.

That sounds absurd until you think about how these ideas travel. Neuromyths almost always start from a real finding, get simplified, and then get packaged for people who are interested in the brain. The more of that material you consume, the more myths you absorb along with the facts. Interest without a filter is a delivery system.

items.label: Share of neuromyth statements the average teacher believed
Teachers surveyed in the UK and the Netherlands

blocks.source: Dekker et al., Frontiers in Psychology, 2012

blocks.text: Myths also stick because they flatter us and simplify life. You have hidden potential locked away in the unused 90 percent. Your struggles in school were not about effort or method, just a mismatch with your style. You are a creative right-brain type, so of course spreadsheets bore you. Each myth offers a story that feels both scientific and personal, and that combination is hard to resist.
Myth one: learning styles

This is the biggest and most consequential of the three. The idea is that each person has a dominant mode of learning, often split into visual, auditory, reading and kinesthetic, and that teaching matched to that mode produces better learning. Questionnaires to diagnose your style are everywhere, and many people can tell you theirs.

In 2008, four prominent learning researchers, Harold Pashler, Mark McDaniel, Doug Rohrer and Robert Bjork, reviewed the evidence. They pointed out what a real test would require: sort people by style, randomly assign each group to different teaching methods, and give everyone the same final test. If the idea were right, visual learners would do best with visual teaching and auditory learners with auditory teaching, a crossover pattern. They found virtually no studies showing that pattern, and several well-designed ones that contradicted it.

The authors were careful about what they did and did not claim. People do have real preferences about how information is presented, and people do differ in specific abilities. What lacks support is the step from preference to payoff: tailoring instruction to someone's preferred style does not appear to make them learn more.

Real-world studies point the same way. In a study of undergraduate anatomy students by Polly Husmann and Valerie O'Loughlin, students took a popular learning-styles questionnaire and later reported how they actually studied. About two-thirds did not even study in line with their supposed style, and those who did got no better grades for it. What predicted grades was what they did, such as practicing with the microscope and reviewing lecture notes, regardless of their label.

Why does the myth survive so well? Partly because the questionnaires feel accurate. Your preferences are real and fairly stable, so when a quiz tells you that you like diagrams, it rings true. The leap that goes untested is from liking a format to learning more from it. Liking and learning are different things, and as the research on desirable difficulties shows, the methods that produce the most learning often feel the least pleasant while you are doing them.
The kernel of truth is that the best format depends on the content, not the person. A circuit is best learned from a diagram. A language's sounds are best learned by listening.

A valve lineup is best learned with your hands on the valves, or as close as you can get. Everyone benefits from the mode that fits the material, and from combining words with pictures. Calling yourself a hands-on learner and skipping the theory is not honoring your style; it is just skipping the theory.
Match the format to the material, not to yourself. Diagrams for systems, sound for sounds, hands for skills, and self-testing for everything.
Myth two: the unused 90 percent
The idea that we use only 10 percent of our brains has been a staple of movies and motivational speeches for a century, and its origins are murky. It falls apart on contact with basic biology.

items.label: Share of body weight that is brain
Share of the body's oxygen, and so its calories, the brain consumes

blocks.source: Raichle & Gusnard, PNAS, 2002

blocks.text: The brain is metabolically expensive. It makes up about 2 percent of body weight but burns about a fifth of the body's oxygen and energy, even at rest. Evolution does not maintain expensive tissue that does nothing; an organ that was 90 percent idle would have been under heavy pressure to shrink. Brain imaging shows activity across the entire brain over the course of a day, though not all regions are maximally active at once, which is a good thing. And damage to virtually any area of the brain produces some effect, which would not happen if most of it were spare.

The kernel of truth here is about potential, not anatomy. You can get dramatically better at things through practice, and the brain does change as you learn. But that improvement comes from strengthening and reorganizing circuits you already use, not from unlocking a dormant 90 percent. There is no hidden reserve to tap with a pill or a trick, only the slower route of practice.

If you want a picture of what is actually going on when you get better at something hard, imagine traffic engineers improving a road network rather than a building with locked rooms. Useful routes get widened, rarely used ones fade, and new connections form where traffic demands them. Every part of the network is already in use. Learning changes how well it is organized.
Myth three: left-brained and right-brained

This one has the most respectable origin. Roger Sperry and his colleagues studied patients whose corpus callosum, the thick bundle connecting the two hemispheres, had been surgically cut to control severe epilepsy. With the halves disconnected, the researchers could test each side separately. The left hemisphere handled speech, writing and calculation; the right excelled at spatial tasks such as drawing three-dimensional shapes and recognizing melodies. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the work.

Specialization is real. What does not follow is that people in general are dominated by one hemisphere and that this shapes their personality. In a 2013 study, a University of Utah team including Jared Nielsen and Jeff Anderson analyzed resting brain scans from 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, looking at about 7,000 brain regions.

Specific functions did tend to sit more on one side. But individuals did not show a whole-brain bias toward a stronger left or right network. Lateralization was a connection-by-connection property, not a personality trait.

In any intact brain, the hemispheres are constantly exchanging information. Doing math involves both sides. So does creativity. Calling yourself a right-brain creative who just cannot do numbers is not neuroscience. It is a horoscope with better branding.

Two more myths from that survey chart deserve a line each. The Mozart effect began with a 1993 report in *Nature* that listening to a Mozart sonata briefly improved performance on a spatial reasoning task. It became a craze, with music marketed to make babies smarter.

A 2010 meta-analysis from the University of Vienna, pooling 39 studies with more than 3,000 participants, found no music-specific benefit for spatial ability. As for sugar, a 1995 meta-analysis in *JAMA* of 23 controlled studies concluded that sugar does not meaningfully affect children's behavior or thinking, though it could not rule out a small effect in some children. Expectations, it seems, do much of the work.

Notice the pattern across all five myths. Each began with something real: a genuine preference, an actual split-brain finding, a single lab result, a parent's honest observation. Each was then stretched far beyond what the evidence could carry. That stretch, from a narrow finding to a sweeping claim about people, is the signature of a neuromyth.

blocks.title: Myth vs what the evidence supports

left.head: The myth
items: Teach to your learning style
Most of your brain sits unused
You are left-brained or right-brained
Your type limits what you can learn

right.head: The evidence
items: Match the format to the material
The whole brain is active and costly
Specific functions lean to one side; people do not
Methods and practice predict learning

blocks.text: What the myths cost you

Neuromyths would be harmless trivia if they did not change behavior. The trouble is that each one gives you a reason to study in a way that feels comfortable instead of a way that works. If you believe you are a visual learner, you might watch more videos instead of testing yourself. If you believe you are right-brained, you might write off math and electrical theory as something your brain is not built for. If you believe in a hidden 90 percent, you might hunt for hacks instead of putting in repetitions.

All three myths share a structure: they move the explanation for how well you learn from what you do to what you are. That is comforting, because it takes away responsibility, and it is corrosive, because it takes away control. The research on learning points firmly the other way. The strongest predictors of how much you will remember are methods that anyone can use: spacing study over time, testing yourself instead of rereading, mixing up problem types, and processing material for meaning.

There is also a hidden cost in time. Learning-styles questionnaires, brain-training apps and right-brain workshops all consume hours that could have gone into methods with decades of evidence behind them. On a deployment, where free time is scarce and comes in fragments, spending it on the wrong method is an expensive mistake. An hour of self-quizzing beats an hour of anything built on a myth.

And labels have a way of becoming self-fulfilling. If you decide you are not a math person, you practice math less, avoid the hard problems and quit sooner when stuck, and then the lack of skill seems to confirm the label. The myth did not describe you. It trained you.

That is good news for anyone who struggled in school and assumed they were just not built for it. Nuclear training proves the point every year: people who never thought of themselves as math types learn reactor theory, because the method and the repetitions do the heavy lifting, not some fixed type.
How to spot the next one
New neuromyths are produced constantly, often by people selling something: brain-training apps, learning programs, supplements. A few questions filter out most of them.

blocks.title: A quick neuromyth filter
items: Does it sort people into neat types, like left vs right or visual vs auditory? Be suspicious.
Does it promise hidden capacity or a shortcut that skips practice? Be very suspicious.
Is there a controlled experiment behind it, or only a brain scan and a story?
Is someone selling a product, course or questionnaire built on the claim?
Is the real finding narrower than the claim, as with hemisphere specialization?

blocks.text: None of this means brain science has nothing to offer learners. It has a lot, and the most useful parts are less glamorous than the myths: forgetting is predictable, effortful recall strengthens memory, sleep consolidates it, and practice changes the brain physically. Those findings will not tell you what type of person you are. They will tell you what to do tomorrow, and that turns out to be more valuable.

takeaways: Learning styles have virtually no experimental support; match the format to the material instead.
The brain is about 2 percent of body weight and uses about 20 percent of its energy; none of it is idle.
Hemispheres specialize in functions, but people are not left-brained or right-brained.
Myths that explain learning by type rather than method quietly remove your control over it.
Be wary of any brain claim that sorts people into types or sells a shortcut.

title: The 10,000-Hour Rule Was Never a Rule
dek: The most famous number in self-improvement came from a small study of violinists. When researchers finally repeated it, the story got more honest, and more useful.

blocks.text: In the early 1990s, three psychologists went to a music academy in Berlin and asked its professors to name their most promising violin students, the ones headed for careers as international soloists. They also recruited good violinists from the same academy and a third group from a program training future music teachers. Then they asked every student to estimate, year by year, how many hours a week they had practiced alone since they first picked up the instrument.

Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer added those estimates up. By age 18, the best violinists had accumulated about 7,400 hours of solitary practice on average. The good violinists had about 5,300. The future teachers had about 3,400. The ranking of skill matched the ranking of hours almost perfectly. Their 1993 paper argued that differences between performers, even at the top, are largely explained by how much of a special kind of practice they had done.

Fifteen years later Malcolm Gladwell's book *Outliers* turned that research into the 10,000-hour rule: put in roughly ten thousand hours and you can become world class at almost anything. It may be the most quoted number in self-improvement. It is also, according to the researchers who have tested it since, a badly misleading summary of the evidence.

It is easy to see why the idea spread. It is democratic: talent is overrated, effort wins. It is measurable: you can count hours. And it gives a clear target for anyone who wants to get good at something. If the gap between you and a professional is just a number of hours, then the only thing standing in your way is discipline. That is a motivating story. The question is whether it is a true one.
What deliberate practice actually means

Ericsson was careful to say that hours alone were not the point, and he spent years objecting to the popular version. His concept, *deliberate practice*, was narrower than just doing a thing a lot. It meant practice designed to improve a specific weakness, usually with a teacher setting the tasks, with a clear goal for each session, immediate feedback, and enough difficulty that it requires full concentration. He argued it is not inherently enjoyable, which is why most people avoid it.

blocks.title: Hours logged versus deliberate practice

left.head: Just playing more
items: Repeat what you are already good at
Effort goes where it feels fun
Feedback is vague or missing
Can run on autopilot

right.head: Deliberate practice
items: Target a specific weakness
Tasks set by a coach or a plan
Feedback right away, every rep
Needs full concentration, so sessions are short

blocks.text: Ericsson later framed the goal of this kind of practice as building better *mental representations*: detailed internal models of what good performance looks like, which let an expert notice errors and plan responses that a beginner cannot even see. A strong musician hears a slightly flat note that a novice misses. A strong programmer looks at a function and senses where the bug probably is. Practice that sharpens those models is the kind that pays off.

That difference is real and useful, and it is why playing ranked matches for a thousand hours can leave someone stuck at the same rank while a player who spends a fraction of the time drilling a specific mechanic climbs. The hours that count are the ones spent working at the edge of your ability with a way to tell whether each attempt was better or worse.
The scientific question, though, is the strong claim: does accumulated deliberate practice explain *most* of the difference between people? That is testable, and it has been tested.
What the meta-analysis found

In 2014 Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick and Frederick Oswald pulled together the studies they could find that measured both practice and performance in the same people, across music, games, sports, education and professions. They asked how much of the variation in performance between people could be statistically accounted for by how much they had practiced.

blocks.title: Share of performance differences explained by practice
blocks.note: For professions, practice explained less than 1 percent.
blocks.source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald, Psychological Science, 2014

blocks.text: A quick word on what "explained 26 percent of the variance" means, because it is easy to misread. Imagine lining up a few hundred chess players from weakest to strongest. If you only knew how many hours each had practiced and used that to predict their ratings, you would capture about a quarter of the spread between them. The rest of the spread would come from other things. It does not mean practice is responsible for 26 percent of any single player's skill; it is a statement about differences across a group.

Practice mattered everywhere. In games like chess it explained about a quarter of the differences between players, which is a lot by the standards of psychology. But that leaves three quarters explained by something else. And the share dropped sharply in education and in professional work, where tasks are less well-defined and feedback is slower and fuzzier.

Why would practice matter more in chess and violin than at work? One likely reason is the structure of the activity itself. In games and music, the task is well defined, the same situations repeat, and feedback is quick: you lose the game, you hear the wrong note. In most jobs, situations vary, the right answer is often unclear, and you might not find out whether a decision was good for months. Practice turns into skill most efficiently when the environment tells you clearly and quickly whether you got it right.

A follow-up focused on sports, published in 2016, found deliberate practice explained 18 percent of the variation overall but only about 1 percent among elite athletes. Once everyone in the group was practicing enormous amounts, more hours no longer separated the best from the rest. The same study found that higher-level athletes had not started their sport earlier in childhood than lower-level ones. Later work by Michael Barth, Arne Güllich and colleagues found that adult world-class athletes had typically done *more* multi-sport practice as kids and *less* practice in their main sport than national-level peers, with slower early progress. The kids who dominate at 14 are often not the adults who dominate at 25.
The replication

The violin study itself had never been directly repeated until Macnamara and Megha Maitra did it, publishing in 2019. They tried to follow the original method closely but added safeguards, including a double-blind procedure so the interviewers did not know which skill group each violinist belonged to. That mattered, because an interviewer who expects the best players to report more practice can nudge estimates without meaning to.

blocks.title: Practice alone by age 18: original vs replication
blocks.note: Group averages from retrospective estimates; the 2019 best and good groups did not differ significantly.
blocks.source: Ericsson et al., Psychological Review, 1993; Macnamara & Maitra, Royal Society Open Science, 2019

blocks.text: The headline result did not replicate. The less accomplished violinists had practiced less, as expected. But the best violinists had *not* practiced more than the good ones; on average they reported somewhat less, and most of the best had practiced less than the average good violinist. Practice explained about 26 percent of the differences in performance, close to the meta-analytic average for music, rather than the 48 percent in the original. By age 20, both top groups averaged more than 10,000 hours, which shows that the hours were real but did not decide who ended up on top.

Ericsson, who died in 2020, disputed these critiques. He argued that the meta-analyses counted many kinds of activity, like group sessions and casual play, that did not meet his definition, so of course they found weaker relationships. Hambrick, Macnamara and Oswald replied that the definition itself had shifted over the years, making the theory hard to test at all. That argument is still not fully settled. What both sides agree on is that the right kind of practice matters a great deal. The disagreement is over whether it is nearly everything or one big factor among several.
What else is in the other 74 percent

If practice explains a quarter of the differences in a domain like games or music, the rest comes from a mix of things, and researchers argue about the proportions. Prior knowledge from related skills matters. So do basic abilities like working memory capacity and processing speed, which partly reflect genes. Starting age matters in some domains and not others. Personality and interest shape how long people stick with something. Quality of coaching, access to good feedback, and plain luck in opportunities all play parts.

There is also a measurement problem that cuts both ways. Almost all of these studies rely on people estimating how much they practiced years ago, sometimes back to early childhood. Those estimates are noisy, and noise pulls correlations toward zero, so practice might matter somewhat more than the numbers show. On the other hand, better players may simply remember or report their practice more generously. Neither side can fully escape that limitation until more studies track practice as it happens.

None of that should be read as fate. Variance explained is a statement about differences between people in a group, not about how much any one person can improve. Even the less skilled violinists in the 2019 study were accomplished players who had put in thousands of hours to get there, and none of them would have reached that level without it. What the research rules out is the promise that a fixed number of hours guarantees an elite result, and the implication that anyone who did not get there must not have tried hard enough.

This has a hopeful side if you are starting something late. One of the original paper's boldest claims was that someone with less accumulated practice at a given age could never catch up with those who started earlier and kept going. The replication found the best violinists were not simply the ones with the biggest head start in hours, and the sports research found that elite adults often specialized later than their peers. Starting to code at 20, or picking up a trade at 30, is not a disqualification. Hours matter, but they are not a race you lost at age eight.

Practice cannot promise you'll be the best. It reliably makes you much better than you were. For almost every real goal, a job, a qualification, a game that people enjoy, the second one is what you actually need.
How to practice like it matters

Strip away the 10,000-hour myth and the core of Ericsson's insight still stands up well: practice works best when it is targeted, hard, and wrapped in fast feedback. That is directly usable whether you are working through a qualification card, learning to script in Luau, or grinding aim in an FPS.

blocks.title: Turning hours into improvement
items: Name one specific weakness per session, not just the general skill.
Design a drill that isolates it: one system, one mechanic, one type of bug.
Get feedback fast: a qualified watchstander checking you, a test that runs, a replay you actually review.
Work at the edge where you fail about as often as you succeed.
Keep sessions short and focused; full concentration does not last for hours.
Track whether the weakness shrinks, and pick the next one when it does.

blocks.text: For submarine quals, that might mean asking the person signing your card to quiz you specifically on the parts of a system you hesitate on, not walking through the parts you already know. For coding, it means building small features that stretch you slightly, then reading the error messages and fixing them yourself rather than copying finished scripts. For aim, it means drilling the one situation you keep losing, then checking replays, rather than queuing another fifty matches on autopilot.

Deliberate practice also stacks with the other tools that make learning stick. Spreading sessions out over days, testing yourself instead of rereading, and mixing problem types all apply here too. A good week of practice on a new skill might be four short, hard sessions, each aimed at one weakness, each ending with a check of whether you can do the thing cold, rather than one marathon on a day off.

And it means setting expectations honestly. You will not know at the start where your ceiling is, and nobody else will either. What the evidence does say is that focused practice moves almost everyone a long way, that hours spent on autopilot move them much less, and that a rule promising mastery at a round number was always too tidy to be true.

takeaways: The 10,000-hour rule came from averages in one small violin study, not a law of learning.
Practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music and 18% in sports: big, but not most.
In the 2019 replication, the best violinists did not practice more than the merely good ones.
Quality beats quantity: target one weakness, get fast feedback, work at the edge of your ability.
Practice may not make you the best, but it reliably makes you far better than you were.

title: What Running Does to Your Brain, and What It Doesn't
dek: Exercise grows new neurons in mice and bigger memory centers in older adults. For healthy young brains the honest evidence is much smaller, and that changes the real reason to train.

blocks.text: In the late 1990s, at the Salk Institute in California, Henriette van Praag, Gerd Kempermann and Fred Gage set up an experiment with five groups of adult mice. One group learned a water maze. One swam in the same pool for the same time without the learning. One lived in an enriched cage full of toys and companions. One lived in a standard cage. And one simply got a running wheel.

Then the researchers counted newly born cells surviving in the hippocampus, a curled structure deep in the brain that is essential for forming new memories. Maze training did nothing. Swimming did nothing. The wheel runners ended up with about twice as many surviving new cells as the standard-cage mice, roughly as many as the enriched group. Voluntary running alone was enough.

The detail that makes the result so striking is what did *not* work. The maze-learning mice were using their hippocampus hard, solving a spatial memory problem day after day, yet their new cell counts did not budge. The swimmers were moving, but swimming for a mouse is stressful and forced. What made the difference was running that the animals chose to do, a lot of it, every night.

That 1999 paper helped launch a whole field, and a popular story that followed it: exercise is fertilizer for the brain, so every workout makes you smarter. Some of that story is solid. Some of it has been badly oversold. The difference matters for how you spend your limited off-watch hours.

It is worth being clear about why mouse results do not translate neatly. A lab mouse in a standard cage is about as sedentary and under-stimulated as a mammal gets, so adding a wheel is an enormous change from its baseline. Mice also run several kilometers a night when given the chance. And counting newborn neurons requires slicing up the brain, which is why nearly all the direct evidence comes from animals. Whether adult humans make meaningful numbers of new hippocampal neurons at all is still argued over by neuroscientists.
A bigger hippocampus, late in life

The most famous human result came in 2011. Kirk Erickson, Arthur Kramer and colleagues randomly assigned 120 older adults to either a year of moderate aerobic exercise, mostly brisk walking, or a stretching and toning program. They scanned everyone's brains before and after.

In the walking group, the front part of the hippocampus grew by about 2 percent. In the control group it shrank, the normal slow decline of aging. The authors estimated the exercise effectively turned back the clock on hippocampal shrinkage by one to two years. The walkers' spatial memory also improved, and the growth tracked with blood levels of a protein called BDNF.

items.label: Older adults randomized to aerobic training or stretching
Growth in hippocampal volume with aerobic training
Age-related shrinkage the training offset

blocks.source: Erickson et al., PNAS, 2011

blocks.text: Notice who was in that study: older adults, at the stage of life when the hippocampus is actively losing volume. That is where exercise has the most room to help. A 20-year-old brain is not shrinking yet, which is the first clue that results like this may not translate directly to someone young and healthy.
BDNF: the molecule everyone mentions

BDNF stands for brain-derived neurotrophic factor. It is a protein that helps neurons survive, grow new connections and strengthen existing ones, and it is heavily involved in the kind of synaptic changes that underlie learning. In animal studies, exercise reliably drives it up in the hippocampus. That made it the go-to explanation for why exercise might help thinking.

In humans you cannot easily sample brain tissue, so researchers measure BDNF in blood. A 2015 meta-analysis by Kristin Szuhany, Matteo Bugatti and Michael Otto pooled 29 studies with 1,111 participants. A single session of exercise produced a moderate rise in BDNF. People who had been training regularly got a bigger rise from each session. Resting BDNF levels after a training program went up only a little.

blocks.title: Exercise and blood BDNF: effect sizes
blocks.note: Around 0.2 is conventionally small, 0.5 moderate. Studies with more women showed smaller changes.
blocks.source: Szuhany, Bugatti & Otto, Journal of Psychiatric Research, 2015

blocks.text: It also helps to know what kind of training produced the bigger responses. The finding that trained people got a larger BDNF spike per session suggests that the body adapts to regular exercise in ways that amplify the response, which is one argument for consistency over occasional heroic workouts. The meta-analysis could not say much about which type, duration or intensity was best, because the underlying studies varied so much.

So exercise does raise BDNF, mostly for a while after each session. The open question is how much that matters for what you can actually learn or remember. Blood BDNF is an indirect signal; some of it comes from outside the brain. And when the same group later tested whether BDNF changes explained exercise's benefits for depressed patients, they could not show that it did. A plausible mechanism is not the same as a proven one.
The plot twist: the evidence in healthy people

By the late 2010s there were dozens of meta-analyses saying that regular exercise improves cognition, and most of them reported positive results. In 2023 a team led by Luis Ciria published an umbrella review in *Nature Human Behaviour* that went back through 24 of those meta-analyses, limited to randomized trials in healthy people, and asked how sturdy the evidence underneath really was.

Not very, they concluded. Many of the original trials were small and underpowered. Meta-analyses picked studies selectively. There were signs that positive results got published more readily than null ones. When the team pooled all the underlying trials themselves, the overall benefit was small, an effect size of 0.22. Accounting for whether the control group did some other activity and for baseline differences cut it to 0.13. Correcting for publication bias brought it to 0.05, which is effectively nothing.

Each of those corrections is worth understanding, because the same problems show up across self-improvement research. If the control group in a trial just sits on a waiting list, any gain in the exercise group could come from expectation, social contact or simply having something new to do. Using an active control, like stretching classes or a social activity, removes much of that. And if small trials with exciting results get published while small trials with null results end up in a drawer, any review of the published literature will overestimate the effect. Statistical tools can estimate how much, and here the estimate was most of it.

blocks.title: Regular exercise and cognition in healthy people
blocks.note: The bias-corrected interval included zero.
blocks.source: Ciria et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2023

blocks.text: This does not mean exercise is useless for the brain. It means that for healthy adults, the claim that a workout program will measurably raise your memory or reasoning scores is not well supported yet. The honest summary today: big benefits in older adults and in some clinical groups, and small or uncertain effects in young healthy people.

blocks.title: What the evidence supports

left.head: Well supported
items: Running boosts new neuron survival in mice
Aerobic training slowed hippocampal shrinkage in older adults
A single session raises blood BDNF
Exercise helps mood, sleep and long-term health

right.head: Oversold
items: Workouts make healthy young adults smarter
Higher BDNF in blood means better learning
Any exercise is a study hack
Effects in mice transfer cleanly to people

blocks.text: Timing: a small, interesting clue

One line of research looks less at long-term brain change and more at what a single bout of exercise does to the memories you just formed. In a 2016 study in *Current Biology*, Eelco van Dongen and colleagues had people learn a set of picture and location pairs. One group then did a session of exercise right away, one did it four hours later, and one did not exercise. Two days later, the group that exercised four hours after learning remembered the pairs better than the others. Exercising immediately did not help.

Other lab work has found that a 20-minute bout of moderate or vigorous exercise before or around learning can improve word-list memory in young adults. These are small studies with simple memory tasks, and nobody should build a study plan on a single result. But the idea fits what we know about memory consolidation: the hours after learning are when the brain stabilizes new memories, and arousal-related chemicals released during exercise may help tag recent experiences as worth keeping.

It is also worth noticing how far these lab tasks are from the learning you actually do. Remembering where a picture appeared on a screen is not the same as understanding how a reactor plant responds to a casualty or why a script throws an error. Nobody has shown that a well-timed workout makes those harder kinds of understanding stick better. It might; the experiments simply have not been done at that level.

A cheap personal experiment: study a qual topic or a coding concept in the morning, work out in the afternoon, and test yourself two days later. Compare that to weeks when you do not. Treat it as a hypothesis, not a hack.
So why train at all?

If the brain-boost claim is shakier than advertised, here is the reframe. The best reasons for a young person to exercise are not about directly upgrading cognition. They are about protecting the conditions that cognition depends on.

Sleep is the clearest example. Your ability to learn depends heavily on sleep, and regular exercise tends to support sleep quality. Mood is another. A 2025 meta-review of high-quality meta-analyses in *World Psychiatry* found large effects of physical activity for reducing depressive symptoms in people with depressive disorders. Low mood and poor sleep are brutal on concentration, so anything that defends against them indirectly defends your learning.

Then there is the long game. The hippocampus results in older adults, and the fact that higher fitness partly protected against shrinkage even in the control group, suggest that the fitness you build and keep now is an investment in the brain you will have at 65. You are not training for next week's exam score. You are training for decades of being sharp.

And finally, exercise is a practical break. Long study sessions in a cramped space, under artificial light, with little movement, wear down attention. A short bodyweight circuit between study blocks will not grow your hippocampus, but it resets your alertness in a way that scrolling a phone does not.

On a boat, all of this collides with real constraints: rotating watches, limited space, a gym that might be a single bench wedged next to equipment. The good news is that the indirect benefits do not require anything elaborate. Regular moderate effort that you can sustain across a long underway will do more for your sleep, mood and long-term health than an ambitious program you abandon after two weeks. Consistency is the variable that matters most, both for BDNF responses and for everything else.

blocks.title: Using exercise for learning, realistically
items: Make regular aerobic and strength training the default for health, mood and sleep, not as a study trick.
Put short movement breaks between long study blocks instead of phone breaks.
Try exercising a few hours after a hard learning session, and see if recall holds up better for you.
Do not skip study time to work out for brain gains; the evidence for a direct boost is small.
Protect sleep first. A workout that costs you sleep is a net loss for learning.

blocks.text: The next time a headline promises that some workout will boost your brain, a few questions will tell you most of what you need to know.

items: Was it done in mice, in older adults, or in healthy young people like you?
Did the comparison group do some other activity, or nothing at all?
How many people were in it? Dozens is a pilot, not proof.
Did it measure a real skill, or a blood marker and a brain scan?
Has anyone repeated it, and did a larger review hold up after correcting for bias?

blocks.text: The van Praag mice made a great headline because they made the brain sound simple: run, grow neurons, get smarter. People are messier. In humans, the strongest evidence points to exercise as a long-term maintenance program for the brain and a short-term support for mood, sleep and alertness, rather than a shortcut to learning faster. That is less exciting than a miracle molecule. It is also a better reason to keep training, because it does not depend on a claim that might not survive the next round of replications.

takeaways: Running doubled surviving new brain cells in mice, and aerobic training grew the hippocampus about 2% in older adults.
Exercise raises blood BDNF, especially right after a session, but that has not been shown to translate into better learning.
In healthy people, the pooled cognitive benefit of exercise programs shrinks to near zero after correcting for bias.
The strongest reasons to train for your brain are indirect: sleep, mood, alertness and long-term protection.
Exercising a few hours after learning helped memory in one study; it is a cheap experiment, not a proven hack.

title: Your Memory Is Not a Recording
dek: Memory is built in three stages, rebuilt every time you use it, and designed to forget. Knowing how it works changes how you should learn.

blocks.text: Try this before reading further. Without looking, draw both sides of a coin you have handled thousands of times. Whose face is on it, and which way does it point?
Where is the date? What words are on it, and where? You have seen this object more often than almost anything else you own.

In 1979, Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams asked 20 Americans to draw a US penny from memory. The typical person correctly recalled and placed only three of the eight main features. Only one person got all eight. In another test, they showed 36 people fifteen drawings of a penny, only one of them accurate, and fewer than half picked the real one as most likely correct. Thousands of exposures had produced almost no memory.

That result is a good doorway into how memory actually works, because it breaks the most common mental model of it: that the brain records what passes in front of it, like a camera, and that remembering is pressing play. Almost every part of that picture is wrong, and the ways it is wrong explain why some studying works and most does not.
Three jobs, not one

Psychologists split memory into three stages. *Encoding* is getting information in: turning an experience into something the brain can store. *Consolidation* is making it stick: stabilizing a fragile new trace into a lasting one over hours to years. *Retrieval* is getting it back out when you need it. A failure at any stage looks the same from the inside, which is simply I don't remember, but the fixes are completely different.

blocks.title: The life of a memory
items: Attention: of everything hitting your senses, only what you attend to has a real chance.
Encoding: the brain processes it, and how deeply you think about it shapes how well it is stored.
Consolidation: over hours and days, the trace is stabilized and gradually woven into what you already know.
Retrieval: a cue brings it back, and the act of retrieving reshapes the memory itself.
Forgetting: traces that are rarely used or easily confused become harder to reach.

blocks.text: A quick way to diagnose your own forgetting: if you cannot explain something even right after studying it, the problem was encoding. If you could explain it yesterday but not today, the trace was never consolidated or reinforced. If it comes back the instant someone gives you a hint, it was stored all along and the problem is retrieval. Each points to a different fix.

The penny is an encoding failure. You never needed the details to use the coin, so your brain never bothered to encode them. Seeing is not the same as storing. Most of what reaches your eyes in a day leaves no lasting trace, because the brain is not trying to keep a log; it is trying to keep what seems useful.

Attention is the first gate. If you are reading a manual while half-listening to a conversation in the mess, the words pass through your eyes but much of the processing that would turn them into memory never happens. Multitasking does not split your learning in half so much as skim the top off it. The quality of the first encounter sets a ceiling on everything that follows.
Encoding: depth beats exposure

If exposure alone does not build memory, what does? In a classic set of experiments from 1975, Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving showed people words and asked them questions about each one. Some questions were about appearance, such as whether the word was printed in capital letters.
Some were about sound, such as whether it rhymed with another word. Some were about meaning, such as whether it fit in a particular sentence. Nobody was told there would be a memory test.

On the surprise test, words processed for meaning were remembered far better than words processed for sound, which beat words processed for appearance. Follow-up experiments in the same paper suggested the advantage was not simply a matter of spending more time on each word. What mattered was how deeply each was processed. Thinking about what something means, and connecting it to what you already know, leaves a much stronger trace than just perceiving it.

This is why staring at a diagram of a system for an hour can leave so little behind. The question to ask is not how long you looked but what your brain did with it. Asking why a valve is placed where it is, what would happen if it failed open, and how this system resembles one you already understand forces deep processing. The details then hang on a structure of meaning instead of floating loose.
You remember what you think about, not what you look at. Turn passive reading into questions: why is it built this way, what happens if it fails, what is it similar to?

Prior knowledge is the hidden multiplier here. Experts remember new information in their field far better than novices, not because they have better memories in general, but because each new fact has somewhere to attach. An experienced electrician hears a new fault story and slots it into a rich mental model of how circuits fail. A beginner has to hold it as an isolated fact. This is why the early weeks of any technical subject feel brutal and later ones feel easier: you are building the structure that later facts will hang on.
Consolidation: the slow save
A new memory is fragile. Much of what we know about how it becomes stable comes from one man. In 1953, a 27-year-old named Henry Molaison underwent experimental surgery for severe epilepsy.

The surgeon, William Scoville, removed tissue from the inner part of both temporal lobes, including large parts of a structure called the hippocampus. The seizures eased. But from that day until his death in 2008, Molaison, known to science for decades only as H.M., could not form new long-term memories of facts or events.

He could still remember much of his childhood, hold a conversation and score normally on intelligence tests. He just could not keep anything new. The psychologist Brenda Milner, who began testing him in 1955, discovered something even stranger. She had him trace a star while watching only its reflection in a mirror, a task that is hard for everyone at first. Over three days he got steadily better at it, while having no memory of ever having done it before.

That split showed that memory is not one system. The hippocampus is essential for laying down new memories of facts and events, but skills are learned through other circuits. Modern research suggests the hippocampus acts like a temporary index, binding together the pieces of an experience scattered across the cortex, while those pieces are gradually strengthened and linked to existing knowledge. Much of that work happens offline, especially during sleep, which has its own article in this library.
Retrieval: every recall is a rebuild

Here is where the camera metaphor fails most dramatically. A memory is not stored as a finished file and played back. It is reconstructed each time from fragments, and the reconstruction is influenced by what is going on when you retrieve it.
In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed students films of car crashes and then asked how fast the cars were going. The only thing that changed between groups was one verb in the question.

blocks.title: Speed estimates for the same crash film, by verb used in the question
blocks.note: Small groups: 45 students in total, nine per verb.
blocks.source: Loftus & Palmer, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 1974

blocks.text: In a follow-up, a week after watching a crash, people were asked whether they had seen broken glass. There was none in the film. Of those who had been asked about the cars smashing, 32 percent said yes, compared with 14 percent of those asked about the cars hitting, and 12 percent of those not asked about speed at all. A single word, used days earlier, had added a detail that never happened. The original groups were small, but the broader finding that questions and later information can reshape memory has been confirmed many times since.

There is even a biological mechanism for this. In 2000, Karim Nader, Glenn Schafe and Joseph LeDoux showed in rats that a well-established fear memory, once recalled, briefly became unstable again and had to be re-saved, a process now called reconsolidation. Blocking protein synthesis in the amygdala right after recall erased the memory; doing it without recall left it intact. Recall is not a read-only operation. It opens the file, and the file can be edited before it is saved again.

items.label: People who falsely recalled broken glass after the word smashed, vs no speed question

blocks.source: Loftus & Palmer, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 1974

blocks.text: This is both a warning and an opportunity. The warning: vivid, confident memories can be wrong, which is one reason the Navy insists on having the procedure in hand rather than trusting what everyone remembers it says. The opportunity: because recall changes memory, practicing recall is one of the most powerful ways to strengthen it, as the article on retrieval practice explains.

Reconstruction also explains a familiar experience in technical work: the procedure you were sure you knew, executed confidently and slightly out of order. Over many recalls, small errors creep in, get re-saved and start to feel like the original. The more often you rehearse from memory without checking against the source, the more confident and the less accurate you can become. Retrieval practice works best with feedback for exactly this reason: recall, then check, then correct.
Context: the cue that unlocks it

Retrieval depends on cues, and the setting you learned in can be one of them. The most famous demonstration is perfect for anyone who works underwater. In 1975, Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley had divers learn word lists either on dry land or underwater, and then recall them in the same place or the other one. Recall was better when the learning and testing environments matched.

It is a great story, and it is less solid than it sounds. In 2021, Jaap Murre repeated the experiment with 16 divers and did not find the effect: recalling in the same environment as learning was not reliably better. A meta-analysis by Steven Smith and Edward Vela found that environmental context effects on free recall are real but often weak, with an average effect size around 0.25. Context matters somewhat, and much less when you have other strong cues.

The practical lesson is the opposite of what people usually take from the diver study. Do not try to study where you will be tested. Instead, study in varied places and ways, so your knowledge does not depend on any single setting. Knowledge that only comes back at your desk, with your notes nearby, is fragile. Knowledge you have pulled out in the mess, on watch and while walking is robust.
Forgetting is a feature

Why do we forget at all? Part of the answer is that memories compete. New information interferes with old, and similar memories blur into each other, which is why the fifth lecture on similar systems is harder to keep straight than the first. Often the memory is still stored but the cue that would reach it is missing, as anyone who has had a name on the tip of their tongue knows.

But a growing view holds that forgetting is not just a defect. In a 2017 review, Blake Richards and Paul Frankland at the University of Toronto argued that the goal of memory is not to preserve the past accurately but to help you make good decisions. Forgetting outdated details helps you adapt when the world changes, and dropping specifics lets you keep the general pattern, which applies to new situations. They compared it to a technique in machine learning that keeps models simple so they generalize instead of memorizing their training data.

Seen that way, the penny result is not a failure. Your brain correctly judged that the details of a penny were not worth keeping. The job, when you are learning something that does matter, is to send your brain the right signals: think about meaning, connect new facts to old ones, pull the information out repeatedly over time, and use it in different settings. Those are the signals that say this one is worth keeping.

takeaways: Exposure is not encoding; thousands of looks at a penny left most people unable to draw it.
Process for meaning: ask why, what if and what is it like, not just what it says.
Memory is rebuilt every time you recall it, so confident memories can be wrong. Use the procedure.
Study in varied places and ways so knowledge does not depend on one setting.
Forgetting is partly a filter; repeated, meaningful use tells the brain what to keep.

title: Why Good Practice Feels Like Losing
dek: Mixing up your practice makes you look worse while you train and better when it counts. The research on desirable difficulties explains why.

blocks.text: In a study published in 1994, a junior college baseball team agreed to an experiment. Thirty players were split into three groups. Ten got no extra practice. Ten got two extra batting sessions a week for six weeks, seeing 15 fastballs, then 15 curveballs, then 15 changeups, in neat blocks. The last ten got the same 45 pitches per session, but in random order, so they never knew what was coming next.

Anyone who has played sports can guess how the sessions felt. The blocked group got into a groove: by the tenth fastball in a row, you are timing it well. The random group kept getting fooled. Yet when everyone was tested at the end on randomly mixed pitches, like a real game, the random group had improved by about 57 percent from their starting level and the blocked group by about 25 percent. The group that looked worse at practice got better at baseball.

That pattern, where the practice that feels worse produces the learning that lasts, has a name. The UCLA psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork call it a *desirable difficulty*. Once you see it, you notice it everywhere, including in the way most people study for exams, train in games and learn to code.
Performance is not learning

The core idea is a distinction that sounds pedantic and turns out to be huge. Performance is what you can do right now, during practice. Learning is the lasting change that shows up later, in a different setting, after time has passed. You can watch performance. You can only infer learning, and the two often move in opposite directions.

Blocked practice is a performance-booster. When you do ten problems of the same type in a row, the method stays loaded in your head from one problem to the next, so you get them right and feel fluent. But that fluency is borrowed from the previous problem, not stored in long-term memory. Take away the crutch, by mixing types or adding a delay, and performance drops in practice. The Bjorks argue that this drop is often what drives durable learning, because it forces you to reconstruct the knowledge each time instead of coasting on what is already in your head.

In the Bjorks' framework, this is the gap between how accessible a memory is right now and how deeply it is stored. Easy practice inflates the first. Effortful practice, where you have to work to retrieve or reconstruct something, builds the second. Your feeling of mastery mostly reads the first, which is why it so often misleads you.

Their list of desirable difficulties is short: space your study sessions out instead of massing them, test yourself instead of rereading, interleave different topics instead of blocking them, and vary the conditions of practice. Spacing and testing each get their own article in this library. This one is about the less famous member of the family, interleaving, and about the crucial word in the phrase, *desirable*.
The math experiment

In 2007, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor at the University of South Florida taught college students to find the volume of four unusual solids, such as a wedge and a spheroid. Everyone did the same practice problems in two sessions. Blockers did all the wedge problems together, then all the spheroids, and so on. Mixers did the same problems shuffled. A week later, everyone took a test.

blocks.title: Blocked vs mixed math practice
blocks.note: Test given one week after the final practice session. Small study: 18 students completed it.
blocks.source: Rohrer & Taylor, Instructional Science, 2007

blocks.text: Practice scores made blocking look like the clear winner. Test scores told the opposite story, by a factor of three. The sample was small, just 18 students who finished all sessions, so treat the exact numbers with caution. But the reason for the reversal is the important part, and it generalizes.

When problems come in blocks, you never have to decide which method to use. The worksheet decides for you: it says Section 4.2 at the top. On a real test, or a real job, nobody tells you what kind of problem you are facing. Identifying the problem type is half the skill, and blocked practice skips it entirely. Mixed practice forces you to ask, every single time, what kind of problem this is and how you know.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Mixing problem types automatically spaces out each type, because between two wedge problems you do three others. Each time you return to a type, you have to pull the method back out of memory rather than reading it off the previous problem. So interleaving smuggles in both spacing and retrieval practice, which may be part of why its effects can be so large.
Blocked practice teaches you how to solve a problem once you know what it is. Interleaved practice teaches you to recognize what it is. Real life mostly tests the second.
From a lab to 787 students

Small lab studies are easy to dismiss, so Rohrer and his colleagues went big. In a randomized trial published in 2020, 54 seventh-grade math classes across five Florida schools used either mostly interleaved homework or the usual blocked kind for about four months. Both groups did the same problems, only in a different order. About a month after a review session, the students took an unannounced test.

items.label: Test scores, interleaved vs blocked homework, one month later
Effect size, which is large for a classroom study

blocks.source: Rohrer, Dedrick, Hartwig & Cheung, Journal of Educational Psychology, 2020

blocks.text: For an educational intervention that costs nothing but reshuffling homework, that is an unusually large effect. It is also one trial, in one subject and one age group, so the precise size should not be taken as a law of nature. But it shows the lab finding survives contact with real classrooms, real teachers and real teenagers.
The illusion that protects bad habits

If interleaving works so well, why does almost nobody do it on their own? Because it fools the people doing it. In a 2008 study, Nate Kornell and Robert Bjork had students learn the styles of 12 painters of landscapes and skies, from Georges Seurat to lesser-known artists, either seeing each artist's paintings in a block or mixed with the others. Later the students tried to identify the artists of new paintings they had never seen. Those who studied mixed paintings were right about 61 percent of the time on the first test block; those who studied in blocks managed about 35 percent.

Then the students were asked which method had worked better for them. Seventy-eight percent said blocking had been as good as or better than mixing, even though 78 percent had actually done better with mixing. They had just experienced the result and still believed the opposite. Blocked study felt like learning. Mixed study felt like confusion.

A second experiment in the same paper repeated the trick, with the same result. Of the students who expressed a preference, 64 out of 72 believed blocking had worked better. The bias was not a fluke of one group. It seems to be how people read their own learning.

This is the real obstacle. Your in-the-moment sense of progress is a performance meter, and desirable difficulties are designed to push that meter down. If you choose methods by how they feel, you will choose the wrong ones almost every time. That makes these techniques less a study tip and more a matter of trust: trusting evidence over your own feeling of fluency.

The same illusion traps teachers, coaches and training programs, not just learners. An instructor mostly sees performance during training: how smoothly the class works through problems, how many get the practice set right, how confident everyone looks at the end of the day. Every one of those signals rewards blocked, predictable, easy practice. Over time, curricula drift toward whatever makes training look good, which is not always what makes people good. Motor-learning researchers have studied this for decades under the name contextual interference, and the baseball study is one of its best-known demonstrations.
When difficulty is just difficulty

The word *desirable* is doing real work. The Bjorks are explicit that a difficulty helps only if you can respond to it successfully. If you lack the background knowledge to make sense of the challenge, it is not desirable, it is just hard. Shuffling problem types before you understand any of them produces confusion, not learning. Learn each method first, then mix.

The evidence also says interleaving is not universal. A 2019 meta-analysis by Brunmair and Richter pooled 238 effect sizes from 59 studies. Overall, interleaving beat blocking by a moderate margin, an effect size of 0.42. But it varied enormously.

Paintings and other visual categories showed the biggest benefit, 0.67. Math showed a smaller benefit, 0.34. Results for expository texts were mixed, and for learning lists of words, blocking actually did better.

The pattern underneath was intuitive. Interleaving helped most when the categories were easy to confuse with each other, when the hard part was telling similar things apart. That is the situation where blocking hides the most and mixing reveals the most. When categories are already obviously different, there is little to gain.

It is also worth admitting how small some of the famous studies are. The baseball study had ten players per group, and the math study had 18 students. The large classroom trial and the meta-analysis are what make the overall picture credible, not any single striking chart.
Building difficulty into your practice

Technical training is full of easily confused categories, which is exactly where interleaving pays off. Electrical faults that present with similar indications. Thermodynamics problems that look alike but need different equations.

Casualty procedures with overlapping symptoms. Bugs that throw similar errors for different reasons. In each case, the real skill is discrimination: noticing the one detail that tells you which situation you are in.

blocks.title: How to interleave without drowning
items: Learn each new method or system on its own first, until you can do a basic example.
Then build mixed practice sets: shuffle problem types so no two in a row need the same approach.
Before solving each one, say out loud which type it is and what tipped you off.
Mix in older material, not just this week's, so earlier topics stay in rotation.
Expect your practice scores to drop. Judge the method by delayed tests, not by how practice feels.

blocks.text: For a board or a big exam, that means quizzing across systems rather than finishing one system completely before touching the next. For math and physics, it means pulling problems from different chapters into one set rather than doing the end-of-section exercises in order. For coding, it means building small projects that need several concepts at once instead of drilling one concept per tutorial. For game skills, it is the same lesson as the batting cage: training against one predictable bot pattern feels great and transfers poorly to opponents who do not cooperate.

Interleaving also changes how you should read your own results. If you switch to mixed practice sets and your scores drop from 90 percent to 60, that does not mean the method failed. It means the old 90 was partly an illusion created by the format. The fair comparison is how you do on a mixed, delayed test, the kind you will face on a board or in a real casualty, and on that measure the 60 is the more honest number and the one that climbs.

Varying conditions counts too. Practicing a procedure only at one panel, in one order, with one instructor watching, builds a skill tied to that setting. Changing the setup, the order of questions, or the person quizzing you makes your knowledge less dependent on any single set of cues.

blocks.title: Same problems, different order

left.head: Blocked
items: Ten of one type, then ten of the next
Method stays loaded between problems
High practice scores, smooth feeling
Weak at telling problem types apart

right.head: Interleaved
items: Types shuffled, no two alike in a row
Must choose the method every time
Lower practice scores, feels messy
Builds recognition of what you are facing

blocks.text: If you doubt all this, test it on yourself. Next time you have two similar topics to learn, practice one in blocks and the other mixed with older material, and quiz yourself on both a week later without warning. Personal experiments are not science, but they are a good way to stop trusting the feeling and start trusting the result.

The hardest thing about desirable difficulties is not using them. It is tolerating how they feel. Every one of them makes you look worse in the short term, to yourself and to anyone watching. The payoff arrives later, quietly, when the pitch you were not expecting comes in, and you hit it anyway.

takeaways: How well you perform during practice is a poor guide to how much you are learning.
Mixing problem types forces you to identify the problem, which is half of real-world skill.
Learn each method first, then interleave; difficulty without background knowledge is just confusion.
Interleaving helps most when categories are easy to confuse, and can hurt for simple word lists.
Judge study methods by delayed tests, not by how smooth practice feels.
