title: Seeing in the Dark With Your Ears
dek: Underwater, light fades within a few hundred meters and radio barely gets in, so the ocean's only long-range sense is sound, and the water itself keeps bending the picture.

blocks.text: In 1826, on Lake Geneva in Switzerland, a physicist named Jean-Daniel Colladon and a mathematician named Charles-Francois Sturm ran one of the most elegant experiments in history. On one boat, a bell hung underwater. At the exact moment someone struck it, a charge of gunpowder flashed in the air above. On a second boat about 10 miles away, an observer watched for the flash and listened through the water for the bell.

Light crosses 10 miles almost instantly. Sound does not. By timing the gap between flash and bell, they calculated how fast sound moves through fresh water: about 1,435 meters per second at 8 degrees Celsius. According to the Discovery of Sound in the Sea project at the University of Rhode Island, that is within 3 meters per second of the value accepted today.

That bell is the ancestor of every sonar system that has ever existed. The basic insight has not changed in two centuries: underwater, sound is the only sense that reaches far. Everything else about sonar is the story of learning to use that sense, and of discovering how strangely the ocean handles sound.
Why sound, and not light

Above water, we see with light and ships detect each other with radar, which is radio. Both are electromagnetic waves, and seawater is brutal to them. Salt water conducts electricity, and conducting materials soak up electromagnetic energy. Sunlight fades within a few hundred meters even in clear ocean water, and radar is useless below the surface. That is why submarines need special arrangements to communicate at all.

Sound is the opposite. It is a pressure wave, a chain of molecules pushing on their neighbors, and water is excellent at carrying it. Water is dense and hard to compress, so a push at one end gets passed along quickly and with little loss. Sound in seawater travels about 1,500 meters per second, roughly four and a half times faster than in air, and it can travel enormous distances.

blocks.title: How fast sound travels
blocks.note: The freshwater value is Colladon and Sturm's 1826 Lake Geneva measurement.
blocks.source: Discovery of Sound in the Sea (DOSITS), University of Rhode Island

blocks.text: Sound also carries information. Every machine has a voice: pumps, motors, propellers, even the flow of water over a hull. Whales and dolphins communicate with it. Earthquakes and storms announce themselves with it. A submarine moving through the ocean is surrounded by a constant, layered soundscape, and the job of sonar is to pull meaning out of it.
Shouting versus listening

There are two basic ways to use sound, and the tension between them shapes everything about how submarines think. You can make a noise and listen for the echo, which is **active sonar**. Or you can stay quiet and listen to what others are doing, which is **passive sonar**.

blocks.title: Two ways to use sound

left.head: Active sonar
items: Send out a pulse and time the echo
Distance is easy: half the round-trip time multiplied by the speed of sound
Works on silent objects like icebergs, wrecks and the seafloor
Announces your presence to anyone listening, often from farther away than your echo returns

right.head: Passive sonar
items: Listen to sounds others make
Direction comes naturally; distance has to be worked out over time
Only detects things that make noise
Gives nothing away, which is why quiet matters so much

blocks.text: The asymmetry in that last row is the heart of the matter. When you ping, your sound has to travel out, bounce off something and travel back, losing strength the whole way. But anyone near your target hears your ping after it has traveled only one way. So the listener often hears you before you hear the echo. Active sonar is like walking into a dark forest with a flashlight: you can see, but everyone can see you.

That is why so much of the history of submarine warfare is a history of quieting. If the other side is listening, your noise is your signature, and the less you make, the closer you can be before anyone knows you are there. Engineering choices that seem odd from the outside, like isolating machinery on special mounts or obsessing over propeller shapes, make sense in that light.
The ocean bends sound

If seawater were uniform, sound would travel in straight lines and sonar would be geometry. It is not uniform, and that changes everything. The speed of sound in seawater depends on three things: temperature, salt content and pressure.

items.label: Faster for each 1 °C warmer
Faster for each extra unit of salinity (1 psu)
Faster for each kilometer deeper

blocks.source: Discovery of Sound in the Sea (DOSITS), University of Rhode Island

blocks.text: Those changes are small, a few percent at most, but they matter because of refraction. When a wave travels through a medium whose speed changes, it bends toward the slower region. You have seen the light version: a straw looks broken in a glass of water. In the ocean, sound rays curve up or down depending on how temperature and pressure are changing with depth.

Near the surface, temperature dominates. Water warmed by the sun is fast, and below it the temperature drops through the thermocline, so sound slows as it goes deeper and the rays bend downward. That can leave regions where almost no direct sound reaches, called **shadow zones**. A sound source on one side of a layer can be hard to hear on the other side, even at a short distance. This is old, publicly understood physics, and it is why oceanographers and navies have spent a century measuring water temperature as obsessively as anything else.
The channel that carries sound across oceans

Go deeper and something remarkable happens. Temperature keeps dropping, which slows sound, but pressure keeps rising, which speeds it up. At some depth the two effects cross, and the speed of sound reaches a minimum. Above that depth, sound rays bend down toward it. Below it, they bend up toward it. Sound that starts near that minimum gets trapped, bouncing gently between faster layers and never touching the surface or the seafloor, where most energy is lost.

In the spring of 1944, Maurice Ewing and J. Lamar Worzel went looking for that channel. They hung a deep hydrophone from the research vessel Saluda, out of Woods Hole, while a second ship dropped small explosive charges set to go off deep in the ocean. On April 3, a charge detonated about 320 nautical miles away, and the crew heard it clearly: a series of pulses building to a sharp finish. The deep sound channel was real.

The Navy's first idea for it was lifesaving. Downed airmen in a raft could drop a small charge, and listening stations on shore could use the arrival times to locate them. The scheme was called SOFAR, for SOund Fixing And Ranging, which is why the channel is still called the SOFAR channel. Soviet scientist Leonid Brekhovskikh independently found the same channel in 1946 in the Sea of Japan.

In the 1950s the Navy put the channel to work in a much bigger way, laying arrays of hydrophones on the seafloor, cabled to shore stations, in a program called the SOund SUrveillance System, or SOSUS. According to DOSITS, it proved very successful at tracking Soviet submarines during the Cold War. It also picked up mysterious loud, low sounds that operators nicknamed the Jezebel Monster. They turned out to be blue and fin whales, which had evidently been using the channel to talk across ocean basins long before humans noticed it.

Scientists borrowed the channel too. Oceanographers built drifting instruments that ride deep currents and either send or receive sound through the channel, so their positions can be tracked for months; one version is called RAFOS, which is SOFAR spelled backward, because it listens instead of transmitting. Because the speed of sound depends on temperature, timing how long a signal takes to cross an ocean basin also works as a giant thermometer, letting researchers track large-scale changes in ocean temperature. A wartime rescue idea became a tool for studying the climate.

blocks.title: Learning to hear underwater
items: Colladon and Sturm measure the speed of sound in Lake Geneva.
Titanic sinks; within weeks, a British inventor files patents for echo ranging.
Fessenden's oscillator detects an iceberg more than two miles away by echo.
Paul Langevin builds an echo-ranging system using quartz crystals.
Echoes are received from a submarine at up to 1,500 meters.
Ewing and Worzel confirm the deep sound channel.
The Navy builds SOSUS seafloor listening arrays.

blocks.text: Finding direction with many ears

You already own a passive sonar system: your two ears. A sound coming from your left reaches your left ear a fraction of a millisecond before your right, and your brain uses that tiny delay to tell you where it came from. Close your eyes in a room and you can still point at someone talking. That is direction-finding by timing.

Underwater hydrophone arrays do the same thing with many ears instead of two. A sound arriving at an angle hits one end of the array slightly before the other. By adding up the signals from all the hydrophones with carefully chosen delays, a processor can make the array most sensitive in one direction and deaf in others, then sweep that sensitivity around like an invisible spotlight. The technique is called beamforming, and the same math is used in radio telescopes, phone microphones and 5G antennas.

blocks.title: How an array points without moving
items: A sound wave reaches the hydrophones at slightly different times depending on its direction.
The processor picks a direction to test and calculates the delays a sound from there would produce.
It shifts each hydrophone's signal by those delays and adds them together.
Sound from the tested direction lines up and gets louder; sound from elsewhere partly cancels.
Repeating this across many directions builds a picture of where sound is coming from.

blocks.text: Two rules fall out of the physics. A longer array, with ears spread farther apart, can tell directions apart more finely. And lower frequencies, with their longer wavelengths, need bigger arrays to get the same sharpness. That is one reason long towed arrays and large seafloor arrays exist: when you want to hear faint, low sounds from far away and still know where they came from, size is the only answer.

The other enemy is noise. The ocean is not quiet. Wind and breaking waves hiss, rain drums on the surface, distant shipping rumbles, whales sing, and in warm shallow water snapping shrimp crackle like frying bacon. Your own boat adds its own sounds right next to your sensors. Detection is never about hearing a signal in silence. It is about picking out a pattern against a background that is always there, which is why signal processing matters as much as the hydrophones themselves.
High notes and low notes

Frequency adds one more trade-off. Seawater absorbs sound, partly through the water itself and partly through dissolved salts, which turn some of the sound's energy into heat. High-frequency sound loses energy much faster than low-frequency sound, so under the same conditions a high note fades over a shorter distance.

That creates a choice that shows up all over acoustics. Low frequencies travel far but give a blurry picture, because long wavelengths cannot resolve small details. High frequencies give sharp detail but do not reach far. Systems built to hear things at great distance lean low. Systems built to map a nearby object, a seafloor or a mine-like shape lean high. Fishfinders, medical ultrasound and dolphin clicks all sit on the high-frequency, short-range side of the same physics.
Range or resolution, pick one. Almost every sensing system, from sonar to your eyes to a camera sensor, lives somewhere on that trade-off.
Sonar is inference, not sight

The deepest thing about sonar is that it is not really seeing. A sonar picture is a hypothesis. Faint tones, shifting bearings and echoes get assembled into a model of what is out there, and that model gets revised as new evidence comes in. The ocean adds layers, shadow zones and its own noise to every clue. A good operator is less a camera than a detective.

That turns out to be how human perception works too. Your brain does not receive a finished picture of the world. It receives messy signals and builds its best guess, filling gaps with expectation. Optical illusions are what happens when that guess is wrong. Sonar just makes the process visible: you can watch a contact get built, tested and sometimes thrown out.

There is a practical lesson in that for anyone who works with incomplete information, whether it is reading an opponent in a game, debugging code or judging people. The first picture is a guess. The skill is in holding it loosely, gathering more evidence, and changing your mind when the data says so. Colladon's bell taught us how fast sound moves. The real art came later: learning how much to trust what it tells you.

takeaways: Seawater kills light and radio within short distances but carries sound fast and far, at about 1,500 m/s.
Active sonar measures distance but announces you; passive sonar is silent but has to work out range over time.
Temperature, salinity and pressure change sound speed, which bends sound and creates shadow zones.
A deep sound channel, confirmed in 1944, can carry low-frequency sound across ocean basins.
Low frequencies reach far, high frequencies show detail: range versus resolution is a universal trade-off.

title: The Bell That Still Holds the Record
dek: The cleanest submarine rescue in history happened in 1939. Here is why getting trapped sailors out is so hard, and how escape suits, rescue bells and robot submarines try to solve it.

blocks.text: On the morning of May 23, 1939, the brand-new submarine *Squalus* made a test dive off the coast of New Hampshire. A main engine air induction valve, a big pipe that feeds air to the diesels on the surface, was open when it should have been shut. The sea poured into the after compartments. Twenty-six men drowned. The boat settled on the bottom at about 243 feet, and 33 men sealed themselves in the forward part of the hull and waited in the cold.

The next morning a strange device was lowered from the rescue ship *Falcon*: a pear-shaped steel bell about the size of a small room, hanging from a cable. Over four trips and roughly 13 hours, it brought every one of the 33 survivors to the surface. By the Royal Australian Navy's reckoning, it remains the only fully successful rescue of a trapped submarine crew from a sunken boat.

Think about that for a second. Nearly a century of engineering, billions of dollars, multiple generations of rescue vehicles, and the clean success case is still a bell from the 1930s. That is not because the later systems are bad. It is because the problem is strange: you are building a machine that must work perfectly on a day you hope never comes, at a place you cannot predict, under conditions you cannot rehearse exactly.

items.label: Squalus survivors brought up by the rescue chamber
Chamber runs needed to reach all of them
Men lost in the flooded after compartments

blocks.source: Naval Undersea Museum; Naval History and Heritage Command

blocks.text: The bell that worked

The *Squalus* rescue did not come out of nowhere. In 1925 the submarine *S-51* sank after a collision, and only 3 of her 37 men escaped. In 1927 the *S-4* went down off Cape Cod; her crew survived the sinking but ran out of air while rescuers on the surface tried and failed to reach them. Those losses pushed the Navy to build something that could actually get men out.

Charles Momsen, a submarine officer shaped by those disasters, drove the idea of a diving bell that could mate with a submarine's escape hatch. Allan McCann led the work to turn it into a practical machine, finished in 1930. The **McCann rescue chamber** is simple to the point of being elegant. It is lowered on a cable, lands on the hatch, and its lower compartment is pumped dry. Once the trapped crew and the chamber are at the same pressure, the hatch opens and men climb up into a dry space. Then the chamber is hauled back to the surface.

Momsen himself directed the *Squalus* rescue. A diver, Boatswain's Mate Second Class Martin Sibitzky, went down to the hull to rig the cable the chamber would ride on, part of the work that earned him the Navy Cross. The Navy's modern assessment robot is named after him. The *Squalus* herself was raised later that year, renamed *Sailfish*, and went back to sea in 1940.

Here is the part that surprises people: the Navy still maintains McCann-style chambers. According to the Navy's Undersea Rescue Command, they carry up to six people at a time and can reach a bottomed submarine at depths of 850 feet. They are kept because they are simple and reliable, and simple and reliable is exactly what you want from a machine that sits on a shelf for decades between uses.

blocks.title: A century of getting men out

S-4 sinks; crew survives but runs out of air before rescue
McCann rescue chamber completed
Squalus: chamber rescues all 33 survivors in four trips

First Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicle launched

blocks.text: Two ways out: escape and rescue

Every plan for a sunken submarine starts with a basic fork. **Escape** means the crew gets themselves out and swims or floats to the surface. **Rescue** means someone from outside comes down, connects to the boat and carries them up in a dry, pressurized vehicle. The two answers fit different situations, and both have been argued over for a hundred years.

blocks.title: Escape versus rescue

left.head: Escape
items: The crew leaves on their own, one or a few at a time
Fast, needs no outside help to start
Exposes people to pressure, cold water and open sea
Limited by depth and by what the body can handle

right.head: Rescue
items: An outside vehicle docks on a hatch and carries people up dry
Keeps rescued people at a controlled pressure
Takes time to fly or ship gear to the scene
Needs a hatch that fits, a ship to work from, and decent weather

blocks.text: The broad logic, as published by navies and rescue organizations, goes like this. If the boat is stable, the air is holding up and help is on the way, waiting is usually the better bet, because a dry transfer is far gentler than a free ascent through cold water. If conditions inside are getting worse faster than help can arrive, from flooding, fire, bad air or rising pressure, escape becomes the option. The hard part is that nobody inside knows exactly how long rescue will take.

Early escape gear looked like a scuba rig made by a coal miner, and in fact the **Momsen lung** borrowed from mine rescue breathing equipment. It was a rubber bag that let a sailor rebreathe air on the way up. The US Navy used it until 1957. The British had a similar device, the Davis apparatus. Then something awkward happened: a 1946 Royal Navy inquiry found that men using the Davis gear did not survive at a higher rate than men who just went up without it. The Royal Navy shifted toward free ascent, and the whole field learned a lesson that applies far beyond submarines: test whether your safety gear actually changes outcomes.
The physics of going up

Escaping from depth is mostly a fight with Boyle's law. The deeper you are, the more the sea squeezes any gas, including the air in your lungs. Rise toward the surface and that gas expands. If you hold your breath on the way up, the expanding air can tear the delicate tissue of the lungs and push bubbles into the bloodstream, which can be fatal. This is why every escape trainer drills the same thing: keep the airway open and let the air out as you rise.

Modern escape suits handle much of this for you. The Submarine Escape Immersion Equipment, the bright full-body suit many submariners know from training, combines a hood that supplies air with an insulated suit and an integrated one-person life raft. According to the Royal Australian Navy's history of escape and rescue, this generation of gear allows escape from as deep as 185 meters, around 600 feet.

blocks.title: How a pressurized escape works, in broad strokes
items: The sailor dons the suit and enters a small escape trunk, which is sealed off from the rest of the boat
The trunk floods while air is fed into the suit and hood
Pressure inside the trunk rises until it matches the sea outside
The outer hatch opens and the suit's buoyancy carries the sailor up quickly
The sailor breathes normally on the way, letting expanding air escape
At the surface, the suit's life raft inflates to keep the sailor out of the cold water

blocks.text: The speed of the ascent is a feature, not a flaw. Divers get decompression sickness because they spend a long time at depth and nitrogen dissolves into their tissues. A fast escape from a boat at normal pressure gives the body little time to load up. That changes, though, if the inside of the damaged submarine has already been pressurized by flooding. Then the crew has been absorbing gas the whole time they waited, and a quick trip to the surface can make them very sick. That single detail shapes the design of modern rescue systems.
From DSRVs to a robot with a cockpit

The loss of *Thresher* in 1963, and of *Scorpion* five years later, made the gap obvious: a modern submarine could sink in water far deeper than a rescue bell could reach. The Navy's answer was the **Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicle**, a small crewed submarine that could be flown to a port in a giant cargo plane, carried to the scene on a host submarine or ship, dive, and dock on the hatch of a disabled boat. Two were built, *Mystic* and *Avalon*. The first launched in 1970, and each could carry 24 people per trip.

In 2008 the DSRVs retired and the Navy fielded the **Submarine Rescue Diving and Recompression System**. Its heart is the Pressurized Rescue Module, a tethered vehicle steered by two operators that can carry 16 rescued sailors per trip. The Navy rates it to 2,000 feet and says it can mate with a submarine lying at up to a 45-degree angle in pitch and roll, which matters, because sunken boats rarely sit level.

The system belongs to the Undersea Rescue Command, based at Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego. It is government-owned and contractor-operated, and it is built to rescue sailors from foreign submarines as well as American ones. That last point is not charity. If your rescue gear can only help your own boats, then on the day it matters you are relying on luck that your boat is the one in trouble and that it sank somewhere convenient.

blocks.title: People carried per trip
blocks.note: Fewer seats per trip in the modern system, but far easier to move and able to reach deeper.
blocks.source: US Navy Undersea Rescue Command fact files; Royal Australian Navy Sea Power Centre

blocks.text: The system comes in pieces. A remotely operated vehicle goes first to look at the boat and clear the hatch. Then the rescue module docks. Finally, a decompression system lets rescued sailors move from the module into recompression chambers *without ever being exposed to surface pressure*, which is the answer to the pressurized-boat problem. Everything is built to travel by truck, aircraft or ship, and to work from a commercial vessel near the scene rather than a dedicated rescue ship that might be an ocean away.

blocks.title: Depths in the rescue story
blocks.source: Naval Undersea Museum; US Navy SRDRS and Undersea Rescue Command fact files

blocks.text: Rescue is a supply chain

Notice what changed between the DSRV and the modern module. The new vehicle carries fewer people per trip. On paper that looks like a downgrade. But the real enemy in a submarine rescue is rarely seat count. It is time. Every hour spent finding a cargo plane, a suitable ship, a crane strong enough, a crew certified to run the gear, is an hour of falling oxygen and rising cold for the people waiting below.

That is why the Navy designs the modern system around a **vessel of opportunity**. Instead of depending on one special rescue ship, the gear is packaged so it can be bolted onto a suitable commercial or military vessel close to the accident. It is a bit like carrying a game save on a USB stick instead of a single console: the value is that it runs on whatever hardware is nearby. Speed comes from flexibility, not from any single heroic machine.

The *Kursk* made this painfully clear in 2000. Help existed in Norway and Britain within reach of the Barents Sea, but it took days of politics before anyone was allowed to use it. Afterward, navies created the International Submarine Escape and Rescue Liaison Office, ISMERLO, to keep track of who has what, which hatches each system fits and how fast it can get anywhere. More than 40 countries operate submarines. Very few could handle every possible rescue alone, which is why rescue forces train together across navies.

The most important rescue technology may be the boring stuff: standard hatch dimensions, pre-arranged agreements, equipment sized to fit a common cargo plane. A perfect rescue vehicle that cannot reach the site in time saves nobody.

There is a broader engineering idea hiding here. When you design something that will only be used in an emergency, you are designing for a moment you cannot fully test. The only ways to get confidence are to keep the design simple, to rehearse it often enough that people stay sharp, and to make sure every interface, from the hatch seal to the paperwork, works with the equipment on the other end. The McCann chamber has lasted because it scores well on all three.
What this means for the crew

The uncomfortable truth is that the odds of survival in any submarine casualty are shaped mostly by the boat's own crew in the first minutes: stopping flooding, fighting fire, keeping the air breathable, and knowing escape procedures cold. Rescue systems buy time and offer a way out. They cannot undo a casualty that was handled badly from the start.

That is also why escape training, the cold water, the trunk drills, the hood, matters even if you never use it. The *Squalus* crew survived because they shut the right doors fast, stayed calm in the dark and cold for more than a day, and kept the forward compartments livable until the bell arrived. The machine got the credit in the headlines. The crew made the machine's job possible.

There is a quiet lesson in the fact that the cleanest success story is still from 1939. Safety systems often look most impressive in the brochure and do their most important work invisibly, by never being needed. A rescue force that trains for decades and never makes a real rescue is not a failure. It is the best outcome anyone could hope for.

takeaways: The 1939 Squalus rescue, 33 men in four chamber trips, is still cited as the only fully successful rescue of a trapped crew.
Escape means getting yourself out; rescue means an outside vehicle docks and carries you up dry.
On the way up, expanding air in the lungs is the big danger: keep the airway open and let it out.
Today's rescue module carries 16 per trip to 2,000 feet and is built to fly anywhere and work from any suitable ship.
In rescue, time and logistics matter more than seat count, which is why navies coordinate through ISMERLO.

title: The Forecast That Was Off by Half
dek: When submarines opened to women, the Navy predicted most would leave. Fourteen years of data tell a different story, and a lesson about how predictions go wrong.

blocks.text: When the Navy opened submarines to women in 2010, it had to make a prediction. How many of the first female officers would stay long enough to become department heads, the mid-career jobs that lead toward executive officer and command? Planners looked for the closest comparison they had, women in the nuclear surface warfare community, and projected that about 12.5 to 15 percent would stay.

The real number for the year groups from 2010 to 2016 turned out to be 29 percent, according to a 2024 Navy briefing to a Pentagon advisory committee. That is roughly double the forecast, and slightly higher than the rate for the men in the same year groups. The Navy did not just underestimate. It picked the wrong comparison.

That gap is the most interesting fact in the whole story of women in submarines, and it says something about predictions in general. But it is only one piece. Integration also brought real problems, design changes, a scandal, and a slow climb up the chain of command that has not finished yet. Here is what the public record shows, about fourteen years in.

items.label: Women assigned to submarines in 2024, out of a force of more than 15,000
Department head retention, female officers from 2010 to 2016 year groups
Reenlistment rate of enlisted women in submarines, FY2017 to FY2024

blocks.source: Navy briefing to DACOWITS, reported by Navy Times, December 2024

blocks.text: The arguments for the ban

For most of submarine history the case against mixed crews felt self-evident to many people inside the force. Submarines are the most cramped warships in the Navy. Racks are stacked tight, privacy barely exists, and there are few heads. Critics worried about berthing, about relationships on long patrols, about the cost of redesigning spaces, and about whether a crew's tight cohesion could survive a change this large. Some of those worries were sincere engineering questions. Some were about culture.

Other navies had already tested the idea. Norway opened its submarines to women in the 1980s and had a woman in command of one in the mid-1990s. Several other navies followed over the next decades. None of that settled the debate in the United States, where the submarine force is larger, the patrols are longer and the culture is famously conservative about change. Still, it showed that the question was practical, not theoretical.

There was also a plain manpower argument on the other side. The submarine force runs on people who can survive nuclear training, which is one of the hardest academic pipelines in the military. Every year the Navy competes with civilian employers for exactly that kind of talent. Shutting half of the qualified population out of an entire community is an expensive habit, whatever the reasons behind it. That argument eventually carried more weight than the worries about berthing.

In 2010, Defense Secretary Robert Gates lifted the ban. The Navy chose to start with officers and with the larger boats. Ohio-class ballistic missile and guided-missile submarines have more room than attack boats, which made it simpler to set aside separate berthing and facilities. Female officers began reporting to boats in 2011, after going through the same nuclear training pipeline as the men.

blocks.title: How integration unfolded
items: Defense Secretary Gates lifts the ban on women serving on submarines
First female officers join submarine crews
Navy begins training enlisted women for submarines; first selected for USS Michigan
A female chief petty officer joins the submarine community
First female submarine executive officer and first female chief of the boat
USS New Jersey, the first sub designed for mixed crews, is delivered
About 2028
Navy projects its first female submarine commanding officer

blocks.text: What the numbers show

The retention story holds up across ranks. An Associated Press review of Navy records in 2018 found that 26 percent of the first female submarine officers signed up to stay for department head, essentially matching the roughly 27 percent of men from 2010. By the 2024 briefing, the department head rate for women in the 2010 to 2016 year groups was 29 percent, about a point and a half above their male peers. On the enlisted side, women reenlisted at 74.9 percent from fiscal 2017 to 2024, about one point above enlisted men.

The 2018 snapshot is worth a closer look because it was the first real test. Of the first 19 female submarine officers, 5 had signed on for department head, and the other 14 had left, were leaving or had moved elsewhere in the Navy. That sounds like a lot of departures until you remember that most junior officers of either sex leave after their first tour. Retention in the nuclear communities has always been a fight. By then, about one-fifth of submarine crews were integrated, and Navy leadership said the early results were encouraging.

blocks.title: Female officer retention to department head
blocks.note: The forecast bar shows the top of the Navy's 12.5-15% projection. Later bars are actual retention.
blocks.source: Associated Press, 2018; Navy briefing to DACOWITS via Navy Times, 2024

blocks.text: Interest is rising too. In fiscal 2024, the submarine force brought in 87 female officers, 20.3 percent of its officer accessions, and 400 enlisted women, 9.5 percent of enlisted accessions. That enlisted number jumped from 271 the year before, an increase of nearly 48 percent and the biggest one-year rise since integration began.

blocks.title: Enlisted women entering the submarine force
blocks.source: Navy briefing to DACOWITS, reported by Navy Times, December 2024

blocks.text: Some honesty about what these numbers can and cannot tell you. The totals are still small: 712 women in a force of more than 15,000 is just under 5 percent. Small groups produce noisy statistics, and a difference of a point or two between women and men is not a meaningful gap in either direction. The early volunteers were also a self-selected group, people who wanted this badly enough to be first, and that can push retention up. The fair reading is not that women outperform men. It is that the predicted collapse never happened.

The Navy's forecast was not wrong because of bias in the math. It was wrong because it borrowed data from the wrong group. When you predict how people will behave, the comparison you choose often matters more than the calculation you run.
The hard parts

Integration was not smooth everywhere. In 2015, the Navy discovered that male sailors aboard USS *Wyoming* had secretly recorded female officers and trainees while they were undressing, and shared the videos. The sailors involved were prosecuted, several of them at courts-martial. It was a serious betrayal, and it became a test of whether the force would treat it as a real crime or as a scandal to manage. Advocates for servicewomen later said the prosecutions showed it had been taken seriously, but the damage to trust on that crew was real.

There were practical problems too. Many boats simply could not be reconfigured cheaply. The older Los Angeles and Seawolf classes are not getting women in their crews and are scheduled to leave service anyway. On boats that did integrate, the Navy added doors, designated washrooms and other changes for privacy, and it has a goal of at least 20 percent women on each integrated crew, partly so that no one is isolated as the only woman aboard. By its own account, it sometimes falls short of that goal.

The plans keep expanding. A 2021 integration plan aimed for 33 integrated crews by 2030. In 2024 the target became 39 by 2033, and a major revision signed by the submarine force commander planned for women officers on 40 submarines, up from 30. Those are plans, not results, and shipbuilding delays on the Virginia class could slow them.
Designing a boat for everyone

Most submarines in service were designed decades ago around the assumption of an all-male crew, and that assumption is built into physical details: where valves sit, how high things are mounted, how much force a handwheel takes. When the Navy announced it would design future subs with women's height, reach and strength in mind, it was admitting something engineers know well. Every design has a model user hidden inside it.

USS *New Jersey*, a Virginia-class attack submarine delivered in April 2024, is the first American submarine designed from the start for a mixed crew instead of being modified afterward. That is the point. The expensive part of inclusion is retrofitting old spaces. Designing it in from the beginning costs far less.

There is a broader idea here, one that shows up everywhere from city sidewalks to game controllers: designing for a wider range of users often makes things better for the original users too. A valve that a shorter sailor can reach easily is also easier for a tall sailor to reach in a hurry, in the dark, with a casualty in progress. It would be overclaiming to say this has been measured on submarines. But it is a pattern worth noticing whenever someone says a change will only help a small group.
Climbing the ladder

The real test of any integration is not whether people can join. It is whether they can lead. In 2022 the submarine force hit two milestones. Lieutenant Commander Amber Cowan became the first woman to serve as executive officer of a submarine, aboard the ballistic missile boat USS *Kentucky*. Master Chief Angela Koogler became the first female chief of the boat, the senior enlisted leader on a sub, aboard USS *Louisiana*.

Anyone who has served aboard knows what that second milestone means. The chief of the boat is the person the whole crew answers to in practice: the enforcer of standards, the voice of the enlisted crew to the captain, the one who knows everyone's name and business. Earning that job requires the trust of a crew that, a decade earlier, had never served alongside women at all.

As of late 2024, 44 female officers had served or were serving as submarine department heads, and four had been designated as executive officers. A female master chief was in training to become an engineering department master chief, set to report aboard in 2026. The Navy projects its first female commanding officer of a submarine around 2028, based on how many women are moving through the pipeline rather than on any single candidate.

blocks.title: The officer path to submarine command, in broad strokes
items: Commission and complete nuclear power training and submarine school
Serve a first sea tour as a division officer and earn the submarine qualification
Return to sea as a department head, such as engineer or navigator
Screen for and serve as executive officer
Screen for command and take a boat of your own

blocks.text: That path takes well over a decade, which is why the first female commanding officer is projected to arrive nearly two decades after the ban was lifted. There is no shortcut. It is the same ladder everyone climbs, and the slowness is not a sign of failure. It is simply how long it takes to grow a captain.
The lesson in the forecast

Go back to that opening prediction. The Navy expected 12.5 to 15 percent of women officers to stay. It got 29. The planners were not foolish. They did what forecasters usually do, which is find a similar-looking group and assume the new one will behave the same. The problem was that the similar-looking group was not actually that similar. Submarine officers chose a different life, in a different community, with a different culture.

This is called the reference class problem, and it is one of the most useful ideas you can carry around. Whenever you predict something, whether a game's retention, a business idea's success, or your own chances at a hard qualification, the group you compare yourself to quietly decides the answer. Pick a bad comparison and your math can be perfect while your conclusion is way off.

The fix is not to stop predicting. It is to ask, every time, what makes this group different from the one you are borrowing data from, and to update fast once real numbers arrive. The Navy deserves some credit here: it collected the data, reported it publicly to an oversight committee and changed its plans as the results came in. That is what good forecasting looks like in practice, not getting it right the first time but correcting quickly when you are wrong.

The integration of submarines is still young, still small and still uneven. Good data will take another decade to mature. But the early record answers the question that worried the force most in 2010. The fear was that women would wash out, leave early or break crews apart. The numbers so far say the people who chose this life have, on average, stayed with it about as often as anyone else.

takeaways: The ban ended in 2010; officers joined in 2011, enlisted women started training in 2015.
Female officer retention to department head reached 29%, about double the Navy's forecast and slightly above men.
Women are still under 5% of the submarine force, so small differences between groups are not meaningful.
The first female XO and COB came in 2022; a first female CO is projected around 2028.
Forecasts depend on the comparison group you choose: pick the wrong reference class and good math still gives a bad answer.

title: Listening Is Not Waiting to Talk
dek: People will give up real money for the chance to talk about themselves. The person who lets them is supplying something everyone wants and almost nobody provides.

blocks.text: In 2012, two Harvard neuroscientists, Diana Tamir and Jason Mitchell, put people in a brain scanner and offered them a strange menu. On each trial, a volunteer could answer a question about their own opinions, answer a question about someone else, or answer a trivia question. Each option came with a small cash payment, and the researchers set it up so that the self-focused choice often paid less. The question was simple: would people pay to talk about themselves?

They would. Across the experiments, volunteers gave up about 17 percent of what they could have earned just to keep the conversation on themselves. In the scanner, disclosing their own thoughts lit up the nucleus accumbens and the ventral tegmental area, the same reward circuitry that responds to food, money and winning. And it got stronger when they believed their answers would actually be shared with another person rather than kept private. Tamir described sharing as doubly rewarding: thinking about yourself feels good, and being heard feels better.

items.label: Share of everyday speech spent telling others about our own experiences
Portion of potential earnings people gave up to talk about themselves

blocks.source: Tamir & Mitchell, PNAS, 2012

blocks.text: Here is the reframe that falls out of that study. In almost every conversation, both people are hungry for the same thing, and it is in short supply. Everyone wants airtime. Very few people give it. So the person who actually listens, and makes the other person feel heard, is not being passive. They are handing out the scarcest resource in the room.
What active listening actually is

The term comes from the psychologist Carl Rogers and his colleague Richard Farson, who wrote a short booklet called *Active Listening* in 1957. Rogers was a therapist, and his insight was that people change and open up not when they are lectured, but when they feel genuinely understood. Rogers and Farson wanted managers to learn the same skill, which is why the booklet was written for the workplace, not the clinic.

Strip it down and active listening has three parts. First, attention: you are actually tracking what the person says, not rehearsing your reply. Second, understanding: you try to grasp both the content and the feeling underneath it, and you check that understanding by reflecting it back in your own words. Third, restraint: you hold off on judging, fixing or redirecting until the person feels you have got it. That third part is the one most people skip.

The sociologist Charles Derber gave a useful name to what usually happens instead. He noticed that conversations are full of what he called shift responses, where a listener takes what someone said and pivots it to themselves. Someone says their division officer chewed them out, and the reply is a story about a worse chewing-out. The alternative is a support response, which keeps the spotlight on the speaker: what happened, what did he say, how did you handle it. Neither is evil. But a conversation made of nothing but shifts is two people taking turns being ignored.

blocks.title: Two ways to reply to the same sentence

left.head: Waiting to talk
items: Hears a topic, reaches for a matching story
Plans the next line while the other person is still speaking
Offers advice before the problem is fully described
Measures the conversation by how much it went well for them

right.head: Listening
items: Hears a person, tracks what they are trying to say
Lets a pause sit for a second before answering
Reflects the point back, then asks if that is right
Measures the conversation by whether the other person felt understood

blocks.text: The hardest single habit to build is tolerating a short silence. When someone finishes a sentence, there is a strong pull to fill the gap right away, either to show you are engaged or because the quiet feels awkward. But that gap is often where the speaker was about to say the real thing. People rarely lead with what is actually bothering them. They lead with the safe version, check whether you are paying attention, and only then go deeper. A beat of silence, with your eyes still on them, tells them you are still listening and the floor is still theirs. It costs you two seconds and it buys you the part of the story worth hearing.
What the evidence says, and what it doesn't

Active listening has a halo, so it is worth being precise about what research supports. In a 2014 study, the communication researcher Harry Weger and colleagues had 115 people talk about a problem with one of ten trained partners. The partner responded in one of three ways: with active listening (paraphrasing and asking about feelings), with advice, or with simple acknowledgments like nods and short replies.

People who got active listening felt more understood than people in the other two groups. Compared with bare acknowledgments, they were also more satisfied with the conversation and found their partner more socially attractive. But compared with advice, active listening did not make the conversation more satisfying or the partner more likable, and the effects overall were small. The lesson is not that listening is overrated. It is that the mechanical version, the robotic line that starts with what I hear you saying, is not a magic trick. What moves people is feeling understood, and that has to be real.

The bigger picture comes from a 2024 meta-analysis led by Avraham Kluger, one of the main researchers in the field. His team pooled 664 effect sizes covering roughly 400,000 observations of about 155,000 people in workplaces. The question: when people feel listened to at work, what else goes with it?

blocks.title: How strongly feeling listened to tracks work outcomes
blocks.note: Average correlations across studies. The last bar keeps only studies where listening and performance were measured by different people or methods, so it is the most trustworthy.
blocks.source: Kluger et al., Journal of Business and Psychology, 2024

blocks.text: The strongest link by far was with relationship quality: trust, closeness and how good the working relationship felt. That makes sense, and it is the honest headline. The authors flagged a real weakness, too. About three quarters of the studies relied on the same person reporting both how well they were listened to and how well things were going, which inflates correlations. When the team kept only studies that measured performance some other way, the link shrank to about 0.21. That is still meaningful for a single soft skill, but it is correlational, and it is a lot smaller than the headline number.
Why being heard changes people

If listening only made people feel nice, it would be a courtesy. The more interesting finding is that it changes how people think. In a set of four experiments published in 2017, Guy Itzchakov, Kluger and Dotan Castro had people talk about their attitudes on various topics to a listener who was either attentive and nonjudgmental or distracted. Speakers paired with good listeners came out with less extreme views. They also became more aware of the contradictions in their own positions, and more comfortable holding them.

The researchers' explanation is that high-quality listening lowers social anxiety in the speaker. A speaker who does not feel judged stops defending and starts thinking. Tellingly, in their fourth study, the effect on how people handled their own contradictions was stronger for people who were more socially anxious to begin with. The person who most needs to be listened to is often the one who seems hardest to talk to.

Apply that to a cramped space with rank in it. A junior sailor comes to you frustrated about the watchbill. If you jump straight to a fix, or to your own worse story, he leaves still defending his position. If you let him finish, reflect it back and ask one question, he often talks himself into a more reasonable view before you say anything. The same works upward. A chief venting about a failed inspection does not need a solution in the first thirty seconds. He needs to see that the point landed.

blocks.title: Listening when someone brings you a problem
items: Stop the task or the screen. Half-attention is visible from across a berthing.
Let them get to the end of the story before you speak.
Reflect the core of it in one sentence, including how it seems to feel to them.
Ask if you got it right, and let them correct you.
Only then ask whether they want ideas, help, or just to be heard.

blocks.text: You already do this on watch

Anyone who has stood a watch in nuclear propulsion already knows a formal version of active listening. An order is given. The receiver repeats it back word for word. The sender confirms the repeat-back was correct, and only then does anyone act. It feels slow the first week and automatic by the second month.

blocks.title: Three-way communication is listening with a protocol
items: Sender gives the order
Receiver repeats it back
Sender confirms or corrects
Receiver acts and reports

blocks.text: The reason that loop exists is that people mishear each other constantly, and in a reactor plant a misheard number is not a social problem. The repeat-back is a paraphrase with the feelings stripped out. Off watch, the stakes are lower, so people skip the check entirely and act on what they assumed was said. Active listening is basically bringing the repeat-back home, then adding one more layer: checking not only the words but what the person meant by them.
Listening up the chain

Most advice about listening imagines two equals over coffee. Military conversations are rarely like that. A lot of the listening that matters happens when someone senior is talking to you, usually fast, often while doing something else. The failure mode there is not shifting to your own story. It is answering the question you expected instead of the question that was asked.

Picture an engineering officer asking why a maintenance item slipped. The anxious move is to launch into the whole history: the parts delay, the other tasking, the qualification board that ate a day. All true, none of it the answer. The listening move is to hear the actual question, which is usually some version of when will it be done and what do you need, and answer that first. The history can follow if he asks for it. Seniors rarely complain that a junior was too brief and too precise.

Listening also means catching what is underneath a question from above. A chief who asks whether you have looked at a procedure lately may not be asking about reading habits. He may be telling you, politely, that you did something wrong. Hearing the second message is a skill, and the people who pick it up early tend to get handed more responsibility, because they need fewer words to get the point.

items: Answer the question that was asked first, in one or two sentences.
If you are not sure what is being asked, repeat it back: you want to know when it will be done, or why it slipped?
Offer background only if asked, or in one line: I can walk through what happened if that helps.
Before leaving, confirm the next step in their words, not yours.

blocks.text: A note for people who talk a lot

None of this means talking is bad. In a 2020 study in *The Leadership Quarterly*, Neil MacLaren and colleagues tested what researchers call the babble hypothesis: the idea that in a new group, whoever talks the most tends to be picked as the leader. They found that speaking time predicted who emerged as a leader even after accounting for intelligence and personality. Talking a lot gets you noticed, and in some settings it gets you followed.

But being seen as a leader and being trusted are different outcomes, and the meta-analysis above says listening is most tightly tied to the second one. If you are someone who fills silence, the fix is not to go quiet and sit there stiff. It is to change the ratio and the type of what you say. Fewer shift responses, more support responses. Fewer stories that start with that reminds me of the time I, more sentences that start with wait, so what did you do.
A simple rule for talkers: before you tell your matching story, say one sentence about theirs. If they keep going after that sentence, your story can wait. If they hand the floor back, now it fits.

There is a quieter benefit, too. A lot of over-talking comes from worry about how you are coming across. Listening is a relief from that worry, because it gives your attention somewhere to go other than yourself. You cannot monitor your own performance and track someone else's story at the same time. Pick their story, and the self-monitoring loses its grip.

The odd thing about the Tamir and Mitchell result is that everyone in the room is running the same reward circuit. Everyone would pay a little to be heard. Most conversations are two people trying to collect that payment at once. The person who decides to pay out first rarely loses. They usually end up being the one people seek out, confide in and, eventually, follow.

takeaways: People find talking about themselves genuinely rewarding, enough to give up money for it. Being heard is the scarce resource in most conversations.
Active listening is attention, understanding checked by reflecting back, and restraint before advice. Scripted paraphrasing alone is not magic.
Feeling listened to is most strongly linked to relationship quality at work; the link to performance is real but smaller once self-reports are removed.
Good listening lowers a speaker's defensiveness, which often lets them reach a more reasonable view on their own.
For talkers: swap shift responses for support responses, and say one sentence about their story before telling yours.

title: The Power Pose Didn't Survive. Here's What Did.
dek: Body language is full of confident claims: stand like a superhero, 93 percent of communication is nonverbal, liars can't hold eye contact. The evidence behind them ranges from shaky to flat wrong, but there is a real core worth knowing.

blocks.text: In 2012 a Harvard social psychologist named Amy Cuddy gave a TED talk with a simple, irresistible promise. Before a job interview or a big presentation, go somewhere private, a bathroom stall if you have to, and stand like Wonder Woman for two minutes: feet apart, hands on hips, chest open. The pose, she said, could change not just how you feel but your body chemistry, raising testosterone and lowering the stress hormone cortisol. By 2016 more than 36 million people had watched it.

It is one of the most watched science talks ever made, and the most famous claim in it did not hold up. The story of how it fell apart is one of the best case studies in modern psychology, and it is worth knowing in detail, because nearly every other piece of body language advice you'll hear works the same way: a small, exciting finding becomes a rule, and the rule outlives the evidence.
The rise and fall of the power pose

The talk was built on a 2010 study by Dana Carney, Cuddy and Andy Yap, published in *Psychological Science*. It had 42 participants. Those who held expansive 'high-power' poses reportedly showed a rise in testosterone, a drop in cortisol, more willingness to take a financial risk and stronger feelings of being in charge. Forty-two people is a small sample for claims that big, but at the time that was common.

In 2015 a team led by Eva Ranehill at the University of Zurich ran the experiment again with 200 participants, measuring the same things. The poses did make people *say* they felt more powerful. But there was no effect on testosterone, no effect on cortisol and no effect on risk-taking. Other labs reported similar results. One 2016 study found no effect on risk-taking and, awkwardly, found that the expansive pose made people feel slightly *less* powerful. Another, which put people through a standard lab stress test, found no hormonal, behavioral or emotional effect at all.

blocks.title: How the power pose story unfolded
items: Carney, Cuddy & Yap report hormone and risk effects from 42 participants
Cuddy's TED talk takes the idea mainstream
Ranehill et al. test 200 people: feelings change, hormones and risk-taking don't
Lead author Dana Carney publicly says she no longer believes the effects are real
A special issue of preregistered studies finds no effect on power behaviors
Cuddy and colleagues argue the evidence for effects on feelings is strong
A meta-analysis of about 130 studies finds effects on feelings, not hormones

blocks.text: Then came the moment that made the story famous. In 2016 Carney, the lead author of the original paper, posted a statement on her faculty website saying she no longer believed power pose effects were real. She pointed to failed replications and said that, looking back, the original analysis had involved choices that made a positive result more likely. NPR called that kind of public reversal almost unprecedented. Cuddy disagreed and said she remained confident that expansive postures affect how powerful people feel.

In 2017 the journal *Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology* published a special issue of eleven new studies whose methods and outcomes were registered in advance, which keeps researchers from fishing for results after the fact. Pooled together, they found no effect on behavior. They found a medium-sized effect on feelings of power, though the authors couldn't rule out that it came from participants guessing what the study was about.
What actually survived

The most complete look so far is a 2022 meta-analysis in *Psychological Bulletin* by Robert Körner, Leonie Röseler, Astrid Schütz and Brad Bushman, covering roughly 130 experiments and about 10,000 people. Its verdict is a useful model of a measured conclusion.

blocks.title: Power posing: the claim vs the evidence

left.head: The original claim
items: Two minutes changes your hormones
You'll take bolder risks
You'll perform better in interviews
The pose is a physiological hack

right.head: What the evidence supports
items: No reliable effect on testosterone or cortisol
No consistent effect on risk-taking
Behavior effects are weak and unclear
Upright, open posture does tend to make people feel a bit more confident

blocks.text: Upright, dominant postures were reliably linked to people feeling more confident and positive about themselves. Effects on behavior, like how long people persisted at a task, showed up but were less robust. The hormone claims found no support. And there's a catch: most studies compared a power pose with a slumped pose, without a neutral group. So it may be that slouching makes you feel a bit worse, rather than that superhero stances make you feel better.

So here's the honest summary. Standing tall before something stressful probably won't hurt and might give you a small lift in how you feel. It will not rewire your chemistry or turn you into a different person in a meeting. If it helps you walk in calmer, do it. Just don't expect it to do the work that preparation does.

It's worth asking why the idea spread so fast and stuck so hard. It asked almost nothing of you: two minutes, no equipment, no practice. It came with a physical mechanism that sounded scientific. And the one part that does seem real, feeling a bit more in charge right afterward, is exactly the part you'd notice when you tried it. People felt the lift, assumed the hormones were doing it, and told their friends. The genuine feeling made the false explanation feel confirmed.

The power pose story has a lesson beyond posture: a confident claim, a great talk and a huge audience are not evidence. Small studies with big, surprising effects are exactly the ones most likely to shrink.
The 93 percent myth

You've probably heard that only 7 percent of communication is words, 38 percent is tone of voice and 55 percent is body language. It shows up in corporate trainings and leadership books as if it were a law of physics. If it were true, you could understand most of a foreign-language film with the sound off.

The numbers come from two small experiments by the psychologist Albert Mehrabian in the late 1960s. In one, 30 women heard single words spoken in positive, neutral or negative tones, sometimes with the tone and word mismatched. In the other, 37 women saw photos of facial expressions paired with spoken words. The task was narrow: judge the speaker's feeling when the cues *conflicted*. In that situation, people trusted tone and face over the literal word.

Mehrabian himself later said the formula doesn't apply to communication in general. On his website he wrote that unless someone is talking about their feelings or attitudes, the equations don't apply. The real finding is narrower and still useful: when someone's words and delivery clash, as in a flat, eye-rolling 'great job,' people believe the delivery. That's worth knowing. It's just not a percentage of all communication.

The flip side shows up whenever the nonverbal channel is missing. In a 2005 set of experiments, Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that people writing emails overestimated how clearly their tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness, would come across to the reader. The writer hears the voice in their head. The reader gets only the words. That is why a dry joke in a text can land as an insult, and why anything with emotional weight, a disagreement, bad news, a correction, usually goes better face to face or at least out loud.
Nobody can read lies from fidgeting

Another durable belief: liars give themselves away by avoiding eye contact, touching their face or fidgeting. Movies, cop shows and plenty of interrogation trainings lean on this. The data are humbling. In 2006 Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo pooled 206 studies covering 24,483 people judging whether someone was lying or telling the truth.

blocks.title: How often people correctly judge lies and truths
blocks.note: Pure guessing would get 50 percent overall. People do slightly better than chance, mostly by assuming others are honest.
blocks.source: Bond & DePaulo, Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2006

blocks.text: Average accuracy was 54 percent, barely above a coin flip. People were better at recognizing truths than lies, mainly because they default to believing others. The reason is that there is no reliable body language tell for lying. Nervousness, gaze aversion and fidgeting come from anxiety, and honest people get anxious too, especially when they suspect they're not being believed.

That cuts both ways for you. You can't reliably read deception off someone's posture, so don't trust anyone who says they can. And if you're nervous in a conversation with a senior person, your fidgeting is far less informative to them than you fear. They're not decoding your hands. They're mostly listening to what you say.

This connects to a well-studied bias called the illusion of transparency: people overestimate how visible their inner nervousness is to others. Your racing heart and the tension in your stomach feel obvious from the inside, but most of it never reaches the surface. Listeners usually rate speakers as noticeably calmer than the speakers rate themselves.
What body language really does

None of this means nonverbal behavior doesn't matter. It matters a lot, just not in the ways the myths claim. The strongest evidence is about impressions, not hidden truths. In a 1993 study, Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal showed strangers silent video clips of college teachers, three 10-second clips per teacher, and had them rate qualities like warmth, confidence and enthusiasm. Those snap ratings tracked the teachers' end-of-semester student evaluations closely.

items.label: Of silent video per teacher (three 10-second clips)
Correlation between snap ratings and end-of-semester evaluations

blocks.source: Ambady & Rosenthal, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1993

blocks.text: That's a strong correlation, though from a small sample of 13 college teachers, plus a high school group with a somewhat weaker result. The lesson isn't that strangers can see your true ability in half a minute. It's that people form impressions of energy, warmth and engagement fast, and those impressions stick. Whether those impressions are accurate is a separate question. What's clear is that they're formed.

Most of what counts is ordinary: facing the person you're talking to, natural eye contact, a relaxed face, not being buried in your phone. None of that is a hack. It's the visible version of paying attention. People read it as interest because it usually is interest.

Context changes the meaning of almost every signal. Eye contact that reads as confident in one culture can read as challenging in another, and common hand gestures carry different meanings in different countries. Military life adds its own layer. Standing at attention or parade rest isn't a personality signal at all; it's a protocol that communicates respect for the situation, and everyone reads it that way. Knowing which rules apply in the room you're in matters more than any universal list of power moves.

blocks.title: Body language worth practicing
items: Stand or sit so you can breathe fully. It helps your voice more than it changes your hormones.
Face people when they talk and put the phone away. It's the clearest signal that you're listening.
Match your delivery to your words. When they clash, people believe the delivery.
Watch for clusters, not single signs: shorter answers, glances away and shifting weight together often mean it's time to wrap up.
Ignore anyone selling lie detection from gestures. The evidence isn't there.

blocks.text: That fourth step is the most useful for anyone who tends to talk too long. Single cues mean little, since someone glancing at the clock might just be checking the time. But when several show up together, replies getting shorter, eyes drifting, body angled away, the other person is usually telling you they're ready to move on. Reading that and wrapping up gracefully is one of the most practical uses of body language there is.

If you want to actually see your own body language, there is a cheap and slightly painful drill. Record yourself on your phone explaining something for one minute, the way you'd brief it to someone senior. Watch it once with the sound off and once with your eyes closed. With the sound off, you'll notice whether you look at the listener or at the floor, and whether your hands help or just wander. With eyes closed, you'll hear pace, filler words and where you trail off. It's the same skill a YouTube creator builds by rewatching footage, and it beats any list of rules because the feedback is about you.

The bigger reframe is that body language works best as a readout, not a costume. Trying to fake confidence with a pose is mostly theater. Being prepared, being interested in the person in front of you and paying attention to how they're responding shows up in your body on its own. The posture follows the substance far more reliably than the other way around.

takeaways: Power poses don't change hormones; upright posture may give a small boost in how confident you feel.
The 7-38-55 rule only applied to judging feelings from conflicting cues, by Mehrabian's own account.
People spot lies at about 54 percent accuracy; there is no reliable body language tell.
Impressions of warmth and energy form fast, so the basics (face people, eye contact, phone away) matter.
Read clusters of signals, like shorter replies plus wandering eyes, as a cue to wrap up.
