title: Nobody Knows When to Leave
dek: Only about 2 percent of conversations end when both people want them to. Hanging on longer won't make anyone like you more. Learning to end well might.

blocks.text: Two strangers sit down in a lab at Harvard. The instructions are loose: talk about whatever you like, for as little as one minute or as long as 45. When you are done, either of you can end it. They chat about classes, hometowns, a show they both watched. Eventually the conversation winds down and they go to separate rooms.

Then each gets a private question. Was there a point when you wanted this to end? If so, when? And when do you think your partner wanted it to end? Neither will ever see the other's answers. That privacy is the whole point, because it lets the researchers measure something polite people never say out loud.

The study, published in *PNAS* in 2021 by Adam Mastroianni, Daniel Gilbert, Gus Cooney and Timothy Wilson, looked at 932 conversations in total. Its headline result is almost funny once you see it: conversations hardly ever end when the people in them want them to.
The 2 percent problem

The research had two parts. In the first, just over 800 people filled out an online survey about the last conversation they had, which was usually with a partner, a relative or a friend. In the second, the lab study, 252 strangers were paired up and talked for as long as they chose. Both studies asked the same core question: how did the actual length compare with the length each person wanted?

items.label: Lab conversations that ended when both people wanted them to
Ended when even one of the two wanted them to
How far off people were, as a share of conversation length, when guessing when their partner wanted to stop

blocks.source: Mastroianni et al., PNAS, 2021

blocks.text: Among the stranger pairs, about 2 percent of conversations ended at the moment both people wanted. Only 30 percent ended when at least one of them wanted. In both studies, the gap between how long people wanted to talk and how long they actually talked averaged around half the length of the conversation. That is not a rounding error. Picture a ten-minute chat in which one person would have preferred about five minutes, or about fifteen.

And the mismatch ran in both directions. In about 46 percent of the stranger conversations, both people had wanted to stop earlier than they did. In about 10 percent, both had wanted to keep going. Roughly 69 percent of strangers said there was a moment they felt ready to leave, and about two thirds of the survey group said the same about conversations with people they knew well.

blocks.title: How stranger conversations actually ended
blocks.note: Categories overlap and are not meant to add to 100. The point: the real ending almost never matched anyone's wish.
blocks.source: Mastroianni et al., PNAS, 2021 (reported in Harvard Gazette)

blocks.text: A coordination problem, not a personality flaw

Why does this happen? Mastroianni's explanation is not that people are bad at conversation. It is that ending a conversation well is a coordination problem with hidden information. Two people almost never want to stop at the same moment. To coordinate, they would have to reveal what they want. But revealing it is rude. Nobody says, at minute nine, I would like to be done in about ninety seconds. So everyone hides the signal, and everyone guesses.

The guesses are bad. When the strangers estimated when their partner had wanted to stop, they were off by about 64 percent of the conversation's length. That number deserves to sink in, because it destroys a strategy that a lot of people run without noticing. The strategy goes like this: I will keep the conversation going until I can tell the other person is ready, so I never seem like I am the one cutting it short. The data says you cannot tell. You are not reading the room. You are guessing, and your guesses are close to random.

For anyone who keeps conversations alive out of fear the other person will not like them, this is genuinely useful news. Staying longer is not a safe default. It is a bet placed with a broken instrument. In nearly half of stranger conversations, the other person was already waiting for an exit too. Your extra five minutes were not buying their approval. They were costing both of you.

The flip side matters as well. Nearly a third of strangers never hit a point where they wanted to leave. So when you end a conversation and the other person seems a little surprised, that is not proof you offended them. Sometimes they would happily have kept going. That is fine. An ending is not a verdict on the relationship. It is just a place to stop.
You cannot reliably read when someone wants to leave, so do not wait for a signal you will never detect. Decide the ending yourself, warmly, and let the next conversation happen.

There is another bias quietly at work here. Research by Erica Boothby and colleagues on what they called the liking gap found that after a conversation, people consistently underestimate how much their partner liked them. Put that together with the 2 percent problem and you get a predictable pattern: we stay too long because we think we need to earn more approval, when we already had more of it than we realized.
How goodbyes actually work

If ending conversations is so hard, how does anyone do it? Linguists have studied this closely. In a famous 1973 paper called *Opening Up Closings*, the sociologists Emanuel Schegloff and Harvey Sacks pointed out that conversations do not just stop. People can't simply fall silent, because in a conversation silence after your turn means something. So closings are built from a short ritual.

The key move is what they called a pre-closing. It is a turn that adds nothing new: okay, well, alright then, so yeah. By saying it, you offer to hand the conversation back without starting a new topic. If the other person also passes, with a matching okay or alright, you have both silently agreed to wrap up, and the goodbye follows. If instead they bring up something new, the conversation reopens. The whole negotiation takes two seconds and nobody has to say I want to leave.

That same year, the communication researcher Mark Knapp and colleagues filmed students interviewing people and coded exactly what they did as they wrapped up. In words, leave-taking leaned on a few predictable moves: a burst of agreement like yeah or right, buffer words like well, expressions of appreciation, and polite follow-up questions. In body language, the strongest signals were breaking eye contact, turning the body toward the exit, leaning forward and nodding. Those cues clustered in the final 15 seconds before people stood up.

Knapp's team concluded that goodbyes do two jobs at once. They signal that you are about to become unavailable, and they reassure the other person that the relationship is fine. Both halves matter. Signal without warmth feels like rejection. Warmth without signal is how you end up still standing in the passageway twenty minutes later.

blocks.title: The anatomy of a clean exit
items: Wait for a natural pause, ideally after a laugh or a point that landed.
Use a pre-closing: alright, well, or so yeah, and let a beat pass.
Add warmth: one line that shows the conversation mattered.
Give a reason or a next step if there is one, kept short and true.
Say goodbye and actually move. Do not open a new topic at the door.

blocks.text: End on a high

There is a reason to leave a little early rather than a little late, and it comes from a very unpleasant experiment. In 1993, Daniel Kahneman and colleagues had people hold a hand in water at 14 degrees Celsius for 60 seconds. On another trial, they did the same 60 seconds, then kept their hand in for another 30 seconds while the water warmed slightly, to about 15 degrees. The second trial contained strictly more pain. It just ended less badly.

items.label: People who chose to repeat the longer, more painful trial because it ended slightly better

blocks.source: Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier, Psychological Science, 1993

blocks.text: When asked which trial they would rather repeat, 69 percent picked the longer one. This became one of the clearest demonstrations of what Kahneman called the peak-end rule: memory does not add up an experience minute by minute. It stores a few snapshots, especially the most intense moment and the ending, and judges the whole thing by those.

To be honest about the evidence, nobody has run the cold-water experiment on conversations. Applying it here is an analogy, not a finding. But it is a reasonable one, and it fits common experience. A conversation that ends right after a good laugh is remembered as a good conversation. The same conversation stretched for another ten minutes until it fizzles into a long silence and a weak see you around is remembered as a bit awkward, even though it contained the exact same good moment. The extra time did not add to the memory. It overwrote the ending.

For someone who worries about being liked, this flips the usual instinct. The fear says: if it is going well, keep it going, because ending is risky. The peak-end rule says: if it is going well, that is the best possible moment to end it, because the ending is what they will remember.
If you are the one who keeps it going

Most people in these studies wanted out sooner than they got out. But some people are the reason conversations run long, and many of them know it. The pattern usually looks the same from the inside: the conversation hits a natural lull, a small spike of worry shows up that the silence means it went badly, and the fix for that worry is one more story, one more question, one more thought. Each extension feels like it rescues the moment. Added together, they turn a good five-minute talk into a draggy fifteen.

The useful move is to catch that spike and treat it as a signal to close rather than to extend. The lull is not evidence that the conversation failed. It is the most natural exit door the conversation is ever going to offer you. Using it is not rude. Walking past it, again and again, is what slowly spends down the goodwill the conversation had built. A rough personal rule helps: when you notice yourself reaching for a new topic just to avoid the silence, say a pre-closing instead and see what happens. Usually the other person takes it gratefully.
Exits that work with rank in the room

On a submarine, a lot of conversations have a built-in end: the watch turnover, the drill, the next evolution. The hard ones are the open-ended ones, in the mess, in a passageway, or in someone's office after the business is done. Rank changes who should end those, and how.

With a senior, the default is to let them close, but to be very quick at noticing the pre-closing. When a chief says alright, glances at his screen or turns back to the paperwork, that is the cue. The polite move is to match it immediately, not to add one more thought. A crisp exit with a senior also tends to read as competence. You said what you came to say and got out of their way.
With peers and juniors, you can and should close. A few lines do most of the work, and they work because they are honest and warm at the same time:

items: I'll let you get back to it. Good talking with you.
Alright, I need to go knock out my quals card. Catch you at chow.
That's a good place to leave it. Thanks for walking me through that.
I've got to run, but I want to hear how the board goes.

blocks.text: Notice what these have in common. None of them apologize. None of them explain at length. Each one signals that you are leaving and reassures that it is fine, which is exactly the double job Knapp's team identified. The over-explained exit, with three reasons and a sorry, often lands worse than the simple one, because it hints that leaving is a problem.

blocks.title: Two ways to leave the same conversation

left.head: Dragging it out
items: Waits for the other person to show they want out
Fills every lull with a new topic
Apologizes and justifies at length
Leaves after the energy is gone

right.head: Landing it
items: Decides the ending without waiting for a sign
Uses a pre-closing and lets it work
One warm line, one honest reason
Leaves while it is still good

blocks.text: The deepest point in the Mastroianni study is not really about time. It is about how little we know about what is going on in the other person's head, and how often we fill that gap with fear. Almost nobody in those 932 conversations got the ending they wanted. That is not a failure anyone can fix by trying harder to read minds. The only real lever you have is your own exit. Pull it a little earlier, pull it warmly, and you will be leaving most people right where they wanted to be left.

takeaways: Only about 2% of conversations in the lab ended when both people wanted; the gap between wanted and actual length averaged about half the conversation.
People guess their partner's wishes badly, off by about 64% of the conversation's length. Staying longer to be safe is a bet you cannot read.
Closings run on a short ritual: a pre-closing like alright or well, a warm line, then the goodbye.
Memory weights the peak and the end. Leaving after a high point beats letting a good conversation fizzle.
With seniors, catch their pre-closing fast; with peers and juniors, end it yourself, warmly and without apologizing.

title: Feedback Backfires More Than a Third of the Time
dek: The biggest review of feedback research ever done found it often makes people worse. What separates the feedback that works, and how to give it, take it and send it up the chain.

blocks.text: In the early 1990s, two psychologists, Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi, set out to answer a question that seemed almost too obvious to ask. Does feedback improve performance? Managers, teachers and coaches all assumed it did. Entire systems, from performance evaluations to report cards, were built on that assumption. Kluger and DeNisi decided to check by pulling together every solid experiment they could find.

They ended up with 607 effect sizes, covering more than 23,000 observations, and published the result in 1996. On average, feedback did help. The average improvement was moderate, about four tenths of a standard deviation. But buried under that average was a number that should have shaken every workplace in the country: in more than a third of the cases, feedback made performance worse than giving no feedback at all.

items.label: Effect sizes pooled in the largest early review of feedback
Average improvement from feedback, in standard deviations
Feedback interventions that lowered performance

blocks.source: Kluger & DeNisi, Psychological Bulletin, 1996

blocks.text: Not occasionally. Not in a few strange studies. More than a third of the time. That means the question is never really whether to give feedback. It is which kind, because the wrong kind is not neutral. It actively costs you.
Where attention goes, performance follows

Kluger and DeNisi's explanation centers on attention. Feedback, they argued, works by redirecting where a person's attention goes. If it points attention at the task, at the specific steps, the details of what went right and wrong, performance tends to improve. If it pulls attention up and away from the task, toward the self, it tends to hurt. Feedback like you are careless, you are a natural, or that was disappointing coming from you turns the conversation from what happened into who you are.

Once a person's attention moves to their own identity, they are no longer thinking about the valve lineup or the paragraph or the free throw. They are defending themselves, or basking, or worrying about how they look. Either way the task is no longer the focus. It is a striking result because it means even praise can backfire if it is aimed at the person instead of the work.

blocks.title: Same mistake, two kinds of feedback

left.head: Aimed at the self
items: You always rush this.
You're not cut out for this watch station.
Great job, you're a natural.
I expected better from you.

right.head: Aimed at the task
items: You skipped the second independent verification on step 4.
Your log entries were late on the last two readings.
The way you called out that alarm was exactly right.
Next time, check the tag-out before you open the panel.

blocks.text: If you think about the best feedback you have ever received, it probably had a few things in common. It was specific. It was about something you did, not something you are. It came soon enough to be useful. And it pointed toward something you could actually change next time. Every one of those features keeps attention on the task, which is exactly what the meta-analysis says matters.
Why good criticism still bounces off

Even accurate, task-focused criticism often fails for a different reason: the person receiving it does not trust why it is being given. Criticism is ambiguous. It could mean I want you to get better. It could also mean I do not like you, or I do not think you can do this. When people are unsure which, they often protect themselves by dismissing it.

A 2014 study by David Yeager, Geoffrey Cohen and colleagues tested a fix. Seventh graders wrote essays, and their teachers marked them up with critical comments as usual. Then, randomly, each student's essay came back with one of two sticky notes. One was bland: I'm giving you these comments so you'll have feedback on your paper. The other made the purpose explicit: the teacher was giving these comments because they had very high standards and believed the student could reach them. The researchers called this wise feedback.

blocks.title: Black students who acted on critical feedback
blocks.note: First pair: share who chose to revise when revision was optional. Second pair: share whose scores improved when revision was required.
blocks.source: Yeager, Purdie-Vaughns, Cohen et al., JEP: General, 2014 (via Stanford SPARQ)

blocks.text: The effect was largest for Black students, a group the researchers expected to have more reason to doubt a teacher's motives. Among them, 64 percent chose to revise with the wise note, compared with 27 percent with the standard note. When revision was required, 88 percent of those who got the wise note improved their scores, compared with 34 percent. For White students, most revised in both conditions, and the note made a smaller, not statistically significant difference. These are school results, in a specific setting, but the principle is general and it applies directly to a division.

A chief who says this is wrong, redo it gets compliance. A chief who says I'm on you about this because you're going to be the one running this space in a year, and I know you can, gets effort. The criticism is the same. The second version tells the sailor how to read it: as investment, not attack.
Taking it: the novice-expert switch

Receiving feedback is its own skill, and there is a revealing finding about who seeks what. In 2012, Stacey Finkelstein and Ayelet Fishbach ran a series of studies across areas as different as learning a language and environmental activism. Novices tended to seek and respond to positive feedback. Experts tended to seek and respond to negative feedback.

The explanation is about motivation. When you are new, positive feedback answers the question you actually have, which is whether you belong and should keep going. Once you are committed, that question is settled, and the more useful question becomes how fast you are improving. Negative feedback answers that one. So the kind of feedback you ask for is a quiet signal of where you are. People who ask what did I get wrong, and mean it, are acting like experts even before they are.

This connects to anything you have trained for seriously. Climbing a competitive ladder in a game, the players who improve fastest are usually the ones who watch their own losses, not their highlight clips. The same is true on a qual card. The checkout that hurts a bit is usually the one that taught you the most.

What about feedback that is just wrong, or delivered badly? It happens, especially in a stressed crew on a long underway. Even then, the useful move is usually to hunt for the part that is true before you deal with the part that is not. A chief who chews you out loudly for something that was mostly someone else's fault may still have a point about the one step you did skip. Take that piece, fix it, and raise the rest later, calmly and in private, with facts. Arguing in the moment rarely works, because both of you are now thinking about yourselves instead of the task.

blocks.title: Taking hard feedback without flinching
items: Let them finish. Do not defend while they are still talking.
Say thanks and mean it. It was probably uncomfortable for them too.
Ask one clarifying question: what would good look like there?
Separate the what from the who. Most feedback is about a task, even when it stings personally.
Decide later, not in the moment, which parts you will act on.

blocks.text: Giving it when you are the senior

Once you pick up a few stripes, you become the one giving feedback, often to people barely younger than you who were your peers a year ago. That transition is awkward for almost everyone. The two common failure modes are opposites. One is going soft: hinting, joking, or saying nothing because you still want to be liked. The other is overcorrecting into a harsh voice you think a leader is supposed to have.

Both miss the point the research keeps making. The junior does not need you to be nice or tough. They need you to be clear about the task and clear about why you are telling them. A useful pattern is short and fits in a passageway: what you saw, why it matters, what good looks like, and that you expect them to get there. You logged the readings twenty minutes late. If the plant had been trending, nobody would have caught it. I need them on time every hour. You are better than that log shows. That is under fifteen seconds and it hits every element of wise, task-focused feedback.

Two more habits help. Give feedback privately when it is corrective and publicly when it is praise for specific work, because public criticism almost guarantees the receiver's attention goes straight to their own image. And give it soon. Feedback delivered a week later is about a version of the event that only exists in two fuzzy memories, and arguing about what really happened is just another way attention leaves the task.
Sending it up the chain

The hardest feedback to give is the kind that goes upward: telling a senior that a plan has a problem, a procedure is wrong, or a decision is going to cause trouble. Research on workplaces suggests most people hold back. In a 2003 study, Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison and Patricia Hewlin interviewed 40 professionals about times they had stayed silent. Thirty-four of them, 85 percent, described at least one occasion when they felt unable to raise an issue they thought was important.

blocks.title: Why people stayed silent with their bosses
blocks.note: Small exploratory study of 40 people; respondents could give more than one reason.
blocks.source: Milliken, Morrison & Hewlin, Journal of Management Studies, 2003

blocks.text: The most common reason was not fear of punishment. It was fear of being seen as a complainer or troublemaker, followed closely by worry about damaging the relationship. This is a small study and should not be stretched too far, but the pattern rings true: most upward silence is social, not disciplinary.

On a submarine, upward silence is not just a career issue. It can be a safety issue. Nuclear training hammers in ideas like a questioning attitude and forceful backup for exactly this reason: in a high-consequence plant, the junior person who sees something off has to say so, even when the senior person seems sure. The culture already gives permission. What it does not give you is the words.

items: Lead with the bottom line and the stakes: I think we have a problem with the lineup on the second pump.
Give the facts, not a judgment of the person: the procedure calls for this valve shut, and it reads open.
Offer a path: can we stop and verify before we start it?
If overruled on a judgment call, accept it, and make sure the concern is on record. If it is a safety or procedure issue, use the backup the system gives you.

blocks.text: Notice that this is just the task-focused rule applied in the other direction. Feedback that goes up the chain lands best when it is about the procedure, the reading, the plan, and not about the senior's competence. Nobody needs to hear you messed this up. Everyone can hear this reading does not match the procedure.
The debrief: feedback without the sting

If you want a type of feedback that reliably works, the military already has one. After-action reviews and debriefs ask a short set of questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why there was a difference, and what to sustain or change next time. Everyone talks, rank is set aside as much as possible, and the focus stays on the event.

Scott Tannenbaum and Christopher Cerasoli pooled the research on debriefs in a 2013 meta-analysis covering 46 samples and more than 2,100 people. Well-run debriefs improved performance by roughly 20 to 25 percent compared with groups that did not debrief. Debriefs that were aligned with real goals got a clear boost, and the authors flagged facilitation and structure as likely to help as well, rather than letting the discussion drift.

items.label: Average performance gain from debriefs over control groups
Samples in the meta-analysis

blocks.source: Tannenbaum & Cerasoli, Human Factors, 2013

blocks.text: Put the two meta-analyses side by side and the debrief makes sense. It is feedback aimed squarely at the task, gathered from everyone involved, given soon after the event, and pointed at what to do next. It is very hard for a well-run debrief to turn into a referendum on who someone is, which is exactly the failure mode Kluger and DeNisi found.

Before giving any feedback, ask yourself one question: will this point their attention at the task or at themselves? If it is about the task, say it plainly. If it is about the person, rewrite it until it is about the work.

The old advice to wrap criticism in praise, the feedback sandwich, gets this partly backwards. People learn quickly that praise is just the bread before the but, and they stop hearing it. Better to say the real thing clearly, explain why you are saying it, and keep it about the work. That is uncomfortable for a few seconds. Then it is useful for a long time.

takeaways: In the biggest early review, feedback helped on average but made performance worse in more than a third of cases.
Feedback works when it points attention at the task and backfires when it points at the person, even if it is praise.
Telling someone why you are critiquing them, high standards plus belief they can meet them, made people far more likely to act on it.
Novices seek praise, experts seek correction. Asking what did I get wrong is an expert move.
Send concerns up the chain with the bottom line, the facts and a proposed fix, never a judgment of the senior.

title: Most Laughter Isn't About Jokes
dek: Scientists who study humor keep finding that laughter is mostly a social signal and that funny lives in a narrow zone between wrong and okay. Knowing where that zone is changes how you use humor at work and with friends.

blocks.text: In the 1990s a neuroscientist named Robert Provine did something odd for a scientist who studied laughter. He stopped showing people comedy in the lab and went out to shopping malls, college campuses and sidewalks with a notebook. Whenever someone nearby laughed, he wrote down what had been said just before. Over years, he collected thousands of examples of natural laughter in the wild.

What he found was that almost none of it followed anything funny. The line before a laugh was usually something like 'I'll see you guys later,' 'are you sure?' or 'it was nice meeting you, too.' By his estimate, only about 10 to 15 percent of the comments that triggered laughter were even remotely humorous. Most laughter was not a reaction to a joke. It was punctuation in a conversation between people who liked each other.

items.label: Of pre-laugh comments that were even remotely funny
More likely to laugh: speakers vs their listeners
More laughter in social settings than when alone

blocks.source: Provine, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2004 (via APA Monitor, 2006)

blocks.text: Two more numbers made the point sharper. Speakers laughed more than their audiences did, about 46 percent more often. And laughter was roughly 30 times more frequent in social situations than in solitary ones. Alone, people were more likely to smile or talk to themselves than to laugh out loud. Laughter, in other words, is something we do *to* each other far more than something that happens *to* us.

That reframes what it means to be funny. The comedian on stage is the rare, extreme case. In everyday life, humor is mostly a bonding tool, a way of signaling 'we're on the same side, we're relaxed, this is safe.' Which raises the real question: if laughter is mostly social, what makes something actually funny when it is?
The benign violation

Philosophers have argued about humor for over two thousand years. Plato and Hobbes thought it came from feeling superior. Later thinkers pointed to incongruity, the surprise of something not fitting the pattern. Freud saw it as a release of pent-up tension. Each theory explains some jokes and fails on others. Puns aren't about superiority. Plenty of incongruous things, like a car crash, aren't funny.

In 2010, Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren at the University of Colorado proposed a simple, testable version. Humor happens, they argued, when three things are true at once: something seems wrong, threatening or a violation of how things should be; it also seems okay, safe or benign; and you perceive both at the same time. If it's only a violation, it's upsetting. If it's only benign, it's boring. The narrow overlap is where laughs live.

blocks.title: The benign violation zone
items: Something breaks a rule, a norm or an expectation
But it is safe, harmless or not really serious
You see both at the same moment
Result: amusement and laughter

blocks.text: Tickling is the textbook case. It's a mock attack, a physical violation, from someone you trust. That's why you can't tickle yourself (no violation) and why a stranger tickling you isn't funny (not benign). Play fighting, teasing between friends and slapstick all fit the same pattern: something looks like a threat, and everyone knows it isn't.

The same logic stretches further than you'd expect. A pun breaks the rules of language, one word doing two jobs it shouldn't, but nobody gets hurt. A game glitch that launches a character into orbit violates physics in a world where nothing is real. That's a big part of why fail compilations and bug clips do so well online: they are pure benign violations. Something has gone badly, obviously wrong, and the stakes are zero.
Testing it on uncomfortable stories

McGraw and Warren tested the idea with scenarios designed to be morally uncomfortable. In one experiment, people read short stories in two versions. One described a mild moral violation; the other described the same situation without it. Violation versions were judged wrong far more often, 69 percent versus 2 percent. They also got far more laughter: 44 percent of readers reported laughing at the violation versions versus 5 percent for the controls.

blocks.title: People who reported laughing at a short scenario
blocks.note: The same readers judged the violation versions wrong 69% of the time.
blocks.source: McGraw & Warren, Psychological Science, 2010 (Study 1)

blocks.text: The more interesting experiments tested what makes a violation feel benign. One way is weak attachment to the rule being broken. In one study, people read about a church that raffled off a Hummer SUV to raise money. Churchgoers and non-churchgoers were about equally disgusted. But non-churchgoers, who cared less about the norm being violated, were far more amused: 92 percent versus 62 percent.

A third route is a competing norm that makes the act seem acceptable. In another scenario, a man rubs a kitten against his body. When the story said the kitten seemed to enjoy it, 61 percent of readers were amused; when it said the kitten whined, 28 percent were. Disgust was nearly universal in both versions. What changed was whether anything was actually being harmed.

Another way is distance. In a different study, people were nudged to feel either far from or close to a bizarre, gross scenario before reading it. Disgust was about the same either way. Amusement wasn't. Among people primed to feel distant, 73 percent were amused, compared with 39 percent of those primed to feel close.

blocks.title: Same gross scenario, different distance
blocks.note: Distance barely changed disgust but nearly doubled amusement.
blocks.source: McGraw & Warren, Psychological Science, 2010 (Study 5)

blocks.text: These were small samples, between 36 and 80 people per study, and benign violation theory is one serious contender among several rather than a settled law. Critics argue it's broad enough to fit almost anything after the fact. But it makes useful, specific predictions, and it explains something everyone has noticed: the same joke can kill in one room and bomb in another, because whether a violation feels benign depends on who's hearing it.
'Too soon' is benign violation theory in two words. Time is a form of distance. Something painful becomes funny once it's far enough away to feel safe, and not a moment before.
Why dark humor thrives in hard jobs

This explains a pattern familiar to anyone in the military, medicine or emergency work: the darker the job, the darker the jokes. Those environments are full of real violations, danger, discomfort, absurd rules, things that genuinely go wrong. Humor reframes them as manageable. When a crew jokes about a brutal field day or a fourteen-hour watch rotation, it isn't denying that the situation is hard. It's declaring together that the situation is survivable.

It works best inside the group that shares the hardship. The same joke told to an outsider can sound callous, because for them the violation isn't softened by shared experience. And it has a limit. When every serious thing gets deflected with a joke, humor stops being a way of carrying the load together and becomes a way of never talking about it. If someone's jokes about how they're doing start sounding less like jokes, it's worth asking them straight.

There's even evidence laughter does something physical for groups. In studies published in 2012, Robin Dunbar's team at Oxford had people watch comedy, including in groups and at live shows at the Edinburgh Fringe, while control groups watched dry factual videos like golf. Afterward they measured pain tolerance with cold, a tight blood pressure cuff and hard exercise. After social laughter, pain tolerance went up by about 10 percent on average; in the control groups it didn't rise. The researchers suspect endorphins released by laughing, though they didn't measure endorphins directly.

items.label: Average rise in pain tolerance after about 15 minutes of laughing at comedy with others

blocks.source: Dunbar et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2012

blocks.text: Dunbar's broader argument is that social laughter evolved as a way to bond larger groups than one-on-one grooming could handle. Whether or not that story is right, the practical point holds: shared laughter seems to make people feel closer and tougher at the same time. On a crew that lives in close quarters for months, that's not a small thing.
Humor at work: a high-risk, high-reward move

So should you try to be funny at work? A set of experiments by Brad Bitterly, Alison Wood Brooks and Maurice Schweitzer at Wharton and Harvard, published in 2017, gives a nuanced answer. Successful humor made people seem more confident and more competent, which raised their status. In one study, people who used humor well were more likely to be picked to lead a group later.

But the effect cut both ways. Any attempt at humor signaled confidence, because joking is risky and only confident people risk it. Whether that confidence turned into status depended on whether the joke landed and fit the moment. Jokes that fell flat, or were inappropriate, signaled poor judgment and lowered status. Confidence plus bad judgment reads worse than quiet competence.

Text makes all of this harder. In person, tone, timing and a grin tell people a line is meant as play. In a message, the words arrive alone, and sarcasm in particular is easy to misread as a real criticism. If a joke depends on delivery, it's usually better said out loud than typed, and in a group chat with seniors, plainer is safer.

blocks.title: Four ways people use humor

left.head: Tends to help
items: Affiliative: joking to bring people together and ease tension
Self-enhancing: finding the funny side of hard situations to cope

right.head: Tends to backfire
items: Aggressive: sarcasm and put-downs at someone's expense
Self-defeating: constantly running yourself down to get laughs

blocks.text: Psychologists Rod Martin and Patricia Puhlik-Doris mapped these four styles in a 2003 questionnaire. Research using it has generally found the first two linked with better well-being and relationships, and the last two with worse. Self-defeating humor is the sneaky one. It can get laughs, and it can feel humble, but a steady diet of it teaches people to see you the way you describe yourself.
Being funny without trying too hard

For anyone who tends to talk a lot, humor has a specific trap. When a joke lands, the temptation is to keep going: a second version, a callback, an extended bit. That's how a moment that raised your status turns into one that lowers it. A good line works partly because it's short and unexpected. Repeating or explaining it removes the surprise, which is the violation, and all that's left is effort.

Teasing deserves its own warning. Between friends with a lot of shared trust, it's affectionate, a mock attack from someone who's obviously on your side, which is a perfect benign violation. Without that trust, the same words are just an attack. That's why teasing a new shipmate, or teasing up the chain of command, carries much more risk than it seems in the moment. The person who tells the joke rarely gets to decide whether it was benign. The target does.

It also helps to separate being funny from being fun. Funny is the ability to produce laughs on demand. Fun is making people feel relaxed and included, and it's mostly about how you listen: picking up on what's amusing in what *they* said, riffing on it with them, letting them get the laugh. People remember who made them feel funny at least as much as who told the best joke.

blocks.title: Practical rules from the research
items: Aim at situations, not people. The shared absurdity of the schedule is safer than anyone's weakness.
Read the room's distance. If something is still painful for someone present, it's too close to be benign.
Keep it short and let it go. One good line beats a routine.
Laugh at other people's jokes. Most laughter is social glue, and being a good audience is half of being fun to be around.
With seniors, let them set the tone first. Humor that fits the moment raises status; humor that misjudges it lowers it.

blocks.text: The deepest lesson from Provine's notebooks may be the most reassuring. You don't need to be a great joke teller to create laughter. Most laughter comes from ordinary, warm, slightly playful conversation between people who feel at ease. Being relaxed, catching the absurd in a shared situation and enjoying other people's humor does more for a room than any rehearsed bit.

And if you want to get genuinely funnier, the benign violation idea gives you a working tool. Notice the small violations around you, the things that are a little wrong, a little ridiculous, a little against the rules, and ask whether the people around you would experience them as safe. When both answers are yes, you've found something worth saying. Then say it once and move on.

takeaways: Most laughter follows ordinary remarks, not jokes; it is mainly a social signal of safety and liking.
Things are funny when they feel wrong and okay at the same time; distance and low stakes make violations benign.
Successful humor raises perceived confidence and competence, but failed or inappropriate jokes lower status.
Joke about shared situations rather than people, and steer clear of steady self-put-downs.
One good line, then stop. Repeating or extending a joke kills the surprise.

title: The Word That Gets You to the Front of the Line
dek: Cialdini's principles of persuasion are some of the most famous ideas in psychology. Some of the evidence is rock solid, some is smaller than the legend, and all of it works best when there is something real behind it.

blocks.text: In the 1970s, a researcher at a university library in New York waited until someone was about to use the photocopier, then stepped up and asked to cut in. The request was small, five pages. The experiment, run by Ellen Langer and colleagues and published in 1978, tested one thing: how the request was worded.

With no reason given, 'Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine?', 60 percent of people let the researcher go ahead. Add a real reason, 'because I'm in a rush,' and it jumped to 94 percent. The interesting condition was the third one. The researcher said 'because I have to make copies.' Which is not a reason. Everyone at a copier has to make copies. Compliance: 93 percent.

blocks.title: Letting a stranger cut in line at the copier (5 pages)
blocks.note: The empty reason worked almost as well as the real one, but only for a small favor.
blocks.source: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1978

blocks.text: The word *because* seemed to do the work by itself. People heard the shape of a reason and said yes without processing the content. But there is a twist that usually gets left out of the retelling. When the favor was bigger, twenty pages instead of five, the empty reason stopped working. It did no better than giving no reason at all. Only the real reason helped. When the stakes rose, people actually listened.

That twist is the key to understanding persuasion psychology as a whole. The famous tricks are shortcuts our brains use when a decision feels cheap. They are real, they can be powerful, and they are fragile. Once someone starts paying attention, substance takes over again.
Six shortcuts, then a seventh

Robert Cialdini, a social psychologist at Arizona State, spent years studying how people get others to say yes, partly by going undercover in sales trainings, fundraising operations and marketing outfits. In 1984 he published *Influence*, which organized what he found into six principles. In 2016, in the book *Pre-Suasion*, he added a seventh. Each one names a rule of thumb that is usually sensible, which is exactly why it can be exploited.

items: **Reciprocity:** we feel obliged to return favors, even small unrequested ones.
**Commitment and consistency:** once we take a stand, we like to act in line with it.
**Social proof:** when unsure, we copy what people like us are doing.
**Authority:** we defer to people who seem to know what they're talking about.
**Liking:** we say yes more easily to people we like, who are similar to us or who compliment us.
**Scarcity:** things seem more valuable when they're rare or about to disappear.
**Unity (added 2016):** we are swayed by people we see as part of our group, a shared 'we.'

blocks.text: If you play games, you have seen every one of these. The free daily login reward (reciprocity). The streak you don't want to break (consistency). '2.3 million players own this skin' (social proof). The limited-time shop item that leaves at midnight (scarcity). The clan tag (unity). Game designers did not invent these. They borrowed from the same playbook used by car dealers, charities and recruiters.
The best evidence, and the shakier stuff
Some of the classic studies hold up well. Some have shrunk on contact with replication. It's worth knowing which is which, because the size of an effect tells you how much to rely on it.

Start with commitment. In a 1966 study by Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, researchers asked California homeowners to put a large, ugly 'Drive Carefully' sign in their front yard. Among people who got that request cold, only 17 percent agreed. But a group who had been asked two weeks earlier to put a tiny 'Be a Safe Driver' sign in their window, a request almost everyone accepted, said yes to the big sign 76 percent of the time.

blocks.title: Agreeing to a big, ugly yard sign
blocks.note: The classic foot-in-the-door result. Later reviews found the average effect much smaller.
blocks.source: Freedman & Fraser, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1966

blocks.text: That is the foot-in-the-door technique, and the original result is huge. The later picture is more modest. Reviews of the many follow-up studies since the 1980s found that the effect exists on average but is much smaller and less consistent than that first study suggested, and in some settings it barely appears. The underlying idea, that a small yes shifts how people see themselves, is plausible. Treat it as a nudge, not a lever.

Social proof has a similar story. In a widely cited 2008 study, Noah Goldstein, Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested signs in hotel bathrooms asking guests to reuse towels. The standard environmental message got 35.1 percent of guests to reuse. A message saying most fellow guests reused their towels got 44.1 percent. It became a textbook example and a favorite of consultants.

Then other researchers tried it. Several later experiments found little or no effect. In 2016 Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues pooled seven towel experiments in a Bayesian meta-analysis. The effect survived, but smaller: in a reanalysis of that pooled data, reuse ran about 50 percent with the plain message and 56 percent with the social norm message.

blocks.title: Hotel towel reuse: original study vs pooled evidence
blocks.note: Pooled values are approximate estimates from a reanalysis of seven experiments.
blocks.source: Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius, J. Consumer Research, 2008; Scheibehenne et al., Psychological Science, 2016, as reanalyzed by van der Linden & Chryst, 2017

blocks.text: So social norms do something, about six points' worth here. That is useful at the scale of a hotel chain or a government tax letter. It is not mind control. The same pattern shows up across a lot of persuasion research: the first flashy study finds a big effect in one place, and the long run settles on something real but smaller.

Reciprocity is one of the sturdier principles, and it shows up in odd places. In a 2002 restaurant study, David Strohmetz and colleagues found that servers who left a piece of candy with the check got bigger tips than servers who didn't, and that both the size of the gift and the way it was offered changed the result. The authors argued that reciprocity explained the pattern better than a simple good-mood boost. Notice what that implies: the candy worked because it read as a gesture, not as a tactic.

A rule of thumb from the replication era: if a persuasion trick claims a giant effect from a tiny change, expect the real-world version to be smaller. Shortcuts work best on decisions people don't care much about.
Scarcity, liking and the messenger

Scarcity has one of the most charming classic demonstrations. In a 1975 study, Stephen Worchel and colleagues offered people a chocolate chip cookie from a jar and asked them to rate it. When the jar held only two cookies, people rated the identical cookie as more desirable than when the jar held ten. The effect was strongest when the jar went from ten down to two in front of them, as if other people had just grabbed the rest. Same cookie. Different story about how rare it was.

That is the engine behind every limited drop and every 'only 3 left in stock' banner. It also explains why things you might lose feel more valuable than things you might gain. A battle pass that expires motivates you more than one that sits there forever, even though the rewards are the same.

Liking and authority are about the messenger rather than the message. People say yes more readily to someone who seems similar to them, who is friendly, who has helped them before. They also defer to people with real or apparent expertise, which is why a confident tone and the right title can carry an argument further than the argument deserves. Stanley Milgram's obedience studies in the 1960s are the darkest illustration of authority, and they have their own long list of critiques about how the experiments were run and reported. The everyday lesson is milder: the same request lands differently depending on who says it and whether they have earned credibility on the topic.

For a junior person, that cuts both ways. You may not have rank, but you can have credibility on specific things: you're the one who actually knows that system, ran that procedure last week, or did the reading. Speaking from that ground, briefly and specifically, is a legitimate form of authority. Pretending to know more than you do is the counterfeit version, and in a technical job it gets caught fast.
Why the shortcuts exist at all

It's easy to read this as a list of human bugs. Cialdini's own framing is kinder and more useful. Each principle is a heuristic that usually leads to good decisions. Copying what others do is a fast way to learn in an unfamiliar place. Deferring to experts is how you avoid relearning everything yourself; it's why you trust the procedure written by people who've thought harder about the reactor than you have. Returning favors is the glue of every functioning group, including a crew.

blocks.title: How a persuasion shortcut gets exploited
items: A rule of thumb works most of the time
People stop checking it on small decisions
Someone fakes the signal (fake scarcity, fake reviews, fake authority)
The fake triggers the yes without the substance
People get burned and grow suspicious of the real thing too

blocks.text: The problem comes when someone fakes the signal. A countdown timer that resets every time you reload the page is counterfeit scarcity. Paid reviews are counterfeit social proof. A guy in a lab coat selling supplements is counterfeit authority. The shortcut fires, but there's nothing behind it. And because these tactics are now everywhere, people have gotten better at smelling them, which is one reason the textbook effects keep shrinking.
Using it without being that guy

Cialdini draws a sharp line between using the principles honestly and manufacturing them. The honest version is simple: if a real reason, a real expert opinion, real popularity or a real deadline exists, make it visible. Don't make people dig for it. The dishonest version invents those things. The first is just good communication. The second works once and costs you trust you won't get back.

blocks.title: Honest persuasion for a normal request
items: Lead with the real reason. The copier study shows a reason helps, and for anything that matters, it has to be a good one.
Point to genuine social proof if it exists: 'the other watch sections already switched to this.'
Borrow real authority: cite the procedure, the tech manual or the person who actually knows.
Ask for a small, reasonable first step rather than everything at once.
Find the shared 'we': same division, same goal, same problem.
Give before you ask: help people when you don't need anything, and you build credit for when you do.

blocks.text: For someone working on speaking professionally, the most practical lesson is the one from the copier. When you ask for something, a schedule swap, a favor, an exception, give the reason in one clean sentence. Then stop. People who over-talk tend to stack reason on reason, apology on apology, and that can backfire: it signals that you don't think your first reason was good enough. One real reason, stated plainly, is usually stronger than five nervous ones.

There's a defensive lesson too. When you feel an urge to decide right now, because it's leaving the store, because everyone's doing it, because the person seemed so likable, that urgency is a good moment to ask a single question: would I want this if the shortcut weren't there? If the item weren't limited, if nobody else had it, if a stranger were offering it? If the answer is still yes, go ahead. If not, you just caught a shortcut doing the deciding for you.

Persuading up the chain of command is where this gets real. A chief or division officer has heard every flavor of pitch and is busy. What tends to work is boring: the request in one line, the real reason, what you've already checked, and what it costs them to say yes. That structure leans on the honest versions of several principles at once. The reason is real, the homework is a signal of competence, and making it easy to agree respects their time. Nothing about it is a trick, which is exactly why it holds up the second and third time you ask for something.

The deeper reframe is that persuasion is not mainly about tricks at all. The strongest form of every principle is the real thing. Real reciprocity is being someone who helps. Real authority is knowing your stuff. Real liking is being decent to be around. Real unity is actually being on the same team. The principles describe why people say yes. The shortcut versions are just attempts to get the yes without doing the work.

takeaways: Persuasion shortcuts work best on low-stakes decisions; when it matters, people check the substance.
Many famous effects are real but smaller than their original studies: hotel towel norms shrank from about 9 points to about 6.
When you ask for something, give one clear real reason and stop talking.
Make genuine reasons, expertise and deadlines visible; never fake them.
If you feel rushed to say yes, ask whether you'd still want it without the scarcity, crowd or charm.

title: The First Minute Is the Worst Minute
dek: Public speaking fear is close to universal, mostly invisible to the audience, and it peaks almost as soon as you start. That is exactly why it can be beaten quickly.

blocks.text: When stress researchers need a reliable way to make healthy people anxious in a lab, they have a favorite tool. It is not a needle, a loud noise or a cold-water bath. It is a speech. In the Trier Social Stress Test, developed in Germany in the early 1990s and used in a huge number of studies since, a volunteer is given a few minutes to prepare a talk, then has to deliver it to a panel of stone-faced judges who take notes and offer no encouragement. It reliably spikes heart rate and stress hormones.

Think about what that means. Out of everything scientists could use to stress a person safely, they chose standing up and talking. Not because talking is dangerous, but because being judged by a group is one of the most dependable alarm buttons the human brain has. If your hands go cold before a brief at quarters, nothing is wrong with you. You are running standard equipment.
Not worse than death, just more common

You have probably heard that people fear public speaking more than death. The claim traces back to a 1973 survey that asked Americans to check off their fears from a list. Public speaking came out on top, checked by about 40 percent of respondents. Comedians ran with it, and it became a cliché that at a funeral, most people would rather be in the casket than at the podium.

In 2012, Karen Kangas Dwyer and Marlina Davidson at the University of Nebraska Omaha tested the cliché properly. They surveyed 815 college students who had not yet taken a speech class, using the same list of 14 fears. When students simply checked which things they feared, public speaking was again the most common, chosen by about 60 percent. But when they were asked to rank their fears, death came first. So the cliché is half right. Public speaking is the fear the most people share. It is not the one they rank as worst.

blocks.title: Share who checked public speaking as a fear
blocks.note: In the 2012 study, death still ranked first when students ordered their fears from worst to least.
blocks.source: Dwyer & Davidson, Communication Research Reports, 2012 (via KIOS/UNO)

blocks.text: It is also worth separating ordinary nerves from a clinical problem. The large National Comorbidity Survey Replication estimated that about 12 percent of Americans meet criteria for social anxiety disorder at some point in their lives, a condition where fear of judgment seriously disrupts daily life. That is real and treatable, and if fear of speaking is wrecking your career or keeping you from basic tasks, a doctor, corpsman or chaplain can point you to help. But the much larger group, the majority who just get sweaty palms before a brief, are dealing with a normal reaction that responds well to practice.
The shape of the fear

Here is a useful fact that most nervous speakers do not know: the fear has a predictable curve. In a 2006 study, Ralph Behnke, Chris Sawyer and Paul Witt at Texas Christian University tracked 96 students giving a five-minute speech. They measured anxiety symptoms like a lump in the throat and knots in the stomach at four moments: the minute before speaking, the first minute of the speech, the last minute, and the minute right after.

For the more relaxed students, anxiety peaked just before they started and fell from the first word onward. For the high-anxiety students, it peaked in the first minute of actually speaking, then declined as the speech went on, dropping substantially by the end. In other words, even for the most nervous people, the worst part was front-loaded. If you can get through the first sixty seconds, the curve starts working for you.

blocks.title: Where speech anxiety peaks
items: Minute before
Peak for low-anxiety speakers. Waiting is the worst part.
First minute
Peak for high-anxiety speakers. Highest symptom load of the talk.
Last minute
Anxiety has fallen for both groups, a lot for the nervous ones.
Minute after
A small bounce back as people replay how it went.

blocks.text: That shape suggests a very specific tactic. You do not need to rehearse the whole talk to the point of memorizing it. That often backfires, because a memorized script shatters the moment you lose a word. You need to over-prepare the first minute. Know your opening sentences cold, so that when your anxiety is at its peak, your mouth is running on rails while the rest of your body catches up.
They cannot see what you feel

A second reason the fear is worse than it needs to be is that speakers badly overestimate how visible their nerves are. Kenneth Savitsky and Thomas Gilovich at Cornell studied this in 2003. In their first experiment, speakers rated how nervous they had looked, and observers rated the same thing. Speakers consistently judged themselves as more visibly anxious than the audience saw them.

In the second experiment, they split speakers into three groups before a short, unprepared talk. One group got no special instructions. One got reassurance that nerves are normal. The third was told about the illusion of transparency: the well-documented tendency to think your inner state is far more obvious to others than it is. That third group gave better speeches, and not just in their own eyes. Observers, who did not know which group anyone was in, rated their speeches higher too.

blocks.title: The same speech, two views

left.head: What the speaker feels
items: Heart pounding, voice shaky
A two-second pause feels endless
Every um sounds like a disaster
Sure the whole room can tell

right.head: What the audience sees
items: Someone a little serious
A normal pause to think
Ordinary speech, barely noticed
A person giving a talk, mostly fine

blocks.text: The interesting part is how cheap that fix was. The informed group did not get coaching or practice. They got one fact about perception, and it changed their performance. Part of what wrecks a nervous speech is the spiral: I think they can see I am nervous, which makes me more nervous, which makes me try to hide it, which takes attention away from what I am saying. Knowing the audience mostly cannot see it breaks the first link.
Call it excitement, with an asterisk

If you cannot calm down, what should you do? A widely cited 2014 study by Alison Wood Brooks at Harvard Business School suggested an odd answer: do not try. In one experiment, 140 people were told they would give a persuasive speech on camera, judged by a committee. Right before speaking, half said out loud I am excited and half said I am calm. Independent raters judged the excited group's speeches as more persuasive, more competent and more relaxed, and their speeches ran longer.

Her other experiments pointed the same way. When people sang karaoke scored by the game's own rating system, those who first said I am excited averaged around 80 percent accuracy, compared with 69 percent for those who said they were calm, angry or sad, and 53 percent for those told to say they were anxious. On a hard math test, people told to get excited scored about 8 percent higher than those told to stay calm.

blocks.title: Karaoke accuracy by what people said first
blocks.source: Brooks, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2014 (APA summary)

blocks.text: The theory is elegant. Anxiety and excitement are both high-arousal states: racing heart, sharp focus, energy. Going from anxious to calm requires dumping all that arousal, which is hard to do on command. Going from anxious to excited only requires relabeling it, from a threat to an opportunity. Same body, different story.

Now the asterisk. In 2025, Michelle Poynter and Marcia Smith Pasqualini published a direct replication of the speech experiment. Saying I am excited again made people report feeling more excited. But this time, independent raters saw no difference in how good the speeches were, and an indirect measure of anxiety showed no change either. So the honest summary is this: reappraisal probably changes how the moment feels, and that is worth something. Whether it reliably makes the speech itself better is not settled. Use it, but do not expect it to replace practice.
How to get better fast

The good news hiding in all of this is that public speaking anxiety is not a fixed trait you are stuck with. It behaves like most fears: it shrinks with repeated exposure that ends without disaster. Each time you speak and nothing terrible happens, your brain gets one more data point against the alarm. The first five briefs are the hardest. By the twentieth, the curve from the TCU study has flattened.

Structure helps too, and the military has already solved part of it. Army correspondence rules have long told writers to put the bottom line up front, usually shortened to BLUF: lead with the conclusion or the recommendation, then support it. That is not just a writing rule. It is the single best structure for a brief to a senior, because it answers the question they actually care about while their attention is highest, and it gives a nervous speaker a short, fixed opening to over-prepare.

blocks.title: Prepping a five-minute brief
items: Write your bottom line in one sentence: what you want them to know or decide.
Pick at most three supporting facts, each a short sentence.
Script and rehearse only the first minute until it is automatic.
Record a full run on your phone once and watch it. It will look calmer than it felt.
Run it out loud two more times, standing, with no notes for the opening.
Right before, breathe out slowly and tell yourself you are excited, not calm.

blocks.text: A few small habits make a big difference in the room. Slow down, because nerves speed you up and a slightly too slow pace sounds confident to listeners. Talk to one face at a time for a sentence or two, rather than the whole room at once. Allow pauses. A one-second silence while you find your next point feels long to you and looks thoughtful to them. And when you finish, stop. A strong last sentence followed by I can take questions beats a trailing so yeah, I think that's about it.

Underway, opportunities to practice are everywhere and mostly low stakes: walking through a system at a qual board, giving a turnover, leading a training session for the division, explaining a drill debrief. Each is a rep. Treat them that way. Volunteer for the short ones on purpose, the way you would choose a drill in a game you are trying to get better at, not a match you are trying to win.
Over-prepare the first sixty seconds and the bottom line. Anxiety peaks right at the start and falls after, so the opening is where preparation pays most.
When the questions start

For a lot of people, the speech is not the scary part. The questions are. You can rehearse a talk, but you cannot rehearse what a department head will ask, and the fear is that one question will expose that you do not know your stuff. In a briefing up the chain of command, that fear tends to produce two bad habits: talking around a question you cannot answer, and over-answering one you can.

The first habit is the dangerous one. Anyone who has been through nuclear training has heard the standard: if you do not know, say so, then go find out. It sounds simple and it feels terrible in the moment. But a senior can work with I don't know, I'll find out and report back by end of watch. What they cannot work with is a confident guess that later turns out to be wrong, because now they have to wonder about everything else you said. An honest gap costs you a little. A bluff that gets caught costs you your credibility for a long time.

The second habit, over-answering, is the nervous speaker's version of filling silence. A yes-or-no question gets a three-minute history. The fix mirrors the bottom-line rule: answer in the first sentence, then stop and let them pull for more. Yes, it is on track for Thursday; the part came in this morning. If they want the backstory, they will ask. Short answers under pressure read as control, and control is most of what an audience means when they say a speaker seemed confident.

Here is the reframe to carry into the next brief. Your nerves are evidence that your brain takes the situation seriously, not evidence that you are bad at it. They are mostly invisible. They peak right at the start and then fade. And they get smaller every time you stand up and speak anyway. Fear of public speaking is common enough that scientists use it as the standard stress test. It is also one of the fears people most reliably get past, by doing the thing.

takeaways: Public speaking is the most commonly reported fear, but people still rank death as worse. Your nerves are standard equipment.
For anxious speakers, anxiety peaks in the first minute and then falls, so script and rehearse the opening most.
Speakers overestimate how visible their nerves are; just knowing this improved speeches in a Cornell experiment.
Relabeling nerves as excitement helps how you feel; its effect on performance did not replicate in a 2025 study.
Lead briefs with the bottom line, then three facts. Collect reps on purpose.
