title: Watch Me Get Better
dek: Why do people watch someone who is not yet good at something? Psychology research on effort, underdogs and progress explains the pull of the journey video, and what it takes to make one that holds.

blocks.text: In a set of experiments published in 2004, the psychologist Justin Kruger and his colleagues showed people a poem. Some were told the poet had spent about four hours writing it. Others were told it had taken eighteen. The poem was word-for-word identical. The people who believed it took eighteen hours rated it better and said it was worth more.

The team ran the same trick with paintings, telling viewers a piece had taken either four or twenty-six hours, and with a photo of a suit of medieval armor said to have taken either fifteen or a hundred and ten hours. Each time, the work believed to have taken more effort was judged higher in quality. People who described themselves as art experts were fooled just as much as everyone else. And the effect grew stronger when the work was harder to judge directly, for example when the armor photo was blurry.

The researchers called it the *effort heuristic*: when we cannot easily judge quality, we use effort as a stand-in. That finding quietly explains one of the most durable formats on YouTube, the journey video. Learning to draw in a year. Going from unranked to a top rank. Coming back to a game after years away and rebuilding a skill that has gone rusty. These videos show the effort that a highlight reel hides, and viewers value what they can see being earned.
Why the struggle is the product

Imagine two clips of the same perfect flick shot. In the first, a stranger hits it, and that is all you know. In the second, you have watched the same person miss that shot for twenty minutes across three episodes, heard them explain what they changed, and seen their aim trainer score climb week by week. The second clip is the same three seconds of footage, but it means something completely different. You know what it cost.

That is the core mechanic of journey content. A highlight shows a result. A journey shows the *gap* between where someone started and where they are, and invites you to watch it close. The result becomes a payoff instead of a spectacle. That is why polished highlight channels and raw progress channels can coexist in the same game without competing. They are selling different experiences.

The pattern is not unique to gaming. Fitness transformations, language-learning diaries, people teaching themselves to draw or play piano, developers building a game in public: all of them run on the same engine. What they share is a measurable skill, a starting point the creator is willing to show, and a destination the viewer can picture. The specific skill matters less than whether the audience can *see* the change from one episode to the next.

blocks.title: Two ways to show the same skill

left.head: Highlight channel
items: Shows the best result
Viewer admires the skill
Value depends on how impressive the clip is
Hard to stand out in a crowded game
Each video stands alone

right.head: Journey channel
items: Shows the gap closing over time
Viewer invests in the outcome
Value depends on stakes and honesty
Your story is yours alone
Each video builds on the last

blocks.text: The effort heuristic comes with a warning label. It works because viewers infer effort from what they see. If they sense that the struggle is staged, that a skilled player is pretending to be bad for content, the inference collapses and tends to turn into distrust. The format runs on honesty. A real starting point, even an embarrassing one, is worth more than a dramatic fake one.
The pull of the underdog

A second line of research explains why viewers root for the person on the journey. In 2007, University of South Florida psychologists Joseph Vandello, Nadav Goldschmied and David Richards published a series of studies on what they called the appeal of the underdog. Using sports matchups, political scenarios and even maps that made one side of a conflict look smaller, they found that people consistently favored whichever side was cast as the underdog.

Two details from that work matter for creators. First, participants tended to believe underdogs were putting in more effort than favorites, which links neatly back to the effort heuristic. Second, the support disappeared when the 'underdog' was expected to lose but had plenty of resources. People do not root for someone who is merely losing. They root for someone who is trying hard against real odds.

For a journey channel, that suggests being honest about your constraints, because constraints are what make the odds real. A player with eight free hours a day who reaches a high rank is impressive. A player who gets there practicing in short windows between long work shifts, with weeks away from a PC at a time, is an underdog. Many adult players live some version of that second situation, and few creators speak to it directly.
Underdog appeal is not about being bad. It is about visible effort against honest constraints. Show the limits you are working within, not just the scores.
Progress is the strongest motivator there is

The third piece comes from Harvard Business School researcher Teresa Amabile and psychologist Steven Kramer. They asked 238 people on 26 creative project teams at seven companies to fill out a short diary at the end of every workday, producing nearly 12,000 entries. Then they looked at what distinguished people's best days from their worst.

items.label: People on 26 project teams who kept daily work diaries
Diary entries analyzed
Share of best days on which people reported making progress

blocks.source: Amabile & Kramer, The Progress Principle, via American Management Association

blocks.text: The single biggest factor was making progress on meaningful work, even in small steps. It showed up in 76% of people's best days, far more than any other kind of event. Setbacks hit even harder: Amabile and Kramer reported that their negative effect was two to three times stronger than the positive effect of progress. They called this the progress principle.

Their study was about people at work, not viewers on YouTube, so it should not be stretched too far. But it hints at why journey content feels good to watch. A viewer following someone's progress gets a small, borrowed version of that same satisfaction each episode: the score went up, the problem got solved, the gap got smaller. And the setbacks, which hit harder, are what make the progress feel earned. A journey with no setbacks is not a journey. It is a victory lap.

The progress principle also works on the creator. Documenting your own improvement gives you a built-in progress tracker, with scores, clips and footage you can compare across months. On days when practice feels pointless, the channel's back catalog is evidence that it is not. Few hobbies give you that kind of record by default.
What actually brings viewers back

Creator advice often says to end every video on an 'open loop', a question left unanswered, because the mind supposedly cannot let go of unfinished business. That idea leans on the Zeigarnik effect, a claim from the 1920s that people remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones. It has been repeated for a century. It has not held up well.

In 2025, Romain Ghibellini and Beat Meier of the University of Bern published a meta-analysis pooling the experimental research on both effects. They found no general memory advantage for unfinished tasks; the classic Zeigarnik effect, they concluded, is not universally valid. But they did find support for a related finding, the Ovsiankina effect: people show a general tendency to go back and finish tasks that were interrupted.

That distinction is useful. A cheap cliffhanger does not burn itself into anyone's memory. What pulls people back is a genuine unfinished goal they care about. A journey supplies exactly that: a clearly stated destination that has not been reached yet. Viewers do not return because you teased them. They return because they want to see whether you make it, the way you go back to finish a game you put down halfway.

There is a practical audience behind the format, too. In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey of 4,594 US adults, 51% of YouTube users said the site was very important for figuring out how to do things they had not done before. That was far more than said it was very important for passing the time.

blocks.title: What US YouTube users say the site is very important for
blocks.note: Share of US adult YouTube users answering 'very important', survey conducted May–June 2018.
blocks.source: Pew Research Center, 2018

blocks.text: That is why the strongest journey channels are also quietly tutorials. Every episode where you learn something the hard way is an episode that teaches it to someone else. A stranger searching for how to fix their crosshair placement may find your week-six video, learn the fix and then stay to see whether you hit your goal. The lesson is how they find you. The journey is why they stay.
Building a journey that holds

Most journey channels fail in predictable ways. The goal is vague, so there is no tension. The progress is not measured, so viewers cannot see the gap closing. The middle stretch, when improvement slows to a crawl, is boring because nothing visibly changes. Or the creator quietly stops, and the story never ends. Each of these is a design problem, and each has a fix.

blocks.title: Designing a journey series
items: Record an honest baseline with a number viewers can track, such as a rank or an aim trainer score.
State a specific goal and a rough timeframe in the first episode.
Name your real constraints, so viewers understand the odds.
Give every episode one lesson someone else could use.
Show setbacks plainly; they are what make progress feel earned.
When improvement slows, change the experiment, not just the episode number.
Plan an ending or a clear next season, so the story resolves.

blocks.text: The plateau deserves special attention, because it is guaranteed. Skill improvement almost always follows a curve that is steep at first and flattens out; early gains come quickly, later ones take far more practice for smaller changes. For a journey channel, that means the first month will produce exciting before-and-after footage, and the third month may not. The answer is to shift what the episodes are about: from 'look how much better I got' to 'here is the experiment I am trying to break through.' A plateau is a new mystery, not a dead end.

The ending matters more than most creators think. A journey that fizzles out teaches viewers that following you is a waste of time. One that reaches its goal, or honestly fails to and says what was learned, rewards everyone who came along. Then a new journey can begin, with an audience that already trusts you to finish what you start.
The camera changes the practice

There is a risk in this format that few creators talk about. Once practice becomes content, it is easy to start practicing for the camera instead of for improvement. Drills that look impressive get more screen time than drills that work. Sessions get cut short because the footage is already good enough. You pick matches that will make a better video rather than ones that will make you a better player. The channel starts measuring something slightly different from the skill it claims to document.

Engineers have a name for this kind of drift: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The guard against it is to keep the practice and the video separate in your head. Decide the training plan first, based only on what will improve your aim, and then film it. If the honest version of a week is boring, that is a storytelling problem to solve in the edit, not a reason to change the training.

The other risk is emotional. Showing your mistakes in public means some commenters will point them out, sometimes harshly, and better players will occasionally sneer. Most people overestimate how closely others are watching their failures, and the viewers who chose a journey video generally came to see someone improve, not to mock them. Still, it helps to decide in advance that the baseline footage is supposed to look rough. It is the 'before' picture. Its whole job is to be worse than what comes next.

Underneath all of this is a reframe worth holding onto. Many people put off starting a channel until they are good at the thing they want to make videos about. The research on effort, underdogs and progress suggests that is backward. Not being good yet is not an obstacle to the content. It *is* the content, as long as you are honest about it and willing to show the work. The only version of this channel that cannot work is the one that waits to be impressive before it starts.

takeaways: People rate work higher when they believe it took more effort. Journey videos show the effort that highlights hide.
Underdogs win support through visible effort against real constraints, not just by losing. Name your limits honestly.
Progress on meaningful work is a powerful motivator for viewers and creators alike; setbacks make it feel earned.
Cheap cliffhangers are overrated. A real, unfinished goal is what brings viewers back.
Plan for the plateau and for an ending. Not being good yet is the content, not the obstacle.

title: The Cut You Don't Notice
dek: Hollywood shots have shrunk from about ten seconds to about four. Fast editing grabs attention, but research shows it can also drown out the message. Good editing is about managing a viewer's brain, not just speeding it up.

blocks.text: Watch a Hollywood film from 1950 and then one from 2010, and something will feel different before you can name it. The psychologist James Cutting and his colleagues at Cornell measured it. Across hundreds of English-language films, the average length of a single shot fell more or less steadily from about 10 seconds in 1950 to about 4 seconds in 2010. Nobody passed a rule. Editors, film by film, learned that audiences would follow faster cutting, and the medium sped up.

YouTube editing went through the same evolution in about a decade. Early vlogs were often a single static shot of someone talking. Today the most-watched videos cut constantly, zoom, insert text, change angles and drop in sound effects. It is easy to conclude that the lesson is simple: cut faster and people will keep watching.

The research says it is more interesting than that. Cuts do grab attention, for reasons wired deep into how vision works. But a viewer's brain has limited capacity, and editing that spends all of it on keeping eyes on the screen leaves nothing for understanding or remembering what is on it. The real skill is not speed. It is knowing when to spend the viewer's attention and when to let them use it.

items.label: Average Hollywood shot length around 1950
Average Hollywood shot length around 2010

blocks.source: Cutting, DeLong & Brunick, Cognitive Research, 2018

blocks.text: Why a cut grabs you

Every cut is a small jolt to the visual system. In their 2018 paper on the rhythm of movies, Cutting, Jordan DeLong and Kaitlin Brunick note that cuts trigger eye movements, which they describe as a low-level demand for attention. Your eyes have to find where to look in the new shot. That reflex is hard to resist, which is exactly why editors use it.

Media researchers call the broader version of this an orienting response: an automatic shift of attention toward something new or sudden in the environment. Annie Lang, whose limited capacity model became one of the standard frameworks for how people process television, built much of her work around it. Structural features of video, like cuts, edits and sudden movement, reliably pull viewers' attention back to the screen, whether or not the content deserves it.

Editors have also learned when to *hide* cuts. The same paper describes how professionals match action across shots, cutting in the middle of a movement so the eye follows the motion and barely registers the edit. The best editing uses the jolt on purpose in some places and smooths it away in others. That is the first hint that speed is not the whole story.

YouTube added its own native cut: the jump cut in a talking segment, where pauses and stumbles between sentences are simply removed and the speaker appears to skip slightly forward. In film, that kind of cut was long treated as a mistake. On YouTube it became a convention, because viewers learned to read it as 'nothing was lost here.' It is a useful reminder that audiences adapt to editing styles. What feels jarring in one era becomes invisible in the next, so the rule is less about any particular technique than about whether the viewer stays oriented.
The overload problem

In 1999, Lang and her colleagues published a study in the *Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media* that should be required reading for anyone editing video. They varied two things in television messages: production pace, meaning how fast the edits came, and how emotionally arousing the content was. Both fast pacing and arousing content made viewers report feeling more aroused, and both led viewers to put more mental resources into the messages.

Then came the catch. When fast pace and arousing content were combined, viewers' processing systems were overloaded, and their recognition and recall of the specific content dropped. The video grabbed them harder and they remembered less of it. In plain terms, attention is not the same as understanding. You can win the first and lose the second.

A cut buys a moment of attention. It is a currency, not a free resource. Spend it during the slow parts that need help, and stop spending it when the content is already intense enough to hold people on its own.

This maps onto gaming footage almost perfectly. A clutch round, a hard fight or a dramatic fail is already arousing. Piling zooms, sound effects, captions and quick cuts on top can turn a great moment into visual noise, where the viewer cannot tell what actually happened. The quiet stretches, the walking, waiting and setup, are where editing tricks earn their keep.

It also explains a common complaint about over-edited videos: they feel exhausting. A viewer can stay alert for a while under constant stimulation, but the experience starts to feel like work. Retention can hold for a few minutes and then fall off a cliff, not because any single moment was boring, but because the whole thing was tiring.

Sound deserves the same caution. Music, sound effects and voice all draw on the same limited pool of attention as the picture. A constant music bed under nonstop commentary and loud game audio forces the viewer to sort three streams at once. Dropping the music during key explanations, or ducking the game audio when you speak, is one of the cheapest ways to make a video feel clearer without changing a single cut.
The attention landscape, measured honestly

Much editing advice leans on a scary claim about shrinking attention spans, often in the form of the widely repeated comparison to a goldfish. That comparison has been criticized for years as having no solid basis, and you should ignore it. But there is real research on how attention behaves on screens, and it is useful as long as you know what it measured.

Gloria Mark, a researcher at the University of California, Irvine, has spent two decades tracking how long people stay on one screen before switching to something else, using computer logging and sensors in people's normal work environments. In a 2023 interview she said the average was about two and a half minutes in her early work around 2004, about 75 seconds by 2012, and about 47 seconds in measurements from more recent years, with a median of 40 seconds.

blocks.title: Average time on one screen before switching
blocks.note: Office and computer-work settings, not video watching. The 2004 figure is approximate.
blocks.source: Gloria Mark, interviewed by the University of California, 2023

blocks.text: Be precise about what this means. These are people switching between windows and tasks on a work computer, not viewers abandoning a video. It does not prove anyone has lost the *ability* to focus; people still binge long series and play five-hour gaming sessions. What it does show is the environment your video lives in: a screen where something else is always one tap away and switching has become a habit. Editing is the craft of making the next tap less tempting than the next second of your video.
A pacing map from the most-watched channel

Some of the most concrete pacing advice available comes from a production manual reportedly used to onboard staff at MrBeast's company, which leaked in September 2024. Its numbers are tied to one kind of high-budget video, so they are a case study, not a law. But the logic behind them is clear and transfers.

blocks.title: Pacing as described in the leaked MrBeast manual
items: Prove the video delivers what the thumbnail promised
Stop describing, start showing; move the story forward fast
A re-engagement moment to re-hook drifting viewers
Simple, fast, highly stimulating scene changes
A bigger re-engagement that pushes the story forward
After 6:00
Viewers who stayed are invested; the pace can ease

blocks.text: Notice the shape. Intensity is not constant. The manual front-loads energy where viewers are most likely to leave, places deliberate spikes where attention tends to sag, and accepts a calmer back half once the audience is invested. That is the opposite of 'cut as fast as possible everywhere.' It is a budget, spent where the retention graph says it is needed.

Your own retention graphs are the best guide to where your sags fall. If viewers consistently drift around the four-minute mark, that is where a re-engagement belongs: a new challenge, a score reveal, a question answered, a change of scene. The pattern interrupt should come from the story whenever possible, not just from a sound effect.
The editing toolkit, used with judgment
Most of what makes a video feel well paced comes from a few basic moves. None of them is new, and all of them can be overdone. The skill is in choosing which one a moment needs.

items: **Cut dead air.** Remove pauses, false starts and repeated sentences. This alone often transforms a talking segment, and it costs the viewer nothing.
**Compress the boring parts of gameplay.** Walking, waiting, lobbies and menus can be cut, sped up or replaced with a quick time-skip.
**Change the frame.** A zoom, crop or switch from facecam to full gameplay resets the eye without adding noise.
**Show, then say.** Put the visual proof on screen before or while you explain it, not after.
**Use text sparingly.** On-screen text helps for numbers and key points, but stacked captions compete with the gameplay for the same attention.
**Let the big moments breathe.** Slow down or replay the payoff so viewers can actually see it.

blocks.text: Aim and skill content has one extra rule: the viewer must be able to *see* the skill. A flick that took real precision looks like nothing at full speed in a busy frame. Slowing the moment down, zooming toward the crosshair, or replaying it once with the target marked turns an invisible achievement into something a viewer can appreciate. The same goes for before-and-after comparisons. Put the two clips or the two numbers side by side, on screen at the same time, rather than asking viewers to remember a score from three minutes ago.

There is evidence that delivery itself matters. In a 2014 study of about 6.9 million video sessions from online courses, Philip Guo and colleagues found that viewers stayed engaged longer, up to twice as long within a given video length, when instructors spoke faster. Energy in the voice is a pacing tool that costs no editing time at all. The same study found that videos planned for the medium held people better than recorded lectures chopped up afterward, which is another way of saying the best edit starts before you hit record.
Editing on limited time

For a creator with a demanding job and little free time, editing is usually the biggest bottleneck. A ten-minute video can take many hours to cut, and the temptation is either to over-polish the first few videos or to give up on editing entirely. Neither works. The answer is an order of operations that puts the cheap, high-value work first.

blocks.title: An editing pass in priority order
items: Plan the video's beats before recording: hook, promise, progress, payoff
Rough cut: remove dead air, mistakes and gameplay downtime
Check the first 30 seconds against the thumbnail and title
Find the slowest stretch and fix it with story first, effects second
Clean up the big moments so viewers can see exactly what happened
Stop. Upload. Let the retention graph tell you what to fix next time

blocks.text: The first two steps deliver most of the improvement. Planning means you record what you need instead of hours you will have to dig through, and the rough cut removes what bores people. Effects, motion graphics and sound design are real skills, but on an early channel they produce smaller gains for much more time than those basics.

Be blunt with yourself about polish. The first twenty videos on a channel are practice reps, and an upload that is good enough beats a perfect one that never ships. Each finished video also produces the most valuable editing teacher there is: a retention graph showing where real viewers left. You cannot get that feedback from a timeline you are still tweaking.

Underneath all the techniques is one idea. An editor's job is to manage a limited resource, the viewer's attention, on the viewer's behalf. Cutting is how you spend it, and pausing is how you let it recover. The editors who grow channels are not the ones who cut most. They are the ones whose cuts the viewer never notices, because each one arrived exactly when the viewer was about to look away.

takeaways: Cuts trigger automatic eye movements and orienting responses, so they reliably grab attention.
Fast pacing on top of already intense content can overload viewers and reduce what they remember (Lang, 1999).
Spend editing tricks on slow stretches and let big moments breathe so viewers can see what happened.
Place re-engagements where your own retention graph sags, and make them come from the story when possible.
On limited time, plan the beats and cut dead air first; polish is the last and least valuable pass.

title: Crossing the Desert: The First 1,000 Subscribers
dek: Almost all of YouTube's views go to a tiny slice of channels. The way out of the empty stretch at the start is not a growth hack. It is a change in what you think a subscriber is.

blocks.text: In 2018, a German researcher named Mathias Bärtl published a statistical study of ten years of YouTube data, drawn from a random sample of channels and videos. His headline finding was brutal: on average, about 85% of all views went to just 3% of channels. The other 97% of channels shared what was left.

A year later, Pew Research Center found the same lopsidedness even among channels that had already made it. Looking at every video posted in the first week of 2019 by about 43,770 channels with at least 250,000 subscribers, Pew found that the 10% of videos with the most views took 79% of all views. Inequality does not stop once you are popular. It is the shape of the whole platform.

blocks.title: How concentrated YouTube attention is
blocks.note: First bar: share of views across a random sample of channels. Second: share of first-week views among popular channels' videos. Third: share of all videos uploaded, produced by the most active 10% of popular channels.
blocks.source: Bärtl, Convergence, 2018; Pew Research Center, 2019

blocks.text: Every new channel starts in that desert. Uploads get a handful of views, mostly from friends, and the subscriber count barely moves for weeks. This is the stretch where most people quit, and it is easy to see why: it feels like shouting into a void. But the desert is not evidence you are failing. It is the default condition, and the question is what to do while crossing it.

Gaming is an especially crowded corner of it. In its 2020 year-in-review, YouTube said there were more than 40 million active gaming channels. In the same post it said more than 80,000 gaming creators had passed 100,000 subscribers, more than 1,000 had passed 5 million and more than 350 had passed 10 million. Those categories may not be counted the same way, so the exact ratio is fuzzy. The shape is not: for every gaming channel with a real audience, there are hundreds that never got one.

items.label: Active gaming channels on YouTube in 2020
Gaming creators past 100,000 subscribers
Gaming creators past 10 million subscribers

blocks.source: Ryan Wyatt, YouTube Official Blog, December 2020

blocks.text: Here is the reframe that helps. A subscriber is not a fan you win by asking. A subscriber is a stranger who watched one of your videos, liked it, and decided they wanted the next one. The count is a lagging indicator of individual videos that worked for people who did not know you. Get good at that, and the count follows. Chase the count directly, and you usually get neither.

It also helps to notice where most growth advice comes from. Almost every 'how I hit 100K' video is made by someone in the top slice of that bar chart. Their advice may be good, but it is filtered through survivorship: you hear from the channels that made it, not from the thousands that did the same things and did not. Treat any single success story as one data point, and look for the advice that matches what YouTube itself says about how its system works.
What the research says about time

Bärtl's study contains a second finding that gets less attention than the 3% figure but matters more to someone starting out. Older channels had a significantly higher probability of building a large viewership. Young channels did have a small chance of becoming successful quickly, but that chance depended heavily on their genre.

Read that carefully, because it cuts two ways. It is partly survivorship: channels that got traction kept going and grew old, while channels that did not were abandoned. But it also says that staying in the game long enough to get good is part of the strategy. Most of the channels that fail do not fail because the creator lacked talent. They stop before the creator has made enough videos to find out what works.

There is a useful comparison in how the Navy trains people. Nobody expects a new electrician to troubleshoot a fault on day one. Qualification happens through repetitions, mistakes caught early, and a growing sense of what normal looks like. The first fifty videos on a channel serve the same function. They are qualification, not performance. The audience they gather is a bonus.
What 1,000 actually unlocks

The number 1,000 is famous mainly because of the YouTube Partner Program, the system that lets channels earn money. In 2023 YouTube added a lower tier in the US and several other countries, later expanding it further. As of the latest rules reported, it works in two steps, though YouTube changes these thresholds, so check YouTube's own help pages before planning around them.

items.label: Subscribers for the lower tier, plus 3 uploads in 90 days and 3,000 watch hours in a year or 3M Shorts views
Subscribers for ad revenue, plus 4,000 watch hours in 12 months or 10M Shorts views

blocks.source: Search Engine Journal reporting on YouTube's Partner Program changes, 2023

blocks.text: The lower tier opens fan-funding tools like channel memberships and Super Thanks. The full tier adds a share of ad revenue. Neither is a living. For a gaming channel at a few thousand subscribers, ad income is usually small, which is one reason not to make monetization the goal of the first year. (The separate article on 1,000 true fans covers the economics of turning an audience into income.)

What 1,000 subscribers really unlocks is evidence. It is hard to reach that number by accident. Getting there usually means at least a few videos found viewers who had never heard of you, and that something in your packaging, topic or personality made enough of them want more. That evidence is worth more than the first payout.
Why subscribers follow videos

Many new creators imagine growth working like this: get subscribers, and then your videos get views from them. On today's YouTube, the order is mostly reversed. YouTube's recommendation system, as described by engineering vice president Cristos Goodrow in 2021, is built around predicting what each viewer will watch and value, using signals like clicks, watch time, survey responses, likes, shares and dislikes. A video that satisfies strangers gets shown to more strangers, whether or not the channel behind it is big.

blocks.title: How small channels actually grow
items: A video satisfies a few strangers
YouTube tests it with more similar viewers
Some of them want the next one and subscribe
The next video starts with a warmer audience
Better videos widen the circle again

blocks.text: This is good news for small channels, because it means the system does not need you to already have an audience. It is bad news for the shortcuts. Asking every viewer to subscribe, buying subscribers, or trading subs with other small creators does not produce people who watch, and people who do not watch cannot send the signals that matter. A thousand subscribers who never click is worse than a hundred who always do.

It also explains why the early numbers are so jumpy. YouTube's help documentation notes that click-through rates for new channels and videos with fewer than 100 views can vary widely. When a channel is small, one video catching a little traffic can double the month's views, and the next can vanish. Judging the channel by a single upload is like judging a training plan by a single workout.

So stop staring at the total on the channel page. A more useful habit is to look at each video on its own: how many viewers it reached who had not seen the channel before, how long they watched, and how many subscribed from that video. YouTube Studio breaks these out per video. Over a dozen uploads, a pattern usually appears. One type of video brings in strangers, another keeps them, and occasionally one does both. That last kind is the one to make again.
What tends to work in the desert

No study has a formula for the first 1,000. What follows is the advice that lines up with how YouTube says its system works, plus the patterns visible in the research above. Treat it as a set of good bets, not guarantees.

items: **Make each video for one specific viewer.** 'People who play shooters' is not a person. 'Someone who used to be good and is scared to come back' is.
**Start with videos people are already looking for.** A useful answer to a common question can find viewers through search even when the channel has none.
**Build a series.** A one-off video gives people nothing to subscribe for. A numbered journey gives them a reason to want episode four.
**Treat packaging as part of the idea.** Write the title and sketch the thumbnail before recording.
**Reply to every early comment.** The first fifty commenters are the closest thing you have to a focus group.
**Change one thing per video** based on what the analytics show, and keep notes on what you tried.

blocks.text: The series point matters most for a channel built around a personal journey, like rebuilding aim after years away from competitive games. The single video 'My aim after two years off' might do fine. But a viewer who enjoyed it has no reason to subscribe unless there is a clear promise of more: the climb back, tracked with real numbers, with a goal at the end. Subscribing becomes the natural response to a story that is not finished yet.

A journey series can also carry useful, searchable material inside it, which helps with the problem of being found at all. An episode about the exact warm-up routine that took an aim trainer score from one number to another is part of the story for subscribers, and at the same time an answer to a question that strangers type into the search bar. Each video then has two ways in: the people following the arc, and the people who only wanted the routine. The second group is where new subscribers come from.

Outside YouTube, the communities around a specific game can help, used carefully. Subreddits, Discord servers and forums for one game are full of the exact viewer a niche video is made for. Most of them have rules against self-promotion, and spamming links burns goodwill fast. Being a genuine member first, and sharing a video only where it actually answers a question someone asked, is slower but tends to bring viewers who stay.

Genre matters too, as Bärtl found. Some topics have big, hungry audiences and fierce competition; others are quiet but underserved. Gaming as a whole is one of the strongest categories on YouTube: Pew found video game content was the most common specific topic among popular channels in early 2019, and gaming videos had median first-week views nearly three times those of all other categories combined. That says the audience exists. It does not say any particular gaming video will find it.
Crossing it on limited time

The hardest version of this problem is the one with an irregular schedule: long work hours, duty days, and weeks or months with no internet at all. That makes the 'upload every day' advice from full-time creators useless. It also makes something else more important: a backlog.

blocks.title: A plan that survives a busy schedule
items: Pick a pace you can keep for six months, even if it is one video every two weeks
Record and edit several videos ahead before any long absence
Schedule them to publish while you are away, using YouTube Studio's scheduling
Make the series format clear, so a gap reads as a season break, not a dead channel
On return, read the retention and comments in a batch and change one thing

blocks.text: Consistency in this sense is not about frequency. It is about not disappearing without explanation and not abandoning the format just as viewers began to recognize it. A channel that posts every two weeks for a year has made twenty-six attempts and learned from each. A channel that posted daily for three weeks and stopped has made twenty-one attempts and learned that it was exhausting.

There is no honest way to promise when the first 1,000 will come. For some channels it is a few months; for many it is years; for most, it never comes, largely because they stop. What the data does suggest is that time in the game, a clear promise to a specific viewer, and a habit of learning from each upload are the ingredients that show up in the channels that make it out.

And here is the part that is easy to miss in the desert. The skills it forces you to build, from writing a promise that strangers believe, to editing out what bores people, to reading feedback without flinching, are the same ones that run any small business. Even a channel that never leaves the desert can turn out to be the best training you ever paid for in hours instead of dollars.

takeaways: On YouTube, about 85% of views go to roughly 3% of channels; the empty start is normal, not a verdict.
Older channels are far more likely to break out. Most channels fail by stopping before they find what works.
Subscribers are a lagging indicator: they come from individual videos that satisfy strangers, so make each video for one specific viewer.
A series gives people a reason to subscribe; a one-off gives them nothing to wait for.
Pick a pace you can sustain for six months and build a backlog before long absences.

title: Pick the Story, Not Just the Game
dek: Gaming is one of the biggest categories on YouTube and one of the most crowded. The channels that last tend to own a format and a story, not just a game.

blocks.text: In 2020, people watched more than 100 billion hours of gaming content on YouTube, according to the company's own year-end review. Minecraft videos alone pulled in 201 billion views that year, more than the next two games combined. If you wanted proof that gaming is a huge audience, there it is.

The same review said there were more than 40 million active gaming channels. That is the other half of the picture. The audience is enormous, and so is the line of people trying to reach it. A new creator who picks the most popular game and makes the most common kind of video for it is entering the busiest marketplace on the platform with the least distinctive stall.

So the useful question is not 'which game should my channel be about?' It is 'which *story* can I tell that a specific group of viewers wants and few others are telling?' A niche on YouTube is not a game. It is a game, a format and a person, multiplied together. The game is usually the least durable of the three.

blocks.title: Most-viewed games on YouTube, 2020
blocks.note: Total views of videos about each game during 2020, in billions.
blocks.source: Ryan Wyatt, YouTube Official Blog, December 2020

blocks.text: Why gaming works on YouTube

There is solid evidence that gaming content is a strong category, not just a big one. In 2019, Pew Research Center analyzed every video posted in the first week of the year by about 43,770 channels with at least 250,000 subscribers. Video games were the most common specific topic, at 18% of the videos Pew coded. Those gaming videos also did well: their median first-week views were 34,347, nearly three times the median of 11,176 for all other categories combined.

Pew also found something that runs against the common belief that online audiences only want short clips. Gaming videos averaged 24 minutes, against 11 minutes for other videos. Gaming audiences sit with long content: full playthroughs, long challenge runs, deep explanations. That matters for format choice, because some of the strongest gaming formats need time to build stakes.

items.label: Median first-week views of gaming videos vs. all other categories
Average length of gaming videos, vs. 11 for other videos
Share of popular channels' videos about video games

blocks.source: Pew Research Center, 2019

blocks.text: A caution about both data sets: they describe channels and games that already had huge audiences, and they are snapshots from 2019 and 2020. They say the category is healthy. They do not say a small channel can borrow that health just by being about games. That depends on what kind of gaming video you make.
The main gaming formats and their trade-offs

No public study ranks gaming formats by how fast they grow channels, and you should be suspicious of anyone who claims one does. What you can do is compare formats by how viewers find them, how long they stay relevant, how much work they take, and how much they depend on the creator's personality. Those trade-offs are real and predictable.

items: **Tutorials and guides**: answer a question people search for, like how to improve flick aim or how a mechanic works. Easy to find through search and useful to strangers, but often tied to a game version, so patches can make them obsolete.
**Challenges**: a constraint creates a story, such as finishing a game without a key tool or climbing ranks with a handicap. Strong stakes and natural tension, but ideas get copied fast.

**Journeys and progressions**: following real improvement over time, from a starting point to a goal. Builds attachment and gives people a reason to subscribe, but early episodes need a hook, because viewers do not know you yet.
**News, patches and meta**: fast-moving coverage of what changed. Can catch big waves of interest, but goes stale in days and rewards speed over craft.
**Highlights and montages**: the best plays, cut tight. Fun to make, but crowded and heavily dependent on elite skill.

**Essays and documentaries**: deep histories or analysis, like the long-form speedrun record histories that built channels such as Summoning Salt. High effort, slow output, but can stay watchable for years.
**Commentary and let's plays**: the creator's personality carries the video. Hardest to stand out in early, because strangers have no reason yet to care about you specifically.

blocks.text: Look at that list and a pattern stands out. Formats that strangers can find and value without knowing you, like tutorials and strong challenge premises, help with discovery. Formats that make people care about *you*, like journeys and commentary, help with loyalty. Most lasting channels combine at least one of each.

Two formats are missing from that list because they behave differently. Live streaming is huge: YouTube said viewers watched more than 10 billion hours of gaming live streams in 2020. But a live stream is only as good as the number of people already waiting for it, which makes it a weak discovery tool for a channel with no audience and a strong one for keeping an audience you have. Most small creators do better treating live streams as a community hangout and uploads as the way in.

The other is the devlog, where a creator documents building a game rather than playing one. It is a journey format with a product at the end, and it can feed both projects at once: the videos find people interested in the game, and the game gives the videos a story with real stakes. Roblox alone drew 75 billion views on YouTube in 2020, so the audience for that world is not small. The risk is the same as any journey: if the building stalls, so does the channel.
Big game or small game

Choosing the game is a bet on two things at once: how many people care about it, and how many creators already serve them. A giant game has a huge audience and an enormous number of channels competing for it. A small game may have a modest audience but almost no one making good videos, so a decent video can become *the* video for that community.

blocks.title: Where to plant the flag

left.head: Huge game
items: Massive search and browse demand
Thousands of established channels
A new video has to beat many alternatives
The topic alone earns you nothing

right.head: Smaller game or sub-topic
items: Limited total audience
Few good videos, so less competition
A solid video can become the reference
Community members share what helps them

blocks.text: Mathias Bärtl's 2018 statistical study of a decade of YouTube data hints at why this choice matters early. He found that young channels did have a small chance to succeed quickly, but that chance depended on genre. The category you start in shapes the odds before you have uploaded anything.

Small games carry their own risk. If the community is tiny or shrinking, even owning it completely may never add up to much, and a game that loses its players takes its niche channels down with it. The sweet spot is usually a topic with steady, real demand that the big channels treat as too small to bother with: a specific role, a specific skill, a specific kind of player.

A common middle path is to pick a big game but a narrow angle within it. Not 'Valorant videos' but 'coming back to Valorant after years away.' Not 'Minecraft' but one specific style of build or challenge. The game brings the audience; the angle gives you something that only you are doing.
The game is the least durable part

Games rise and fall. In early 2019, Pew found that videos with Fortnite in the title drew more than five times as many views at the median as other videos. A year later, Fortnite was still in the top five on YouTube but well behind Minecraft. Channels whose entire identity was one game have had to rebuild from scratch when its audience moved on.

Formats and stories travel better. A channel known for brutal self-imposed challenges can take that format to a new game and bring its audience along, because the audience came for the challenge. A channel known for honest progress tracking can start a new journey in a new game. The question to ask about any niche is: *if this game died next year, what would my channel still be?*
A good niche survives a change of game. If the only thing tying your videos together is the title on the box, your channel is renting its audience from a publisher.

The third factor, the person, is the one creators most often underrate. Two channels can make the same format about the same game and feel completely different, because one creator explains with dry humor and the other with obsessive detail. Viewers who come back are often coming back for that. You cannot invent a personality for a channel, but you can stop sanding yours off. The quirks that feel embarrassing on camera at first, the way you talk when frustrated, the odd analogies, the honest admissions, are frequently the parts people remember.
Where 'rebuilding my aim' fits

A channel about returning to competitive shooters after years away is, in format terms, a journey with a built-in tutorial. That combination is strong on paper. The journey supplies the reason to subscribe: will they make it back? The tutorial side supplies a way for strangers to find it: every routine, drill and setting change that actually moves the numbers is something other players search for.

It also has a real audience behind it that few creators speak to directly. Plenty of players who were once good have stepped away for work, school, the military or family, and wonder whether they can still compete. Most aim content is made by people at the top, for people grinding daily. A creator showing the honest climb back from rust, with real numbers, is speaking to a different and often ignored viewer.

The creator's own situation is part of the angle, too. Someone practicing in short windows between demanding work shifts, with weeks away from a PC entirely, is living the exact problem many adult players have: how do you improve when you cannot grind eight hours a day? Showing what a few focused sessions a week can and cannot do is useful information, and honest content about limits is rarer than content about the grind.

The weaknesses are worth naming bluntly. A journey only works if there are stakes and visible progress, so the channel needs a measurable starting point and a clear goal, such as a rank or an aim trainer score. Viewers will not care about episode one because they do not know you yet, so early videos need a hook that works on strangers: the shock of how far the aim fell, or a specific bold target. And if progress stalls for weeks, the story needs a way to stay interesting, which is where the tutorial and experiment side earns its keep.

blocks.title: Testing a niche before committing
items: Write the niche as one sentence: game, format, and the specific viewer it is for
Search for it on YouTube and note how many good, recent videos already exist
Ask whether the channel would survive moving to a different game
List ten video ideas; if you cannot, the niche is too thin or too vague
Make three videos, read their retention and comments, then adjust the angle rather than the whole channel

blocks.text: The last step matters most. A niche is a hypothesis, not a vow. The first few videos are how you test it, and the analytics tell you which part of the idea strangers respond to. Sometimes the tutorial episodes pull far more viewers than the story episodes, or the other way around. The right move is usually to lean toward what works while keeping the thread that makes the channel yours.

There is one more trap to avoid: niche-hopping. Switching game and format every month because the views are low resets every lesson and confuses whatever small audience you had. Give a niche a fair test, measured in videos rather than days, before deciding it failed. The channels that eventually take off rarely look like they were working at video five.

Seen this way, choosing a gaming niche is less like picking a game to play and more like designing a product. You are deciding who it is for, what need it meets, what makes it different from what already exists and whether it can outlive the platform trend it started on. Those are the same questions behind any business that lasts, and a gaming channel is a cheap place to practice answering them.

takeaways: Gaming is a strong YouTube category: in Pew's 2019 data, gaming videos had nearly triple the median views of other categories and averaged 24 minutes.
A niche is a game, a format and a person. The game is the least durable part.
Mix a format strangers can find (tutorials, strong challenges) with one that builds loyalty (journeys, commentary).
A big game with a narrow angle often beats both a crowded general channel and a tiny game nobody plays.
Test a niche over several videos, adjust the angle based on data, and avoid hopping between games.

title: The Line That Shows Where You Lost Them
dek: Every video comes with a second-by-second record of when viewers gave up. Learning to read it is the closest thing a creator has to a coach watching over their shoulder.

blocks.text: Imagine giving a talk to a room of a hundred people, and every time someone got bored they quietly stood up and walked out. Afterward, someone hands you a chart showing the exact second each person left. Most speakers never get that feedback. Every YouTube video comes with it automatically.

It is called the audience retention graph, and it lives in YouTube Studio under each video's analytics. It starts at the left with everyone who pressed play and slopes down to the right as people leave. New creators tend to glance at it, feel bad about the slope, and move on. That is a waste. The shape of the line is a diagnosis, and once you know how to read it, it tells you which minute of your video needs work and often why.

The idea worth holding onto: a retention graph is not a grade. It is a map of where your video stopped matching what the viewer wanted. Every steep drop is a broken promise, a confusing stretch or a dull one. Every flat stretch is something working that you should do more of.
Why the line matters so much

YouTube's recommendation system has cared about watching, not just clicking, for over a decade. In a 2021 post on the official YouTube blog, engineering vice president Cristos Goodrow explained that the company added watch time to its recommendations in 2012 after learning that clicks alone were a poor signal, and later added viewer surveys to measure what it calls valued watch time. (A separate article covers the algorithm itself; here the point is simply that minutes watched carry weight.)

The retention graph is where those minutes are made or lost. It turns a single number, average view duration, into a story with a beginning, middle and end. Two videos can have the same average and very different graphs: one loses half its audience in the opening and then holds the rest, the other bleeds viewers steadily from start to finish. Those are different problems with different fixes, and only the graph tells them apart.
How to read the graph

YouTube's help page on retention describes a few landmarks it highlights for you, under the label key moments for audience retention. They appear only when YouTube detects them, and only on videos at least 60 seconds long with at least 100 views. Retention data usually takes a day or two to process, so the morning after upload is too early to read anything.

items: **Intro**: the percentage of viewers still watching after the first 30 seconds. A strong number suggests the opening matched what the title and thumbnail promised.
**Top moments**: stretches where almost no one left. YouTube suggests that if these come late, consider moving that kind of material earlier.
**Spikes**: moments viewers rewatched or shared. They can mean something was great, or that it was unclear and people scrubbed back to catch it.
**Dips**: moments viewers skipped past or where they quit entirely.
**Typical retention**: a comparison against your own 10 latest videos of similar length, with an option to compare against all YouTube videos of similar length.

items.label: Point at which YouTube measures your intro retention
Your latest similar-length videos used as the comparison
Minimum views before key moments appear

blocks.source: YouTube Help, Measure key moments for audience retention

blocks.text: Notice what YouTube compares you against by default: yourself. Not a universal benchmark, not the top channels in your niche, but your own recent videos of similar length. That is a quiet admission that there is no single good retention number. A 40-minute documentary and a 4-minute clip live in different worlds. The useful question is never 'is this line good?' but 'is this line better than my last ones, and where?'

One more detail matters. Replays count. If a viewer scrubs back and watches a section three times, that section can register more views than the video has viewers, which is why the line can rise above where it started. A bump in the graph is a moment people chose to see again.
The cliff at the start

Nearly every retention graph begins with a drop, and it is usually the steepest part of the line. Some of that is unavoidable: people click by accident, or realize within seconds that a video is not for them. But much of it is the gap between the promise and the first impression. A viewer clicked on a thumbnail of a dramatic before-and-after and got forty seconds of channel intro, a sponsor read and a recap of last week. They leave, and they were right to.

The most closely studied creator on the platform seems to agree. A production manual reported to be MrBeast's onboarding document for new staff, which leaked in September 2024, calls the first minute the most important one in a video and says it should confirm, quickly, that the video delivers what the thumbnail showed. It also tells producers to stop *describing* what viewers will see and start *showing* it.

That gives a practical test for any opening. Pause at 0:30. Has the viewer seen evidence of the thing they clicked for? For a video about returning to a shooter after years away, that might be the first embarrassing aim trainer run with the score on screen, inside the first ten seconds. Context and backstory can come later, once the viewer is already invested.
Before uploading, watch only your first 30 seconds as if you were a stranger who just clicked the thumbnail. If the promise is not visibly being kept by then, rewrite the opening, not the thumbnail.
The slope through the middle

After the opening, a healthy graph tends to flatten into a gentle slope. Viewers are now choosing to stay, and losses come from moments that ask too much of them or give too little. There is no published YouTube benchmark for what that slope should look like, and you should distrust anyone who offers one. But there is useful research on what flattens it.

The best-known study is not about YouTube at all. In 2014, Philip Guo, Juho Kim and Rob Rubin analyzed about 6.9 million video-watching sessions from four edX online courses. They found that the median time students spent watching topped out at around six minutes, no matter how long the video was. Students often watched less than half of videos longer than nine minutes, while the shortest videos, under three minutes, had the highest engagement: in 75% of those sessions, viewers watched more than three quarters of the video.

items.label: Cap on median engagement time, regardless of video length
Sessions on 0–3 minute videos that watched over three quarters
Engagement gain linked to faster speaking rate within a length range

blocks.source: Guo, Kim & Rubin, ACM Learning at Scale, 2014

blocks.text: Do not take this as a rule that videos must be six minutes long. These were lecture videos for online courses, watched by students with a different goal from someone relaxing with gaming content, and the data dates from 2012. Gaming audiences in particular watch long: a Pew Research Center analysis of popular channels in early 2019 found gaming videos averaged 24 minutes, against 11 minutes for everything else, and still drew more views at the median.

What transfers is the *why*. Guo's team found that within a given length, videos where the speaker talked faster held people longer, up to twice as long; that videos where the instructor drew and talked through a problem beat static slides; and that courses whose videos were planned for the medium, rather than recorded lectures chopped up afterward, kept viewers more engaged. Energy, visible process and planning beat length. A long video earns its length by giving viewers a reason to stay every minute, not by being long.

In gaming footage, the usual slope killers are easy to spot once you look for them: walking back to the objective, waiting in a lobby, a long menu, a round where nothing happens. To you, the player, those moments are part of the experience. To the viewer, they are dead air. Line up your steepest mid-video drops against the footage and you will often find one of these sitting right underneath.
Spikes, dips and what they really mean

The most misread features of the graph are its bumps. A spike looks like pure good news, but YouTube's own help page notes the ambiguity: a rewatched section might be a highlight people loved, or a moment so unclear they had to go back. A dip might be a boring stretch, or it might be a section viewers skipped because they already knew it, a sign your audience is more advanced than you assumed.

blocks.title: Same bump, different story

left.head: Good sign
items: Spike on a clutch play: people rewatched a highlight
Dip on a recap: returning viewers skipped what they knew
Flat stretch through a hard lesson: viewers were hooked

right.head: Warning sign
items: Spike on an explanation: people missed it the first time
Dip on a key setup: the video lost them before the payoff
Steady decline with no flat spots: nothing re-hooked them

blocks.text: The only way to tell which is which is to go to that exact timestamp and watch it with fresh eyes. This is where the graph becomes a coach. You are not asking what is wrong with the video in general, a question with too many answers. You are asking what happens at 4:12 that made a slice of viewers leave, a question with one.

The MrBeast manual describes deliberate re-engagement moments placed around the three-minute and six-minute marks, segments designed to re-hook viewers who might be drifting. You do not need a crane or a budget to borrow the idea. In a gaming video, a re-engagement can be a new challenge, a reveal of a score, a switch in setting or a question answered that the opening raised. The graph tells you where your own drift begins, which is where yours should go.

Watch the far right of the graph too. Many videos show a final drop in the last stretch, as viewers sense the ending coming and leave before it arrives. A long thank-you, a slow fade or a spoken 'that's it for today' all announce that the value is over. If the closing minute contains nothing a viewer would miss, they are behaving rationally by leaving. Ending on the payoff, or pointing straight to the next video while interest is still high, keeps the last part of the line from collapsing.

Finally, be careful which number you chase. Average view percentage, the share of a video the typical viewer watches, is easy to raise by making videos shorter. But a three-minute video watched to the end can deliver fewer total minutes than a fifteen-minute video watched halfway. The leaked MrBeast manual reportedly treats percentage watched as a lesser concern for its producers, since video length is decided above them. For a small creator, the better question is whether each section earns its place. Cut what does not, keep what does, and let the length be whatever is left.
A ten-minute retention review

Reading graphs is a skill, and like any skill it improves with repetitions done the same way each time. Here is a simple routine to run on every upload once it has enough views for key moments to show up.

blocks.title: After each upload
items: Wait a few days for retention data to process and views to accumulate
Check intro retention at 30 seconds against your recent videos of similar length
Find the single steepest drop after the intro and watch that exact moment
Find the flattest stretch and name what was happening there
Check every spike: highlight or confusion?
Write one sentence: next video, do more of X and less of Y

blocks.text: That last step is the whole point. One concrete change per video, carried forward, compounds. After twenty uploads, a creator who did this has run twenty small experiments on their own audience. A creator who only checked view counts has twenty data points about luck.

There is an honest limit worth stating. Small channels get noisy graphs. With a few hundred views, one or two viewers leaving can make a dip, and YouTube will not even show key moments under 100 views. Early on, look for patterns that repeat across several videos rather than reacting to a single bump. The habit of looking matters more than any one reading.

The deeper lesson reaches beyond YouTube. Most of the things people try to get better at, from a presentation to a workout plan to a game they are building, come with feedback that is slow, vague or flattering. A retention graph is fast, specific and indifferent to your feelings. Creators who learn to welcome that kind of feedback, rather than avoid it, tend to improve faster at everything else too.

takeaways: A retention graph is a map of where your video stopped matching what viewers wanted; read it, do not just grade it.
YouTube measures intro retention at 30 seconds and compares you with your own 10 latest similar-length videos, not a universal benchmark.
Show the thing you promised in the opening seconds; backstory can wait until viewers are invested.
Spikes and dips are ambiguous. Watch the exact timestamp to tell a highlight from a confusing moment.
Make one concrete change per video based on the graph; twenty small experiments beat twenty guesses.

title: Two Doors Into the Same House
dek: Shorts now pull in hundreds of billions of views a day. The question for a new channel is not whether to make them, but what job each format is actually doing.

blocks.text: In June 2025, YouTube CEO Neal Mohan walked onto a stage at the Cannes Lions festival and dropped a number that is hard to picture: YouTube Shorts were averaging 200 billion views a day. Fifteen months earlier, in March 2024, the company had put the figure at 70 billion. Whatever you think of vertical video, that is not a side feature anymore. It is one of the largest attention machines ever built.

For someone starting a gaming channel, that number creates a strong pull. Long videos take days to script, record and edit, and the first ones usually get a few dozen views. A Short can be cut in an hour and occasionally gets thousands of views from strangers. It is natural to wonder why anyone bothers with the slow format at all.

items.label: Average daily Shorts views, announced June 2025
Average daily Shorts views, reported March 2024
Logged-in users watching Shorts each month, June 2022

blocks.source: Neal Mohan via TheWrap, 2025; YouTube via TechCrunch, 2022

blocks.text: The useful way to think about it is that Shorts and long-form are two different doors into the same house. Each door lets in a different kind of visitor, in a different state of mind, for a different reason. A channel that understands which visitor comes through which door can use both. A channel that treats them as the same thing tends to get the worst of each.
Two different machines

Think about how a viewer actually meets each format. A long video is usually *chosen*. Someone sees a thumbnail and title on the home page, in search or next to another video, and decides to click. That decision is a small act of intent. They wanted something specific, and they picked you to provide it.

A Short is usually *served*. The viewer is swiping through a feed, and your video simply arrives. They did not pick it, and they will leave the instant it stops being interesting. The feed is closer to channel surfing than to choosing a show. That makes Shorts superb at reaching people who have never heard of you, and weak at telling them who you are.

blocks.title: How viewers arrive

left.head: Long-form
items: Viewer chooses from a thumbnail and title
Found through search, home page and suggestions
Judged on whether it delivers what the package promised
Room for a story, a personality and a payoff
Builds viewers who come back for you

right.head: Shorts
items: Video is served in a swipe feed
Reaches strangers with no prior interest in you
Judged in the first second or two
Room for one idea, one moment or one joke
Builds awareness, sometimes loyalty

blocks.text: Neither of these is better. They solve different problems. Long videos build depth: a viewer who sits through fifteen minutes of your aim training session has learned how you think, how you talk and whether they like you. Shorts build breadth: thousands of people see one slice of you for twenty seconds, and a few of them get curious about the rest.

The catch is that breadth does not automatically become depth. Many creators report Shorts that got huge view counts and barely moved their subscriber count or their long videos. That makes sense once you remember how the viewer arrived. Someone who swiped onto a clip did not ask for your channel. Converting them takes a reason to want more, and a single great flick shot does not always supply one.

There is a second difference that matters even more for a beginner: what each format teaches you. A long video forces you to practice structure. You have to open strongly, hold attention through a middle and land an ending, and the retention graph shows you exactly where you lost people. A Short teaches compression: what is the single most interesting second of this idea? Both are real skills, and the creators who last tend to have both. But if you only ever make Shorts, you never learn to hold someone for ten minutes, and that is the skill a journey channel depends on.
What YouTube claims, and how to read it

YouTube has been pushing creators to do both formats for years. In June 2022, when it announced that Shorts had passed 1.5 billion logged-in monthly users, Tara Walpert Levy, its vice president for the Americas, said channels posting both formats were seeing better overall watch time and subscriber growth than channels posting only one. The company held up creators like Ian Boggs, who had built billions of views largely through Shorts, and Rosanna Pansino, who said her views more than doubled after she adopted them.

Treat that claim the way a good technician treats a gauge reading from someone else's watch: as useful, but not verified. YouTube gave no numbers for the watch-time gain, and TechCrunch's reporter called the claim somewhat suspect at the time. There is also an obvious selection problem. Creators who are already doing well have more time and staff to make both formats, so 'channels that do both grow more' could partly mean 'channels that are growing can afford to do both.'

The case studies have the same weakness. YouTube picks its most successful Shorts creators to showcase. You never hear about the thousands of channels that posted Shorts every day for a year and stayed small. None of this means the advice is wrong. It means that 'do both' is a reasonable bet, not a law of nature, and you should test it on your own channel instead of taking it on faith.

When a platform tells you which feature to use, it is also telling you what it currently wants more of. That can line up with your interests, and often does, but the platform's goal is a fuller feed, not necessarily a bigger channel for you.
The money is different too

The two formats also pay differently. Since 2007, YouTube has given creators 55% of the ad revenue earned on their long-form videos. Shorts work another way, because ads run between clips in a feed rather than inside one video, so there is no single video to pin an ad to. When Shorts revenue sharing began on February 1, 2023, YouTube set it up as a pool: Shorts ad revenue is gathered together, part of it goes toward music licensing, and the creator portion is divided among eligible creators, who keep 45% of what is allocated to them.

blocks.title: Creator share of ad revenue by format
blocks.note: The Shorts figure is 45% of a creator's slice of a shared pool. YouTube has not said how much of total Shorts ad revenue goes into that pool, so the two bars are not directly comparable.
blocks.source: MIT Technology Review, 2022

blocks.text: That second number looks close to the first, but it is not an apples-to-apples comparison. As MIT Technology Review pointed out when the program was announced, YouTube did not disclose what fraction of total Shorts ad revenue flows into the creator pool, so the effective payout per view is unknown from the outside. Creators who publish their own numbers almost always report that a Short earns far less per view than a long video, though the gap varies widely by audience and topic.

YouTube says the gap is shrinking. On Alphabet's earnings call in July 2024, the company's finance chief said YouTube was continuing to close the monetization gap with Shorts, especially in the United States. It gave no figures. The practical point for a small channel is simpler: Shorts revenue is unlikely to be the reason to make Shorts. If they help, it will be by bringing people to the rest of the channel.
The line keeps moving

The boundary between the formats is also less fixed than it looks. On October 15, 2024, YouTube began allowing Shorts up to three minutes long, for videos that are square or taller. A three-minute vertical video is not really a snack anymore. It can hold a small story with a setup and a payoff.

For a journey channel, that extra room opens a middle option. A two-to-three-minute vertical recap of a week, with a clear starting score, one key change and an ending score, is a complete mini-story that lives in the feed. It will never replace a full episode, because it cannot show the struggle in any depth. But it can do something a ten-second clip cannot: make a stranger care about the outcome before they have ever seen your long videos. YouTube said in its announcement that it would keep working on recommendations for these longer Shorts, which is another way of saying the system was still learning how to handle them. Expect the rules here to keep shifting.

blocks.title: How Shorts grew up
items: Long-form ad revenue sharing starts, at 55% to creators
Jun 2022
YouTube says Shorts passes 1.5 billion logged-in monthly users
Feb 2023
Shorts revenue sharing begins, using a creator pool
Mar 2024
Shorts reported at 70 billion average daily views
Oct 2024
Shorts can run up to three minutes
Jun 2025
Shorts reported at 200 billion average daily views

blocks.text: That change reveals what actually separates the two formats. It was never really length. It is the *context of arrival*: chosen versus served, searched versus swiped. A three-minute Short still lives in a feed where people leave the moment they are bored, so it still has to hook in a heartbeat. A six-minute long video still has to earn the click with its packaging. Design each video for the door it comes through, not for the stopwatch.
How to tell whether Shorts are helping

Because the public evidence is thin, the honest approach is to run your own experiment and judge Shorts by the job you gave them. If their job is to bring strangers to the journey, raw Short views are the wrong scoreboard. A Short with 40,000 views that sends nobody to the long episodes did less for the channel than a Short with 3,000 views that brought in a handful of people who watched three episodes each.

So look at what happens *after* the swipe. Do subscriber counts move in the days after a Short does well? Do the long videos pick up new viewers at the same time? Do the comments on long episodes start mentioning a clip? None of these signals is perfect on its own, and small channels have noisy numbers, so give any test several weeks and several Shorts before drawing conclusions.

It also helps to decide in advance what would change your mind. For example: if eight Shorts over a month bring no visible lift to the long videos, try a different style of Short, such as lessons instead of highlights, before giving up on the format. If one style clearly pulls people through, make more of it. This is the same discipline as tuning a training routine: change one variable, give it enough reps to judge, and keep what works.
Using both on a channel about rebuilding aim

A journey channel is a good fit for the two-door approach, because the journey naturally produces both kinds of material. The long videos are the episodes: where you started, what you tried, what worked, where you are now. They are where viewers get attached to the outcome. The Shorts are the moments: a clean clip, a before-and-after aim trainer score, a ten-second lesson that took you a week to learn.

The trick is to make each Short point somewhere. A random highlight is a dead end for the viewer. A Short that says, in effect, 'Week 6 of rebuilding my aim after two years away: this one drill finally fixed my crosshair placement' tells a stranger there is a bigger story and invites them into it. The clip is the trailer; the long video is the film.

blocks.title: A simple two-format workflow
items: Record each practice block or match session once, with the long episode in mind.
Edit the long video first, around one question: what changed this week, and why?
While editing, flag two or three moments that stand alone in under a minute.
Cut those as vertical Shorts, each with a one-line setup that names the journey.
Check after a few weeks which Shorts sent viewers to the long videos, and make more like those.

blocks.text: This approach also suits an irregular schedule. Long stretches away from a PC are a real constraint, and batching is the natural answer: record and edit during the windows you have, then release on a steady rhythm. Because Shorts can be cut from footage you already captured, they cost far less than separate productions, and a small bank of them can keep a channel visibly alive between the bigger episodes.

Watch for one trap. Shorts give fast, loud feedback: views move within hours, which feels like progress. Long videos give slow, quiet feedback over weeks. It is easy to drift toward whatever gives the quicker hit, until the channel becomes a stream of disconnected clips with no story holding them together. If the journey is the reason people subscribe, the long episodes are the part that cannot be skipped.

So the real decision is not Shorts *or* long-form. It is what each one is for on your channel. Shorts are how strangers meet you. Long videos are how they get to know you. A channel that needs both, which is most of them, should be clear about which door each video is built for, and should measure each format by whether it does its own job.

takeaways: Long videos are chosen; Shorts are served. Design each for how viewers arrive, not for its length.
YouTube says doing both helps growth, but it has published no numbers. Test it on your own channel.
Long-form pays creators 55% of ad revenue; Shorts pays 45% of a share of an undisclosed pool. Shorts are rarely worth making for the money alone.
Make every Short point to the bigger story. A clip with no path to the long video is a dead end.
Cut Shorts from footage you already recorded, so a small bank can keep the channel alive between episodes.
